0100136c-d21e-52a5-b03f-fb11f9499ed7.name: 'A Giant Fish Rescues Abu Ubayda and his Men from Dying of Starvation'
0100136c-d21e-52a5-b03f-fb11f9499ed7.description:
The style of the miniatures from this manuscript is slightly old-fashioned compared with the otherwise refined Timurid painting, and it has in fact been called Shah Rukh’s historical style. Its inspiration was undoubtedly the illustrations made about a century earlier for Rashid al-Din’s famous ‘History of the World.’  
  
The rescue of the close companion of the Prophet, Abu Ubayda, from starvation is one of Islam’s early miracles. His desperate men have eaten the leaves from the trees and although they do not look quite as emaciated as the two dromedaries lying on the ground, the yellow desert underlines the gravity of the situation. When a giant fish appears, the Muslims are saved from dying of starvation.
keywords: Water; folio; miniature; manuscript; Herat; Timurids

021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.name: Jar
021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.description:
This container for transporting and storing date molasses was made from the stomach lining of an animal, such as a sheep or goat.  
Made from raw leather, this jar has been waterproofed with several layers of natural resin. It has a large stained wooden stopper. The rim of the opening is made of gypsum and three layers of leather to ensure a truly waterproof seal. This use of animal leather demonstrates the commitment of populations living on seasonal pastures in the desert and involved in the production and trade of date syrup.  
  
In Qatar, it's known as a *dabba*.
021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.obtention: Object has been in the National Museum's permanent collection since 1975.
021fc9a2-4a62-5d59-a094-931252cd0fe5.author: Tania Abdulmonem Al Majid

0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.name: Ceramic tile with a picture of the Ka‘ba.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.description:
Blue, green and red pigments have been used on a white background. A border with a chain-motif, drawn in black on a blue background, frames the single-piece tile. This is enriched by a second border made up of blue palmettes which ends at the top of the tile in a *mihrab* shape. The *mihrab*'s two corners are decorated with interlacing *rumi* (split-palmette) motifs on a dark-blue background. In the middle of the *mihrab*, also on a dark-blue ground, is a symmetrical pediment motif decorated with arabesques, at the bottom of which is an inscription in three rows of black *naskhi* script. The inscription contains *sura* 3, verses 96–7 of the Qur'an: 'Lo! the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind was that at Becca \[Mecca\] a blessed place, a guidance to the peoples; Wherein are plain memorials (of Allah's guidance); the place where Abraham stood up to pray; and whosoever entereth it is safe.' Below this text, the Masjid al-Haram is depicted within a rectangle drawn in green and blue. The Ka'ba is shown in the middle of the Masjid al-Haram, recognisable by its porticoed courtyard. The various buildings, gates, sacred spots (*maqams*), and water-wells located within the porticoes are represented and identified with their names.  
  
Introducing the holy cities of Islam (Mecca and Medina) and the sacred sites therein with books, and reinforcing this introduction with pictures, is seen from the early period of Islam. Detailed pictures of these holy places were put in pilgrimage certificates, which were made especially in the Ayyubid period, and which have an important place in the Museum's collection. These documents begin with the banner of the caliph of the time and show painted images of Mount Arafat, Muzdalifa, the Sacred Enclosure (al-Haram al-Sharif), Medina, and even Jerusalem. Similar pictures of the holy places were made for pilgrimage certificates in Ottoman art. Beginning at the end of the 10th / 16th century images of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca are also found depicted on tiles in certain mosques.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.short_description: This tile panel is assumed to have been produced at Iznik for the Mosque of Neslişah Sultan in Edirnekapı, Istanbul. The purpose of tile panels depicting the Ka'ba was to feel its presence, the most sacred shrine of Islam, during prayer at the mosque.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.initial_owner: Sultan Neslişah (d. 987 / 1579; granddaughter of Sultan Bayezid II).
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.dates: Hegira last quarter of the 10th century / AD 16th century.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.method_for_datation: The panel was originally embedded in the wall of the Neslişah Sultan Mosque built in the late 16th century. Since such panels are not found in every mosque, and the quality of the work suggests that it was made for a structure built by an important person, it is plausible to think it was specially made for the aforementioned mosque.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.method_for_provenance: The materials, techniques and colours used are typical of an Iznik-produced tile.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.obtention: The tile was transferred to the Museum in 1914 from the mosque of Neslişah Sultan, the grandchild of Sultan Bayezid II, in the Edirnekapı section of Istanbul.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.bibliography: Ölçer, N. *et al, Museum of Turkish and Islamic Art*, Istanbul, 2002, p. 282.
0356286a-7b78-54d7-b0a8-bf8bfd97a059.author: Cihat Soyhan
materials: Iznik tile of white clay, with a painting of the Ka‘ba in underglaze.

03c579c8-fe6c-5cb4-a41d-f10cb2e3df25.name: Basin
03c579c8-fe6c-5cb4-a41d-f10cb2e3df25.description: A basin in the form of a deep container with a prominent rounded rim, ornamented with a band of lobed medallions adorned with pictorial scenes of mythical creatures, a rider on horseback and others with inscriptions and vegetal motifs depicting a tree with branches, rosettes and birds. The decorative band is enclosed between two narrow friezes of undulating foliate motifs and irregular lozenge shapes. The exterior is adorned with cylindrical and circular medallions enclosing representations of birds, mythical creatures and human figures. The underside of the basin is decorated with interlaced lines in the form of a braid. The basin has a circular lid, adorned with oval and circular medallions enclosing depictions of mythical creatures, birds, animals and human figures. It is surmounted by a neck ornamented with vegetal arabesque motifs, topped by a protruding circular element. The rim of this element is adorned with interlaced braided lines, while its field is adorned with horizontal bands of repeated inscriptions, framed above and below by simple vegetal ornament.
03c579c8-fe6c-5cb4-a41d-f10cb2e3df25.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
03c579c8-fe6c-5cb4-a41d-f10cb2e3df25.author: Zeina Al Amad

03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.name: Pilgrim flask
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.short_description: The basic form of the canteen, which is still in use today, may be traced to Roman times; it has changed little over the centuries. While medieval Islamic canteens are sometimes referred to as pilgrim flasks, most seem to have played a more quotidian role as water vessels. There are large numbers of such unglazed canteens, mainly ranging in date from Hegira 6th–8th centuries / AD 12th–14th centuries and attributable to Iran, Syria, and Anatolia. A few canteens are glazed as well, such as this example; all have applied handles, which would allow for suspension.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.dates: Hegira mid-6th century / AD mid-12th century
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.method_for_datation: The carved relief decoration, a central rosette surrounded by a leafy scroll on one face and a rabbit circumscribed by the same leafy scroll on the other, is related to similar designs on ceramic wares from Syria, which are generally dated to the 12th century.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.method_for_provenance: The canteen’s carved relief decoration is related to similar designs on ceramic wares from Syria.
03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.obtention: Collection of Maan Z. Madina (1926-2013), New York, until 2002 (sold to); LACMA, The Madina Collection of Islamic Art, gift of Camilla Chandler Frost.

03d9bf39-2820-5bbc-b5ab-da3243697172.author: LACMA Staff

055c7844-a362-5d7c-b2fc-0a48c99ed65b.name: Calligraphy
055c7844-a362-5d7c-b2fc-0a48c99ed65b.description:
This calligraphy is by Reis-ül Hattat Hasan Çelebi. It reads:  
  
"Ey misafir, kıl namazın, kıble bu câhiptedir.  
İşte leğen, işte ibrik, işte peşkir iptedir."  
("O guest, perform your prayer — the *qibla* is in this direction. Here is the basin, here is the ewer, and here hangs the towel.")
055c7844-a362-5d7c-b2fc-0a48c99ed65b.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
055c7844-a362-5d7c-b2fc-0a48c99ed65b.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
055c7844-a362-5d7c-b2fc-0a48c99ed65b.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

056dead0-e9f9-5694-939a-2d3d5752e145.name: "Jonah and the Whale"
056dead0-e9f9-5694-939a-2d3d5752e145.alternate_name: Folio Probably from a Jami al-Tavarikh (Compendium of Chronicles)
056dead0-e9f9-5694-939a-2d3d5752e145.description: The story of Jonah and the Whale, mentioned in the Qur'an (37:139), was popular in the Muslim world and frequently illustrated in manuscripts of world history. This large-scale painting, however, never formed part of a manuscript. Rather, it may have been used during oral recitation or storytelling. Scholars have also suggested that with its strong palette, monumental figures, and spare composition, this work may reflect a now-lost wall painting tradition. Here, we see Jonah after his release from the belly of the fish. Above him, a gourd vine grows—sent by God to protect him from the elements—and, gliding across the top of the painting, a spirited angel with colorful spreading wings offers Jonah a garment.

057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.name: Saliha Sultan Fountain
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.short_description: Robertson’s photographs of landscapes and monuments were usually printed in a roughly 25 by 30cm format. In the early years of his career as a photographer, he appears to have preferred the albumen-on-glass method of taking negatives, switching to the wet collodion process around 1855. For his positive prints, he used salt paper until about 1858; after that, prints were made on albumen paper even if they were made from negatives taken before that year. Robertson’s photographs are concentrated mainly in and around the districts known as Sultanahmet, Beyoğlu, Galata and Tophane today. This photo captures the Saliha Sultan Fountain in Galata.
057b0a91-5753-5a0f-a506-60b096d9eeb0.author: Bahattin Öztuncay

05ccd63e-f481-509d-af73-29ae3f2e3135.name: Hookah base

065ee648-ada2-516d-a7cd-4adf36e94026.name: *Habb* water jar
065ee648-ada2-516d-a7cd-4adf36e94026.description: This large water jar (*habb*) combines a utilitarian function with ostentatious decoration. It occupied a place of honour in the domestic space. Water was drawn from it with a jug or pitcher as needed for daily living. The surface is adorned with stylised female figures that reflect the persistence, through millennia and civilisations, of the mother goddess.

06703762-5053-5671-b110-5b6f3f755b04.name: Wellhead
06703762-5053-5671-b110-5b6f3f755b04.description:
Ceramic wellheads of this type are distinctive for southern Spain throughout the entire period when the region was under Muslim dominance (AH 2nd to 9th / AD 8th-15th century). This wellhead, however, comes from the AH 4th - 6th / AD 10th-12th century, and holds a monumental decoration in two bands. The wider, lower band features a procession of graceful, long-eared gazelles alternating with birds set in roundels. Above it is a beautifully conceived Kufi inscription, which is illegible.  
  
The whitish decoration, which was originally green, provides an elegant contrast to the earthenware’s red ground and, like the size of the wellhead, bears witness to the virtuosity of the ceramist.
materials: Earthenware painted in green and a manganese-colored glaze

06945f29-b3f5-5c43-b860-5d861b0794e2.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
06945f29-b3f5-5c43-b860-5d861b0794e2.description: Apricot paste is made from an apricot very specific to the Damascus oasis, the so-called *klabi*, a small, very juicy apricot with a bitter pit that grows on large trees with abundant foliage. Klabi apricots notably were found in some of the villages of Eastern Ghouta, south of the Barada valley. Klabi is characterised by its rapid ripening, with the fruit falling off as soon as it is ripe. As a result, the fruit had to be picked up from the ground day after day. Workshops for making *Qamr ad-Din* are always set up in sunny open fields in an oasis.
06945f29-b3f5-5c43-b860-5d861b0794e2.bibliography:
Bianquis, A.-M., “Modernisation d'un artisanat traditionnel: la pâte d'abricot dans la ghouta de damas”, *Bulletin d'études orientales*, T. 56 (2004-2005): 301-328.  
  
Denker, J., "'Moon of the Faith:' A History of the Apricot and Its Many Pleasures", (14 June 2016).
06945f29-b3f5-5c43-b860-5d861b0794e2.author: Hiba Bizreh

073cada1-b5a8-5fa6-bce4-4879f04d6814.name: Iznik jug
073cada1-b5a8-5fa6-bce4-4879f04d6814.short_description: An Iznik jug with one handle decorated with tulips and stems carrying small blue flowers. It was bought by Alexander Benaki in 1919 by the Cairo based dealer Boghos Ispenian whose name is handwritten in ink under the base, next to an etiquette indicating that it was part of the 1925 Alexandria exhibition.

074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.name: Healing bowl
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.description: This brass talismanic healing bowl, dated to the 12th–13th century Seljuq and Anatolian Beyliks period, was traditionally used in Anatolian folk medicine for spiritual wellbeing, protection from the evil eye, and relief from night terrors and insomnia. Water placed inside the bowl was blessed through recitation, then either drunk or applied to the body to transmit its sacred power. The bowl is richly adorned on both its inner and outer surfaces with finely engraved Kufic inscriptions.
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.method_for_datation:
Date of production was determined by Islamic metal artefacts expert Güner Liman.  
The inscriptions on it were also read by Fuat Recep, an expert in Ottoman archival texts.
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.method_for_provenance:
Its date was determined by Islamic metal artefacts expert Güner Liman.  
The inscriptions on it were also read by Fuat Recep, an expert in Ottoman archives.
074fe362-9f4c-5b1b-b022-d07db8b96020.obtention: It was displayed for 20 years in the window of the antique shop of “Parisli Mustafa” in the Cevahir Bedesten (Grand Bazaar) and was sold at auction after his death.

076badd5-59ef-5ded-a02b-e7d343ffb7a0.name: *Maada*
076badd5-59ef-5ded-a02b-e7d343ffb7a0.description: The *maada* is a traditional water distribution device used in Moroccan irrigation systems to allocate water shares fairly among rights-holders. Constructed of stone or wood, the system channels water into precisely measured outlets that correspond to established rights, often determined by ancient legal texts or community agreements. The museum’s model reproduces this system at a smaller scale so visitors can understand how communities combined hydraulic engineering with social contracts to regulate a scarce resource. The *maada* reflects the sophistication of traditional Moroccan water law (*qanun al-maʾ*), which was deeply rooted in equity, transparency, and sustainability. By ensuring exact water allocation, it minimized conflicts and symbolised the sacred responsibility of water stewardship. The display preserves not only the technical ingenuity of past engineers but also the social and ethical dimensions of water management in Morocco’s arid regions.
076badd5-59ef-5ded-a02b-e7d343ffb7a0.holder: Mohammed VI Museum of Water Civilisation
076badd5-59ef-5ded-a02b-e7d343ffb7a0.owner: Mohammed VI Museum of Water Civilisation

076badd5-59ef-5ded-a02b-e7d343ffb7a0.obtention: Museum commission or acquisition for exhibition (details not available).

076badd5-59ef-5ded-a02b-e7d343ffb7a0.author: MUSEUM Staff, Layan Shahin

078b6eae-ee80-5e07-bece-2ad30be691e7.name: Ewer and basin
078b6eae-ee80-5e07-bece-2ad30be691e7.description: A ewer with a round base and pear-shaped body, ornamented with circular bands, beginning with vegetal motifs in the form of inverted crenellations, followed by a band inscribed with Persian script interspersed with round medallions containing human figures, followed by a wider band decorated with human figures, mythical creatures and birds, alternating with lobed medallions bearing Persian inscriptions and round medallions with human figures. The upper body ends with arched panels filled with depictions of humans, birds and mythical creatures. These bands are interspersed with small frames ornamented with meandering vegetal scrolls sprouting trifoliate leaves. The neck begins with a ridge and widens towards the round mouth, decorated with lobed, pointed-arch motifs enclosing human and animal figures, along with floral rosettes of many petals. The curved handle extends from the lower body to the mouth. The spout is missing.
078b6eae-ee80-5e07-bece-2ad30be691e7.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum

082c7eda-5670-536a-867f-e0373b2e15a8.name: Rectangular sling or back support (*quffah*) or tree-climbing harness (*habūl*)
082c7eda-5670-536a-867f-e0373b2e15a8.description: To climb the date palm tree, a specially made harness (*habūl*) is used consisting of a rectangular sling or back support (*quffah*) and a thick climbing rope (*suw’*). The climber works his way up the tree by looping the *suw’* around the trunk, leaning back against the *quffah*, and stepping upward.
082c7eda-5670-536a-867f-e0373b2e15a8.type: Rectangular sling or back support (*quffah*) or tree-climbing harness (*habūl*)
materials: Cotton fabric and date palm fibre rope

088cf3bb-ffc3-56ca-8a23-9d69924c19fa.name: Port of Alexandria
088cf3bb-ffc3-56ca-8a23-9d69924c19fa.short_description: The Port of Alexandria during the departure of King Fu`ad on a trip to Europe. The Eastern Port of Alexandria is one of the oldest ports in the world. It was established in 2000 BCE, at the ancient village of Rakotis, to serve the coastal areas of the Pharos island (now the area of Ra's al-Tin in Alexandria). To its west lies the Bay of Anfushi.
keywords: Alexandria Port; King Fouad I; Trips to Europe

08b6e3c0-94d9-573c-a123-ddbc53534246.name: Ewer with epigraphic decoration
08b6e3c0-94d9-573c-a123-ddbc53534246.description: In Iran, during the Seljuq period, a large number of moulds were produced, typically with epigraphic expressions, though figures or foliage are also found. The potters shaped ewers that often borrowed forms developed by coppersmiths. The turquoise glaze replaces with colour the detailed decoration of carving and silver inlay found in metal pieces.

0a0e3c68-6be2-5140-b568-bf800fe28f33.name: *The Religious Pilgrimage of the Mohammadans - Makkah (Arabia) - General View of the City, the Precinct and Enclosure of the Al-Haram Mosque and the Holy Kaaba*
0a0e3c68-6be2-5140-b568-bf800fe28f33.short_description: This print was originally published in 'La Ilustracion Espanola y Americana', a newspaper published in Madrid on the 15th of April, 1882. Entitled 'La Peregrinacion religiosa de los mahometanos: Vista general de la Meca, del patio y claustro de la mesquita El-Haram y de la Santa Kaaba', it was copied from the first known photograph (at the time) depicting the Makkah precinct, taken - according to the newspaper - by the English traveller Mr [John Fryer Thomas] Keane.  Keane (1854-1937) was a clergyman, who converted to Islam and visited Makkah in 1877. In 1881, he published two books about his experiences in the Hijaz, 'Six Months in Meccah' and 'My Journey to Medinah'. The image shows the courtyard of the Makkah mosque with hundreds of pilgrims clustering around the Ka'bah at the centre. Beyond, the hills of Makkah with their traditional houses, many of them multistoreyed, can be seen.

0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.name: Incantation bowl
0a0edfc8-af4f-5ae8-9755-2f42463320c3.description:
A copper dish with a small, inverted dish at the canter, known as an incantation bowl. The entire surface, inside and out, is ornamented with religious inscriptions and talismanic numbers.  
  
The exterior rim is inscribed with Qur’anic verses: “In the name of Allah, the Gracious, the Merciful”; “Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The parable of His Light is as a niche and within it a lamp”; “Allah the Sufficient, Allah the Healer”; “In the name of Allah, the Gracious, the Merciful”; “In the Name of Allah, Who with His Name nothing can cause harm in the earth nor in the heavens, But Allah is the Best to guard and He is”; “In the name of Allah...the healer…”. The inner rim is ornamented with a band enclosed between two frames, each inscribed with repeated numbers (81 / 12).  
  
The band is inscribed with Qur’anic verse in Thuluth script: “Allah, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting by Whom all subsist, there is no god but Him. Neither slumber seizes Him, nor sleep; to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. Who is there who might intercede with Him save with His leave? He knows what lies before them and what is hidden from them, whereas they cannot attain to anything of His knowledge save what He wills them to attain. His Dominion overspreads the heavens and the earth, and their upholding wearies Him not. He is All-High, All-Glorious”.  
  
The inner base is surrounded by fifteen lobed medallions arranged in horizontal registers containing invocations reading: ”Allah the Sufficient / Allah the Healer / In the name of Allah,” repeated. At the very centre is a small, inverted dish. Its decoration begins with a band inscribed in Thuluth script repeating ”O Allah, grant us well-being”. Above it runs a row of pointed arches containing horizontally written numbers (II/II). The central surface of the dish is adorned with a star-shape formed of interlaced script reading ”O the most Compassionate, O the most Generous”.  
  
The exterior body is decorated with ornamental bands consisting of inscriptions and motifs. The outer rim begins with a band of Qur’anic verse: “Allah, the Ever-Living, the Self-Subsisting by Whom all subsist, there is no god but Him. Neither slumber seizes Him, nor sleep; to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth. Who is there who might intercede with Him save with His leave? He knows what lies before them and what is hidden from them, whereas they cannot attain to anything of His knowledge save what He wills them to attain. His Dominion overspreads the heavens and the earth, and their upholding wearies Him not. He is All-High, All-Glorious”. This is followed by a frame of repeated numbers (II/II).  
Around the outer rim of the bowl are fifteen lobed medallions arranged in horizontal registers, each inscribed with repeated invocations: ”Allah the Protector / Allah the Healer / In the name of Allah / Allah the Comforter”.  
Next comes a frame whose decoration is effaced, but traces of the number (81/12) remain visible.  
The recessed base begins with a band in thuluth script containing invocations: ”O Allah, grant us health / O Allah, be pleased with us”. This is followed by a row of pointed arches inscribed with numbers (81/12 and II/II). At the very center, a hexagram encloses the numbers (81/12).

0a6a863f-3205-5785-8137-feaae00e4cbf.name: Kırkçeşme water-supply system.
0a6a863f-3205-5785-8137-feaae00e4cbf.description:
As the population of Istanbul increased during the AH 10th / AD 16th century, so did its problems with water shortages. Tradition holds that once, while Sultan Süleyman was out hunting, he noticed possible water sources and ordered their investigation. The head architect of the palace at that time, Mimar Sinan, surveyed the area and recommended the construction of a water system to convey water to the city. Süleyman consequently ordered in AH 961 / AD 1554 that construction of the water system was initiated. The project was completed in AH 970 / AD 1563, but parts of it were soon damaged by floods and had to be rebuilt in AH 971 / AD 1564. The system cost about 50,000,000 *akche*s, the main currency unit during the Ottoman Empire.  
The system collects water from various springs located about 25 km northwest of Istanbul, in two branches, namely east and west, which join south of Kemerburgaz village and continue as a single line to the city of Istanbul. The system is composed of covered galleries (measuring 55 cm x 175 cm in section and extending about 55 km in total), 33 aqueducts as well as collection and distribution centres, and provided water to the areas of the town below 34 m in altitude. A number of reservoirs were built at a later stage, between AH 1029 / AD 1620 and AH 1234 / AD 1818, and so were further aqueducts. A small section of the water-supply system dates to before Süleyman, such as that extending between Eğrikapı and Cebeciköy, which dates to the reign of Mehmed II. Other parts of the system, such as that of the Kovuk Kemer, were built partially on Byzantine remains.  
Of the 33 aqueducts that make up the Kırkçeşme water-supply system, five are monumental, with two or three tiers of arches and of considerable length. Paşa Kemeri or Balıkzade is 102 m long, 16.4 m high and has two tiers. Uzunkemer is 711 m long, 25 m high and is also two tiered.The plastered gallery on top of it is 60 cm x 175 cm and covered with stone slabs. Kovukkemer or Kırıkkemer is 408 m long and 35 m high and makes a turn of 90 degrees. Its first section is single tiered while the second is triple-tiered. Mağlova or Muallak Aqueduct, the greatest part of the entire system, is 258 m long and 36 m high. It is two-tiered with eight large and eight small arches. Güzelcekemer or Gözlücekemer aqueduct is 165 m long, 34.5 m high and is also two-tiered. Other important but single-tiered aqueducts are Ayvad (195 m), Kurt (305 m), Karakemer (62.6 m), Balıklıkemer (125 m) and Valide Kemeri (38.8 m).  
The entire system is built of stone masonry and uses bossed stones.  
The system originally provided water to over 300 fountains in the city, 135 of which were built as pious foundations of Süleyman the Magnificent. Later additions raised the number to about 580 fountains. Parts of the system located outside Istanbul's city walls have been functioning for over 400 years.
0a6a863f-3205-5785-8137-feaae00e4cbf.short_description: Kırkçeşme water-supply system was built by the great Ottoman architect Sinan on the order of the Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent in order to solve Istanbul's growing problems with water shortage. The system comprises 33 aqueducts and numerous collection and distribution centres. It supplied more than 300 fountains in the beginning but this number later rose to 580. Parts of the system located outside the city walls are still functioning and serving the megapolis of Istanbul.
0a6a863f-3205-5785-8137-feaae00e4cbf.method_for_datation: The dates of the construction for the water system are mentioned in the Tezkiretü'l-Bünyan and in Tezkiretü'l-Ebniye, both of which Sinan dictated to his friend Saî Mustafa Chelebi. Also the Tevzi Defteri, which Sinan wrote, includes detailed information on the parts of the system located within the city.

0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.name: The revenge ground of al-Mukhtar (Persian: *Dar al-entegham-e Mokhtar*)
0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.short_description: The tragic martyrdom of the Prophet’s grandson al-Husayn and his companions at Karbala' near Kufa, where they were massacred by an Umayyad army in 61/680, played an important role in the consolidation of the *Shi'i* ethos; it also led to the formation of radical trends among the *Shi'i*. The earliest of such trends became manifest in the movement of al-Mukhtar, who won control of Kufa in an open revolt in 66/685. Aiming to avenge al-Husayn’s murder, al-Mukhtar launched his own movement and proclaimed Ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Husayn’s half-brother Muhammad, as the *Mahdi*, 'the divinely guided one', the messianic saviour imam and restorer of true Islam who would establish justice on earth and deliver the oppressed from tyranny.
0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.obtention: Purchased 1996 in Isfahan by Dr Axel Steinmann, curator at the Museum für Völkerkunde, during his fieldwork in Iran.

0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.name: Strainer.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.description:
The reddish-grey earthenware fragment comes from a vessel that was provided with a slightly convex strainer. The lattice of this strainer is a geometrical design composed of circles and curved lines. The basic unit of the pattern is a circle filled with a four-sided border bent inwards to form a star with a holed circlet at the centre and four circles in the middle of the sides. The whole design is composed of three of these circles. The space between them is filled with a pointed motif flanked by two tiny holed circlets, which repeats a section of the basic pattern. An incised zigzag line bordered by two curved lines surrounds the openwork at the centre. The zigzag line is a characteristic element of Fatimid strainer designs.  
The strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of an earthenware vessel to protect the stored liquid from insects and pollution. Most strainer vessels of the Islamic period were manufactured of clay. The vessels remained unglazed in order to allow evaporation through the porous material, if it was wished to keep the stored liquid, mostly water, cool.  
Designs put together on the basis of simple geometrical shapes such as circles, lines or triangles, the repetition of these elements and their rearrangement in new patterns are a feature of Fatimid strainers. Geometrical compositions are dominant among the strainer designs of this period followed by zoomorphic and epigraphic motifs. Decorative strainers are known from excavations from the AH 2nd / AD 8th century to the AH 9th / AD 15th century, but Fatimid period was the high point of their development.
0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.short_description: Earthenware fragment which was integrated in a vessel as a strainer. The latticework is composed of a geometrical design of circles and curved lines. The strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the earthenware vessel to protect the stored liquid from insects and pollution.

0d3e43d7-9082-5cb7-bb0c-3a25c1f1ccc9.method_for_provenance: Similar strainers were excavated at al-Fustat and their place of manufacture ascribed to the city. According to F. R. Martin, this strainer comes from excavations at al-Fustat.

0d8a58c2-5da1-5c7f-a4bc-5bc61e7ad347.name: Bath scraper or pumice stone
0d8a58c2-5da1-5c7f-a4bc-5bc61e7ad347.description:
This object might be related to bath scrapers or pumice stones displaying a similar conical shape and attributed to the Safavid period.  
  
This example is decorated with yellow and blue chevron motifs. Its flat side is left purposely untreated to be used as an abrasive surface that would be suitable for hammam rituals of exfoliation and purification of the skin.

0e56903a-9b5a-5b71-84c1-c4e82186198b.name: Yoke (*nīr*)
0e56903a-9b5a-5b71-84c1-c4e82186198b.description: This yoke was used for animals to raise water from a *zājrah* well. Donkeys and bullocks typically work side-by-side to pull together against the weight of the water.

0e671219-31d0-5818-8e46-222c869924d9.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
0e671219-31d0-5818-8e46-222c869924d9.description: After being weighed, sorted and washed, then treated with sulphur, apricots are placed on a large cement platform sheltered from the sun. Exposing the apricots to sulphur vapour before pressing is a major innovation in the process. After some trial and error, sulphurisation is now a well-established part of the process; although the main argument in favour of it is commercial, the operation has the essential advantage of purifying or sterilising the fruit, therefore allowing better preservation of the *Qamr ad-Din*. A suction pump on the platform is used to load the press. A worker in boots enters the platform and pushes the apricots towards the mouth of the suction pump with a wooden shovel.

0e6ba665-360e-507e-b3aa-df4042629de0.name: Al Qanāt, Abu Dhabi
0e6ba665-360e-507e-b3aa-df4042629de0.description:
The tranquil waterway of Al Qanāt in Abu Dhabi is a modern landscape feature where urban architecture meets a natural waterway. At sunset the gentle canal becomes a reflective corridor linking the city’s contemporary skyline with the silhouette of the Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, creating a dialogue between heritage and modernity. In the Gulf region, waterways such as Al Qanāt play a vital role in shaping urban life. They cool the environment, support marine activity, and provide communal spaces for recreation and movement.  
  
Water remains a central element in the identity of Abu Dhabi — a functional resource and symbol of serenity, continuity, and connection.
0e6ba665-360e-507e-b3aa-df4042629de0.author: Dina Turkieh

0ec56979-2b66-516d-a77f-a6c3c80db240.name: Ewer with Design of Animals and Inscriptions
0ec56979-2b66-516d-a77f-a6c3c80db240.short_description:
A stoneware, brown and white Luster-painted ewer with cylindrical body that swells slightly as it rises toward the shoulder; rounded shoulder from which extends a flat handle, neck, and spout. The handle extends upwards from the shoulder and turns at a 45 degree angle to connect to the neck just below the rim. The neck is funnel-shaped with and everted rim; there is a hollow collar at the base of the neck, just above where it joins to the shoulder.  
The decoration consists of a yellow-brown Luster painting over an opaque, white glazed background and is concentrated in two zones of the ewer: the bottom section of the body and the upper section, including the neck, shoulder, handle and spout. This leaves a large, central section of opaque white glaze on the body on which a single line of inscription has been added in the yellow-brown Luster. The inscription, a quatrain in Persian, reads as follows:  
*man mihr-i tu dar miyan-i jan awardam / ba u hama khurda dar miyan awardam / akhir zi hama jahan bar awardam sar / ta 'ishq-i tu bar sar-i jahan awardam  
li-katibihi katabahu Abu Zayd bi-khattihi dar sana sittami'a*  
I brought your love to the midst of my soul / I discussed the smallest matters with it / Until I overcame the entire world / In order to bring your love to the world.  
\[This belongs\] to its writer.  
Abu Zayd wrote it in his own script in the year six hundred.  
In the lower zone is a second inscription written in reserve in large, Kufic script on a background of the yellow-brown Luster with small, delicate scrolls and spirals. This inscription mainly repeats the word *al-'izz* ("glory") along with one or two instances each of *al-dawla* ("good fortune") and al-salama ("well-being").  
The upper zone of decoration is comprised of three registers. The lowest register contains a series of plump birds with their feet on the ground and their wings in mid-flap. They are painted in Luster against a background of light scrolls. The middle register contains a chase scene moving from right to left with a cheetah, placed to the immediate left of the handle, pursuing a series of gazelles that fill the remainder of the register on either side of the spout. The cheetah is represented wearing a collar with a ring, indicating that it is a trained cheetah rather than a wild one. The animals are painted in reserve against a background of Luster with fine scrolls. The upper register of the shoulder has another *Kufic* inscription, possibly the phrase *al-'izz al-da'im* ("perpetual glory"), written in Luster and fitted tightly around the base of the neck. The neck is painted with a small-scale chain pattern. The exterior of the rim is painted in solid Luster while its interior contains *Kufic*\-style pseudo-epigraphy. Finally, the outward facing side of both the handle and the spout appear to have been painted with ascending palmette motifs.  
There are numerous hairline cracks throughout the vessel, and the spout, handle, and rim have all been partially restored. The central *Kufic* band has a notable area of blurring and streaking of the glaze.

0f4a0527-db26-5775-bfd1-e8fdba819736.name: *Sabil* (public fountain) of Yussef Dey.
0f4a0527-db26-5775-bfd1-e8fdba819736.description:
This monument stands in a public square which overlooks the old port and is the meeting point of several arterial roads used by merchants. It is a square construction of cut stone with a rim of green round tiles. There is a marble column on either side, each capped by an Ottoman-style foliate capitol. These provide the framework for a marble rectangle decorated with a horseshoe arch with *ablaq* type black and white arch-stones, a typical Tunisian feature since the Hafsid period. At the base of the rectangle, engraved in the marble, is a Turkish-style vase of flowers decoration. Two symmetrical foliate scrolls with stylised trefoil fleurons emerge from the vase. On the interior of the arch, slightly in relief, is a bilingual Arab and Turkish inscription which consists of the following poem written in 13 lines of *thuluth* script:  
“God has chosen a lord of our times / to produce benefits and to undo the chains of the needy: / This most honourable citizen, the Dey Yussef, has realised how spending on public finances will ultimately be to his own profit. / He has caused water to spring forth on all sides / awaiting the reward of quenching his thirst beside the river al-Kaoutari. / How fine he is and how deeply the public is in his debt! / Thanks to him Bizerte has become a beauteous place to contemplate. / Drink, O thirsty one, from this delicious fountain / whose limpid water is so sweet! / Such a fine fountain built in 1041. / The chief of all the soldiers built us this fountain.”  
“By the master mason Ali ibn Disim Andalusi, at the beginning of *rabi* II in the year 1041 \[AD 1632\]”.  
The old marble drinking-trough has completely disappeared. Formerly, there was a room behind the fountain occupied by a waterwheel or *noria* and which was worked by a camel or by a mule.
0f4a0527-db26-5775-bfd1-e8fdba819736.short_description: This fountain was built in a public square that overlooks the old port of Bizerte and joins several main roads, and it remains the architectural highpoint of the district. It would have been supplied with water using a camel- or mule-powered *noria*. The old marble drinking trough has completely disappeared. The fountain was built by a Spanish emigrant and it has a very beautiful arch of alternating black and white marble voussoirs beneath a ledge of round, green tiles.

0f56194e-aa8f-5ad8-a874-6e567cfd390b.name: Large Water Bottle
0f56194e-aa8f-5ad8-a874-6e567cfd390b.description:
In the modern Arab world, and particularly in the Gulf region, the purchase and use of bottled water have become an essential part of daily life. Due to limited natural freshwater resources and the high salinity of groundwater, most domestic water is desalinated sea water — suitable for cleaning and household use, but often not preferred for drinking or cooking.  
  
As a result, many communities rely on bottled or filtered water for consumption. Large refillable containers like this one are delivered directly to homes by water companies, part of an organised urban distribution network. The practice reflects both environmental adaptation to arid climates and the consumer culture of modern Gulf societies, where water — once scarce and precious — remains a vital symbol of comfort, safety, and modern living.
0f56194e-aa8f-5ad8-a874-6e567cfd390b.author: Dina Turkieh

0f8edbbb-ebb5-5b6a-b92d-27d539424298.name: Drawing water from a well in the village of Tell Halula (Syria)
0f8edbbb-ebb5-5b6a-b92d-27d539424298.description: This image serves to illustrate the day-to-day existence of communities inhabiting arid regions of Syria. It portrays a local woman engaged in the collection of water from a well, thus offering a glimpse into the domestic practices of these communities. As demonstrated in the background, the architectural design of the local construction is informed by the availability of materials in the immediate area. The architectural style employed is a simple and functional house type that has been adapted to provide protection for the local communities against the high temperatures typically experienced in the region.
0f8edbbb-ebb5-5b6a-b92d-27d539424298.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

1004e44b-7e21-5cde-b4c6-d9be0ce7c721.name: Dried Gourds - Various Shapes and Sizes
1004e44b-7e21-5cde-b4c6-d9be0ce7c721.description:
This type of gourd, grown in Hit, Anbar Governorate, Iraq, is among a number of varieties of calabash or "bottle gourd" of different shapes and sizes that were historically used as multipurpose vessels, including water bottles and containers for agricultural produce including beer and wine, milk and other dairy products, honey or grains. Cut segments of these gourds could also be used to make kitchen utensils such as ladles and bowls. They have been cultivated in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas for thousands of years for similar purposes.  
  
While the same gourds can be harvested young for consumption as a vegetable, if grown as containers or utensils they are left to grow for longer and harvested when mature. After harvesting, they are dried for several months until the outer shell becomes hard. The dried gourds are usually cut at the top to make an opening through which the seeds are removed and contents added for storage.  
  
In this image, the double holes pierced near the top of some gourds enabled them to be tied together for transportation. These holes can later be plugged with sticks.
1004e44b-7e21-5cde-b4c6-d9be0ce7c721.holder: Open Museum Initiative for Water Culture

keywords: Water; gourd; calabash; container; vessel; utensil.

10750e4a-16c1-59c9-9ca2-1fd0ff0f88a6.name: Palace of the Emir Bashir Shihab II
10750e4a-16c1-59c9-9ca2-1fd0ff0f88a6.description: The image depicts the principal courtyard of Beiteddine Palace, featuring a circular stone fountain. The construction of the Beiteddine Palace was initiated in 1788 under the authority of Emir Bashir Shihab II, who ruled Mount Lebanon during the Ottoman period, and was largely completed by 1812. The palace functioned as an administrative and residential complex and is an important example of Ottoman-influenced architecture in the Levant. The surrounding façades are constructed from coursed limestone masonry and incorporate arcaded galleries, staircases and balconies with wooden railings and decorated door and window surrounds. Today, the Beiteddine Palace is a major cultural heritage site and tourist destination. It houses museum collections and hosts cultural events, contributing to its continued use as a site of historical interpretation and public engagement.
10750e4a-16c1-59c9-9ca2-1fd0ff0f88a6.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

10f5e2b1-957c-5ea1-a0fb-f3b0d036fa44.name: Noria Jisriyya and Ma’muriyya
10f5e2b1-957c-5ea1-a0fb-f3b0d036fa44.description:
These norias have been carefully restored in recent years. The Jisriyya is known to have irrigated a wide expanse of orchards called Bustan al-Shahiqa and a long part of its aquaduct arcade is still standing. The Ma’muriyya is the largest noria on the Orontes, second only to the Muhamaddiya located to the north of the city. It measures a diameter of 21 meters with a total of 120 buckets. All these norias are known to have been used since early Roman times, as indicated by archaeological findings at the tower bases below the water, and they were certainly strengthened and restored during Nur al-Din's reign, and continued to be resoterd regularly to this day. But unlike most of the noria, this one carries an inscription commemorating the noria’s renovation by an Ottoman governor in 857/1453.  
Next to the Ma’muriyya are two smaller norias called al-Uthamaniyya and al-Mu’ayadiyya. These smaller wheels are some of the smallest on the Orontes, the former has a diameter of 11 m while the latter a mere 7. They were originally meant to function as mills and, in more recent times, serve as workshops for the water-wheel carpenters.

112c53a7-9492-5a54-9745-591f4c96202c.name: Hand-held plough (*haīs*)
112c53a7-9492-5a54-9745-591f4c96202c.description: Ploughing with a *haīs* is the first stage in the traditional cultivation process. The *haīs* is drawn by a draft animal, usually a bullock. A ploughman walks along behind, using a sturdy guide rope and verbal commands to steer the animal while directing the path of the *haīs* by means of a tall wooden handle.

122ed70a-7520-546e-8a64-a6c09c9fef31.name: C.E. Heinke & Co. ‘Pearler’ Diving Helmet
122ed70a-7520-546e-8a64-a6c09c9fef31.description:
Pearl diving was an extremely dangerous and physically demanding occupation, which often discouraged white Australians from undertaking such work. To meet the labour demands of the industry, many Malay workers were brought to Australia in the early 1900s. By 1900, Malays made up 38% of the pearl divers in Western Australia.  
  
The introduction of C.E. Heinke & Co. diving helmets played a crucial role in improving diver safety, enabling them to work at greater depths and reducing the risk of fatal accidents.  
  
This particular helmet was recovered from a pearling lugger that sank in Princess Charlotte Bay during the catastrophic 1899 Mahina cyclone. The cyclone claimed over three hundred lives and destroyed numerous vessels engaged in the pearling industry.  
  
In addition to the damage caused by the cyclone, the helmet shows evidence of multiple repairs carried out over its working life, reflecting its extensive use.  
  
Courtesy of Queensland Museum.

12c86eff-6117-5981-a2db-6fc7d1b3ebdb.name: Abu Ishaq Ibrahim b. Muhammad al-Farisi al-Istakhri, *Kitab Suwar al-Aqalim* (Book of Images of the Lands)
12c86eff-6117-5981-a2db-6fc7d1b3ebdb.short_description: The cartographic treatise called “*Tarjamat al-Masalik wa al-Mamalik*” was written in Arabic by Abu Ishaq Ibrahim b. Muhammad al-Farisi al-Istakhri (c. 340 AH / 951–2 AD), one of the most famous geographers. This 16th-century Persian copy, referred to as “*Kitab Suwar al-Aqalim*” (Book of Images of the Lands), may have been made in Constantinople or in another centre of Turkish power in the first half of the 16th-century. The colophon offers no contextualising information except for an erroneous attribution of the work to Nasir ad-Din Tusi, who was an astronomer and theologist in the 13th-century. On fol. 1a and 157b, there are two almond-shaped Turkish-Ottoman *tughra* stamps, with the name of Ahmad Muzaffar Khan indistinctly recognizable. This shows that the manuscript must have been part of Ottoman collections before it came to the Austrian National Library in 1820/30. The text opens with a typical ornamental panel (*‘unwan/sarlauh*) and includes 21 full-page map illustrations. These brightly coloured miniatures represent stylised maps, occasionally showing decorative motifs, figures, and scenic elements. The quality of the depictions may suggest that they were made by a Persian painter who had emigrated to Turkey. The painter may have also used older models, particularly comparable to a 15th-century manuscript, possibly from Shiraz, in the Topkapı Sarayı (B. 334).

The doublures are made of light brown leather with a medallion, two extending pendants and corner spandrels depicted. These motifs are filled with a dense arabesque work in delicate brown leather filigree on a white background. The binding was likely created in 16th-century Turkey.

12f5d5fd-1263-5c49-9096-319d47fa4f1b.name: Hemispherical cup on trumpet foot
12f5d5fd-1263-5c49-9096-319d47fa4f1b.description:
The hemispherical cup resting on a trumpet-shaped foot belongs to a typology that developed in Iran between the late 12th and early 13th centuries, also spreading to the Syro-Mesopotamian area.  
The outer wall is engraved with apical medallions decorated with arabesques and rosettes with geometric motifs and stylized flowers.  
The upper rim of the cup features an inscription characterized by rods ending in human heads, while the lower part of the letters features recognizable animal heads, including birds, which are also found in the interstices on the swirled base.  
The animated inscriptions are typical of Khorasan metalwork and are reflected in the ornithomorphic inscriptions on ceramics from the Samanid period.  
The auspicious inscription on the rim reads: "Everlasting glory, healthy life, complete prosperity, full success, increasing fortune, favorable destiny, eternal delight, happiness, health, favor, generosity, peace, intercession... long life to the owner." The inscription on the body reads "for Khalīf son of al-Jūlakī (?).  
The cup was probably used to hold beverages and drinking water, which was traditionally stored in large clay jars that preserved its freshness and were covered with cloth, palm branches, or other leaves.

13234dce-e760-5f68-9ead-fa6944333432.name: Magic Bowl
13234dce-e760-5f68-9ead-fa6944333432.short_description:
Protective verses from the Qur’an, blessings and magic letters encase this bronze bowl. This vessel belongs to a group of objects known as magic bowls in Islamic metalworks, intended to ward off fear, evil and demons (*jinn*).  
  
While this bowl originates from Karbala in Iraq, the place of pilgrimage for Shiite Muslims, these objects have appeared in Syria, India and Iran since the 12th century. Earlier Sasanian magic bowls with Aramaic inscriptions embodied similar amuletic qualities, however were made of clay instead of metal and invoked the powers of demons and Liliths.  
  
The Throne Verse (*Ayat al Kursi*) of the Qur’an guards the exterior of the bowl in the *thuluth* style of Arabic calligraphy, granting talismanic protection. A hexagram (six-pointed star) invokes prophet Sulayman (Solomon), while the surrounding inscriptions bear blessings for one's body and the senses. Twelve panels on the vessel allude to the twelve Imams in Shia Islam. The science letters (*ilm al huruf*) ascribes magical properties to the assortment of letters marking the panels.

1433647b-a363-527b-a739-01058ae49638.name: Ritual ladle for the Taghounja festival
1433647b-a363-527b-a739-01058ae49638.description: The ritual ladle used in the Taghounja festival reflects the intersection of water, fertility, and collective ritual in Moroccan rural life. During this traditional celebration communities would gather to invoke rain, fertility, and divine blessing. The ladle, carved from wood, was used to pour or sprinkle water in symbolic gestures of renewal and abundance. Its simplicity belies a profound cultural meaning: water as the essence of life, shared collectively through ritual. Its preservation illustrates how intangible heritage and material culture merge to tell the story of Morocco’s spiritual relationship with water.

1480f971-0e51-5521-a651-32af3d9dcb61.name: *Shasha* reed bundle raft
1480f971-0e51-5521-a651-32af3d9dcb61.description:
The *shasha* (reed boat) of the Iraqi marshlands is a type of raft constructed from reeds, using a bundle technique similar to that of architectural structures such as the *mudhif* (reed meeting-house). This ancient boat type exists around the world wherever there are wetlands.  
  
The simplest and smallest *shashas*– around 2-3 metres in length – were seen in the marshes until at least the AH 1390s / AD 1970s, typically made and used by children for play or fishing. The bundles were bound with cordage made from twisted strips of reed. Larger *shashas* may have used cordage of palm leaf or palm fibre (as does this reconstruction). They largely disappeared from use during the first half of the AH 14th / AD 20th century as the industrial era made wood more accessible to marsh dwellers; previously, only local elites could afford wooden boats, and reed boats of various types were far more common.  
  
Textual archaeological evidence suggests sea-going ships of Sumerian times used vast tonnages of reeds and of palm-fibre rope. There is much debate over their form and building technique. In AH 1397 / AD 1977, Thor Heyerdahl experimentally reconstructed a Sumerian ship based on a similar form to the *shasha*: the “Tigris”, measuring 18m x 6m, followed trade routes from Iraq across the Indian Ocean to Pakistan, then westward to Djibouti. Rashad Salim, who was among the crew, questions whether such craft could have carried cargo, as they lack a hold and have considerable drag even without additional weight. An alternative design for Sumerian trading ships could resemble the *zaima*, another marsh boat made of many narrow bundles of reeds connected in parallel to create the shell of a boat with a central hold.  
  
The *shasha* in the collection of the Open Museum for Water Culture (Basra) was built in AH 1443 / AD 2021 by a team of craftsmen skilled in reed architecture, as part of the Material Cultural Heritage Lab, where architecture students from Basra University studied traditional building techniques.

15d5bb62-3545-5377-b7b5-4a45f3ceb8d6.name: 'Funeral Procession'
15d5bb62-3545-5377-b7b5-4a45f3ceb8d6.description: This illustration is associated with a story related by the hoopoe as a response to a bird who complains about his fear of death. In the story, a son grieves the death of his father in front of his coffin and a sufi soothes him, explaining that his father had experienced much pain and that no one can avoid death. Here, the painter depicts the incident as occurring in front of a cemetery gate. The scene behind the gate is replete with motifs that are irrelevant to the story itself. The viewer at the court may have enjoyed deciphering them.

1757e7cf-1d29-556c-9e11-f2696aaa848e.name: Madrasa and Mosque of Sultan Qaytbay.
1757e7cf-1d29-556c-9e11-f2696aaa848e.description:
The principal, northern face of the *madrasa* contains the entrance. The form of the entrance follows the style typical of Mamluk entrances, commonly crowned with a tri-lobed arch that includes carved *muqarnas*. To the left of the entrance is the *sabil*(water dispensary) and above the entrance, a *kuttab* (Qur'anic school). There is a minaret to the right of the entrance, which is considered one of the most complete Mamluk examples as it represents both the architectural harmony and decorative skill of the age.  
The ground plan of the *madrasa* consists of a square courtyard with a polychrome marble floor and a ceiling with a central skylight. The courtyard is surrounded by four *iwan*s, the biggest of which is the *qibla iwan*, which overlooks the courtyard by means of a horseshoe arch. This *iwan* includes a magnificent *minbar* made of wood and inlaid with ivory and mother-of-pearl, decorated with intricate geometric ornamentation. Stuccoed windows, inset with coloured glass characterise the upper portion of the walls. The designer of the building was extremely skilled in filling the interior spaces with a variety of decorations: the embellishment of the wooden ceiling, its gilding and its painting; the arches that assume a number of forms; the stonework, decorated and carved with vegetal designs; the marble floors of the *madrasa*, mausoleum and water dispensary as well as the stucco windows.  
The mausoleum is accessed through a door on one of the side walls of the *qibla iwan*. Its floor plan is square and it is covered by a dome. The transition zone from a square to the circularity of the dome consists of nine tiers of intricately detailed stone *muqarnas*. The dome is decorated on the outside by ornamentation carved in stone, which consists of repetitive vegetal forms and geometric motifs in harmony with it. The design of this dome is considered to be an example of Mamluk stone decoration at its peak.  
The Complex of Qaytbay is considered one of the most innovative and beautiful of architectural complexes in Islamic Egypt. Its importance lies in the detailed decoration, the beauty of its proportions and the harmony of its architectural components, which include the *madrasa*, mosque, water dispensary, Qur'anic school and the mausoleum.
1757e7cf-1d29-556c-9e11-f2696aaa848e.short_description: This monument stands in the Mamluk (Northern) Cemetery and is described as the most beautiful of the architectural complexes in Islamic Egypt. It is notable for its fine decoration, its perfect balance and the harmony of its components, which include a mosque, a *sabil* (water dispensary), a *kuttab* (Qur'anic school for children) and a mausoleum, and became known as the 'jewel' of Islamic architecture. Sultan Qaytbay, its patron, ruled for 29 years and has left many charitable monuments in Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem and Egypt.
1757e7cf-1d29-556c-9e11-f2696aaa848e.method_for_datation: The complex is dated based on bands of epigraphic inscription, which record the name and title of the builder and the date of construction. There is an inscription band beside the entrance to the *madrasa* and another in the higher reaches of the *qibla iwan*, both of which include the date when construction started (877 / 1472). Furthermore, there is an inscription band inside the mausoleum, which includes the date when the construction of the dome was finished (879 / 1474).

177765c0-4c0d-540e-9196-1b9816f5e481.name: Ewer
177765c0-4c0d-540e-9196-1b9816f5e481.description: The rounded body has flat sides, and is inscribed with Arabic script. It stands on a conical base with a long, slender neck bearing seven protrusions. The vessel has a lid, broken at the riveted section. From the body rises a long spout, inclined forward, with a hexagonal surface; its tip ends in a spur. An S-shaped handle joins the shoulder to the rim, with two perforations at its lower end and a notched ornament at the centre. The conical base and neck are undecorated, while incised floral motifs adorn the shoulder and body.

17f38219-908a-521a-bc48-bdfa982ef72d.name: Small decorated glazed jar
17f38219-908a-521a-bc48-bdfa982ef72d.description:
The small size of this jug and its decoration make it a delicate piece of tableware. It has three rounded handles on the shoulder and is entirely covered with an opaque glaze on the inside and out, now stained grey. The cobalt-blue decoration has been reconstructed as an oval above two curling branches, probably a plant motif, and is repeated between each of the three handles. A bright green vertical line runs down the outside of each handle.  
  
Originally this jug would have looked bright and striking, with dark blue-and-green painted designs against a white or cream colour.
17f38219-908a-521a-bc48-bdfa982ef72d.short_description: It could have been a table vinegar pot used to contain sweet and sour sauces that were very popular in the AH 3th / AD 9th century. The painted design and technology indicate that this was manufactured either in Iraq or Iran.
17f38219-908a-521a-bc48-bdfa982ef72d.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.name: Goblet.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.description:
A goblet in the shape of a truncated cone. The upper part is undecorated and spreads out slightly into a chalice shape. The base is concave (for stability) and retains the navel-like mark where the glass-blower's pipe broke away.  
The glass is transparent, slightly smoky and has very few air-bubbles. It has an iridescent and pearly appearance. The lower part is decorated with a grid of incised lines forming two rows of seven diamond shapes and two rows of seven triangles. Topped by a double circumferential band, the upper rows are decorated with oblique tapering grooves whereas the lower rows have opposing lobes. This grid is decorated at each intersection with an ellipsoidal groove shaped like a segment of a circle. Around the base are more notches, linked to the wall of the goblet with quarter-circle shapes. This goblet is similar to some found at Fustat, Raqqa and Damascus, and to others discovered in the cargo of the wreck discovered off the Turkish coast during the Serce Limani seabed excavations. The goblet's straight profile reminds us of those drinking vessels held by the *caliph*s and high dignitaries shown on the Fatimid wood carvings in Cairo.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.short_description: This goblet in the shape of a truncated cone has a concave base, and its slightly tinted transparent glass contains some air bubbles. The goblet is comparable to similar objects found during submarine excavations along the Turkish coast.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.dates: Hegira, second half of the 4th–first half of the 5th centuries / AD 10th–11th centuries.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.dimensions: Height 11 cm, diameter 4 cm to 6 cm, thickness of glass at rim 0.1 to 0.15 cm.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.method_for_datation: Although this object is similar to articles found at Raqqa dating from the 3rd / 10th century, it was, however, discovered at the Sabra al-Mansuriyya site. This capital city of the Fatimids was founded in the mid-4th / 9th century. As for the likeness of the goblet to the above-mentioned Serce Limani wreck cargo, we know that the ship sank in the second quarter of the 5th / 11th century. Sabra was completely abandoned after the Hilalian invasions in 449 / 1057. We can therefore date this goblet with assurance between the second-half of the 4th / 10th and the beginning of the 5th / 11th centuries.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.method_for_provenance: This goblet was discovered by chance in 1992 at the Sabra al-Mansuriyya site. Brick pickers broke open a large jar with a pick-axe and found contents of priceless value: carafes, goblets, flasks and cups. The shape and decoration of other similar objects found in the Sabra excavations suggest that this object was either produced at the Sabra glass-works, which were highly reputed at that time, or at those of Kairouan, the nearest economic capital.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.obtention: After its discovery in 1992 this piece was kept at the Bardo Museum. It was then acquired by the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada, on its inauguration. It is currently on display there.
183bf3a2-aeed-5d42-afde-1232d1908e44.bibliography: Marçais, G. et Poinssot, L., *Objets kairouanais*, XI, fasc. 2, Tunis, 1952, pp.388–9, cat. no. 8.

197c66bc-cc66-5bb1-87c4-c6327477449c.name: Box trap/Spindle traps
197c66bc-cc66-5bb1-87c4-c6327477449c.description: A rectangular trap made of fine bamboo sticks, and tied with coir rope or nylon twine. The Ghuni is constructed with specially designed involuted front and back walls that create vertical openings to guide fish inside, and it also includes an upper opening for collecting the catch. The clever device is typically used in beels, derelict waterbodies, and inundated paddy fields, especially in rural areas, for catching small-sized fish, prawns, and shrimps.

1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.name: Norias (*nawa’ir*) of Hama.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.description:
The waterwheel, or *noria* (properly pronounced *na'ura* (singular) and *nawa'ir* (plural)), is an ancient hydraulic structure designed for collecting and distributing water by utilising the power of a running stream. It is also the visual and aural hallmark of the city of Hama, 226 km north of Damascus, straddling the meandering River Orontes. The use of waterwheels in Syria dates to the Classical and Hellenistic periods, possibly even the Nabataean period (2nd century BC–AD 2nd century), and the first visual depiction of a *na'ura* is found on a mosaic from the ancient city of Apamea, 55 km north of Hama, dated AD 469. During the medieval period, however, there was a marked increase of references to *nawa'ir* in Islamic geographical writing, indicating their improved and multiplied development.  
Under the Seljuq sultanate and their various Atabeg, Zangid and Ayyubid vassals, when Syria's cities witnessed robust urban development, the *nawa'ir* of Hama received special attention. Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi went on a rebuilding campaign after the earthquake of AH 551 / AD 1157, which included the restoration of Hama's water system and *nawa'ir*.  
The earliest of the surviving *nawa'ir* are attributed to the Ayyubid period (late AH 6th – 7th / AD 11th - 12th centuries) while the earliest inscribed *na'ura* tower, named al-Muhammadiyya, dates to the Mamluk period in AH 763 / AD 1361. This is also one of the two largest *nawa'ir* of the city: 21 m in wheel diameter and 17.5 m in aqueduct height. The aqueduct of al-Muhammadiyya is particularly long as it supplies water for the Great Mosque quarter, nearly a kilometre away from the banks of the River Orontes. The second largest *na'ura*, also 21 m in diameter and known as al-Mamuriyya, is early Ottoman, dated AH 867 (1453).  
*Nawa'ir* are constructed basically in two parts: the mobile wheel, usually made of poplar wood, and the static aqueduct, usually made of stone. The wheel consists of a group of broad beams fixed perpendicularly around the axle, creating a quadrangular formation in the centre, and radiating out towards the wheel's periphery. These beams are held together by circular frames and further supported by more beams that are nailed in at successive angles. At the periphery of the wheel are paddles that facilitate the wheel's circular movement and compartments (*sanadiq*) that collect the water. Given that the wheel is largely a wooden construction, its beams need regular maintenance and changing every 15 years or so.  
Stone constructions, like the aqueduct for transporting water and the small dam controlling the river's water level, are also part of the *noria's* successful construction. The aqueduct is a tall rectangular receptacle standing parallel to the wheel and designed to be as wide as possible in order to receive maximum water per rotation. Attached to this receptacle is the long duct set on an arcade that serves the adjacent areas, providing them with water for domestic and irrigation purposes. On average, a *na'ura* can raise 50 litres of water per second, and irrigate no less than 75 hectares.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.short_description: The city of Hama is famous for its waterwheels, or *norias*, which charmingly dot the meandering River Orontes, which passes through the city. The technique for building these waterwheels is an ancient one, but remarkably effective and still in use. The wheels are typically made of poplar wood, requiring regular maintenance, while their supportive structures, like aqueducts and dams, are made of stone. The dimensions of the total hydraulic construction are inter-related, depending on each other to collect the maximum amount of water efficiently and ensure its most effective distribution.
1a0d6f2a-0a7e-5fdf-98b4-9f6cc792909b.method_for_datation: Some *nawa'ir* are dated by inscriptions but mostly by approximation based on archaeological evidence and historical sources. Recent excavations that have taken place under water are proving that most *nawa'ir* have ancient origins and have been continuously restructured throughout the ages.

1a2dd605-e515-506f-b3e0-89e24d47949b.name: Apod bowl
1a2dd605-e515-506f-b3e0-89e24d47949b.description: This flattened subglobular bowl, apodal with a rounded base, has a short rim flared upwards and a wide mouth. The external decoration is distributed in horizontal bands, the lowest of which depicts a series of intertwined arches ending at the bottom with palmettes. In the central band, ten epigraphic cartouches with benevolent inscriptions are alternated with ten large medallions with hunters riding horses and pairs of musicians. The upper band depicts animals, including hares, felines, sphinxes, caprids and dogs. The interior decoration,  at the bottom of the bowl, features a radial motif in the centre, a solar symbol, around which alternating fish and harpies rotate. The bowl was intended to hold water. The iconographic repertoire, including court scenes and motifs alluding to water and sunt, expresses the wish for eternal life for the owner of the object. This type of bowl was highly sought after during the Ilkhanid period in Iran, as demonstrated by the examples of the Freer Gallery of Art in Washington and of the Galleria Estense in Modena.

1b4970b4-bc60-53bb-887d-df1ef0e3270d.name: Waterskin
1b4970b4-bc60-53bb-887d-df1ef0e3270d.description: A traditional container used for the natural preservation of water, commonly employed in rural and Bedouin communities. The water skin is made from goat hide that is tanned, cleaned and stitched before being filled with water. It was often carried during desert journeys lasting several days. The vessel is crafted so that the goat’s neck forms the spout, while the legs serve as handles for carrying or for fastening the container onto the back of an animal during transport. The sewing is done with leather threads obtained from the neck of a camel, or from the legs of sheep, goats, or cattle. Goat hide was chosen for its thinness and flexibility, and thanks to the fine pores of the leather, the water remained cool even in hot conditions, making it comparable to modern-day coolers.

1b6254e3-cc23-516a-85ce-ff122e61f5e2.name: *Saliha sultan fountain and sabil*
1b6254e3-cc23-516a-85ce-ff122e61f5e2.description:
This work was exhibited in the “Miniatures and Fountains” exhibition held within the scope of Istanbul’s 2010 European Capital of Culture program.  
  
This miniature illustrates a well-known Ottoman story about Saliha Sultan, whose life changed through a moment of honesty at a neighborhood fountain.  
In the district of Azapkapı in Karaköy lived a young girl named Saliha. At that time, homes in Istanbul had no running water, and people fetched water from communal fountains. One day, while filling her clay pitcher, Saliha accidentally broke it and began to cry in grief. Coincidentally, Emetullah Gülnuş Sultan, the wife of the reigning sultan, was passing by in her imperial carriage. Seeing the weeping girl, she asked her attendants to offer the child some money to comfort her. Saliha, however, refused the gift, saying:  
"I am not crying because I lost the pitcher or its value. I am crying because I failed to complete the task entrusted to me."  
Impressed by her sincerity and sense of responsibility, palace officials conveyed the incident to Gülnuş Sultan. Soon after, Saliha was invited to be educated and raised in the imperial palace. When Gülnuş Sultan’s son, Prince Mustafa, came of age, he married Saliha. Mustafa later ascended the throne as Sultan Mustafa II, making her Saliha Sultan.  
Their son, Mahmud, became Sultan Mahmud I upon his father’s death, and thus Saliha Sultan rose to the rank of Valide Sultan, the Queen Mother—one of the most influential positions in the Ottoman court.  
  
Wishing to commission a charitable fountain, Saliha Sultan began preparations, but she passed away before its completion. Her son, Sultan Mahmud I, fulfilled her wish by constructing the Saliha Sultan Fountain and Sebil, the structure depicted in this miniature.  
According to popular tradition, the incident of the broken pitcher inspired an Anatolian custom: during weddings, clay pitchers are broken so that the bride’s fortune may be open and the household blessed.

1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.name: Clogs
1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.description:
*Nanule* – clogs (Tr. *nalın*) are a major category of Ottoman footwear, worn both by men and women. They were carved from a single piece of hardwood, such as walnut, beech, boxwood or ash, held on the foot by a leather strap and usually decorated with mother-of-pearl inlay or metal plaques. The wooden soles of the clogs have two high wedges, as they were designed for use on wet floors in the hamam – a Turkish bath. The height of the clogs also protected the foot from the heat generated by underfloor heating in the bath.  
  
These clogs, from the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade (a.n. TC-265 (1924), are made of wood. They have flared wedges, the back one expanded at the rear. The toe of the sole is square, and the heel is pointed. The soles and wedges are inlaid with mother-of-pearl and metal wire. The inlay design features mother-of-pearl triangles set within metal wire frames. The leather straps are covered with purple velvet and embroidered with vegetable motifs in couched supported technique, using metal thread and spangles. The clogs had an important place in the shared dress and living culture of the urban population in the Ottoman Balkans, which had diverse confessional and ethnic backgrounds.
1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.
1c5f02d2-2470-50be-8d9d-69e9381c662f.obtention: The item is a part of the collection of Serbian painter and engraver Ljuba Ivanović (1882–1945). The collection was purchased by the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade in 1951 and comprises 3,116 items, bearing witness to the early modern and modern visual culture of the Balkans: urban and folk dress,  jewelry, metalwork, casting molds and tools, items carved in wood, horn, and mother-of-pearl, wood-carved and painted icons, etc. The items were collected in the field, mostly during the interwar period.

1cb28b3d-969a-57af-a358-58c996f87905.name: 'The Funeral of Isfandiyar'
1cb28b3d-969a-57af-a358-58c996f87905.description: From a dispersed copy of the Ilkhanid manuscript referred to as the Great Mongol Shahnama, this folio depicts the funeral procession of the Persian hero Isfandiyar. The bier is accompanied by a group of mourners, some wailing and pulling at their hair, which is worn loose as a sign of mourning. The painting technique, with its strong linear quality and thin washes of color, recalls contemporary Chinese brush painting.

1dec3c6e-e957-5322-afe4-42cea2c75ee9.name: Ewer and Basin Set
1dec3c6e-e957-5322-afe4-42cea2c75ee9.description:
In this set, the entire body of the ewer, together with the basin's rim and part of the lid strainer, is reeded. The ribs are alternately engraved with simple leaf ornaments. The ewer has a swan-neck spout, a cast handle and a thumb piece in the form of a bird on the top of the domed lid. The basin has a very wide, flaring reeded rim, decorated in the same manner as the ewer.  
  
The bottom of the lid is perforated, while the highly raised central section serves as a stand for the ewer. An Ottoman inscription with the craftsman's name and date is engraved on the body of the ewer and on the rim of the basin: Sa’âdetlü Zernâb Kalfa AH 1307/ AD 1889-1890. The rim of the lid bears an unidentified stamped Ottoman mark.

1eb58eb2-a356-5cc6-8d6f-3bf073afed7e.name: Photographic print

1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.name: Solomon’s Pools.
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.description:
The Pools of Solomon comprise three neighbouring pools that were arranged in such a manner that the first pool poured into the second, and the second into the third, and from which canals branched out. The first pool is 116 m long and approximately 72 m wide. Its depth ranges from between 6 m and 12 m, and its capacity was 85,000 cu m. The middle pool is 129 m long and 76 m wide. It is 12 m deep and its capacity was approximately 90,000 cu m. The lower, third pool (Mamluk), is the biggest of the three at 177 m long and 86 m at its widest point. It is around 15 m deep and had the greatest capacity of around 113,000 cu m. Thus the total capacity of all three pools exceeded a quarter of a million cu m.  
Water was channelled from naturally occurring springs in the region to the pools by use of an aqueduct system which was more than 70 km long; the pools also served as reservoirs collecting rainwater. The pools provided the city of Jerusalem – which suffered constantly from drought – with water necessary for drinking, domestic use and for ablutions. Located on high ground, water from the pools flowed to Jerusalem by exploiting the inclined slopes and *wadi*s of the natural landscape. The canal and aqueduct system took a zigzag course running for the equivalent of double the geographical distance between Jerusalem and the pools – about 22 km.  
A mandate was issued by the Ottoman Sultanate for the protection and preservation of the water system which meant that the villages through which the system passed were responsible for its security. In AH 1027 / AD 1618 Sultan ‘Uthman II (Osman II, r. AH 1027–32 / AD 1618–22) constructed a fortified castle several meters to the north of the first pool.
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.short_description: These large water reservoirs located to the south of Bethlehem were named after Ottoman Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent who restored and developed them. Three large pools collected water and were connected to a complicated system of canals that channelled water from springs located tens of kilometres away. Canals transported the water from the pools to Jerusalem. The system was begun in the Roman period and was improved over the ages. A third pool was added in the Mamluk period. The improvement of the system to provide Jerusalem with water was considered a measure of the success of the ruling administration.
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.dates: The construction of the first and second pools dates to the second half of the 1st century BC. The third, lower pool was built between hegira 865–72 / AD 1461–7.
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.method_for_datation: The water system is dated with the support of information handed down by the Roman historian Josephus (died after AD 100) and the Arab historian Mujir al-Din al-Hanbali (d. 928 / 1521).
