Berchem, M. van, *Materiaux pour un Corpus Inscriptionum Arabicarum* (Part II), Cairo, 1922.  
Al-Hanbali, Mujir al-Din, (d. 927 / 1520), *Al-Uns al-Jalil fi Tarikh al-Quds wa al-Khalil \[The Magnificent Ambiance in the History of Jerusalem and Hebron\]*, Amman, 1973.  
Natsheh, Y., “The Architecture of Ottoman Jerusalem”, in S. Auld and R. Hillenbrand (eds), *Ottoman Jerusalem: The Living City 1517–1917* (Part II),London, 2000.  
Salama, O., and Zilberman, I., “Aspakat ha-mayim li-Yerushalayim ba-meot ha-16 ve-ha 17, \[The Water Supply System of Jerusalem in the 16th and 17th Centuries\]”, *Cathedra*, No. 41, 1985, pp.91–106.  
  
*Pilgrimage, Sciences and Sufism: Islamic Art in the West Bank and Gaza*, pp.191–2.
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.patrons: It is not known who sponsored the construction of the water system in the pre-Islamic period when the first and second pools were built. The third pool was commissioned by the Mamluk sultan, Khushqadam (r. AH 865–72 / AD 1461–7). Restoration and renovation of the pools and the aqueducts known as al-Qanat al-Sabil (the Aqueducts of the Sabil), were undertaken by the Mamluk Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96) and after him, Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66).
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.architects: Documents in the archives of the Shari’a Court in Jerusalem cite the appointment of Murad al-Nasrani the Armenian, in the position of “Architect of the Aqueducts of the Sabil” in AH 970 / AD 1562.
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.dynasty: The first and second pools date to the Roman period, the third dates to the Mamluk period.
1f743996-b211-5583-a401-77554e5bfc79.author: Yusuf al-Natsheh

1f9cc409-36e4-51f2-828e-77a94d820a08.name: Istanbul water pipeline map
1f9cc409-36e4-51f2-828e-77a94d820a08.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. The Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902. The station is located at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique reminder of Ottoman architecture. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – with water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane, propelled by steam pump machines.

1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.name: Calligraphy
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.description:
Considered one of the masterpieces of Ottoman classical literature, *Su Kasidesi* (*Water Ode*) is Fuzûlî’s celebrated ode (*kaside*) written in praise of the Prophet Muhammad. The poem employs water (*su*) as its central metaphor, intertwining themes of purity, life, longing and spiritual elevation. Throughout the *kaside*, water appears as an entity filled with devotion—flowing, bowing, crying, evaporating and kneeling—mirroring the poet’s own yearning for the divine.  
  
Fuzûlî’s intricate wordplay transforms water into a symbol of both physical and spiritual life, reflecting the Islamic belief that all creation originates from water. By personifying water as an admirer of the Prophet, the poem situates natural elements within an emotional and devotional universe.  
The musical rhythm of the *aruz* metre, the repetition of sound patterns and the carefully layered imagery create an atmosphere of reverence. The poem’s rhetorical brilliance lies in its fusion of mystical Sufi thought, high literary artistry and deep emotional sincerity.  
  
*Su Kasidesi* continues to be celebrated as one of the finest examples of Ottoman poetic expression, demonstrating Fuzûlî’s mastery in blending spirituality, metaphysics and lyrical beauty.
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.method_for_provenance: Date and origin are written on the piece.
1fa972c1-55d3-529e-8a54-27ed5bbaf7a3.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

20876879-3e64-5a45-850f-5156e63e55b7.name: Zamzam Water Bottle
20876879-3e64-5a45-850f-5156e63e55b7.description:
This plastic bottle of Zamzam water, purchased during the pilgrimage (*‘Umrah*), represents how sacred traditions coexist with modern systems of production and distribution. Drawn from the Zamzam Well in Mecca, this water holds deep spiritual significance for Muslims worldwide, symbolising divine mercy and blessing.  
  
Today, Zamzam water is bottled and sealed in modern factories to ensure hygiene and facilitate safe transport. Pilgrims can purchase it directly at airports or distribution centres, allowing them to carry home a sacred element of their journey. In Mecca itself, public coolers and dispensers provide pilgrims with direct access to the holy water, continuing a practice of hospitality and devotion that has endured for centuries.  
  
This object embodies how faith, modern technology, and global mobility intersect, preserving tradition in contemporary life.
20876879-3e64-5a45-850f-5156e63e55b7.author: Dina Turkieh

2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.name: Calligraphy
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.description:
This artwork features the phrase "*Su gibi aziz ol*", written in classical Ottoman Turkish and rendered in Hasan Çelebi’s refined *sülüs* calligraphy. The expression—literally "May you be as precious as water"—is a traditional Anatolian blessing that conveys wishes of purity, value, and life-giving goodness. Water, regarded in both Islamic thought and Ottoman culture as the origin and sustainer of life, becomes a symbol of virtue, generosity, and spiritual clarity.  
  
The calligraphic composition is shaped in a fluid, droplet-like form, echoing the blessing’s meaning. Surrounding the central inscription is an intricate *tezhip* (illumination) border in deep blue and gold, reminiscent of traditional Ottoman manuscripts.  
  
The visual contrast between the delicate floral motifs and the strong, sweeping calligraphic lines highlights the harmony between ornamentation and the written word.  
Through its union of devotional aesthetics and cultural symbolism, this piece reflects the enduring legacy of Ottoman calligraphy and the masterful craftsmanship of Hasan Çelebi, one of the leading contemporary heirs of this artistic lineage.
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
2128703e-9b93-51af-ae89-1e8e1b75f0d3.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

221afe73-7d15-546e-aadf-50258ff042fd.name: Subterranean Passage to Fountain of the Virgin, Jerusalem
221afe73-7d15-546e-aadf-50258ff042fd.description: A local Silwani woman carries a water jug and candle down to the Fountain of the Virgin to collect water. Another figure in the background is emerging into the daylight, having completed a similar trip. The Fountain of the Virgin, or Gihon Spring, is a freshwater spring in the Kidron Valley that represents the only local water source for Jerusalem. Other pools, like the Bethesda pool in the north of the city, held water transported from the springs at Artas, near Bethlehem. It is part of a complex and ancient water management system dating back at least to the Middle Bronze Age (c 2,000 BCE) that continued to represent a major source of fresh water for the Silwani and Jerusalem community until recent years.
221afe73-7d15-546e-aadf-50258ff042fd.method_for_datation: Watercolour is dated 1869 and signed by the artist.
221afe73-7d15-546e-aadf-50258ff042fd.obtention: Donated to the PEF by Walter Morrison, 1872.

221afe73-7d15-546e-aadf-50258ff042fd.author: Felicity Cobbing
keywords: Fountain of the Virgin Gihon Spring, Silwan, Jerusalem
materials: Watercolour and pencil on paper. Created in the studio from a pencil and ink sketch made on site.

22832cf5-d8f3-561b-aeea-71694ea3b574.name: Spouted jug
22832cf5-d8f3-561b-aeea-71694ea3b574.short_description:
The jug is covered with a transparent turquoise glaze and has two feline-shaped handles and two bullhead-shaped spouts. The designs are vertical compositions of leaf motives intercepted by curving peacock feathers.  
Two bands of inscriptions, *en reserve* on a black background read a Persian poem in the form of a *ruba\`i* (quatrain) that was a popular type of verse established by the end of the 10th century. The interior is with a group of fish.
keywords: Jug; Iran; Glaze; Persian poetry; Calligraphy motifs; Fish motifs
materials: Frit ware, underglaze painted in black

22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.name: Citadel of Amman (Water Reservoir).
22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.description: Within the Umayyad Citadel to the east of the palatial complex is a round water cistern, 6 m deep with a diameter that exceeds 17.5 m, and which could hold up to 1300 cu m of water. This cistern was the most important source of water at the Citadel. It was fed through inlet channels connected to a system for the collection of rainwater. These channels and the associated settling tank are partially preserved to the west of the cistern. Some earlier architectural elements including columns, shafts and capitals were incorporated into the wall of the cistern as building materials, such as the shaft of a stone column which was placed in the centre of the cistern and re-used as a depth gauge. The base and the walls were covered with a thick layer of hydraulic plaster which can still be seen. Stone steps along the western side lead down into the cistern. This access was necessary in order to clean the interior from the debris collected with the run-off water and to prepare the cistern for the rainy season. A deep well adjacent to the cistern from the north may be part of the water installations necessary to feed water to the bath complex located to the west of the citadel. This round cistern is closely related architecturally and stylistically to the local tradition of rectangular cisterns, despite the superficial similarity to the round Aghlabid cisterns found at Kairouan Tunisia
22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.short_description: The water cistern on the Amman Citadel lies to the east of the Umayyad palatial complex. It is round, 6 m deep with a diameter of over 17.5 m, and could hold up to 1300 cu m of water. This cistern, fed by inlet channels connected to a rainwater collection system, was the most important source of water at the Citadel. Some earlier architectural elements were incorporated into the cistern wall, and a column shaft was re-used as a depth gauge. The interior was covered with a thick layer of hydraulic plaster. Stone steps along the western side led down into the cistern.
22d721a5-3840-5af9-8c84-912b213423e2.method_for_datation: By way of archaeological excavations within the palatial complex the cistern was dated to around 730 / the first half of the eighth century AD.

23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.name: Pilgrimage proxy scroll.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.description:
This pilgrimage proxy scroll includes handwriting, painting, and drawing on an expensive yellow glazed paper known as *abadi*. It is in fragmentary condition and its title, as well as the section containing the *basmala* (the formula 'In the Name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful'), are missing. The first of the two fragments includes a pair of standards bearing the name of the contemporary Abbasid caliph, al-Nasir (r. AH 575–622 / AD 1180–1225); the standard on the right is partially preserved. Below this emblem is a colour depiction of Mount Arafat flanked by candlesticks. Below this are depictions of the Maqam-i Ibrahim, a stone associated with the Prophet Abraham, and the water wells. Further below this is a depiction of al-Muzdalifa, where pilgrims spend the night as part of their pilgrimage duties, and al-Mina, which is the third most important site for pilgrims. The empty spaces in between the drawings are filled with inscriptions describing the requirements for the pilgrimage.  
  
The depiction of the Ka'ba unfortunately has not survived in this scroll. The second fragment features depictions of al-Safa and al-Marwa (two locations that pilgrims visit in Mecca), the city of Medina (where pilgrims visit the tomb of the Prophet Muhammad), the city of Jerusalem, which pilgrims customarily visit after the pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina, and al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem. This proxy certificate was prepared for a person identified as Umm Abbas, wife of Ghalib. The person performing the pilgrimage on her behalf is Ahmad ibn Fadl al-Andalusi. The document was prepared in AH 602 / AD 1206.  
  
In the Middle Ages it was difficult for people, especially women, to go on pilgrimage. Therefore, people who went on pilgrimage themselves, and those who sent a proxy on their own behalves, wanted to own a certificate proving that they had visited the holy sites and fulfilled all the requirements for the pilgrimage (perhaps in order to leave them to the future generations). Such pilgrimage and proxy certificates are invaluable documents for they describe the pilgrimage ritual, depict the holy sites, and provide information regarding the social life of the period.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.short_description: Pilgrimage certificates document pilgrimages to the Holy Lands, culminating in circumambulation of the Ka'ba. The certificates or proxy certificates (for those unable to make the hazardous journey themselves) give the names of the pilgrim and the proxy, the places visited and worship performed, accompanied by pictures.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.dimensions: 4737: Height 55 cm, width 26.5 cm.; 4746: Height 51 cm, width 26.5 cm.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.method_for_datation: The document's inscription specifies the date 602 / 1206. Both the style of writing and the name of the contemporary caliph support this dating.
23e8db58-0148-5dc3-98b4-98cb5313ba16.obtention: Ismet Bey, the mayor of Istanbul and a member of the board of directors of the Museum of Islamic Foundations (the old name for the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts), visited the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus while travelling. He had a number of items in the Qubbat al-Hazine (Treasury) of the mosque, including Qur'ans and this pilgrimage document, transferred to the Museum where they were registered in the inventory in around 1332 / 1914.

253606f2-42fd-5770-a8f6-cd970b12f2cb.name: Nubian Boy
253606f2-42fd-5770-a8f6-cd970b12f2cb.short_description:
The painting provides a glimpse of everyday street life, probably in Cairo. A tired water seller rests on a wall in front of a building entrance. The boy depicted is carrying on his back a large portable water jar similar to SM1996-219 whilst holding in his hand small drinking cups.  
Ferraris was a renowned Orientalist painter, pupil of Jean-Léon Gérôme, who encouraged him in 1885 to set off on a journey to Egypt with another famous Orientalist painter, Ludwig Deutsch.
253606f2-42fd-5770-a8f6-cd970b12f2cb.author: Hazelle Page
keywords: Painting; Water seller; Water jar; Everyday life; Cairo; Nubian; Ferraris

258aa7cd-e30a-5c77-8172-b842a88bc371.name: The Oil-Press of Midoune
258aa7cd-e30a-5c77-8172-b842a88bc371.description:
In Jerba, traditional oil-presses or mills were all underground, but certainly not for reasons of security; it seems that the choice of this type of architecture was justified for climatic reasons: these underground constructions created a constant microclimate favourable to the extraction of oil which usually takes place during the cold season. The variety of olives cultivated in Jerba bear fruits whose oil becomes solid at a certain degree of temperature, in winter.  
  
Most oil-presses can only be viewed from the outside as they are entirely dug out of the tender rockface whilst the harder layer is used as a roof. But some of them, like that of Midoune, have more elaborate architecture and a constructed roof. From outside, this oil-press is not distinct for its white dome, preceded by an inclined vault, and flanked by two long barrel vaults, the whole of which is built on ground level.  
  
The interior space having been dug out, one could only descend with the help of a staircase, reaching a corridor onto which opens the small recesses which act as storerooms for the olives. One then reaches a circular room that houses the press at its centre, with the oil-presses placed to the right and to the left. The dome is pierced with square holes that let in a very low level of light, whilst the vaults receive rays of sunlight through rectangular holes pierced into the south-eastern side. The recesses are endowed with circular holes at their summit, which enabled olives to be poured in from outside. The design of the whole orchestrates the space into a circular motion around the central element that is the press, in such a way that one imagines an animal turning under the dome, continuing to animate this space despite his absence. This type of oil-press only stopped functioning a few years ago.
258aa7cd-e30a-5c77-8172-b842a88bc371.author: Aziza Ben Tanfous

25aa9b13-028b-5543-8ed7-576c61474cc2.name: Climbing rope (*suw’*)
25aa9b13-028b-5543-8ed7-576c61474cc2.description: To climb the date palm tree, a specially made harness (*habūl*) is used consisting of a rectangular sling or back support (*quffah*) and a thick climbing rope (*suw’*). The climber works his way up the tree by looping the *suw’* around the trunk, leaning back against the *quffah*, and stepping upward.
materials: Cotton fabric and date palm fibre rope

2778ce78-5836-53cd-89f8-bb048bc613b1.name: Bottle with stamped design
2778ce78-5836-53cd-89f8-bb048bc613b1.description:
The overall shape of the object consists of four distinct parts: neck, handle, and upper and lower hemispheres of the body. The decoration, of great complexity, consists of patterns frequently found on jewellery, which gives the impression of a goldsmith’s work transposed to clay. Included in this profusion are roundels framing a bird downed by a hawk or passing lion, twisted columns topped with discs in the shape of flowers, fish, lotus buds, palmettes, and palm trees, circular marks…  
It is a utilitarian but decorative piece intended for pouring water in apartments or reception rooms.
2778ce78-5836-53cd-89f8-bb048bc613b1.holder: Museum of the Arab World Institute

28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.name: Coping of a well.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.description:
Cylindrical on the inside and hexagonal on the outside, this coping rests on a thick base forming a ridge and opens up with an outcurving rim, flat on the upper part and cut in eight vertical sections. A green glaze covers the stamped decoration. It is distributed in eight vertical panels, each one divided into five horizontal sections, three of which are decorated with friezes of poly-lobed arcatures. They are in turn separated by one section covered only by a green glaze and another with an inscription in cursive characters engraved on a green glaze. The inscription names the owner of the workshop and the date the coping was made. The inscription says: 'This was made in Haj Buluqin's house on the (…) day of the seventh of the month of *Rabi* II the last in the year five hundred eighty-six \[AD 1190\]'. The opening of the coping is crowned by several patterns, laid out in two superposed friezes. One is formed by squares filled with eight-pointed stars whereas the other is thinner and has a herringbone pattern.  
During the Almohad period, this type of coping was widely used in both the Maghreb and al-Andalus. They were built with the purpose of protecting the wells in the middle of the courtyards in houses. They also served as decoration, and that is the reason why ceramicists built them with special care and were proud to sign their work.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.short_description: This type of decorated coping, bearing the date and name of the workshop, was equally common in the Maghreb and al-Andalus. They were used to protect wells sunk in the centre of interior domestic courtyards, and to enhance their beauty.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.method_for_datation: The engraved inscription in cursive characters on the fourth section mentions the place of manufacture (the workshop of Haj Buluqin) and the date, the seventh day of the month *Rabi* II in the year 586 / 1190.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.method_for_provenance: Chance archaeological find in Sebta (Ceuta), at the place known as Llano de las Damas.
28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.bibliography:
Bazzana,A., *Maroc, les trésors du Royaume*, catalogue, Paris, 1999.  
Cambazard-Amahan, C. and Erbati E., *6000 ans d'Art au Maroc*, catalogue, Paris, 1990.

28d76422-01a9-5e8c-8c76-2776985164f6.author: Naima El Khatib-Boujibar
keywords: water; architectural decoration; geometric decoration; epigraphic decoration

2a51dcfa-cb1d-50b4-aa78-fe06eed41edc.name: Plan of Temple Mount, called “Harem ech-Cherif” by Muslims. (In French)

2b25ab30-94ca-55a9-a78a-5a565bd5aef1.name: Leveller
2b25ab30-94ca-55a9-a78a-5a565bd5aef1.description: This land-levelling tool, locally known as *azun* or *awzan*, was traditionally used after ploughing to flatten agricultural soil and improve water distribution in oasis farming systems. Pulled by two individuals using ropes, it ensured even irrigation of cultivated plots. The object illustrates sustainable agricultural practices rooted in collective labor and a deep understanding of hydraulic management in arid and semi-arid regions of southern Morocco.

2cdcf470-1102-576a-8d96-463131d599c4.name: Container
2cdcf470-1102-576a-8d96-463131d599c4.description: A traditional leather container used for storing and transporting water, commonly employed by desert tribes and in rural areas. It has a slightly swollen spherical body made of dark leather, now hardened and cracked due to age and dryness, with a short cylindrical neck and a narrow round mouth. Leather containers such as this were widespread before the use of pottery and metal, as leather was a readily available raw material. Its porous nature allowed slight evaporation, cooling the liquid inside and keeping the water cool. Such vessels were carried on pack animals or kept in homes.

2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.name: "The Story of the Princess of the Blue Pavillion: The Youth of Rum Is Entertained in a Garden by a Fairy and her Maidens"
2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.alternate_name: Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
2d816e3d-dd49-518b-8af2-f3ada0d2875b.description: Approximately one century after the Persian poet Nizami wrote his Khamsa (Quintet), the Indian poet Amir Khusrau Dihlavi composed a response using Nizami’s structure but varying his stories slightly. This painting comes from the Mughal emperor Akbar’s (r. 1550–1605) copy of Amir Khusrau’s verses. It depicts a story told by a princess to the king Bahram Gur, about a youth and the fairy queen he imagines meeting nightly in a lush garden.

2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.name: Column capital.
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.description:
A stone column capital, one of 18 capitals that belong to the water reservoir at the Umayyad palace at al-Muwaqqar, with an inscription that reveals that the reservoir was built by order of the Caliph Yazid II (r. AH 101–5 / AD 720–24). It was found in May 1943 in a yard belonging to a private house located within a few hundred meters of the ruins of the palace. It was broken into two pieces which fit together neatly.  
  
Three sides of the capital are decorated with a row of acanthus leaves separated by paired volutes. One side contains a ten-line Arabic inscription that stands out in relief from a plain background. This inscription reads: 'In the name of the most merciful God. Has ordered the building of this pool the servant of God, Yazid Commander of the Faithful, may God favour him and prolong his life and happiness and bestow upon him blessings and bounties in this world and the next. It has been built by the care of ‘Abdallah the son of Sulaym.' Between the eighth and ninth line of the inscription three words are incised in smaller characters, they read: 'Khamsat Ashara dhira' (15 cubits). The drums of the column, upon which this capital once sat, would have been immersed in the pool; each drum with other incised words indicating the number of cubits; thus forming a water gauge. The highest measurement is on the capital itself, being 15 cubits.  
  
A second inscription in relief runs around the abacus of the three decorated sides, it is interrupted in the middle of each by a circular boss with an inscribed trefoil which reads: 'Allahma salli Ala Abdka Rasul Allah' ('O God bless your servant and messenger Muhammad').
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.short_description: Limestone capital from al-Muwaqqar with a ten-line Arabic inscription in relief mentioning the building of a pool ordered by Yazid II (r. AH 101–5 / AD 720–4). The capital and its drum formed a water gauge and incised words indicate measurements. The last was 15 cubits, recorded within the inscription.
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.owner: Now on display at Jordan Museum
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.method_for_datation: The capital is datable by the inscription which bears the name of the Umayyad Caliph Yazid II (r. 101–5 / 720–24).
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.method_for_provenance: Literary sources indicate that the palatial residence at al-Muwaqqar belonged to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik (Yazid II) who reigned from 103–4 / 722–3. Furthermore the capital was found only a few hundred meters from the palace at al-Muwaqqar.
2f8de84c-6136-535a-a12d-f37d60e59baa.obtention: The Museum obtained the capital directly from the owner of the house in which it was found.

310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.name: *Dhiil*
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.description: The *dhiil* is a traditional Somali milk container, both practical and finely crafted, used mainly to collect and store milk from different livestock, and sometimes water. Traditionally made by Somali nomad women, the *dhiil* can be woven from the thorny *qabo* (a plant from the *Euphorbia* genus), as featured, or crafted from wood. Its construction involves peeling and softening the spiny *qabo* stems into long strips, which are then coiled and bound in a basketlike technique. The vessel has a hemispherical base that widens to a central ridge (*kelli*) before narrowing toward the top, capped with a fitted lid (*bugul*). Once woven, the *dhiil* is treated with *asal*, a dye and sealant made from red acacia bark (*qaroon*), giving it a rich colour and protective finish. The interior is traditionally smoked over *shilin* (wood) and cleaned carefully, a process that imparts a distinct smoky flavour to the milk. Milk is shared from the cup of the *dhiil*, called *harrubi*, in a tradition known as *waddagid* ("sharing").
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.method_for_datation: Date not precisely known; established as at least three generations old based on family oral history.
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.method_for_provenance: Provenance established through oral history provided by the lender, supported by family inheritance records.
310da155-3663-5beb-b8de-caa608f5aade.provenance: Belonged to Mohamed family in Somalia; passed down through generations before being inherited by Salim Mohamed.

31375bcb-5762-5e4c-858e-10020d55be9a.name: The Sealed Fountain
31375bcb-5762-5e4c-858e-10020d55be9a.description: One of the springs which feeds into Solomon's Pools at Artas. This watercolour shows a vaulted structure which is now known as the Spring House, in which water from 'Ain Farujeh is fed into the Lower Pool, which is the largest of the three reservoirs. The Spring House is situated in the eastern dam wall of the Lower Pool. Recent excavations and refurbishments have revealed the complex history of the pools over two millennia.

315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.name: *Reposadero* or vat-base
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.description:
It has a cylindrical, hollow body with a straight base and a square-shaped rim, featuring a hole that would have served as a conduit for drainage. Both the base and the rim are slightly concave, the latter also has a whitish colour that could be interpreted as calcareous remains.  
  
The decoration is concentrated on the wall and consists of an epigraphic frieze between concave mouldings with marked edges. The central frieze is stamped with the inscription al-mulk with a six-pointed star positioned above the “m”.  
Functionally, the objects are known as *reposaderos* and served as supports for large water vats, which were both placed either in the courtyard or in domestic interiors. They preserved the water from impurities and kept it fresh, while also collecting any oozes liquid. By the spout of the *reposadero*, the water was transferred to basins or other vessels and could be used for washing hands or for human consumption. Furthermore, the stamped decoration, which repeats the word "*al-mulk*" or "the power", alludes to prophylactic practices of protection and praise of God.
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.dates: Second half of Hegira 6th century / AD 12th century
315f5403-c2b3-5aaf-8a31-139f4ec1548a.method_for_datation: Art-historical and archaeological studies have demonstrated the proliferation of different types of *reposaderos* in the domestic environments of al-Andalus from the end of the Hegira 6th / AD 12th and beginning of the Hegira 7th / AD 13th centurycenturies, following oriental models (Navarro 1995). This coincides with the generalisation of stamped decoration on ceramics for everyday use.

322a4b7e-8f5e-533a-a286-39eb5ff67781.name: Falaj al-Qattārah — The Heart of Traditional Water Management
322a4b7e-8f5e-533a-a286-39eb5ff67781.description:
This is a key distribution point of Falaj al-Qattārah, one of Al Ain’s most important historical irrigation channels. Flowing water reaches a communal basin where it is measured, allocated, and directed toward different agricultural plots. Such structures reflect the sophisticated engineering and social organisation behind the *Aflāj* system, which has sustained oasis life for millennia.  
  
The term *Aflāj* (singular: *Falaj*) derives from the Arabic root ف-ل-ج, meaning to split, channel, or divide, capturing the system’s purpose: the fair and continuous distribution of water. These basins served not only as hydraulic hubs but also as social spaces where timings, rights, and maintenance responsibilities were agreed upon within the community.  
  
Recognised by UNESCO as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, the *Aflāj* remain a living testament to the environmental knowledge, cooperative governance, and technical mastery that shaped desert settlements. Falaj al-Qattārah stands today as an example of these ancestral systems that continue to feed the palm groves and gardens of Al Ain Oasis — one of the UAE’s most significant World Heritage landscapes.

33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.name: Sahrij Swani (Basin of the Norias).
33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.description:
According to the Meknès historian Ibn Zaydan, Mulay Isma'il had an ornamental lake, large enough to sail pleasure boats on, built inside the *kasbah*. In fact, the 'Alawid prince, a contemporary of Louis XIV, had this lake constructed to guarantee the supply of water, in times of siege or drought, to the palaces and mosques of the town, as well as to the public baths, homes, gardens and the orchards that surrounded the town and provided for its daily fruit and vegetable requirements.  
The masterpiece of the complex known as Hri Swani, the Basin of the Norias, Sahrij Swani, is an artificial lake notable for its size (148.75 m by 319 m with a depth of 3.20 m). Three tall crenellated walls that stood around the lake have today been reduced to an isolated section of rampart located on the southwest side towards the Bani Ahmad district and the remains of the base of an enclosure wall more than 2 m thick.  
The size of the lake is reminiscent of the lakes of the Middle Atlas mountains located to the south of the town. The lake was filled from two sources:  
\- Water from the ten wells dug near the Sahrij, below the silo, brought up using ten norias and ceramic channels. Water from the wells was used at times of trouble (war, etc.) and drought.  
\- Water from the Wadi Bufekrane which descends from the Middle Atlas mountains, crosses the southern part of Meknès and feeds the lake and part of the town of Meknès.  
Today the lake attracts tourists visiting the town and also its inhabitants, who come at weekends to cool down during the summer.
33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.short_description: Located beside the building containing the Meknès grain silos within the enclosure wall of the Royal Palace, the Sahrij Swani lake, or Basin of the Norias, or House of the Ten Norias, was created in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. A rectangular artificial reservoir, like the one at the Menara in Marrakesh, this hydraulic structure was intended to provide water for the buildings and monuments in Mawlay Isma'il's town in times of siege. It was supplied by the ten norias (waterwheels) of the neighbouring building and surrounded by three tall crenellated walls more than 2 m thick. This site has been restored very recently.
33362f44-34f0-5545-a2a1-056208f5dff6.method_for_datation: Ibn Zaydan provides the approximate date of 1107 / 1695 in *al-Ithaf*.

337a5b55-9969-5549-aa3c-b41b8507f129.name: Traditional water gourd of the *guerrab*
337a5b55-9969-5549-aa3c-b41b8507f129.description:
The *gerba*, or leather water gourd, is the emblematic tool of the *guerrab*—the traditional water seller of Marrakech and other Moroccan cities.  
For centuries, *guerrabs* played an essential social and cultural role, distributing potable water in marketplaces, festivals, and urban quarters before the advent of modern supply networks. Often recognisable by his bright attire and brass cups, the *guerrab* was not merely a vendor but also a living symbol of water as a sacred resource to be shared.  
The *gerba* itself is made of tanned goat leather stretched over a wooden or reed frame, stitched with strong thread, and treated with natural substances to ensure watertightness. A brass or wooden spout is attached to allow water to be poured, and straps enable it to be carried on the back. Its design preserved coolness through the evaporation of water across the leather's porous surface, allowing a single gourd to serve dozens of people.  
Today, while modern infrastructure has largely replaced the *guerrab*’s profession, the gerba remains a striking testimony of Morocco’s intangible heritage, illustrating the intersection of craftsmanship, social practices, and the cultural symbolism of water.

344f16f7-3c16-5c30-926c-39ba140ff180.name: Ewer
344f16f7-3c16-5c30-926c-39ba140ff180.description:
During the Middle Ages, handwashing had a profound significance, linking hygiene, spirituality, and socialisation. This importance is attested to by the profuse production of ceramic and metal ewers and is also reflected in literature and poetry. Generally, stories and inscriptions, whether on the objects themselves or in architecture, refer to this act of purification in both secular and religious settings.  
  
In relation to this cultural importance, ewers were not only found in religious spaces for ritual ablution prior to prayer but also played a role in secular spaces. At the entrances to domestic and palatial premises, as a sign of hospitality and generosity, the *tacas* (small openings in the walls) probably held containers of perfumed water to welcome visitors. In addition, banquets and receptions were preceded by a washing ritual that not only emphasised hygiene, but also power and social hierarchy.  
  
Furthermore, pieces such as this one have led to historiographical debate about their place of production, ranging from al-Andalus to Sicily, or even the Asian Levant.

34f94cfa-2246-5c81-93dc-34dc25afa481.name: al-Ghuta ash-Sharqiyya
34f94cfa-2246-5c81-93dc-34dc25afa481.description:
Stainless steel trolleys are used to transport the apricot paste to the drying area in the oasis, where it is spread onto the wooden boards. In this last operation, we find the traditional gestures: the workers coat the board with olive oil, and the boss, the most experienced, spreads the paste with a sure hand and using the old measure *kayl* (about 2.5 kg) of liquid paste.  
At daybreak, the apricot paste is left to dry on boards that are placed on the open ground. From the small workshop with rudimentary equipment to today’s industrial enterprise, this vast drying area in full sun remains the essential element of the *Qamr ad-Din* installation. The dough stays in the drying area for several days until it can be peeled off in long dark orange strips at the end of the day. Strips are folded and transported to the workshops, where the second phase of preparing the *Qamr ad-Din* takes place: the dough is cleaned, cut and packaged for the local market or for export.

35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.name: *A Ferry Crossing the Gagos River*
35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.short_description:
This is one of the both unnecessary and revolutionary illustrations in Abdallah ibn al-Fadl’s copy of Dioscorides’s medical treatise.  
The text states that on the shores of the Gagos River, jet can be found effective against pain in the uterus, but the artist took the opportunity to depict a ferry with a helmsman, two rowers, and eight passengers looking out of a porthole.
35dafca1-8ab1-5d22-8ffd-d39248a402df.type: Miniature from a copy of *Kitab al-hashaish*, a translation of Dioscorides’s *De Materia Medica*, scientific manuscript, miniature
keywords: Illustration; Abbasid; scientific manuscript; De Materia Medica; science; medicine; medical plant

3603d007-07c7-5d43-ad14-c40d81e1d215.name: A Sinner’s Plea to God
3603d007-07c7-5d43-ad14-c40d81e1d215.alternate_name: Folio from the Manuscript of Kulliyat (Collected Works) of Sa`di
3603d007-07c7-5d43-ad14-c40d81e1d215.description: Marked as page 177 in the manuscript, this is the 12th and final painting to appear in the Bustan. It depicts group of sages in the wilderness: two debating over books, one praying alone, and one washing in a stream. Below the painting is an inscription in red naming the painter Hiranand, who was assigned by the workshop master to complete this illustration.

37eeebe2-30b7-5a11-b819-7445bc61c961.name: Tile
37eeebe2-30b7-5a11-b819-7445bc61c961.description:
Large rectangular ceramic plaque in a vertical arrangement. Its outer surface is completely covered with a symmetrical decoration based on scrolls twisted around themselves, from which different types of leaves emerge. The coat of arms of the Banda, characteristic of the Nasrid monarchy, is also found throughout the composition, flanked on all occasions by a pair of wading birds. The upper part and the right-hand side are framed by a gold herringbone motif, and the fact that the left-hand and lower sides do not have this border suggests that it was part of a larger ensemble. All the decoration on the tile is in blue, yellow and gold on a white background, although due to a manufacturing defect, the blue has run on part of the surface.  
  
Within this cultural context, water plays a prominent role in Andalusian architecture, often serving as a common thread. Present in numerous texts of Islamic sacred literature, it is presented as a symbol of life itself, thus reflecting the architectural design of the palace. We see it in ponds, fountains and irrigation channels with a practical, symbolic and aesthetic function, intertwining with the vegetation and evoking paradise. In this case, we are looking at a tile that was possibly used for a door jamb or a window frame, in which water is present indirectly, but its evocation is still clear: wading birds, vegetation and bluish tones contribute to an iconographic programme that revolves around this element.
37eeebe2-30b7-5a11-b819-7445bc61c961.method_for_datation: Comparative study with other similar pieces and iconographic analysis.

3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.name:
The constellations Andromeda and Pisces  
Folio from a dispersed *Kitab Suwar al-Kawakib* (Images of the Fixed Stars)
3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.short_description: The lady in this saffron-coloured robe and crown-like helmet is a personification of the constellation Andromeda, which was identified by the second-century CE astronomer Ptolemy and continues to be considered a major constellation. With the translation of Ptolemy’s *Almagest* in the court of the ninth-century Caliph al-Ma’mun in Baghdad, astronomers working under the patronage of the Muslim rulers in modern-day Iraq and Iran adopted the Greco-Roman astronomical knowledge and expanded on it from the indigenous Arab (*Anwa’*) and Indian astronomical traditions, in this illustration combining Andromeda with Pisces. The most prominent example of this tradition is 'Images of the Fixed Stars' written by the Iranian astronomer ‘Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi (died 986), which contained two representations of each constellation, one looking up at the constellation from Earth and the other looking down on it from above. Al-Sufi’s work continued to be in broad circulation, and various copies exist in major museum collections.
3820f22f-64c5-54c7-80da-20ed18f8af7b.obtention: Former Prince Saddrudin Aga Khan Collection
keywords: Folio; work-on-paper; works-on-paper; figure; female-figure; constellations; science; space; astronomy; astronomical; stars

38793766-f653-5775-9feb-93b915baf247.name: Ewer
38793766-f653-5775-9feb-93b915baf247.description: A ceramic ewer with a transparent turquoise glaze, painted in black and blue, in the form of a rooster. Composed of a base, body, neck, spout and handle, it is decorated with vegetal motifs. The circular base, which is smaller than the body, is glazed and undecorated. The body is pear-shaped, and adorned with vegetal motifs in black. The decoration begins at the lower body with a three-petaled leaf surmounted by a wide band, while the rest of the surface is adorned with vegetal designs composed of twisting branches sprouting bud-shaped leaves and half-palmettes. A plain band separates the body from the neck, which is short, cylindrical and decorated with impressed dots. Above it rises the spout in the form of a rooster’s head, featuring a comb, beak and circular eyes.
38793766-f653-5775-9feb-93b915baf247.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
materials: Ceramic/Mold-formed, with underglaze decoration in black beneath a turquoise glaze

38c8715f-fcca-5d98-afc6-976902eb06dc.name: Coconut shell dipper
38c8715f-fcca-5d98-afc6-976902eb06dc.description:
This dipper is inscribed in Arabic with the verse:  
*"Wa ja‘alnā mina’l-mā’i kulli shay’in ḥay"* (Surah al-Anbiyā, 21:30), "And We made from water every living thing."  
  
It also bears the Basmala — *"Bismillāhi’r-Raḥmāni’r-Raḥīm"*, "In the name of Allah, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful."
38c8715f-fcca-5d98-afc6-976902eb06dc.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
38c8715f-fcca-5d98-afc6-976902eb06dc.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu
keywords: Water; Dipper; Coconut; Qur'an; Basmala; Ottomans

38e58977-4147-5180-845f-11ffcd1daba9.name: Pulley
38e58977-4147-5180-845f-11ffcd1daba9.description: A wooden pulley in the form of a circular wheel with a recessed rim, around which the rope was wound to facilitate drawing a water bucket from the well. At its center is a round wooden piece fitted with various wooden boards arranged in a circular manner. Animals were used to pull the rope passing through the pulley.
38e58977-4147-5180-845f-11ffcd1daba9.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum

392b1e4c-50c0-588d-b32e-20bc09dc65d1.name: Glass Water Bottles
392b1e4c-50c0-588d-b32e-20bc09dc65d1.description:
These glass water bottles, from various brands and countries, reflect the habits of modern urban societies where convenience, design, and sustainability intersect. As daily life in cities becomes increasingly fast-paced, bottled water has become an essential commodity, consumed at home, in offices, and on the move.  
  
While plastic bottles dominate global markets, glass bottles are valued for their reusability, purity, and lower environmental impact. Their simple yet elegant design mirrors contemporary aesthetic preferences that balance function with minimalism.  
In the modern Islamic world, the widespread use of bottled water illustrates both the urbanisation of lifestyle and the growing awareness of environmental responsibility in daily consumption.
392b1e4c-50c0-588d-b32e-20bc09dc65d1.author: Dina Turkieh

398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.name: Ewer
398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.description:
This delicate mouth-blown transparent glass ewer has a very tall neck ending in a spout. An elegant handle attaches to the base of the spout and extends to the body. The base is decorated with a ring of yellow paint. The same yellow colour is used to create a floral pattern. However, the upper edge of the bottle and the top of the spout are covered with a purple paint.  
  
Such ewers were used by women to hold rose water, perfume or scented oil. In Arabic, this object is known as an *abriq*.
398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.obtention: Object has been in the National Museum's permanent collection since 1975.
398744ea-4e6d-5503-a7ea-34197a9a2473.author: Tania Abdulmonem Al Majid

39ef25b0-8d27-55d5-b4e9-761de510e7f7.name: Bath scraper
39ef25b0-8d27-55d5-b4e9-761de510e7f7.description:
This object has been associated with a series of bath scrapers and pumice stones attributed to the Middle East of the AH 5th–6th / AD 11th–12th centuries. They were moulded in a variety of geometric shapes displaying animals in profile or facing each other.  
  
This piece shows two birds symmetrically placed around a central axis created by their almost-touching beaks, wings, and tails, along with decorative drop-shape motifs. Their bodies and legs face outward, creating a dynamic composition.  
  
This piece is left untreated to allow its abrasive surface to act as an exfoliating tool used in hammam rituals of purification of the skin.
39ef25b0-8d27-55d5-b4e9-761de510e7f7.bibliography: Boghanim, H. and Carayon, A., *Parfums d'Orient*, Paros: Skira, 2023: p.123.
39ef25b0-8d27-55d5-b4e9-761de510e7f7.author: Dounia Handis
materials: Unglazed clay with modeled decoration and slip

3a31c191-2d71-5f90-af12-d4c3fb392a26.name: Glazed bowl with cobalt-blue and green decoration
3a31c191-2d71-5f90-af12-d4c3fb392a26.description: This high-walled straight bowl has a painted cobalt-blue and green decoration on a white opaque glaze. It has a repeated geometric pattern of alternating blue vertical lines and green shapes. The shape of this bowl and the colours used are highly typical of early Abbasid decorated glazed wares and were originally inspired by AH 2nd-3d / AD 7th–8th-century Chinese ceramics.

3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.name: Nejjarin Funduq.
3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.description:
Although they were constructed almost one century apart, the *funduq* (caravanserai) and *seqqaya* (fountain) of the Place Nejjarine (Carpenters' Square) constitute a single social and civic entity.  
Usually erected charitably and often as an annex to a mosque, this fountain is unusually connected to a hostel.  
The Nejjarin *funduq* occupies an almost regular rectangular space and faces northeast/southwest. It is accessed through a large opening extending onto a straight hallway. Two steps give access to the courtyard. This rectangular courtyard is surrounded on all four sides by galleries that in turn lead to bedrooms of different sizes.  
There are two upper floors above the ground floor. The façades of the courtyard are symmetrical.  
The building is noteworthy for its large portal (5 m high by 3 m wide) that dominates the square and the building. The composition of the portal is uniform and harmonious. Its decoration is based on a horseshoe arch resting on two full brick pillars set into the wall. This arch is surrounded by a second poly-lobed arch in sculpted plaster, whose spandrels are tiled with *zellij* (small tiles) bearing floral, and epigraphic decoration. Above the arch there is a band bearing an inscription and a succession of arcades in sculpted plaster or wood. The ensemble is crowned by consoles that support a large canopy in sculpted wood. They are marked by series of arches resting on pillars and wooden beams.  
The interior, similar to all *funduq*, was restored in 1998 and converted into a museum of woodwork.  
The Nejjarin fountain opposite the *funduq*, located near the centre of the square, is a rectangular pool which served as a drinking trough, in particular for the horses of the customers of the *funduq*. Its upper part and the back of the pointed horseshoe arcature that rises behind it are covered with ceramic marquetry. On either side of the arcature, two demi-columns support overhanging wooden lintels and cornices.
3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.short_description: Al-Nejjarin Funduq is a *caravanserai* built in the AH 12th /AD 18th century by Sultan Mulay Isma'ïl to house the large numbers of passing merchants in Fez. Built on a rectangular site, the *funduq* is noteworthy for its gateway, which dominates the square. The ground floor was used exclusively for stabling, with the guest rooms on the first floor. At the beginning of the 20th century, the *funduq* was used as a police station by the Protectorate. It was recently restored (1998) and turned into a museum of woodwork. It stands beside a beautiful 19th-century fountain.
3b8b9f68-e0cc-5ffc-84c6-1dee91c19a09.method_for_datation: There are no dates on the monument or the fountain, but classical texts such as Ibn Zaydan's *Ithaf* date the *funduq* to 1123.

3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.name: Endowment Charter (*Waqfiyya*) of Haseki Hürrem Sultan.
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.description:
This deed of trust for a pious foundation (*waqf*) belonging to the wife of Sultan Süleyman 'the Magnificent,' Haseki Hürrem Sultan, is written in Arabic on 49 pages of delicate finished (*aharlı*) paper and is dated AH 964 / AD 1557. The official monogram or *tuğra* of Sultan Süleyman (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66) is found on page 1a. The text, which begins with a single-page heading, is written nine lines to the page in black ink within gold-ruled margins. The heading on page 1b and the spaces between the lines on page 2a are illuminated with gilding whose edges are traced in black.  
  
The work's brown leather binding reflects the stylistic characteristics of 10th / 16th century bookbinding with its sunken oval medallion with pendants and corner-pieces. It was executed with a mould and painted with gilding. The inner covers are decorated with oval medallions cut out and pasted on. The medallions are decorated with arabesques (*rumi*) and Chinese-inspired (*hatayi*-style) floral motifs.  
  
On pages 9b–10a of the deed are mentioned the buildings Sultan Süleyman ordered built in Jerusalem near the Dome of the Rock for his wife Hürrem Sultan, known from historical sources as the Haseki Hürrem Sultan Mosque, *Madrasa* and *Imaret* (soup-kitchen). Pages 12a–14b contain a detailed explanation as to how expenditures will be made to take care of the endowment's operations, such as the care and cleaning of the buildings, the salaries of the people who worked in them, and so forth. On pages 15b and 27a the number of commercial estates, mills, etc. donated from among Hürrem Sultan's landholdings to ensure revenue to the endowment is mentioned. But no information is given as to where these estates were located. The signatures of witnesses and Hürrem Sultan's seal are found on page 49a.  
  
The deed, which also includes the signatures of witnesses, is an outstanding example of the arts of the book in the Classical Ottoman period, as well a valuable source of historical information about the Ottoman system of pious foundations and how it worked.
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.short_description: The *waqfiyya* or endowment charter of the charities in Jerusalem of Hürrem Sultan, wife of Süleyman the Magnificent, known for her political involvement, elegance and charitable works, is not only a historical document but also a beautiful example of book arts of the AH 10th / AD 16th century.
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.initial_owner: Haseki Hürrem Sultan (also known as Khassaki Sultan, or as Roxelana, d. AH 965 / AD 1558).
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.method_for_datation: According to the document's colophon it was written in 964 (1557).
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.method_for_provenance: The deed was written in 964 / 1557. In addition, the calligraphy, the *tuğra* of Sultan Süleyman 'the Magnificent,' the binding and the quality of the illumination show that the work was probably prepared in the 10th / 16th century in the palace atelier in Istanbul.
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.obtention: Brought from the Directorate of Pious Foundations in 1919.
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.bibliography: *Soliman le magnifique*, Paris, 1990, pp.38–9, cat. no. 17.
3b9a8d6f-7ca1-5e34-9c8f-c212c393a3de.author: Sevgi Kutluay
keywords: Paper; gilding; ink; leather (binding); watercolour; tooling; painting; waqf system; women
materials: Delicate finished (*aharlı*) paper, written using ink, watercolour, gilding; tooled leather (binding).

3bade1c0-e889-52a3-9c4f-df066605f2cc.name: Beni-Isguen Dam
3bade1c0-e889-52a3-9c4f-df066605f2cc.description:
The great Beni-Isguen Dam is also known as *ahbas* and this name has spread to the whole surrounding region. Upstream of the *qsar*, it is built over the bed of the N'tissa Wadi, spanning one of the narrowest gaps between the two hills that flank the palm grove.  
The dam is 430 m long, 8 m high, 3 m wide at its base and 1 m wide at the top. It is divided into two main parts.  
Firstly, the spillway and distributor, which is 77 m wide and runs down on a slightly diagonal path; 74 vertically set stones break the power of the water current and allow the *umanas* (flood water management commission) to measure the height of the floods from the level at each stone. At the top of the spillway a post (*sham'a* or candle) of predetermined height indicates a dangerous flood level. If the water rises to this height, an immediate alert is given to evacuate the whole palm grove and the *qsar* area further downstream.  
The second part of the dam is the natural reservoir which feeds the ground water. Two wells dug out at the level of the dam accelerate and ease the feed to the ground water and so reduce the effect of evaporation caused by the extensive surface area of the stored water, especially during hot weather.
3bade1c0-e889-52a3-9c4f-df066605f2cc.short_description: The great Beni-Isguen dam is situated upstream of the *qsar* in the bed of the N'tissa Wadi. It consists of two parts; the spillway, along which are set stones for measuring the water level and to give the alert in case of dangerous floods; and the reservoir in contact with the ground water via two wells.
3bade1c0-e889-52a3-9c4f-df066605f2cc.bibliography:
Didillon, C. and Pierre D., *Habiter le desert, les maisons mozabites*, Brussels, 1986.  
*Rapport sur les sites et monuments de la vallée*, OPU, Algiers, 1986.
3bade1c0-e889-52a3-9c4f-df066605f2cc.author: Lakhdar Drias

3c0a8afd-9a9e-52f1-a2f3-a48c17f4d63f.name: Great Mosque of Mahdiyya.
3c0a8afd-9a9e-52f1-a2f3-a48c17f4d63f.description:
This mosque was built on a rectangular plan measuring 75 m x 55 m. It is flanked by two round towers which served to catch the water running from the terraces. It seems the mosque did not have a minaret. The call to prayer was probably proclaimed from one of the towers. In front of the main entrance stands a porch claimed to be the first to figure in Maghrebin architecture. Harmoniously proportioned, this porch is roofed with a round horseshoe arch with *mihrab*\-shaped niches placed high up on either side. Lower down, the different faces of the porch are ornamented with flat-backed niches. This decoration, a main feature of Fatimid monuments (best exemplified by the lateral façade of the Great mosque at Sfax) was carried over into the early Zirid period. This porch is reminiscent of the triumphal arches built by the Romans.  
This entrance porch leads into a courtyard surrounded by four galleries with a room at each corner. These are supported by arches and pillars rising from the courtyard on each side. Pointed arches for the north gallery simply rest on pillars whilst the three other galleries have round horseshoe arches and columns with capitals. From the southeast gallery one comes into the prayer-hall which has nine naves and three bays. The central nave and the transept form a T-shape. At their intersection is a dome supported on multifoil columns, under which a reproduction of the AH 5th-/ AD 11th-century *mihrab* has been built. This comprises a niche with fluted walls, each flute terminating in a shell motif. A *cul-de-four* on top of the niche is bordered by a horseshoe arch positioned on small corner columns incorporating Zirid capitals. The Great Mosque at Mahdiyya was the inspiration for several Egyptian mosques, notably al-Hakim and al-Aqmar mosques in Cairo.
3c0a8afd-9a9e-52f1-a2f3-a48c17f4d63f.short_description: The Great Mosque of Mahdiyya was built by the caliph al-Mahdi. It was modified on several occasions before being rebuilt by the French architect A. Lézine between 1961 and 1965. The mosque does not appear to have had a minaret, with the call to prayer being made from the top of one of its towers. The Great Mosque of Mahdiyya inspired a number of mosques in Fatimid Egypt, such as al-Hakim Mosque and al-Aqmar Mosque in Cairo. This monument owes its beauty to the simplicity of its forms and materials, as the absence of any superfluous decoration.
3c0a8afd-9a9e-52f1-a2f3-a48c17f4d63f.method_for_datation: Historical sources, for example Ibn Idhari (7th / 13th century), as well as geographical authorities such as al-Bakri (5th / 11th century), attribute the Mahdiyya mosque to the Fatimid caliph al-Mahdi. However, the north gallery and the old *mihrab* can be dated from the Zirid era through comparisons with contemporary monuments such as the Great Mosque at Sfax and the *mihrab* of the Great Mosque at Monastir.

3c0a8afd-9a9e-52f1-a2f3-a48c17f4d63f.history: The mosque was built on a fairly tangential piece of land which was in-filled and reclaimed from the sea. Several re-workings of the original building have taken place, mainly during the Zirid period after the collapse of the *qibla* wall. Other works were carried out during the Ottoman era in the 11th / 17th century. The mosque was rebuilt between 1961 and 1968. Only the porch and the north gallery are authentic.

3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.name: Frescoed architectural fragment from a bathhouse.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.description:
A frescoed architectural fragment that once formed part of a bathhouse, consisting of a niche with a pointed arch. The imagery within the niche portrays a figure, executed in black and red watercolours against a white background, executed in the fresco technique. The subject is a seated youth – who might have been a prince – and who holds a cup in his hand. He is wearing a loose robe-like garment, which is decorated with red vegetal motifs. His upper arms are encircled by two bands, and his head is covered by a pleated turban. A complete circular halo appears around the youth's head, perhaps to emphasise his status. He wears a scarf placed around his back, the two ends emerging from under his armpits and then left hanging down, suspended in mid-air. Two parts of the youth's hair can be seen beneath the turban, one in the front and the other at the back.  
The niche is framed by an arch composed of bead-like roundels. The fresco itself resembles paintings found in Samarra, Iraq in terms of both the figures; the shape of the heads and the circular halo, for instance, as well as in the repetitive decorative motifs; the frame in the form of an arch, for example. In addition the implementation of style is far from realistic, and leans more towards the decorative, with clear Persian influences. The Fatimid frescoes are not too different in form, style, or thematic content from depictions executed on metallic lustre ceramics, which were being produced in Egypt during this period. It is possible to study the pictorial representation on this architectural fragment by comparing it to similar Fatimid-period examples executed on various media: ceramics, some wooden pieces and on many textiles. Furthermore it is interesting to consider the role of painting itself as a distinctive decorative component of the applied arts during the Fatimid period.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.short_description: Baths were buildings of importance in the Islamic world due to their role in purification and hygiene. The walls of bathhouses were commonly decorated with frescoes, like the example we see here.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.method_for_datation: Painting on all the applied arts is a distinctive feature of the Fatimid period, it also makes comparison with other paintings of the period a useful means of dating an object.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.method_for_provenance: Fustat was narrowed-down as the place of production for this architectural fragment as the piece was discovered *in situ* in a Fatimid bathhouse.
3c8378b6-b15a-5c21-874e-d7a334e3dab5.obtention: Archaeological excavations undertaken by the Centre of Arab Antiquities in 1932 revealed the presence of a Fatimid bathhouse in the region of Fustat. Some of its constituent parts, including this architectural fragment, were transferred and registered as acquisitions of the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo in 1934.

3ce9d4f4-ee92-5a23-b01e-6209cae6e2dc.name: Celestial Globe
3ce9d4f4-ee92-5a23-b01e-6209cae6e2dc.description:
This precisely executed globe, made of two hemispheres, is the sixth earliest surviving celestial globe. The maker’s name is given twice on the globe. The first, and shorter inscription, states that the globe was made by Muhammad ibn Mahmud ibn ‘Ali al-Tabari. His name appears again in the longer five-line inscription, where he omits the name of his grandfather and his nisbah, but emphasizes instead his trade as an astrolabe-maker, al-asturlabi. And indeed the globe does reflect the work of a professional instrument maker.  
  
The long inscription, situated near the south pole of the instrument, states that its maker, Muhammad ibn Mahmud based it on the illustrations in the AH 4th / AD 10th-century astronomer al-Sufi’s *Kitab suwar al-kawakib al-thabitah* (‘Book of the Fixed Stars’), adapting it to take account of the 200-year lapse of time and rectifying errors of placement and spelling and that the maker had written the identifications of the various constellations of the Zodiac, fixed stars, lunar mansions, and of some non-Zodiacal constellations as well. These show certain discrepancies with al-Sufi’s figures, and, further away from the ecliptic, the star-positions are increasingly misleading. And, although the maker does not say so, he would also have been responsible for calibrating the globe, a necessary condition of its being used for astronomical purposes.

3e779188-7463-53b1-8360-81f5e5086837.name: *Kitab al-Masalik wa’l-Mamalik of al-Istakhri*
3e779188-7463-53b1-8360-81f5e5086837.description:
The AH 4th / AD 10th-century Persian geographer al-Istakhri was one of the most important figures in the evolution of Arab cartography. He travelled widely, but his account of Arabia (Hijaz, Yemen and the Gulf) is curiously sketchy, particularly given the importance of the Pilgrimage. This is partly because, as the title of this treatise, *Kitab al-masalik wa’l-mamalik* (‘the book of postal routes and kingdoms’), suggests, it is based on lists of stations on the postal routes of the Abbasid heartlands and in Iran, which were not available for Arabia and Egypt.  
  
In its present state the manuscript is incomplete. It opens with a splendid page of illumination in gold and silver, and on the penultimate page (folio 120a) is a colophon with the date AH 706 / AD 1307, possibly a later addition. It contains the following maps: Arabia (Hijaz, Yemen and the Gulf); Egypt; the Mediterranean (Bahr-i Rum); Iraq (central and upper Mesopotamia); Khuzistan; Fars; Kirman; Sind; lower Mesopotamia and western Iran (‘Iraq-i ‘Ajam); Tabaristan; the Caspian; the central Iranian desert between Fars and Khurasan; Khurasan; Central Asia, from Transcaspia to beyond Bukhara; Ceylon (Sarandib), with Adam’s Peak and the west coast of India. The map of Sind is a later replacement, and a number of maps announced in the text are now missing. They were obviously lost when the original manuscript was unbound, perhaps for repairs, and the remaining folios rebound in the wrong order.

3e86a5e0-7d9c-53ee-a0db-449ac4bf412d.name: Hand-towel (*Peşkir*)
3e86a5e0-7d9c-53ee-a0db-449ac4bf412d.description: A densely woven, cream-coloured cotton towel with fringed short edges. The border is embroidered in red thread with a running water motif. The main border features six stylised floral motifs worked in sequence. The embroidery employs the counted-thread technique using green, pink, brown, purple, yellow, and red threads. The towel is stained in places.

3ecd0c7a-1b74-5c15-9202-2b4414a57d9c.name: *Port of Algiers*
3ecd0c7a-1b74-5c15-9202-2b4414a57d9c.short_description: The artist studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Algiers in 1905, under Hyppolite Dubois' supervision, and was taught to paint by Léon Cauvy and Georges Rochegrosse. In 1909 he was awarded a scholarship to study in France, and so entered the Atelier Cormon. In 1919 he won the Grand Prix Artistique de l'Algérie for his work "La Famille Attali" and returned to Paris, where he won his second Grand Prix de Rome. He regularly took part in Algerian and Orientalist artists' salons, and in 1934 he received his first commission. In 1936 he completed his first fresco, made of 8 wooden panels, for the Algiers opera house.
3ecd0c7a-1b74-5c15-9202-2b4414a57d9c.author: Dalila Orfali

3ed0bda5-ca9d-536f-b3ed-1c1519674199.name:
The rocky lotus: Sumulutun  
Folio from the manuscript of *Khawass al-Ashjar* (The Characteristics of Trees)
3ed0bda5-ca9d-536f-b3ed-1c1519674199.short_description:
Born around 40 AD in Anazarbus in Cilicia (today’s Turkey), Dioscorides exerted a great influence on scholarship and practice from the Middle Ages until the 16th century. His treatise *De Materia Medica* was first translated into Syriac, a language generally familiar to physicians in the Abbasid empire (750–1258).\[1\] The earliest Arabic translation directly translated from a Greek copy\[2\] was made by two scholars, Istafan ibn Basil and Hunayn ibn Ishaq, in the mid 9th century in Baghdad under the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mutawakkil (r. 847–61).1 Ibn Ishaq was a physician, Arab scientist, and Nestorian Christian. Known as the “master of translators,” he was active in the Bayt al-Hikm (House of Wisdom) in Baghdad.  
According to sources, in 948, Byzantine Emperor Romanus I offered a Greek copy of *De Materia Medica* as a gift to the Umayyad caliph of Cordoba, ‘Abd al-Rahman III (912-961). There is no evidence to suggest a full Arabic translation of this copy was ever made in Cordoba.\[3\] In the intervening years, both the Greek text and accompanying illustrations continued to undergo revision as new copies were made.  
A famous Arabic copy made in the first quarter of the 13th century was widely recopied and distributed and is now dispersed throughout many private and public collections, including the Aga Khan Museum Collection. Known as the Khawass al-Ashjar, it describes the fabrication of medicines from some 500-600 plants; animals, like fish and shellfish; and minerals that serve as the basis for pharmacology in Near Eastern countries and beyond.

3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.name: Ewer.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.description:
A ewer made of copper and inlaid with silver. Decorated with ornamentation and inscriptions in *naskhi* script; the text reads: 'The honourable Excellency, Tabtaq. Glory to his triumph'. Blazons decorate the surface of the ewer, bearing depictions of a goblet, thereby alluding to the position of cupbearer. Adorning the upper section of the ewer's body is a decorative band featuring a series of prominent roundels inside each of which is depicted a pair of confronting birds. The mouth is decorated with vegetal motifs and is equipped with a two-hinge cover and a strainer, which sits inside the mouth. The spout of the ewer has three decorative bands: the middle one carries propagandistic inscriptions in the *naskhi* script, while the other two are adorned with diamond-shaped units filled with vegetal motifs. The name on the ewer dates back to Amir Tabtaq, one of the elite officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, who ruled from AH 689–93 / AD 1290–4. Tabtaq was Governor of the City of Qus in Upper Egypt during the third reign of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. A.H. 709–41 / AD 1309–40).  
The crafting of ewers was an industry that flourished in Iran; it then transferred to Iraq and from there to Egypt, during the Ayyubid and Mamluk periods. The different forms of ewers and the roles that they played were manifold; they were used to pour water for bathing, for hand-washing, or for *wudu* (obligatory ablutions before prayer). However, ornamental ewers were used to decorate the palaces and houses of *amirs* and sultans.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.short_description: The importance of this ewer stems from its fine decoration. It bears the name of Amir Tabtaq, a follower of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad, and a cup blazon, the emblem of his post as cupbearer. Ewers came to Egypt and Iraq from Persia and took many shapes. They were used in palaces and houses for bathing, hand-washing and obligatory ablutions.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.dimensions: Height 40 cm, diameter (of base) 15 cm; diameter (of mouth) 10 cm.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.method_for_datation: The ewer is dated based on the name that it carries: Amir Tabtaq, who was one of the officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, and the Governor of the City of Qus, during the third reign of the Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (r. A.H. 709–41 / AD 1309–40).
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.method_for_provenance: The ewer was crafted in Egypt, specifically for Amir Tabtaq, a fact verified by the inscription. Furthermore it was uncovered during an archaeological excavation in the Egyptian City of Qus. Likewise, the technique of inlay used is typical of the style that flourished in Egypt during the Mamluk period.
3f16b552-d46e-5615-93a4-6d3aa09a3cdd.obtention: This piece was uncovered during the course of archaeological excavations in the City of Qus in Egypt in 1966.

3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.name: Wellhead
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.description:
Wellhead in the shape of an external octagonal and internal semicircular prism, made of sifted reddish clay on which various decorative motifs have been stamped and complemented with green glaze. On a circular and smooth base, a prismatic shape rises, which is reinforced by the moldings that vertically decorate each of the walls, ending at the top with lobed modillions. Two decorative motifs alternate on its eight fronts. The first consists of a decoration of quadrilobed flowers included in a rhomboidal pattern, in the manner of the sebka network, all glazed in green and bordering its contours with manganese oxide. The second has a trilobed arch, whose central lobe is a sharp pointed horseshoe arch, and which houses a decoration with a mirror pseudoepigraphic motif ending in palmettes that end in a twisted stem. It ends, under the mouth of the border, with two borders: the lower one with a stamped seven-point star decoration, on which three bands with incised zig-zag lines and a central one with knife-corded thread, and the upper one contains a inscription in florid Kufic, transcribed by Sahwki Zayed (2015) as *at-tawfiq*, "The Providence", repeated five times on each side of the octagon. The presence of this inscription is confirmed in numerous Almohad works, and is common in the Merinid and Mudéjar works, but not in the Nasrid works. Its upper edge, thickened on the outside and rectangular in profile, is octagonal and smooth.  
  
Such wellheads can be understood within the broader development of water management systems in al-Andalus. Methods and objects were introduced and disseminated to optimise the water usage, an essential resource that significantly shaped everyday life. As part of these innovations, systems for water collection, distribution, and storage were devised. Among these, wells played a key role in accessing underground water, and wellheads such as this one were installed both in public spaces and in domestic courtyards.
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.initial_owner: Unknown / Daniel Aguilera Camacho (owner of the Córdoba house)
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.method_for_datation: The techniques of stamping and the *cuerda seca* technique (original and innovative technique, created in al-Andalus at the end of the 10th century that will continue to be used in later centuries), become widespread and reach their best expression in the AH 6th - 7th / AD 12th–13th centuries. Decorative motifs such as stars are frequent in pieces from the Almohad, Mudejar and Nasrid periods, throughout the AH 6th - 8th / 12th–14th centuries.
3fb68c28-e2b3-5087-9283-6b67b63e3936.method_for_provenance: The stamping and the dry rope techniques (which were created in al-Andalus at the end of the 10th century and would continue to be used long afterwards) became widespread and reached their best expression in the Hegira 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th centuries. Decorative motifs such as stars are frequent in pieces from the Almohad, Mudéjar and Nasrid periods throughout the Hegira 6th–8th / AD 12th–14th centuries.

40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.name: Jug with Design of Five Sphinxes and a Standing Figure
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.short_description:
A biconical jug with handle and buff-colored composite body, wheel thrown with painted decoration and gilded highlights over white glaze. A straight collar rim sits on the large truncated biconical body on a small flared unglazed foot, a vertical strap handle with an applied flat disc thumb rest. There is a dark blue-gray scalloped band on the lip. The rim has a frieze of gray-blue rectangles outlined above and below in black and divided by vertical red lines; each panel is filled with delicate black arabesque patterns and a small square gold leaf central highlight.  
A red and black line defines the carination between neck and shoulder. The shoulder contains five spotted sphinxes with hats and collars, each a different color (blue, red, green, blue, red) walking to the viewer's left toward a vine or sprig with alternating red and blue buds. A figure in a long patterned blue robe and brown conical cap stands at the back of the procession. Gold leaf highlights the figure's shoulders, three areas on the body of each sphinx and the circular elements between them. A series of stylized buds in black and red sit below the top of the register and a second set rests on the decorative baseline. This decorative band is light green and filled with a pattern of red four-petaled rosettes drawn in black with white centers and blue dots above and below, separated by vertical blue lozenges. Some centers still preserve square gold foil elements.  
The bottom half of the body is undecorated except for a series of simple floral elements painted in black just under the band; a similar design is applied below the rim interior. The handle has a black *Kufic* inscription with blue highlights on the sides, the thumb rest is red. The glaze is badly cracked overall; six major areas of loss are in-filled and painted.
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.dimensions: Height: 13.7cm; Diameter of mouth: 8.3cm; Diameter of body: 14cm; Diameter of foot: 5.4cm
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
40152862-7ac2-51ab-a591-e95b3acc0ced.method_for_provenance: During the 12th and 13th centuries, the Persian city of Rayy was an important political, economic, and cultural center. It produced a variety of pottery, of which the most costly were called Minai wares.  These thin-walled vessels were first glazed with an ivory or white ground, although some have a turquoise or blue underglaze.  They are usually embellished with figural decoration not unlike contemporary manuscript painting.

40301340-cb49-5d31-8fc4-0266c8f1e953.name: *Medbasa* (Dibs/date-molasses Extraction Room)
40301340-cb49-5d31-8fc4-0266c8f1e953.description: Many markets in the UAE had medbasas, which were special rooms that contained grooves in the floor for collecting *dibs* (date molasses). Date palm leaf bags full of dates were piled on top of each other above the grooved floor. The combined weight of the bags pressed molasses out of the dates. The molasses drained between the grooves and into a pot where it could be collected and sold. Several *medabasa* rooms still exist in Sharjah and can be visited at Al Hisn (Fort) Museum and Souq Shinasiyya.
40301340-cb49-5d31-8fc4-0266c8f1e953.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century

4161ef6b-9657-5bfe-b8cd-b675c40d0f5f.name: Small bowl
4161ef6b-9657-5bfe-b8cd-b675c40d0f5f.description:
Nielloed silver bowl (*çamça*) made in Van during the Ottoman period. The handle features a stylised bird figure, while the interior center contains a movable stylised duck motif.  
It bears both an Ottoman Turkish "Van" hallmark and an Armenian master’s mark with the initials “K.KH."

42efdee4-d0a0-588e-8606-1ebc9cb0a6cb.name: Jar with green glaze
42efdee4-d0a0-588e-8606-1ebc9cb0a6cb.description: This jar is covered with a green glaze on the outside and inside. The jar has an annular base and two small handles attached to the base of the short neck. The clay used is red. This vessel would have been used to store liquids and food.

43c5ab5f-241d-5114-a0de-5364612ff8df.description: This small jar was discovered during an excavation in a house in Murwab, northwest Qatar in AH 1402 / AD 1981. The jar was in fragments, but it was possible to piece together the top part and restore it. It has a slightly flared rim with a rounded end and a small straight neck. The jar widens into a rounded shape with two small handles that have brown spots of paint. The jar is painted in turquoise blue with drips inside and outside and is covered with an opaque glaze. The jar is made from beige earthenware and may have been made by potters in Basra or Samarra in Iraq or Susa in Iran during the early Abbasid period.
