45320add-79cd-5e4e-a505-b843b89eb3f3.name: *The Green Valley*
45320add-79cd-5e4e-a505-b843b89eb3f3.description:
Educated at the Beaux-Arts in Cairo, Samir Rafi displays some distance from his academic training. In AH 1366 / AD 1946, he co-founded *Le Groupe d'Art contemporain* (Contemporary Art Group) with Egyptians Al Gazzar and Nada. Leading the modern art movement in Egypt, they rejected storytelling, were inspired by local subjects, and simplified their styles. In this bucolic picture the rise of the Nile fertilises the earth.  
  
Through this symbolic scene Rafi combines a common past with a hopeful present at a time in which British troops were withdrawing from the Suez Canal.

457749e2-01c8-568d-b28d-68edb462699d.name: Date-harvesting basket (*al-mikhrafa*)
457749e2-01c8-568d-b28d-68edb462699d.description: The rigid, tray-like *al-mikhrafa*, traditionally used for harvesting dates, is designed to support heavy loads and is raised and lowered from the top of the date palm tree by means of a palm fibre rope. The *al-mikhrafa* is woven from split lengths of *al-isqah*, the woody, long-grained stem from which the date clusters hang.

458f12d6-11aa-5aa1-8e81-ad3731f1366c.name: Panel of six tiles
458f12d6-11aa-5aa1-8e81-ad3731f1366c.short_description:
The panel depicts the holy sanctuary of the mosque at Mecca. Within the compound the Ka\`ba is shown in the centre among other sites such as the *minbar*, the well Zamzam and the structures of the different religious schools, all identified by their names.  
Such topographical works, with a votive or commemorative function, are typical of the Iznik workshops of the 17th century and follow analogous illustrations in manuscripts from the 16th century onwards.
458f12d6-11aa-5aa1-8e81-ad3731f1366c.type: Ottoman ceramic, fritware with polychrome underglaze decoration

4774c55a-a1aa-5860-91ed-a7105da0298d.name: Water bottle
4774c55a-a1aa-5860-91ed-a7105da0298d.short_description: This polychrome Iznik water bottle, *orsürahi*, is decorated with striking, stylised vegetal and arabesque motifs. The decoration was sketched out into the surface of the slip with a sharp instrument before the colours were applied, giving the artist a template from which to work but also allowing him to add additional painted details as he wished. The unusually large size of this bottle, and the spirited quality of its decoration, make it a particularly fine example of its genre.

47a9e1ed-a000-5cfc-8164-b1d48f168b3d.name: Al-Naoor Waterwheel
47a9e1ed-a000-5cfc-8164-b1d48f168b3d.description:
A wooden waterwheel known locally as naoor (plural: nawa'ir), traditionally used to lift water for agricultural irrigation along the upper Euphrates, from Syria into Anbar governorate in western Iraq. The town of Hit (north-west of Baghdad) is at the south-eastern limit of the area of their use.  
  
The example pictured (around 5 metres in diameter) is a small replica constructed by a waterfront coffee shop owner around the year 2000, but most nawa'ir were larger, ranging from 8-12 metres in diameter. They were constructed from lengths of mulberry wood (known for its durabiliity), cut to size and connected with wooden pegs hammered into place. No metal was traditionally used in the waterwheel's construction: this modern example has corrugated metal paddles to power its rotation , but traditionally this function was served by similar rectangular paddles made of small straight sticks attached together in parallel.  
  
A traditional naoor had twenty-four wooden spokes and twenty-four ceramic jars attached to its outer circumference, tied on with palm fibre cordage. As the river current caused the wheels to rotate, the jars would raise water from the river and pour it into an aqueduct at the top of the stone platform, which fed into irrigation channels leading to nearby farms. Traditionally, several farms or families would share a waterwheel and distribute the water between them, each using it during agreed hours of the day; this whole community would also be involved in its construction and installation, which could take up to a month.  
  
According to local sources, this technology has been in use since Akkadian times to solve the problem that the river level in this region is much lower than the surrounding ground. The stone foundations (dahlia) supporting today's nawa'ir are estimated to be around 400 years old, and were built using a specific type of lime-based mortar that hardens underwater.  
  
Many traditional nawa'ir were destroyed in 1967 by a devastating flood on the Euphrates. Although some were rebuilt, electric pumps began to take over their function in the 1970s. The nawa'ir remained an important feature of local memory and were celebrated in reconstructions such as the one pictured. Between 2019-2021, a campaign by local residents led to the rehabilitation of four large waterwheels in Hit, and to their inscription on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2021. Similar revivals have taken place in other parts of Anbar, notably in Haditha, where 24 waterwheels are said to be in operation.

48dbd98b-5340-5f05-be6e-39f0d4addb1f.name: Water-bag

49271df4-3589-5288-9f2d-848a3ad34181.description: Cup decorated with a series of lozenges with floral and leaf motifs. In the center a circular medallion dispays three fish and the number 25.

49a6379f-cd3f-5da3-80ce-ed27270c14f7.name: Bowl
49a6379f-cd3f-5da3-80ce-ed27270c14f7.description:
A short metal bowl with thick walls, decorated with incised or hammered circumferential motifs of lines and vegetal or epigraphic ornamentation (including the inscriptions *“Lā ilāha illā Allāh” and “Al-ḥamdu lillāh”*). The surface shows green and blue copper oxidation.  
This type of bowl was known in that period as *Ṭāsat al-Ruʿwah* (“The Bowl of Fright”). Before medical prescriptions were written on paper, and before people understood anxiety or shock as they do today, Arab households relied on their faith and ancestral wisdom. In one such home, a small metal vessel — this very bowl — was kept and cherished as *Ṭāsat al-Ruʿwah*. Adorned with delicate engravings and Qur’anic inscriptions encircling it like a protective barrier, it was kept by women on the upper shelf of the family wooden chest, wrapped in white cotton cloth. It was used only in moments when the heart trembled in fear or panic.  
When a family member experienced sudden fright, the bowl would be filled with clean water, or sometimes rosewater, and the inscriptions around it would be recited — not as a magical ritual, but as a reminder that tranquillity comes from God alone, and that the Qur’an was never just letters, but a source of serenity that flowed into the soul, even from a small copper vessel held by trembling hands.

4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.name: Plate.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.description: A deep dish with an underglaze-painted design showing a European-style sailing ship at sea, its sails billowing as it rides the cresting waves. Three tadpole-like fish are seen swimming below. In the rim of the dish, groups of simply drawn spirals, ultimately descended from the Chinese 'wave-and-rock' border pattern, reflect the oceanic theme. This dish is one of a number of similar pieces depicting sailing ships of either European or North African build. They were produced around the second quarter of the 17th century, when the Iznik ceramic industry had declined from its heyday of 50 or so years previous. Yet this plate retains considerable charm, especially the jaunty air the artist has given the ship.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.short_description: A deep dish with a representation of a ship at sea. Similar depictions of European and North African ships appear on a number of Iznik wares from the second quarter of the AH 11th / AD 17th century. Although the industry was in economic and artistic decline, examples like this retain a considerable charm.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.method_for_datation: Comparison with similar pieces of the same period.
4a348cc6-05a3-5e8a-8b61-a980db3a8b21.method_for_provenance: Iznik was the centre of quality ceramic production in this period.

4a51e3f4-294d-54c9-a5ea-baa4868a2d16.name: Sickle (*mijaz*)
4a51e3f4-294d-54c9-a5ea-baa4868a2d16.description: The sickle is a tool that has been employed worldwide for its utility: it is a manual agricultural tool that consists of a curved blade that is usually used for harvesting grain crops or cutting weeds used to feed livestock.

4aed1631-e500-5b52-9093-ae36e5e2ea38.name: *Les foggaras*
4aed1631-e500-5b52-9093-ae36e5e2ea38.description:
An ingenious system of drawing and distributing water simultaneously in an extremely dry area, foggaras consist of a row of wells on a gentle and uninterrupted slope that allows surface water to flow to gardens.  
  
The well shafts are made by drilling a tunnel at the base of a mountainous area and following an aquifer, with the goal of bringing water to the surface for irrigation of agricultural land. The tunnels are horizontal and dug with extreme precision on a regular slope to allow the water to flow steadily.  
  
The tapped foggara water table is deeper than the water table under the dunes, but closer to the surface in the nearby plateau of Tadmaït (to the east), which makes it accessible by digging horizontally. The size of this network of wells is estimated at thousands of kilometres between the Gourara and the Touat; seven kilometres for just the Mghayer, the foggara of Timimoun. The punishing work of digging could not have been accomplished without the exploitation of many slaves. For this reason maintaining foggaras that collapse or become silted is problematic.  
  
The term foggara refers not only to this system of pumping from the water table, but also to the pooling of water to irrigate the palm groves. The oases of Gourara and Touat have comb-like structures (kesria) that direct the water flowing between the “teeth” (kiel el-Ma). The water is distributed according to the requirements of the private gardens, and routed through channels (seguias) that drain into ponds (majens) from which farmers draw water to the extent allowed. This system, specific to Saharan regions, is evidence of its early use, and of the people’s deep desire to live in harmony by sharing with each other the meagre resources of the Sahara in a strict but fair manner.
4aed1631-e500-5b52-9093-ae36e5e2ea38.author: Farida Benouis, Houria Cherid, Lakhdar Drias, Amine Semar

4c2706b3-1aef-5df4-b5b2-4acc99b47143.name: Jar
4c2706b3-1aef-5df4-b5b2-4acc99b47143.description:
This transport jar was handmade and has a typical kitchenware profile. Its high neck with a wide rim allowed it to be covered with a lid (ceramic, wood, textile). Its ovoid body supports a single handle. The entire body is covered with a cream-coloured slip and geometric decoration painted in brown in a series of panels across the body.  
  
Although it was found in Al Zubara, in north-western Qatar, the characteristic grainy clay, as well as the manufacturing technique, shape and decoration, identify it as Julfar pottery. This type of pottery was made in Ras al-Khaymah (in the modern United Arab Emirates) and exported throughout the Gulf, particularly from the AH 12th-13th / AD 18th to the mid-20th century.

4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.name: Tankard
4c9c682b-e3ff-589b-807b-5e22f9819c18.description: A cylindrical tankard with one handle. The body is decorated with a series of white flowers with a blue centre and green leaves on a red ground. On the top and bottom there is a band in the form of a chain. The handle is decorated in blue and white.

4ccbf41b-58c9-561b-9afc-21680166f66c.name: Shell with inscriptions
4ccbf41b-58c9-561b-9afc-21680166f66c.description: This palm-size, perfectly shaped mother-of-pearl shell displays an elegant design and an intriguing function. Its luminous surface is engraved with eight concentric rings containing verses from the Qur’an and religious supplications. The variety of the calligraphic styles and their layout make the design both dynamic and quite dignified. Although the intensity of the decorative program on the shell and the attention given to the minutest detail are unique, the shell may have been designed for a specific purpose that demonstrates how Muslims evoked the Qur’an in their everyday life. The concave shape of the shell and some of its decorative motifs suggest that it may have been used as a drinking vessel. In line with the belief in the protective and therapeutic power of the Qur’an, some Muslims drank water that came into direct contact with Qur’anic verses in order to obtain blessings and protection. Could this have been the role of this singular shell?

4d43096d-e741-5b21-a636-ccbb17e263cf.name: *Windows*
4d43096d-e741-5b21-a636-ccbb17e263cf.description:
Wafa al-Hamad’s exploration of doors and windows delves into the intersection of heritage and visual transformation within the Gulf region. These architectural elements, often crafted with precision, symbolise entry and exit-gates to the past, present, and future. Drawing from the historic buildings of Qatar, UAE, and Bahrain, she captures their ornate facades as a means of preserving fading architectural traditions amidst rapid modernization. Her paintings, such as this one, function as portals, inviting viewers into spaces where the past remains alive.  
  
Rooted in Islamic art, al-Hamad’s work frequently incorporates geometric abstraction and calligraphy, though these elements are not present in this piece. In the 1990s (AH 1410), she has additionally woven Arabic proverbs into her compositions, enriching her art with cultural depth. These proverbs serve as visual metaphors, blending the functionality of objects with poetic symbolism and allowing her to explore concepts within a contemporary framework.  
  
"I have developed a strong interest towards these ancestral doors, in their excellent craftsmanship, a sublime beauty, uniqueness and inspirational representation of faith…My paintings convey such meanings especially door panels which truly express what I believe in. Door panels stand at the crossroad of our ancestral heritage. They pave the way to the realm of Islamic art, its form, decorative accents and inscriptions." - Wafa al-Hamad
4d43096d-e741-5b21-a636-ccbb17e263cf.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art

4d52d723-2eaf-5fc7-ba06-13ce4807735a.name: Deep glazed bowl with pseudo-epigraphic inscription
4d52d723-2eaf-5fc7-ba06-13ce4807735a.description: This bowl was discovered on the site of a house during the Qatari-French archaeological mission in 2009. The bowl itself dates to the 9th century. It is covered in an off-white opaque glaze with a wide band of turquoise glaze or paint around the upper part. The black-brown paint around the outside resembles Arabic script, but it is unclear whether real words were intended or this is simply a design. This kind of stylised painting is known as 'pseudo-epigraphic' decoration and is particularly associated with workshops in Samarkand and Nishapur (present-day Uzbekistan and Iran, respectively). These types of wares illustrate the influence of Islamic design and Arabic script throughout the Muslim world during the early Islamic period.
4d52d723-2eaf-5fc7-ba06-13ce4807735a.dates: AH late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

4dbcd917-010c-5ebd-8b39-646ec4f29059.name: "Bahram Gur Sees a Herd of Deer Mesmerized by Dilaram' s Music"
4dbcd917-010c-5ebd-8b39-646ec4f29059.alternate_name: Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
4dbcd917-010c-5ebd-8b39-646ec4f29059.description: Approximately one century after the Persian poet Nizami wrote his Khamsa (Quintet), the Indian poet Amir Khusrau Dihlavi composed a response using Nizami’s structure but varying his stories slightly. This painting comes from the Mughal emperor Akbar’s (r. 1556–1605) personal copy of Amir Khusrau’s verses. It shows the king Bahram Gur with his beautiful slave girl, Dilaram, who could make animals sleep or awaken with the sound of her music.

4df535c3-b510-5c68-a479-e3f13cd24179.name: Morocco. Irrigation channels in Marzuga
4df535c3-b510-5c68-a479-e3f13cd24179.description: The irrigation channels of Morocco, locally known as khettaras, are predominantly located in the southern areas of the country, on the margins of the Sahara Desert. Isolated oases, such as Merzouga, have relied on the khettaras for irrigation and survival since the 14th century AD. Functioning similarly to the aflaj of Oman, they work by drawing groundwater from areas of higher altitude to oases via underground tunnels that can be several kilometres long. In these images, we see them in use in local contexts, with water arriving to the village to irrigate the land.

4e79bace-bc0e-55dc-9c99-de21e6fc0f6b.name: *Kelek* raft
4e79bace-bc0e-55dc-9c99-de21e6fc0f6b.description:
The Iraqi word for raft is *kelek*, a name that can be traced from Sumerian (*ka-la*) via Akkadian (*kalakku*). Most *keleks* were made on banks of the Tigris in mountainous areas of what is now Iraqi Kurdistan and southern Turkey. *keleks* were traditionally constructed using a grid of long, straight poles made from tree saplings – an important export from the northern highlands to Mosul and Baghdad since ancient times, used in construction and for a wide range of purposes after the rafts had been dismantled.  
  
The *kelek* differs from log rafts as its poles are supported on floats to increase buoyancy: traditionally these were made from inflated animal skins (more recent versions have been known to use tyre inner tubes). The poles and floats are tied together with cordage made from leather, goat-hair, or other materials sourced from further afield.  
  
Some *keleks* were used simply to transport the wooden poles that made up the raft; others carried additional heavy cargoes, including giant millstones and the raw stone used to build ancient Mesopotamian cities. *Keleks* from the northern highlands generally made only one downstream journey before being dismantled and used for their materials. *Keleks* were photographed on the Tigris in the early AH 14th / AD 20th century and were used by archaeologist A. H. Layard to transport statues from Nineveh downstream to Baghdad in the AH mid 13th / AD mid-19th century.  
  
*Keleks* are depicted on at least two Assyrian reliefs from the reign of Sennacherib (705-681 BC): in one scene the raft carries passengers and a fisherman, while another shows it carrying two large stone blocks. Both rafts are propelled by oarsmen seated at the front of the raft. One is guided by a swimmer on an animal skin float.  
  
The *kelek* in the collection of the Open Museum for Water Culture is a reconstruction made in AH 1446/ AD 2024 by a craftsman from Sulaymaniyah, Iraqi Kurdistan.

50179dc4-4e0f-5796-85ea-539270a46a71.name: Cooking pot
50179dc4-4e0f-5796-85ea-539270a46a71.description:
This kitchen utensil was discovered at the al Wakra site during excavations carried out in 2011.  
It is a cooking pot that was made in Julfar (in the Emirate of Ras al-Khaymah) and used for storing and preparing foodstuffs and liquids. With a globular body and a flat base, this pot bears a grey slip, and some of the specific decoration painted in red from the Julfar production workshop can be discerned on the upper part of the body, neck and shoulder. This bears witness to the import of pottery and to Qatar's commercial links and activities.

517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.name: Textile Panel
517b9478-f631-507d-9c9f-4381e1f51b61.short_description: Most of the textiles that survive from Fatimid Egypt, mainly fragments, were made or reused as burial shrouds and were preserved on account of the dryness of the Egyptian climate. This comparatively large panel may therefore derive from a funerary context; to compensate for areas of loss, it appears to have been pieced together in modern times from four parts of the same cloth, suggesting the original panel was once much longer. Its materials (bleached linen and silk), tapestry-weave technique, and bands of geometric decoration all mark it as a product of the Fatimid period. There are several bands of inscription that can be read as a repetition of “Help from Allah,” but because it lacks a royal or historical inscription, this cloth was likely made for a humbler clientele rather than for the ruling elite. However, it is otherwise very similar in style and manufacture to the so-called Cadouin Shroud (Abbey of Cadouin, France), inscribed in the name of the caliph al-Musta‘lī (r. Hegira 487-495/ AD 1094–1101).

52262e70-2860-5b5b-8fff-109c9c07916c.name: Janissary water jug
52262e70-2860-5b5b-8fff-109c9c07916c.description:
The pitcher is copper, coated with tin, and bears Janissary symbols.  
It is inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the text:  
  
*"Es-SeCenturyid Salih Beşe, sene \[H.\] 1232, Bölük 25.”*: "Es-SeCenturyid Salih Beşe, Year \[AH\] 1232, Regiment 25."  
  
Additionally, the body is decorated in engraved workmanship with stylised motifs of a naval anchor and a fish, symbolising maritime affiliation.  
  
This pitcher was owned by Agha (commander) of the 25th Janissary Regiment.

5337eb4c-b40b-5fbe-9d53-67905e8aef78.name: Water Distribution in Urban Life — Abu Dhabi
5337eb4c-b40b-5fbe-9d53-67905e8aef78.description:
A delivery truck transports large refillable water dispensers, a familiar sight in many Gulf cities. In Abu Dhabi, where natural freshwater sources are scarce, and tap water is often not preferred for drinking, bottled and delivered water play a central role in daily life. These large containers — ordered through coupon systems and delivered to homes, offices, and public buildings — are part of the infrastructure that secures safe, drinkable water for urban communities.  
  
Water, though readily available in modern cities, remains a resource managed by desalination, distribution, and consumption patterns unique to the Gulf.
5337eb4c-b40b-5fbe-9d53-67905e8aef78.author: Dina Turkieh

54e4dfd7-48fc-5972-94f5-cea81c315201.name: Bowl.
54e4dfd7-48fc-5972-94f5-cea81c315201.description:
Wide-mouthed bowl with a slightly convex base. As in the majority of examples of this type of object, the decoration, which covers the whole of the outer surface, consists of a wide band, interrupted by medallions, made up of a series of scrolls bearing inscriptions in Mamluk cursive characters known as *thuluth*. The underside decoration includes typical motifs, such as phoenixes in flight and peonies, peculiar to Mamluk metalwork, revealing the influence of Far Eastern naturalism tempered by its Iranian background.  
  
The inscriptions, which offer a typical example of the titles used in Mamluk protocol for objects intended for high-ranking persons, include "*al-maqarr*…*al-âli*" (High Excellency), "*al-mawlawî*"(the Master), "*al-mâlikî*" (the Sovereign), "*al-âdilî*" (the Just), "*al-amîri*" (the Amir) and "*al-mâmâlk*" (the Mamluk). The bowl probably belonged to an unknown high-ranking official of the sovereign’s court, who is referred to in one of the inscriptions.  
  
The bottom of the inside of the bowl bears a particularly interesting motif made up of a series of fish in a whirlpool pattern. This is a very common decorative element in Islamic metalwork, particularly during the Mamluk period. The fish motif, as well as being obviously linked to the intended use of the piece (to hold water), probably also holds a special magical or symbolic significance as fish are bearers of good omens in the East and specifically in this case for the owner of the piece.
54e4dfd7-48fc-5972-94f5-cea81c315201.short_description: This bowl, used for holding water and decorated with inscriptions and zoomorphic motifs (fish and phoenixes in flight), is a good example of calligraphy being used for decoration and as a good omen in the Muslim world.

556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.name: Ablutions basin.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.description:
This parallelepipedic tank marked with plain striations on the inside, the short sides and the corners, was beautifully adorned on the outside, and almost all of the decoration has survived on two sides. The design on the decorated face, whose inscription has been destroyed, is divided into two styles. The first one, rising from the base, consists of a large frieze of grooved foliage, dotted with buds and rosettes and wide-veined plain palms with calyxes, and double ones with acanthus leaves and buds. The second comprises a strip in relief with two lines of grooved intersecting knotwork, one curved and the other straight, bearing fleurons and veined palms. It is framed by an edge, set back, formed by vegetal knotwork accentuated with small stylised palm leaves in the shape of six-pointed stars.  
The short side is occupied by two identical animal scenes, sculpted on two vertical panels separated by an empty space. On each panel, there is an eagle spreading its tail, carrying two quadrupeds on its wings and two gazelles from its claws. Two winged ibex confronting each other on either side of a fleuron finish the scene in the lower part.  
Most of the ornamentation on the other two sides has been destroyed, leaving only the text in *kufic* characters sculpted in relief on the rim and the decoration of the framing ribbon on the large side, which consists of a frieze of aquatic birds and fish alternating on a plant background.  
The surviving elements of the inscription that crowned the entire rim of the tank include the last digit of the hegira date (300), and the name of the patron, 'Abd al-Malik, *hajib* (chamberlain) of Hisham II.  
The design and animal scenes of this beautiful example of Caliphate artwork are reminiscent of the tank at al-Mansur and would appear to be from the same Madinat al-Zahira marble workshop in Córdoba.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.short_description: This basin is the work of a marble workshop in Madinat al-Zahira, Córdoba, the princely city built by al-Mansur. It was brought to Marrakesh by 'Ali ibn Yusuf and placed in the ablutions room of the Great Mosque.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.dimensions: Height 70 cm, length 155 cm, width 82 cm, depth 50 cm, thickness of sides 10 cm, thickness of base 20 cm.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_datation:
1\. The inscription, partially destroyed, sculpted on the upper rim of the tank reads '(the year) three hundred, in the name of God! God's blessing. Victory and divine assistance to the Hajib \[followed with his honours\] Abu Marwan 'Abd al-Malik ibn Amir (…), this is part of what he commissioned (…)'.  
2\. We know that 'Abd al-Malik was appointed *hajib* of Hisham II between 381 and 398 / 991 and 1008) by his father al-Mansur.
556ddc9e-29c0-523e-bb8e-eb53f4c45d06.method_for_provenance: Although it was discovered in the Ibn Yusuf Madrasa in Marrakesh, which belongs to the Sa'did period (10th / 16th century), the name of the patron and the comparative study with the al-Mansur basin in the National Archaeological Museum in Madrid suggest that it was originally from Madinat al-Zahira in Córdoba.

5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.name: Ablutions font.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.description: Ablutions font with a circular bowl, formed with eight lobes in the style of a flower. It has a unique decoration on the outside of the rim, a band in relief bearing an epigraph. Water has worn this away, obliterating the letters on the outer curves, with just a few remaining on the corners where the lobes meet. On one of them it is possible to read the beginning of the *Basmala* (first verse of the Qur'an) and everything leads us to suppose that this was completed with a quotation from the Qur'an, as was common on facilities of this kind related to ritual ablutions at the entrances to mosques. Another specimen of similar characteristics and probably from the same period is known in the Lisbon area.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.short_description: Almohad ablutions font decorated on the outside of the rim with a band inscribed in relief with the beginning of the *basmala*, which suggests that it also included a Qur’anic inscription. This piece was probably related to the ablutions ritual practised when entering a mosque.
5656dd0b-ba48-5ef4-a959-1d9718ee9e56.method_for_datation: The style of lettering dates it to the Almohad period.

58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.name: Large pitcher
58467eac-791f-5968-9787-74e5c5043757.description:
This pitcher is inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the following text:  
  
*"Bu güğümden su içene şifalar olsun; eğer dahi kâfir içerse İslamla müşerref olsun. Tarih 1266’dır, cümle hakkında hayr olsun."*: “May those who drink water from this ewer be granted healing; and if an unbeliever drinks, may he be honored with Islam. The date is \[AH\] 1266; may it bring goodness to all.")  
  
It also reads *"Fet oğlu Hüseyin Ağa, tûl-i ömrü ile muammer olsun."*: "May Hüseyin Ağa, son of Fet, live a long and prosperous life."

5873b7f8-20de-5178-a5f8-4103250abc6c.description: A very long queue, mainly of Bedouin women, waiting to collect water rations in an open area with domestic buildings behind. To the left are two mounted Allied soldiers. There is a third mounted soldier facing the line of women on the right. 58752dc4-a710-5e08-bb58-f1e52b715cb4.name: Axe
58752dc4-a710-5e08-bb58-f1e52b715cb4.description: The traditional hand-forged axe is a simple but highly functional implement which dates back to antiquity in Oman. It is used to shape, chop and split wood, with its steel head serving as a wedge to force wood fibres apart and its wooden handle acting as a lever to increase force at the cutting edge.

587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.name: Model of traditional pearling boat
587837e2-ba2c-5d56-b39a-b5dcb62c7f11.short_description: This type of boat represents the most common type of vessel that was involved in the pearling trade in Sharjah. Throughout the Arabian Gulf, several types of boats such as the Jalboot, Sambooq, Battil and the Sama'a, although in fact multi-purpose, were used for pearling at the peak of the industry in the 19th and early 20th centuries. Depending on the boat and size, the boats had the capacity to carry between 10 and 100 crew. This model is of the 'Saku', a Sama'a-type boat originally belonging to Juma Al Sari, the father of the model donor.

58a491a4-71cc-5b24-a1a9-764a71488439.name: *Works for the opening of the Corinth Canal*
58a491a4-71cc-5b24-a1a9-764a71488439.short_description:
The Corinth Canal being dug. Photographer unknown.  
The Corinth Canal separates the Peloponnesian peninsula from the Greek. The idea of the canal was revived after Greece gained independence but soon abandoned due to economical reasons. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 gave an new impetus and the following year, the Zaimis government passed a law authorising the construction of the canal, which was formally inaugurated on 23 April 1882. Zaimis assigned the project to the Hungarian István Türr who set up the Société Internationale du Canal Maritime de Corinthe but the company failed and the project was finished by the company of Andeas Syngros. The canal was designed by the Hungarian engineer Béla Gerster with the assistance of the French Vincent Dauzants, a chief engineer of the Suez canal.
58a491a4-71cc-5b24-a1a9-764a71488439.author: Maria Dimitriadou

The glaze and decoration remain only on the outside, with alternating vertically painted lines in red and yellow running from the lip to the foot. The glaze above the painted decoration is transparent. 59e80b7c-1bba-5071-b131-361159bba754.description:
Istanbul was a lively center of trade, and many ships, both Turkish and Western, called at its harbor. Most of the Turkish vessels were light, fast ships with lateen sails, like the one depicted on a flask (11/1971). Western European galleys were much heavier, and this dish shows a monumental oceangoing three-master on the raging sea.  
  
What were presumably the muzzles of threatening cannons were transformed by the Turkish potter into flowerheads. An early example of the slogan Make Love, Not War?

5afe91bf-fea8-55d3-82ee-a8b6233aab07.name: Haram al-Sharif (Noble Sanctuary).
5afe91bf-fea8-55d3-82ee-a8b6233aab07.description:
The Haram al-Sharif is of great importance in the Islamic faith. It is where the Prophet Muhammad set out on his midnight journey from Mecca to Jerusalem (*Isra'*) and from where he ascended to the heavens (*Mi'raj)*. Furthermore, God blessed the Haram in the Holy Qur'an, and made it the first *qibla* (or direction of prayer) for Muslims.  
The Haram takes an elevated position up in the hills of Jerusalem. It is composed of a rectangular platform of approximately 1450,000 sq m forming one-sixth of the old city of Jerusalem.  
Scholars agree that as it exists today the Haram al-Sharif is devoid of any visible remains that precede the arrival of the Muslims in Jerusalem in AH 15 / AD 638, due to the fact that the buildings which were standing were destroyed by Titus and his legions in AD 70.  
When the Arab-Muslims arrived, Jerusalem surrendered peacefully as part of a contractual agreement set up by Caliph ‘Umar bin al-Khattab (r. AH 13–23 / AD 634–44) with the Patriarch, Sophronius. The Arabs did not destroy any buildings in the area of the Haram and the agreement made with Sophronius guaranteed the protection of the inhabitants, their households and their possessions. Most of the city was inhabited, with the exception of the Haram area, which at the time was neglected.  
The Haram site slopes from the north to the south. The highest point of it is in the centre where the Dome of the Rock is located. This tendency to slope is addressed by a platform that traverses it. One section of the platform is known by the name of al-Aqsa al-Qadim, while the other is known as al-Musalla al-Marwani.  
Development of the Haram is focused on its northern and western borders, although this was following construction at the centre, along with some important buildings such as the Dome of the Rock and the Qubbat al-Silsila (Dome of the Chain). The eastern edge of the Haram inclines towards a slope running down to the Wadi Jahannam (Qidron Valley), used as an Islamic cemetery from the very beginning of the Islamic conquests. On the southern side there is an even steeper inclination that offers better structural support to the architecture, and because of this, Umayyad edifices on the southern limit, best represented by the Dar al-Imara in the south of the Haram, have been continuously inhabited throughout history.  
The Haram al-Sharif is composed of three levels. The ground level includes Bab al-Rahma (Gate of Mercy), Bab al-Tawba / Bab al-Dhahabi (Gate of Repentance / Golden Gate), al-Musalla al-Marwani, al-Aqsa al-Qadim (Old Aqsa) and the Masjid of Buraq. The middle level includes the Aqsa Mosque, the Islamic Museum and the side arcades in the western and northern walls, along with a multiplicity of gates and buildings such as *sabil*s, *madrasa*s, *mastaba*s, minarets and domes. The highest level is that of the Dome of the Rock, reached by a series of stairwells, and where there are a series of magnificent domes and some *khanqa*s (Sufi retreats), also the Minbar Burhan al-Din and the Mastabat al-Kark, and a number of cisterns and fountains.
5afe91bf-fea8-55d3-82ee-a8b6233aab07.short_description: This is the third oldest Islamic site after Mecca and Medina and the oldest and most important sacred Muslim site in Palestine. It is a large complex with an area of some 145,000 sq. m. It includes the Dome of the Rock, al-Aqsa Mosque, the Dome al-Silsila (Chain) and the Bab al-Rahma (Gate of Mercy) as well as more than 90 other commemorative buildings. The complex thus represents diverse Eastern Islamic architectural arts in different styles over the course of various periods, transforming it into an outdoor architectural museum. The site is linked with Islamic stories, specifically that of the *Isra'* and *Mi'raj* (Night of the Prophet's Ascension).
5afe91bf-fea8-55d3-82ee-a8b6233aab07.method_for_datation: The Haram al-Sharif is dated by the inscriptions it bears, by historical sources and finds from archaeological excavations.

The most prominent was the Umayyad caliph, Abd al-Malik bin Marwan (r. AH 65–86 / AD 685–705). Subsequent renovations were undertaken by several Muslim sultans and caliphs, the most prominent being: the Fatimid caliph, al-Zahir (r. AH 411–27 / AD 1021–36) and sultan Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi (known as Saladin, r. AH 564–89 / AD 1169–93) and the Ottoman sultan, Sulayman al-Qanuni (Sulayman the Magnificent; r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66).

5ba1e422-156b-52c9-b178-d1de57501788.name: Piri Reis b. Hajji Mehmed, *Bahriye* (Navigation or Sailing Manual)
5ba1e422-156b-52c9-b178-d1de57501788.short_description: The important manual on navigation and sailing called “*Bahriye*” was authored by Piri Re’is b. Hajji Mehmed (died 962 AH / 1554–55), an Ottoman navigator and cartographer. This 17th-century copy was penned in large *naskh* script, possibly in Ottoman Istanbul. Piri Re’is, a Turkish captain and later admiral of the Ottoman fleet, is credited with the creation of two famous world maps as well as this sailing manual for the entire Mediterranean. While the latter is relatable to Catalan and Italian *Portolane* and *Isolarii* (Sea Atlases or Naval Manuals, and Island Books respectively), the work of Piri Re’is is considered quite independent and original as it contains detailed descriptions of the coasts and islands of the Mediterranean, starting from the Bosporus and the Dardanelles. Interestingly, this manuscript is a late copy of his first version of 1521, while a separate second version, which included a longer and more detailed text, was made five years later and was dedicated to Suleyman the Magnificent. The earlier text consists of 132 chapters with descriptive texts of historical, geographical, and navigational content. Moreover, this copy contains 133 half– to full-page map sketches that accompany the text, of which most feature a black compass rose in the centre. Like the other more than 20 surviving copies, it likely served primarily practical purposes. In contrast, the second version of the text is extant in about ten surviving copies which reflect a representative courtly quality both in their elaborate calligraphy and illustration. This suggests that these manuals were rather intended for the education of the nobility. It has been postulated that the Vienna copy, with its schematic, rather inconsistently oriented sketches that sometimes even extend into the text block, was produced by sailors or members of the Ottoman Navy in the arsenal or in cartographic workshops. The map sketches show port cities and fortresses identified by toponyms and other representational details added in bright colours. These representations seem to follow a fixed compositional formula with stylised landscape depictions. Small offshore islands or reefs, for example, are usually highlighted in red. Judging from the illustrations, this manual is stylistically comparable to the copy kept in the University Library of Bologna (MS 3613, dated 977 AH / 1569 AD), and it has been argued that the Vienna manuscript may be a copy of the Bologna manuscript from the second half of the 17th-century. The owners’ notes and stamps on fol. 1a reveal that the manual was part of the collections of a certain Zeynül'Abidin Evliyazade as well as of Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall.

5cb50de2-2586-516f-843e-945e72d7f294.name: Miniature
5cb50de2-2586-516f-843e-945e72d7f294.description:
In this miniature, an entire world of living beings—mothers and children, animals, plants, and all forms of life—is depicted within a single drop of water. Beneath the drop appears an Arabic inscription from the Qur’an, Surat al-Anbiya (21:30):  
"*Ve ce‘alnā min al-mā’i kulla shay’in ḥayy*" —  
“We created every living thing from water.”  
  
The work symbolises the idea that all beings are bound together through water, sharing a common origin and interdependence. Reflecting this message, the Istanbul Water Museum has embraced the motto “Su Kardeşliği” — "The Brotherhood of Water."

5e718b75-a6e3-5eae-9b65-a96062887c90.name: *Dlu*
5e718b75-a6e3-5eae-9b65-a96062887c90.description: The *dlu* is a traditional leather bucket used in Moroccan oases to draw water from deep wells. Typically crafted from thick goat leather treated with natural oils, it was strong enough to withstand constant immersion while remaining flexible. Attached to a rope and pulley system, the *dlu* was lowered into wells to collect water, then hoisted up for domestic, agricultural, and animal use. Its design reflects both simplicity and efficiency, adapted to arid environments where groundwater was the primary source of survival. In Tafilalet, where *khettaras* and wells structured daily life, the *dlu* was indispensable to communities before mechanised pumps. It represents the resilience of rural craftsmanship and the crucial role of traditional tools in sustaining livelihoods in desert societies.

5ed0eaf8-52ab-5071-826a-912d48b8619d.name: *Perahu*
5ed0eaf8-52ab-5071-826a-912d48b8619d.description:
This scale model represents a *perahu padewakang*, a traditional sailing vessel of the Makassans and Bugis peoples of South Sulawesi, Indonesia. The *padewakang* was one of the largest and most important maritime crafts of the Indonesian archipelago from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries. It was widely used for long-distance trade and is closely associated with the historic Makassan voyages to northern Australia.  
  
The visits of the Makassans to the northern shores of Australia are thought to have begun between 1650 and 1780 CE, according to different scholarly interpretations. Their primary aim was the collection of trepang (sea cucumber), a valuable commodity in Chinese markets. Sailing from the port of Makassar, the heart of this trade network, the Makassans established seasonal camps along the Arnhem Land coast where they harvested, boiled and dried the trepang before transporting it back to Indonesia and onward to China. These voyages represent some of the earliest sustained contact between people from outside the continent (Southeast Asian Muslims) and the Indigenous Australian communities, a history remembered in Aboriginal oral traditions and depicted in rock art and later bark paintings.  
  
The *padewakang* was a relatively large vessel, able to carry around thirty crew members, provisions and the processed trepang cargo. Its form, with high stern and prow, made it a seaworthy vessel for the open waters of the Timor and Arafura Seas.  
  
**Cataloguing Information**:  
This particular model was commissioned in 2019 by the IMA from Premier Ship Models, a specialist firm. Crafted abroad in Mauritius as a representational piece, it reflects the essential features and proportions of the historic *padewakang*. It serves as an educational tool and visual record of one of Indonesia’s most significant indigenous ship types and its role in cross-cultural maritime history.
5ed0eaf8-52ab-5071-826a-912d48b8619d.method_for_datation: The maker (Premier Ship Models) provided documentation confirming the model was produced in 2019. Vessel type identified as perahu padewakang, traditionally built and used in South Sulawesi, Indonesia, based on characteristic design features and historical records.

5f76f108-6ffb-5c2b-8fe2-0ec05a6fae48.name: Various hydraulic machines used in Egypt to water the land. The first method is constructed in a linear manner and provides the land with water whenever it is in need. Part of "Dyke A"
5f76f108-6ffb-5c2b-8fe2-0ec05a6fae48.short_description: The captain of the Danish Royal Marines Fréderic-Louis Norden (1708–1742) was sent to Egypt to draw monuments. His collection, *Voyage d’Égypte et de Nubie*, was published posthumously in 1755, and was added to in 1795 by the inclusion of scientific commentaries by Louis Langlès (1763–1824), founder of the École Spéciale des Langues Orientales and curator of oriental manuscripts at the Bibliothèque Impériale. This new edition, a product of Europen "Egyptomania", introduced some splendid new illustrations. In this particular page, the artist has focused on traditional hydraulic machinery.

5ff2f6bf-6eef-590b-81ac-758e18790131.name: Calligraphy
5ff2f6bf-6eef-590b-81ac-758e18790131.description:
This artwork blends modern calligraphy with classical Islamic *sülüs*– and *tuğra*–inspired forms. The central inscription features the Qur’anic verse from Surah Al-Anbiyā’ (21:30): “And We created every living thing from water.” The phrase emphasises the essential and sacred nature of water as the origin of life, reflecting a cosmological theme deeply rooted in Islamic thought.  
  
On the right side, the intricate calligraphic motif expresses a devotional invocation, rendered in fluid, interwoven lines that echo the movement and vitality of water. The turquoise background reinforces the symbolism of purity, creation, and continuity. Together, these elements merge spiritual meaning with visual harmony, inviting viewers to contemplate the relationship between nature, divine creation, and artistic expression.
5ff2f6bf-6eef-590b-81ac-758e18790131.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
5ff2f6bf-6eef-590b-81ac-758e18790131.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
5ff2f6bf-6eef-590b-81ac-758e18790131.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

5ffeeb7c-0b57-5dd4-a331-6d70ed986d0d.name: Bottle with wide rim
5ffeeb7c-0b57-5dd4-a331-6d70ed986d0d.description: This black glass bottle has a spherical body supported by a ring-shaped base. The tubular neck narrows slightly towards the top and ends with a flat rim. At its base it is circled by a twisting black glass ribbon overlay, the sole design element. Blown glass existed from the first century AD, making possible a considerable increase in the production of glass objects. The process became popular and played a significant part in the fabrication of vessels.

611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.name: Aghlabid Reservoirs.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.description:
These two reservoirs were built using the same method. They are constructed of rubble and surfaced with a waterproof coating. The walls are consolidated by internal and external buttresses which alternate, thus providing maximum resistance against the water pressure. These buttresses are semi-cylindrical in shaped and topped with semi-spheres, combining aesthetics with technical performance.  
They are composed of three main sections:  
– The small reservoir measures 17 m in diameter and is reinforced by 17 internal and 26 external buttresses. Its holding capacity is 4,000 cubic metres. It is a filtering basin which receives the untreated water and rids it of most of the debris that it carries before decanting it into the large reservoir.  
– The large reservoir is circular in shape, measures 128 m in diameter and is 4.8 m deep. Its holding capacity is 57,000 cubic metres. No less than 182 buttresses were needed (118 external and 64 internal) to contain the pressure and guarantee the viability of the project, which was to store enough water for the needs of daily life in the town. A squat poly-foil pillar rises up from its centre. Formerly surmounted by a dome, it was used as a leisure pavilion.  
The water travels from here into two parallel dispensing water-tanks set perpendicular to the reservoirs. They are covered with barrel vaults held up by arch-beams that rest on pillars. Six openings at the top of the vaults allow the water to be drawn.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.short_description: These hydraulic structures are the most famous in the Muslim world. They were among 15 pools outside the city walls that provided water to Kairouan. The imposing majesty of these installations earned Kairouan the epithet ‘city of water tanks’ in the Middle Ages. There are two semi-cylindrical pools supplied by an ingenious system for draining rainwater and the water from a nearby depression filled by tributaries of the *wadi* Merguelli.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.method_for_datation: Historical sources: Ibn Khaldoun, *Histoire des Berberes*.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.bibliography:
Lezine, A., *Architecture de l'Ifriqiya, recherches sur les monuments Aghlabides*, Paris, 1966.  
Maoudoud, K., *Kairouan*, Tunis, 2000, pp.37–9.  
Solignac,M.M., *“Les installations hydrauliques de Kairouan et des steppes tunisiennes du VIIIe au XIe siecle”*, t.X, Algiers, 1953, pp.187–92.  
*Ifriqiya: Thirteen centuries of Art and Architecture in Tunisia*, pp.162–3.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.history: The Aghlabid reservoirs, of which only two survive, were part of a group of about 15 reservoirs, located outside the city walls, which supplied the town with water. They are considered to be among the most important hydraulic works of the Muslim world. They provoked the admiration of travellers and led to the town being given the name 'city of the cisterns'. They were filled by draining rainwater as well as water from the tributaries of the *wadi* Merguelli, which flow in the surrounding lowlands. Its waters were harnessed by small dams and a conveyance canal which transported it to the small pool. In 350 (961), the Fatimid Caliph al-Mu'izz built an aqueduct that brought water from the Shreshira springs, located 40 km to the west of Kairouan.
611b1a5d-121e-5d2d-aabc-4a2151130229.author: Jamila Binous
keywords: Aghlabid; Umayyad; reservoirs; buttresses; filtering pools; aqueducts; hydraulic works; cisterns; leisure pavilion

6177d6e0-4105-5c92-a2c3-cf308dc051e6.name: "Alexander Fights a Sea Battle"
6177d6e0-4105-5c92-a2c3-cf308dc051e6.alternate_name: Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
6177d6e0-4105-5c92-a2c3-cf308dc051e6.description: In the episode illustrated, Alexander the Great has ordered the construction of a tall tower surmounted by a revolving mirror in order to battle the pirates menacing the Mediterranean Sea. The protagonists appear as contemporary Indians wearing turbans and tunics, rather than ancient Greeks, and one of the fighters uses a gun, an invention from nearly two millennia after Alexander’s time.

61c3680d-7e1f-5627-a43b-1ebb99008f0e.name: Folio with two miniatures from Persian translation of 'The Wonders of Creation and the Oddities of Existence' by Zakaria Qazwini
61c3680d-7e1f-5627-a43b-1ebb99008f0e.short_description: A folio from Persian translation of a popular cosmography treatise "The Wonders of Creation and the Oddities of Existence" by Zakaria bin Muhammad al-Qazwini. The book, written in AD 13th century, covers the fields of geography, astronomy, astrology and natural history, in a mixture of science and superstition. Both sides of the folio are embellished with miniatures featuring fruit-bearing trees.

628ff64b-bf4e-573e-86cb-55190cee5fba.name: Water women 1/5
628ff64b-bf4e-573e-86cb-55190cee5fba.description: The photograph, entitled *Water Women* (2016), is a striking work from the Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts that fuses portraiture, landscape and cultural symbolism into a multilayered visual narrative. By employing the technique of double exposure, the artist superimposes an image of a smiling woman carrying a water container on her head upon the typically rugged sandstone terrain and ancient steps that are characteristic of Petra. This merging of human and environment transforms the subject into a living embodiment of endurance and heritage, connecting the labour of daily survival with the monumental legacy of Jordan's desert civilisation. The photograph is indicative of themes of resilience, gender and ecology. The subject's countenance, characterised by a poised yet radiant expression, serves to create a pronounced visual contrast with the arid landscape, thereby underscoring the pivotal role women play in the sustenance of life in such inhospitable environments. The water jug positioned on her head functions as both a literal vessel of survival and a metaphorical burden, thereby echoing the carved steps and eroded stone, which are symbols of persistence and continuity through time. From a visual perspective, the warm ochres of the sandstone blend harmoniously with the cool tones of her embroidered clothing. This creates a dialogue between tradition and adaptation. The presence of an additional veiled woman, walking in the background and carrying bottled water, serves to anchor the image in contemporary realities of scarcity and modernity. Collectively, these elements form a layered composition that evokes a poetic meditation on the intersection of nature, culture and feminine strength. This work is situated within a broader discourse of Middle Eastern identity and environmental consciousness in modern photographic art.
628ff64b-bf4e-573e-86cb-55190cee5fba.holder: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts

62a33986-22ab-54e6-b59d-861e59b608f3.name: *Khabia*
62a33986-22ab-54e6-b59d-861e59b608f3.alternate_name: Water storage jar; Large earthenware jar; clay cistern jar
62a33986-22ab-54e6-b59d-861e59b608f3.description:
The *khabia* is a large earthenware jar traditionally used in Morocco for the storage and preservation of drinking water. Handcrafted by skilled potters from the Marrakech region, the *khabia* was an indispensable element of both domestic and communal life before the spread of modern water supply systems. Its substantial size, often exceeding two metres in height, allowed families, mosques, or fountains to store large quantities of water drawn from wells or *khettaras*.  
The process of making a *khabia* required specialised knowledge—shaping and assembling clay coils, smoothing the surface, and firing in traditional kilns — reflecting centuries of artisanal heritage. Beyond its utilitarian role, the khabia embodied the cultural significance of water conservation in Moroccan society.  
The *khabia* displayed at the Mohammed VI Museum of Water Civilisation offers insight into vernacular technologies of storage and sustainability, serving as a reminder of how communities safeguarded water in arid environments long before industrial systems.

62e625a3-a3f0-51a2-b3d3-9ee1fce45141.name: Süleymaniye Complex.
62e625a3-a3f0-51a2-b3d3-9ee1fce45141.description:
The Süleymaniye Mosque is considered a work of the architect, Sinan's, fellow-master or *kalfa* period, with the Selimiye Mosque representing the absolute pinnacle of his career in his master (*usta*) period. The mosque is part of a *külliye*\-type complex, where the mosque occupies the central position, occupying about 60,000 sq m in a district of Istanbul also known as Süleymaniye. The mosque is independent of the other buildings, standing within a courtyard measuring 216 m x 144 m. There is a graveyard adjoining the mosque to the south. The tombs of both Sultan Süleyman and his wife Hürrem Sultan are found in the graveyard, as well as a tomb-keeper's room. The other buildings of the complex are arranged around the mosque and graveyard on the east, west and north in a 'U' shape. To the north of the mosque are the guest rooms (*tabhane)*, the soup-kitchen (*imaret*) and hospital (*darüşşifa*); to the west are the primary school, medical school, the first and second *madrasa*s and the Tiryaki Market with its 36 shops; to the east are the third and fourth *madrasa*s; and to the southeast are the school of traditions of the Prophet (*darülhadis*) and the bathhouse (*hammam*). The modest baldachin tomb of the mosque's architect, Sinan is in the northeast corner of the complex.  
The Süleymaniye Mosque consists of a rectangular, nearly square prayer hall measuring 69 m x 63 m and a courtyard with porticoes. There is a rectangular pool in the middle of the courtyard. All the bays of the porticoes are domed. The building has four minarets, two on the northeast and northwest corners of the prayer hall and two on the northeast and northwest corners of the courtyard. The minarets rising from the prayer hall are 76 m high and have three balconies each, while those rising from the courtyard are 56 m high and have two balconies each. The prayer hall is covered by a central dome, 27.40 m in diameter, which is carried on four monumental piers, each measuring 6.20 m x 5.10 m and joined by pointed arches. The dome rises to 49.50 m off the ground. The rectangular spaces to the north and south of the central space are each covered by a half-dome; those on the east and west are covered by domes of different sizes. The monumental piers in the central space are joined to pointed arches which connect to monumental buttresses placed in the main walls. To break up any monotony the buttresses might create the east and west walls of the building are enlivened with porticoes and galleries.  
All the buildings of the complex are faced with fine cut stone. Elements such as the portal of the mosque, the *mihrab*, and the *minbar* are covered in marble.  
The most richly ornamented buildings in the Süleymaniye Complex are the tombs of Süleyman and Hürrem Sultan, which are decorated with tiles and painted (*kalemişi*) designs. The decoration of the mosque is fairly simple. The principal elements of decoration are the *kalemişi* designs of the domes in the prayer hall and courtyard, the inlaid designs of mother-of-pearl and ivory in the wooden shutters of the lower row of windows, and the stained-glass windows of the south wall which are original. In the 13th / 19th century the Fossati brothers added ornament in the style of the day over the painted decoration of the prayer hall; this was removed during the restorations 1961–7, and the original decoration was revealed. The other buildings of the complex are not decorated.  
The mosque continues to function as a place of worship to this day. The other buildings in the complex are used for a variety of purposes.
62e625a3-a3f0-51a2-b3d3-9ee1fce45141.short_description: The complex has many structures with various functions such as mosque, *madrasa*, *tabhane* (guest-rooms), *imaret* (soup-kitchen), hospital, children's school, mausolea, *darülhadis* (school of traditions of the Prophet), bathhouse and market. The great Ottoman architect Sinan, who built the complex, is buried here. The central mosque is considered to be a work of Sinan's *kalfa* (fellow-master or intermediate) period. It is covered with a dome 27.4 m in diameter rising 49.5 m above the ground and resting on four large piers. This central dome is flanked with a semi-dome on the south and north and five lesser domes each on the east and west.
62e625a3-a3f0-51a2-b3d3-9ee1fce45141.method_for_datation: An inscription in Arabic by the calligrapher Karahisari Ahmed Effendi on the north portal of the prayer hall states that the building's construction began in AH 957 / AD 1550 and was completed in 964 / 1557. The *Tezkiretü'l-Bünyan* (*Memorial of Buildings),* dictated by Sinan to his close friend Mustafa Sai çelebi, states more exactly that construction began on 27 Jumada I 957 / 13 June 1550 and finished on 21 Dhu'l-Hijja 964 / 15 October 1557. According to documents, the first and second *madrasa*s were completed in 960 / 1553, and the third and fourth in 966 / 1559. The tomb of Hürrem Sultan was built in 965 / 1558, that of Süleyman in 974 / 1567.

63941bb7-1c0a-5e01-8b06-e6ae1b313ece.name: Water bottle/jar
63941bb7-1c0a-5e01-8b06-e6ae1b313ece.description: A red pottery water jar used for filling and pouring water. It has a cylindrical body rounded at both ends, with a circular mouth at the centre flanked by two prominent handles, allowing it to be tied with ropes, hung, or carried easily - especially during travel. Due to the porous nature of pottery, the container also helped in cooling the water.

647040db-954c-553c-b7b9-c7c2901d4516.name: Album of calligraphies including poetry and prophetic traditions (*hadith*)
647040db-954c-553c-b7b9-c7c2901d4516.short_description: This album contains samples written by one of the most celebrated Turkish calligraphers, Shaikh Hamdullah (d. 1519), who developed the *naskhi* and *thuluth* styles from masters of the past to suit Ottoman taste. These pages, which show control, exactitude, and gentle flow, but also exaggeration of some letters to create a lively rhythmic pattern, demonstrate the calligrapher’s mature phase. The text comes from the hadith, the compilation of the Prophet Muhammad's words and deeds that is an important source for moral and legal guidance in the Islamic tradition. On each page, several lines of a small script (*naskhi*) are framed by one or two lines in a larger script (*thuluth* or *muhaqqaq*) and then pasted onto sheets of marbleized paper, which developed in Turkey and came to be much favored for calligraphic works.

64e3e4fa-1a13-5862-88d5-b4956e026fd7.short_description: A doughnut-shaped bottle made of bubbly translucent amethyst glass, blown with marvered opaque white trail decoration and dragged into a feather pattern. Opposing S-shaped handles applied in amethyst glass at shoulder and pulled up to neck. The globular form is flattened and tooled into an asymmetrical donut-shaped body. The thin elongated neck, tooled to constrict at its base and thus flattening the shoulder, is pulled up into a long tapering form with the rim rounded by heating. The base is flattened and kicked retaining a pontil mark; four small prunts of amethyst glass are applied on the sides as vestigial, but useless feet. There are losses in the neck and the body.

678d0b51-8dc7-59f3-818b-402d1bec24d6.name: *The Barrage or Nile dam*
678d0b51-8dc7-59f3-818b-402d1bec24d6.short_description: This picture, from the book *A Pilgrimage to Egypt: An Account of a Visit to Lower Egypt*, shows the Delta Barrage dam built by the French engineer Mougelle during the reign of Muhammad 'Ali Pasha to maintain the Nile water at a balanced level all the year. The barrage also served as a fortification against attack on Cairo or Upper Egypt. It consisted of a double bridge, the eastern part spanning the Damietta branch of the Nile, the western the Rosetta, with the head of the Delta between the two. The barrage had to be improved from 1883 by Sir Colin Scott Moncrief to solve structural problems with the foundations and the gates of the dam. The barrage and other dams testify to the importance of these structures to provide the water needed for irrigation in Egypt since antiquity.

68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.name: Pair of clogs
68860d9a-5a4b-577c-8584-cef6ff62671a.description:
The high heeled clogs (ar. *qabqab*, tr. *nalın* are an emblematic item of the hamam reflecting the atmosphere of such public baths. They were worn when entering the bath complex to protect the wearer from the dirty water as well as from the hot marble floor. Wearing these shoes meant that the wearer was obliged to walk slowly to avoid falling. This slower pace was in tune with the temporality dictated by the rhythms of the hamam and its cleansing rituals.  
  
This pair of clogs is attributed to Syria. They are made of wood inlaid with silver and multi-coloured triangular pieces of mother-of-pearl. The front and rear parts of the sole are incrusted with repoussé silver bands decorated with floral motifs encircled with two dotted lines. They are embellished with long silver chains ending in trinkets which must have created a gentle tinkling with each step highlighting the sound dimension of the hamam.  
  
The strap holding the foot is made of various layers of leather for comfort. It is topped with a large silver band intricately designed and solidly nailed to the sole.  
  
This pair of clogs is particularly high, suggesting that it might have been the property of the hamam owner who traditionally wore sophisticated clogs with heels higher than those of the clients. Often offered as part of the dowry of the bride in a toiletry trousseau providing her with all the hamam essentials, the clogs were a statement on the social status of their owner and could also bear many symbolic meanings through their decoration.  
  
Although strongly associated with femininity, hamam clogs, with lower heels and different ornamentation, were also worn by men in their own establishments.

695016ec-c554-5ddd-ae3f-8d50aadf22b4.name: *Guffa* coracle
695016ec-c554-5ddd-ae3f-8d50aadf22b4.description:
The *guffa* is the central Mesopotamian coracle, a round boat whose shell is a coil basket made of a single spiral bundle of grass wrapped with palm leaf. It is braced inside with pomegranate wands, then saturated inside and out with pitch. After drying completely under the sun, it is painted all over with a layer of tar, then coated with clay on the exterior to protect the tar from melting. The diameter of an Iraqi *guffa* ranges from around 1.6m (a standard-sized fishing *guffa*) up to 6m, with the larger versions used to transport cargo such as watermelons, bricks, and even livestock, and as ferries or passenger craft.  
  
Coracles are among the earliest recorded boat types in the world: the earliest known representation of one is a pottery model boat found in Lower Saxony, dating from 5500 BCE. The Babylonians described the Ark of the Flood as a *guffa* – suggesting these boats were already perceived as ancient. The *guffa* becomes visible in Mesopotamian art from Assyrian times, when reliefs of the 9th century BCE depicted them carrying chariots and other cargo. They were famously described in Herodotus’ “Histories” (450 BCE); other travellers to Mesopotamia have often mentioned them, as did Arab literature. *guffas* appeared in popular songs as a venue for secret lovers’ trysts. They also figure in the work of early Iraqi landscape painters (AH 13th-14th / AD 19th-20th century) such as Abdulqadir al Rassam.  
  
These examples were made in Sadat al-Hindiya, Hilla Governorate, Iraq, in AH 1441/ AD 2019, as part of a series of workshops organised by Safina Projects to reconstruct traditional fishing *guffas* in collaboration with local makers, supporting intergenerational transfer of this ancient and endangered craft skill. Before that date, production of traditional *Guffas* had diminished since at least the AH 1400s/ AD 1980s (although similarly shaped coracles were made using metal). The elderly woman who advised on the workshop was the last known maker in Sadat al-Hindiya and had ceased her craft after the AH 1424/ AD 2003 invasion.

69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.name: *Noah’s Ark*
69bdb01a-4161-5c8b-8079-4bbee1cbfb1d.short_description:
Timur’s son Shah Rukh (r. AH 808-851 / AD 1405-1447) ordered the historian Hafiz-i Abru to write a continuation of Rashid al-Din’s famous history of the world, Jami al-tawarikh. Like the Il-Khanids, the Timurids were concerned with legitimizing their right to rule, and Hafiz-i Abru’s “A Collection of Histories” covers a period that included the time of Shah Rukh himself.  
  
The style of the manuscript’s miniatures is slightly old-fashioned compared with the otherwise refined Timurid painting, but the scene on the stormy sea is quite dramatic, with the fluttering sail, the ark breaking out of the picture frame and the swollen bodies. The animals that are to populate the earth are rendered both humorously and fairly realistically.

6a7f88ad-e38f-5e65-b83b-d07699dcfcd7.name: *Zubdat al-Tawarikh* (‘Cream of Histories’)
6a7f88ad-e38f-5e65-b83b-d07699dcfcd7.short_description: Muslims consider the Qur’an the third and final portion of God’s revelation to mankind: it completes, but does not supplant, God’s earlier revelations to the Jews and Christians. The prophets of the Old and New Testaments are therefore also prophets in Islam. This manuscript is a history of the world beginning with Adam and ending with the Ottoman sultans of the sixteenth century. It includes depictions of various prophets common to all three religions (such as Abraham and Ishmael), as well as specifically Islamic prophets (such as Alexander and Khizr). The manuscript ends with a depiction of Sultan Murad III (r. AH 982–1003 / AD 1574–95), during whose reign the manuscript was produced. Each prophet or sultan is identified by an inscription.

6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.name: *Sabil* (Water Dispensary) and *Kuttab* (Qur’anic School) of ‘Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda.
6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.description:
This monument has a special artistic importance, for it is a free-standing complex that consists of a *sabil* (water dispensary) and a *kuttab* (Qur'an school) both of which display many of the glories of Islamic art specific to the Ottoman period. The building represents the style of *sabil* that has three windows and which is a blend of the Mamluk and Ottoman styles.  
The *sabil* has three facades (south, north and west) that are identical and equal in length. Each façade contains a semi-circular arch, which is supported by two spiral marble pillars. In the middle of the arch is a large opening from which cups of water may be obtained for passers-by (windows for the procurement of water or *tasbil*).  
The opening seen here sits within a semi-circular arch supported by two marble spiral pillars. The *tasbil* are covered with copper grills in the form of intersecting tri-lobed arches; these allow drinking-cups to be passed through them. The spandrels of the arches are decorated with splendid geometric designs executed in fine polychrome marble. The walls of the outer façade contain interlocked stone courses in the form of whirling vegetal leaves. The façade of the *sabil* is crowned with nine tiers of *muqarnas*, which bear the floor of the first storey containing the *kuttab*. The entrance to the *sabil* is located on Tambakshiyya Street, to the left of the southern façade, and resembles the Mamluk portal. The entrance is composed of a recessed wall crowned with a tri-lobed arch and a semi-dome decorated with tiers of *muqarnas*. In the middle of the recessed wall is the door to the *sabil* the straight, top lintel of which is adorned with carved verses of poetry. Above the lintel there is a marble decorative unit comprising a central circle. It contains the foundation text surrounded by four tiny circles.  
The entrance to the *sabil* leads to a small vestibule, which contains three doors: the first is located to the right of the entrance and leads to the cistern chamber; the second is to the left of the entrance and leads to the room from which the water is distributed *hograt al-tasbil* (water dispensing room), and the third is at the rear of the vestibule leading to the stairs and up to the *kuttab*. The floor-plan of the water-dispensing room is rectangular (3.50 m x 4.50 m). Three windows are located within the recessed areas of the room's three walls, which overlook the street. The walls of the room are panelled with blue-glazed ceramic tiles and decorated with a multiplicity of vegetal decoration. The southern wall contains a panel of glazed tiles depicting a view of the Holy Ka'aba and the buildings surrounding it.  
The *kuttab*, or school room, has a rectangular floor-plan of the same dimensions as the *hograt al-tasbil*. The *kuttab* overlooks the street from three directions by means of three *mashrabiyya*, and it has seven marble pillars, which resemble the pillars on the façade. The pillars are topped by six stone pointed arches, crowned with an inclined wooden awning. A balcony projects from the *kuttab,* characterised by 14 exquisite slim wooden pillars which bear 15 arches supported by balustrades, made from beautiful turned wood. The balcony is roofed with a wooden awning that is lower than the first.
6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.short_description: This building has special artistic importance as a freestanding establishment in the heart of al-Muizz Street. It consists of a *sabil* (water dispensary) with three façades and three windows covered with iron grills for distributing free drinking water to the local population, passers-by and travellers. The second floor is occupied by a *kuttab* (Qur'anic school for children) with a balcony overlooking three sides through *mashrabiyya* screens. The Mamluk and Ottoman styles blend harmoniously in the construction of this monument.
6a900d8a-d3e6-5851-b145-8c3ebfc27556.method_for_datation: The building was dated based on an inscription above the entrance that includes the name of the sponsor and the date of construction. Furthermore, a *waqf* deed is preserved in the archives of the Ministry of Awqaf or Endowments (file no. 941, dated 1158 \[1745\]), it also gives the name of the builder.

6af5bf51-a5aa-558d-8578-3ac815792a90.name: *Zaima* reed boat
6af5bf51-a5aa-558d-8578-3ac815792a90.description:
The *zaima* is a small reed canoe from the Marshlands of southern Iraq, made of reed bundles of narrow diameter sewn together to form a flat base and sides. Its internal bracing may be made from flexible stems such as cane, palm frond, date bunch stalk (forming the prow), or small branches of trees such as willow, acacia or *gherib*, and it is waterproofed with an outer coating of bitumen. Evidence of these boats' existence in recent decades is sparse, but reports from earlier centuries suggest they were once much more common. Travellers to Mesopotamia in the AH 12th / AD 18th and AH 13th / AD 19th centuries reported that the Marshes were full of canoes made from reeds and cane, tarred on the outside.  
  
During the AH 14th / AD 20th century, especially in the 1970s when the extent of the Marshes and the density of boat traffic reached a peak, the majority of canoes (*meshoufs*) were made of planked wood joined with nails. Images and accounts of reed or cane canoes in this period are exceptional. The only known photographs identified as a *zaima* were taken by the British explorer Wilfred Thesiger in the AH 1370s / AD 1950s. Rashad Salim, during his fieldwork in AH 1438-1441/ AD 2016-19, gathered a handful of oral accounts of reed and cane boats, some known as *zaimas* and some with other names. These were among the simplest and cheapest types of boat made locally by Marsh dwellers.  
  
The boatbuilding community of Huwair, where Safina Projects’ Meshouf-building workshops were held, had no direct experience of constructing *zaimas*, but they agreed to attempt to reconstruct reed and cane canoes, drawing on their familiarity with these widely available local materials (also used in vernacular architecture). They also applied knowledge Rashad Salim had collected in the form of oral history interviews – recorded in both Huwair and Amara – and the photographs and writings of Thesiger. The *zaimas* in the collection of the Open Museum are the result of these experimental workshops.

6c54efb2-f695-580b-805f-f38df23ae55f.name: Hand basin
6c54efb2-f695-580b-805f-f38df23ae55f.description:
It was a widespread custom in the Islamic world to wash one’s hands before entering a house, and basins like this one were used before meals as well. The lid is perforated so that the sight of dirty water did not bother the guests. An equally richly decorated ewer once made up a set with the basin.  
  
The embossed silver basin has elegantly conceived and deeply engraved decorations featuring gazelles, flowers and other ornamentation filled out with transparent enamel. There are less costly basins with simpler decoration of the same type made of bronze and bidri metal.

6ce9b353-6fa5-545f-8dcd-8780df1109a4.description: This scythe-like agricultural hand tool is traditionally used for cutting weeds in cultivated fields. It also finds use as a reaping tool for crops and animal fodder. The hand-forged steel blade of the cutter is angled for maximum efficiency and attached to a handle made of fig, jujube or lime wood.

6f53c50b-23a7-5c94-9dc1-8ba00ad40bc2.name: Mulay Isma‘il Mausoleum.
6f53c50b-23a7-5c94-9dc1-8ba00ad40bc2.description:
Built near to the tomb of the saint Sidi 'Abd Al-Rahman al-Majdub, a famous AH 10th / AD 16th century poet and mystic, the mausoleum houses the tomb of Mulay Isma'il. This royal funerary complex, located away from the palace, attracts visitors with its majesty and rich decoration, and is divided into three main sections.  
The first section, which includes the entrance to the mausoleum, consists of a vast entrance hall and annexes.  
The hall is square plan with sides measuring 9.88 m. The walls are covered with *zellij* (small tile) decoration to a height of 1.60 m, on top of which there is an anepigraphic sculpted plasterwork band. In the middle of the hall, a fountain overflows into an octagonal basin. A door gives access to latrines located around a pool.  
The second section is made up of three very large trapezoid courtyards. The very high walls (9 m) of the first courtyard are decorated with *zellij* up to a height of 0.56 m. The floor of the second, plain courtyard is tiled with monotone *zellij* that extend up the walls to what height of 0.56 m. The third courtyard is noteworthy for its two porticoes that face one another on the east and west sides. The centre of the courtyard is embellished with a deep round pool. A *mihrab* has been built into the wall of the east portico and a minaret stands in the south-west corner of the courtyard.  
The third section consists of the funerary halls and a courtyard. The large open-air trapezoid hall located on the south side contains two *qubba*. To the northeast of the complex there is a square courtyard surrounded on all four sides by porticoes 1.87 m deep and groups of three marble columns crowned with various types of capitals. The capitals that have a cylindrical part with a double row of leaves next to a heavy prismatic part extensively decorated with palms and palmettes, engraved rather than sculpted, can be classified as Hispano-Maghrebian.  
A marble pool occupies the centre of the courtyard, which leads to three funerary rooms of different sizes: a sort of oblong antechamber, richly decorated with bronze lustre, and main square room containing the tomb of the Sultan Mulay Isma'il and finally an oblong room containing the book cabinets.  
Its majesty makes the mausoleum a continuous reminder of the era of Sultan Mulay Isma'il.
6f53c50b-23a7-5c94-9dc1-8ba00ad40bc2.short_description:
The mausoleum, a veritable royal funerary complex to the south of Mulay Isma'il's palace, was built near to the burial site of the saint Sidi 'Abd al-Rahman al-Majdub, a mystic of the AH 10th / AD 16th century.  
Restored by Sultan Mulay Isma'il's successors, the building has a complex layout of Hispano-Maghrebi influence, complete with *zellij* (small tile) and stucco decoration, in which the structural elements are arranged in a row, similar to three rooms of the Rauda at the Alhambra in Granada, Spain.  
The sultan's tomb is at the centre of the complex. A *mihrab* linked to the courtyard and burial rooms was constructed for prayers.
