7045f484-1e6a-55ad-9fd3-497bdc3dd415.name: *Meshouf* (canoe collection)
7045f484-1e6a-55ad-9fd3-497bdc3dd415.description:
The Open Museum for Water Cultures (Basra) holds in its collection 11 *meshoufs* of various types and sizes. *Meshouf* is a generic term for a flat-based canoe made in the region of Iraq's southern marshlands. *meshoufs* range from 3-11m in length and have a narrow form, often with a distinctive crescent-shaped prow.  
  
Variants range from small flat-prowed canoes like the *matour* (a one-man canoe used for hunting waterfowl), to larger types with a prominent curved prow such as the *chilaika*, the prestigious *tarada* (hunting and war canoe of the Marsh Sheikhs), and working vessels like the *barkash*, used for harvesting and transport.  
  
*Meshoufs* became almost extinct from the Iran-Iraq war (1980s) onwards. In Huwair, once a well-known centre for their making, modernised boatbuilding methods and carpentry remained common forms of livelihood. *Meshouf* production was revived with the support of the Safina Projects initiative from AH 1440 / AD 2018 onwards. In addition to the Open Museum’s collection, by AH 1447/ AD 2025 over 70 *meshoufs* were in use across the Iraqi Heritage Boat Clubs Network established by Safina.  
  
Boats of a comparable form have been recorded since the Sumerian period (from around 2500 BC), although in the modern-day *meshouf* the prow is typically much taller than the stern, whereas in the Sumerian version prow and stern are of equal height.  
  
Rashad Salim’s research with Safina Projects has concluded that the AH 14th/ AD 20th century *meshouf* was strongly influenced by the availability of industrially manufactured nails and tools and imported wood. In the pre-industrial period, wood was scarcer, and many marsh dwellers made *meshoufs* from reeds.  
  
The extended family who built the *meshoufs* in this collection are among the most renowned boatbuilders of Huwair. They are part of the Beni Asad tribe, who came to the marshes 300-400 years ago from Arabia, learned boatbuilding methods from the Mandaean-Sabean population, and gradually took over as the main practitioners of the craft.

707e3119-1895-51ef-95aa-cf18a89fd850.name: Ewer
707e3119-1895-51ef-95aa-cf18a89fd850.description: A narrow-necked body rises to a considerably wider main body, with a total of eleven projections of varying sizes extending outward from its upper surface. The handle is riveted at one end to the center of the body and at its two other ends to either side of the mouth; a clasp at the top of the handle secures the lid. The handle is decorated with cross motifs. The spout, designed for pouring, is beak-shaped, open at the top and adorned with floral motifs. The lid begins broadly and tapers into a minaret-shaped neck. Both the top surface of the lid and the base feature four rounded, outward-pointing reliefs. The ewer is in good condition and retains a brown colour.

70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.name: Abu Yahya Zakariyya' ibn Muhammad al-Qazwini, *'Aga'ib al-makhluqat wa-ghara'ib al-maujudat* ('The Wonders of Creation and the Marvels of Creation')
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.short_description: Abu Zakariyya' ibn Muhammad al-Qazwini (600-682 AH / 1203-1283 AD) wrote the famous treatise ‘The Wonders of Creatures and the Marvels of Creation’ (*'Aja'ib al-Makhluqat wa Ghara'ib al-Mawjudat*). According to the colophon, this copy was written in 1174 AH / 1761 AD by al- Hajji 'Ali, one of the freedmen of 'Abdalhaiy Auda Pasha and likely created in Ottoman-dynasty Cairo, Egypt. As the owners’ stamp indicates, the manuscript later belonged to Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall, and was acquired by the Austrian National Library in 1842. In the early 19th century, the manuscript and binding were probably supplemented and restored, yet their original look has been preserved. Its contemporaneous leather binding exhibits Ottoman-style decoration, while its 455 paintings of various sizes and shapes seen throughout the manuscript. They seem to have been created to mimic medieval models of painting, which were not fully understood, or perhaps just poorly preserved. Interestingly, the images are in stark contrast with the neat Egyptian writing style in *naskh* script. The flat painting style throughout includes raw outlines and bright colours, all of which give the paintings a dramatic and, at times, comic expression that may be comparable to later Coptic painting.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.method_for_provenance: On fol. 312b, an owner's stamp by Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall dated to 1223 AH / 1808 AD is visible.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.obtention: Acquired  in 1842 from Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.bibliography: Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften II. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 5, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1992: 111-116.
70d82e89-b0df-5268-a49f-ceb3a92a2ba4.binding_desc: The brown leather binding features gilt inlays of thin light-brown leather, which are stamped with floral motifs in the Ottoman style. The binding consists of a flap that has a recessed pointed medallion with pendants at its centre. Hand-painted cord or interlace motifs are visible on the overall frame, and immediately inside this frame are small, stamped floral details. The binding was likely produced in 18th-century Cairo, Egypt.

materials: Ink, opaque watercolour and gold on paper. Calligraphic *naskh* script of 23 lines per page.

718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.name: Page from a Qur’an.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.description: Al-Takathur *sura* ('The Rivalry', 102: 8) and al-Asr *sura* ('The Time', 103: 1). This page is taken from a Qur'an written in black *kufic* script. The vowels are marked with red diacritic dots and the *hamza* and *shadda* are indicated by green and yellow marks in the style of Abi al-Aswad, the Arab grammarian (d. AH 61 / AD 681). The verses are divided by a gilded green-centred rosette outlined in brown dots. The magnificent title of the *sura* is contained within an ornamental line of *kufic,* terminating in a palm-leaf motif which projects into the margin of the page. This palm-leaf is composed of stylised, gilded leaves and floral arabesques and is illuminated in blue and green with delicate touches of brown. These motifs are part of the decorative repertoire of Muslim illuminators and calligraphers from the AH 5th / AD 11th century.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.short_description: Written in black *kufic* script, this page contains two Qur'anic quotations (102: 8 and 103: 1). The division of verses is marked by a gold rosette with a green centre. All of the motifs belong to the decorative repertoire of Muslim illuminators and calligraphers after the AH 5th / AD 11th century.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.dates: Hegira, beginning of the second quarter of the 5th century / AD 9th century.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.method_for_datation: The Qur'an was given as a legacy (*habus*) by the Zirid prince, al-Mu'izz ibn Badis to the Great Mosque of Kairouan. The deed of gift dates from later than the break with Cairo, since it mentions the hatred of the prince for the Fatimids. According to historians this split began in 424 / 1033 and came to an end by 441 / 1050.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.method_for_provenance: This Qur'an was left to the Great Mosque by the reigning Zirid prince. Given that Kairouan was at that time a great centre of book production, it is highly likely that this example was copied and bound at Kairouan on locally tanned parchment.
718874e8-d67c-57c0-aabc-505af50ed024.obtention: This Qur'an was obtained by the National Library in 1967 after the abolition of the *habus* foundation in Tunisia, and was transferred in 1983 to the Centre of Islamic Art and Civilisation at Raqqada. It has been displayed in the Museum of Islamic Art at Raqqada since 1986.

71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.name: "How Rustam Found a Spring"
71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.alternate_name: Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi
71b58e2a-590f-5062-b329-444a2fef694c.description: The two miniatures 69.74.8 and 69.74.9 illustrate the first and second of Rustam's seven ordeals. The first depicts the frequently illustrated scene of Rustam's gallant horse Rakhsh killing a lion while the hero sleeps. The subject of the second miniature is, on the other hand, rarely depicted. Rustam and Rakhsh nearly die of heat and thirst in the desert before, with the help of divine providence, they find a spring. Rustam bathes and grooms his faithful steed by the water's edge, as seen here. The painter is very sympathetic to the closeness between the hero and his trustworthy Rakhsh.

72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.name: Plate and ablution ewer
72d97a33-faa9-5945-a6f9-e8d7c8992dc4.description:
The porcelain plate depicts a ritual washing ceremony, in which a servant pours water from an ewer for ablution. This scene illustrates the importance of cleanliness and ritual purity in Ottoman daily and religious life. The accompanying basin and ewer set, produced in the Süleymaniye workshop tradition, reflects the same function represented in the image. Such basin–ewer sets were commonly used indoors for ablution (*wudu*), particularly before prayer, as well as for washing hands after meals.  
  
Beyond their practical purpose, these objects held symbolic meaning, emphasising purity, hospitality and respect for religious practice. Through both the visual narrative on the porcelain plate and the physical form of the basin and ewer, the work highlights the central role of water in Ottoman ceremonial, domestic and spiritual culture.

74a255de-faae-533b-ad80-5e73500284f7.name: *The Perfect Pearls*
74a255de-faae-533b-ad80-5e73500284f7.description: Riki Salam’s *The Perfect Pearls* is a tribute to family, ancestry and cultural continuity. Dedicated by the artist to “those who came before us,” the work draws inspiration from his Uncle Seaman Dans’ song "Perfect Pearl". At its centre is Salam’s great-grandfather, Hardie Salaam Snr., depicted as a deep-sea diver. Born in Malaysia, Hardie migrated to Australia to work on a pearl lugger in the Torres Straits, embedding his story within the broader history of migration and maritime labour. Within the pearl shell are portraits of Salam’s grandparents, Hardie Salaam Jnr. and Maude Louise Savage, accompanied symbolically by their seven children, who are represented as pearls. The branching black coral evokes the artist’s immediate and extended family tree, which stretches from Mossman, on Kuku Yalanji Country, across Cape York, the Torres Straits and into the Northern Territory and Broome. The crayfish point to contemporary Torres Strait commerce, while the trochus shells and sea cucumber reference the historic trade networks linking Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples with the Makassans.

74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.name: Muhammad Jandarajizada (?), *Muraqqa'* (Album)
74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.short_description: This *muraqqa‘* (album) was compiled for the Ottoman Sultan Murad III (reigned 1574-1595) in Istanbul in 980 AH/1572-73 AD. The term *muraqqa’* (‘patched garment’) refers to the patchwork character of the collection of calligraphy, drawing, and painting in codex-format, which was significant for Safavid and Ottoman cultures as a means of collecting and displaying artworks. Likely created according to a systematic and aesthetic process of selecting materials, the specimens of this album were arranged in a particular order. It includes 18 ornamental pen-and-ink drawings, eight figural pen-and-ink drawings, 16 paintings, eight figural lacquer paintings, eleven pages with paper cutting, and 54 pages with calligraphy as the main motif. These specimens are mounted within perforated boards of variously decorated frames. The introduction to the album names a certain Muhammad Jandarajizada as its artistic compiler, while the scribe’s name is Haidar al-Husaini. The dedication to Sultan Murad III can be found on fol. 2b, and it appears that it was gifted to him at least two years after its completion. A red lacquer seal of Franz von Ottenfels-Gschind, the Austrian *internuntius* in Constantinople, on fol. 1a reveals the person who brought the album to Austria as a diplomatic gift for the Austrian emperor, after which it became part of the Austrian National Library in 1833-34.
74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.method_for_provenance: On fol. 2b, dedication to the reigning Sultan Murad Khan ibn Sultan Selim Khan. On fol. 48b, a cut-out and affixed owner's stamp of a so-called Mustafa as-Selaniki with the date 978 AH / 1570-71 AD. On Fol. 1a,  red lacquer seal of Baron Franz von Ottenfels-Gschind incnluding the name Ottenfels and an Arabic motto in Arabic script.
74c8d2f0-d499-5753-a385-cea7dbf6cb7a.obtention: Baron Franz von Ottenfels-Gschind, Austrian Internuntius at Constantinople, donated the album to the Austrian National Library in 1833/34.

75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.name: Two glasses
75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.description:
The Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade houses highly significant utilitarian glass objects that reflect the courtly culture of the Obrenović dynasty. These objects are not only testaments to a bygone era, but they also reflect the aesthetic sensibilities of the ruling dynasty, as well as their cultural refinement and enlightenment. The royal family paid special attention to the culture of dining, salons, and dining rooms. In this context, a need arose for acquiring certain exclusive glassware sets, including those intended for private ceremonies, which were imported from abroad and ordered according to specific typologies.  
The Obrenović dynasty ruled Serbia from 1815 to 1842, and again from 1858 to 1903. Its progenitor was Miloš Obrenović (1783–1860), also known as Miloš the Great, leader of the Second Serbian Uprising against the Ottoman Empire and Prince of Serbia twice, from 1815 to 1839, and from 1858 to 1860. During the rule of Prince Miloš Obrenović, in 1830, Sultan Mahmud II issued a hatt-i-sharif granting Serbia the status of an autonomous principality, while Serbia’s full independence was confirmed at the Congress of Berlin, in 1878, during the rule of Prince (later King) Milan Obrenović (1854–1901).  
Among the Obrenović dynasty-related objects from the collection of the Museum of Applied Art is a pair of water glasses, skilfully decorated with an engraved royal cypher of King Alexander Obrenović (1876–1903). Made using the glass casting technique, the glasses have exceptionally thin walls and a characteristically flat base. In their central section, the initial letter "A", topped with a royal crown, is lavishly engraved. The glasses were acquired by the Museum of Applied Art in 2008. They were originally owned by the Kozinc family from Slovenia, and later became part of the Višnjić family collection in Belgrade.  
King Alexander Obrenović was the last ruler of the Obrenović dynasty. Together with his consort, Queen Draga, he was assassinated in Belgrade, in the May Coup, on the night of 10–11 June \[O.S. 28–29 May\] 1903, which resulted in the dynasty’s extinction.
75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analisys with related material.

75271db6-a634-5c80-87e5-b32e543ed713.author: Jelena Vukadinović, Draginja Maskareli
keywords: tableware, glass, Serbia, the Obrenović dynasty.

76bd886e-d945-5f5e-b0b1-071c229a6721.name: "The Castle Water Clock" from al-Jazari's "Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices"
76bd886e-d945-5f5e-b0b1-071c229a6721.description:
In the early AH 8th / AD 13th-century, a scholar and engineer named Isma‘il Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari wrote a famous treatise called *Kitab fi ma‛rifat al-hiyal al-handasiyya*, or The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices. The text offered detailed descriptions of a series of elaborate machines designed to delight and impress the elites at the court where he served, in eastern Anatolia. Al-Jazari’s text and its illustrations belong to a long tradition of studies about these kinds of devices, including Greek compendia on mechanics and mathematics. This page belongs to a copy of the text that was produced in Mamluk Egypt in AH 755 / AD 1354, and was copied by Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Izmiri for a Mamluk ruler.  
  
This folio illustrates elaborate hydraulic clock in the form of a palace gateway.
76bd886e-d945-5f5e-b0b1-071c229a6721.obtention: By 1912, Victor Goloubew (b. 1879 - d. 1945), Paris; 1914, sold by Goloubew through M. Meyer-Riefstahl to the MFA.
materials: Ink, watercolour and gold on paper

781670ca-b4db-57b9-b537-ff501442790e.name: Dar Ibn ‘Abd Allah.
781670ca-b4db-57b9-b537-ff501442790e.description:
The different sections of the Dar Ibn 'Abd Allah Palace stand on either side of a small square, which used to be a private passageway protected by doors.  
The grand entrance is a large studded door set in a surround of richly-sculpted pink stone. The first hallway contains benches set under walls which are covered with Quallaline ceramic panels. The vault is lined with sculpted plaster. The courtyard is protected by two further off-set hallways.  
The courtyard is surrounded on four sides by porticoes, both on the ground floor and on the first floor. The lightly fluted columns with neo-Corinthian capitals are of Carrara marble from Italy, as are the door and window frames, the paving and the fountain with its three basins.  
Under the galleries, the facades are identical. In a wall panelled with green and yellow ceramic tiles, there are two windows on either side of a central door with a salient surrounding frame. The upper portion consists of a wide strip of carved stucco representing vases of foliate scrolls on a smooth background. The apartments on both floors are in the classic 'T' formation. They consist of a sunken central floor, opposite the entrance, furnished as a salon with three benches. This area is flanked by two small bedrooms. There are two lateral alcoves containing beds with wooden canopies.  
Among the richest elements of this palace are the wooden shelf panelling, the canopies and the ceilings, which combine the geometric decoration typical of al-Andalus with Turkish floral ornamentation. The panelled doors are carved in the Italian style.  
The service areas are arranged around a small courtyard which has a door leading to the main courtyard and an entrance opening direct from the street. The storehouses, the stables and the gardens are on the other side of the small square.
781670ca-b4db-57b9-b537-ff501442790e.short_description: This palace was named after one of its former owners, the wealthy silk-weaver Mohamed Talar bin Abd Allah. Extensively refitted and extended during the 19th century, the palace reveals Italian influences in its columns, capitals, door and window frames, and the marble fountain in the centre of the courtyard. Dar Bin 'Abd Allah has been the home of the Museum of Popular Art and Tradition since 1978, holding some of Tunis’s extensive museum collections, including clothes, jewellery, bathroom and kitchen utensils, and weapons.
781670ca-b4db-57b9-b537-ff501442790e.method_for_datation: Deeds quoted by Revault, *Palais et demeures de Tunis*.
781670ca-b4db-57b9-b537-ff501442790e.bibliography:
Binous, J., *Maisons de la Medina de Tunis*, 2001, pp.108–13.  
Revault, *Palais et demeures de Tunis (XVIIe et XIXe siecles)*, CNRS, Paris, 1971, p. 99.  
*Ifriqiya: Thirteen centuries of Art and Architecture in Tunisia*, pp.84–6.
781670ca-b4db-57b9-b537-ff501442790e.history: We have known the history of this palace since 1796, from the deeds which quote Hadj Muhammad al-Kossentini as owner of the premises. In 1801, Sliman al-Hanafi took possession of them. He was promoted from high military functionary to commander of the army on marrying the daughter of the *bey.* The palace benefited from extensive improvements and refurbishments. In 1875 Tahar ibn 'Abd Allah, a silk weaver and landowner, acquired the palace and gave it his name. In 1905, a French Orientalist painter by the name of Albert Aublet bought the palace and occupied it until 1941. At that date, the Directorate of Fine Arts and Public Instruction installed the Office of Tunisian Art there. After Tunisian independence, the Minister of Cultural Affairs converted the premises into the Centre of Popular Arts and Traditions on the first floor and into the Tunis Regional Museum (Tunisian life in the 19th century) on the ground floor.
781670ca-b4db-57b9-b537-ff501442790e.author: Jamila Binous
keywords: Palace architecture; ceramics; painted wood; Italian marble; Andalusian decoration; Italian decoration; Turkish decoration

79528dd8-b305-5d0a-99c2-94a3c8d75553.name: Clogs
79528dd8-b305-5d0a-99c2-94a3c8d75553.description: *Nanule* (Tr. *nalın*) – clogs from the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade (a.n. TC-283 (1942)), are made of wood. They have a slightly flared front wedge and a concave back wedge. The toe of the sole is square, and the heel is round. The sole is decorated with intarsia of leaf-shaped medallions with carved vegetal motifs, while along the edges runs a frame of inlaid mother-of-pearl rhombi. The wedges are adorned with carved geometrical motifs. The leather straps that hold the clog on the foot are plain. The clogs were used in the hamam, and belong to the shared dress and living culture of the urban population in the Ottoman Balkans, which had diverse confessional and ethnic backgrounds.
79528dd8-b305-5d0a-99c2-94a3c8d75553.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analisys with related material.

79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.name: Wash basin and jug.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.description:
The jug and basin were used at court on dining tables for the washing of hands. Medieval Arabic sources include descriptions of this sort of utensil. The daughters of amirs, viziers, high-ranking noblemen, officials and merchants all had this hand-washing equipment as part of their trousseau. Judging by the iconographic motifs of its decoration, the Berlin jug and basin look as if they were made for a lawyer. The inscriptions include blessings of a general nature (well-being, wealth, health, knowledge and leniency) for the unknown owner. Its original magnificence is clearly visible, as it has been excellently preserved.  
Judging by its shape, with its flap lid and straight spout, the jug has been made as a sculpted three-dimensional form. Its body, shoulder and neck are decorated with three friezes featuring figurative motifs within medallions of different sizes. The medallions are filled with depictions of thrones and riders and images of planets. The base of the neck shows 11 arched fields with standing figures in the style of Christian representations. A unicorn is being hunted in the animal frieze on the jug’s shoulder. There are additional Arabic well-wishing inscriptions within the friezes or spread over the jug.  
In the bottom of the basin, six planets are drawn encircling the sun, and in a second frieze, the signs of the Zodiac are depicted in relationship to particular planets. As on the jug, the outer surface of the basin is decorated with six large medallions that depict a prince flanked by two bodyguards, scenes of hunting and revelry. They are linked together by an inscription wishing for strength and victory, knowledge and leniency, qualities belonging to Allah.  
The complexity of the design and the highest quality of craftsmanship substantiate the high status of the person who commissioned its making. The jug and the basin are even signed with the name of the craftsman, which demonstrates that the artist was also held in very high regard.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.short_description: The extremely fine design and workmanship of this basin and jug demonstrate the skill of the metal craftsmen working in Mosul around 1270. Commissioned by someone of high rank and depicting the planets and scenes of courtly life, the set may have been used for washing hands on special occasions.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.dates: Hegira second half of 7th century / AD second half of 13th century.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.dimensions: Jug: height 37 cm, diameter 20.6 cm; basin: height 17 cm, diameter 43 cm.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.method_for_datation: The artist, ‘Ali ibn ‘Abdallah al-‘Alawi, who signed both the jug and the basin, lived during the mid-7th / mid-13th century.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.method_for_provenance: The artist, who signed both the jug and the basin, includes in the inscription of his name an indication of his town of origin: al-Mawsili, ‘from Mosul’, signifying where he was born or where he worked. The signature and the motif of the figure with a crescent in front of its body suggest that it is very probable that this piece originates from Mosul.
79968466-a94b-5053-a5e9-1155df32e285.obtention: From a private art gallery in 1938.

7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.name: Qarawiyyin Mosque.
7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.description:
A simple oratory of about 100 m2, the original mosque was made up of four naves parallel to the *qibla* wall, a courtyard, a *mihrab* and a minaret.  
In the AH 5th / AD 11th century, the Almoravids enlarged and enriched it with elements borrowed from Andalusian ornamental style fashionable at that time: plasterwork sculpture, *muqarnas* (stalactite) domes, sculpted marble capitals, epigraphic and geometrical floral motifs, etc. The *mihrab* dates from this time, as do the earlier domes. The mosque is embellished with *kufic* inscriptions and floral compositions that are reminiscent of Islamic art in Spain.  
During the Almohad era, AH 6th–7th / AD 12th–13th centuries, the Qarawiyyin was again endowed with new ornaments and practical additions such as the latrines in the north of the building and an underground warehouse on the northeast side used to store oil, mats and other material from the mosque. To bolster the monument's existing hydraulic infrastructure, a pool was constructed and water was channelled from one of the wells of the *medina* ('Ayn Farmal). Lighting was provided by a large chandelier in the ribbed dome of the axial nave and by bells along the central aisle that were imported from al-Andalus and transformed into chandeliers.  
The Mosque reached its heyday during the Marinid era (AH 7th–9th / AD 13th–15th centuries) with its 270 pillars forming 16 naves of 21 arches each, 15 large doors reserved for men and 2 small doors for women. With its 509 lamps, the large central chandelier weighed 1,763 pounds. The building could accommodate 22,700 people in its halls.  
Unlike most mosques in the Muslim west, the naves of the Qarawiyyin are not perpendicular but parallel to the *qibla* wall, which suggests an oriental influence (probably the Great Mosque of Damascus).  
The minaret, which is as old as the original mosque, was built in freestone and subsequently covered with plaster and carefully polished whitewash.  
The Sa'dids (AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries) took inspiration from the Alhambra in Granada for the two magnificent pavilions of the *sahn* (courtyard), which is evident in their layout as well as their decoration and architectural elements.  
The 'Alawids were responsible for restoring the chandeliers, the walls and pillars.  
The Qarawiyyin was also a real university, playing a major role in the diffusion of knowledge and the training of the intellectual elite. The Marinids provided two libraries and organised the institution and the teaching programmes, with 140 teaching posts throughout the establishment and the *madrasa*.
7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.short_description: It was in the AH 8th / AD 14th century that the simple oratory founded in the AH 3rd / AD 9th century by Fatima al-Fihriya in Fez old town, having become a Friday mosque, reached its apogee with its 270 pillars, 17 large gateways, a library and enough space for 22,700 worshipers. A university of great prestige and an important spiritual centre, Islam's most celebrated scholars came from Córdoba and Damascus to study or to teach at one of the Qarawiyyin's 140 chairs, located throughout the establishment or in the town's different *madrasas* and mosques.
7ac3ea27-a8cb-553d-b1c3-19067190a3c3.method_for_datation: Written sources such as the *Rawd al Qirtass* (The Mausoleum of Writing) by Ibn Abi Zara al-Fassi and the *Jana Zahrat al-Aas* (Myrtle Flower) by al-Jaznaï enable us to date the foundation and extensions (see Bibliography).

7b607aac-e5db-517f-aaf5-04ce4eb5e62c.name: *Project for a Garden or Park*
7b607aac-e5db-517f-aaf5-04ce4eb5e62c.short_description: This project for a park with fountain, covered, possibly, with tiles decorated in Neo-Mudéjar style. The development of urban design was an important subject from the mid-19th century onwards. The Neo-Mudéjar style was selected by the architects for important buildings such as theatres or bull rings or urban spaces as the International exhibition of Barcelona 1888. One of the characteristics of this style is use of brick and tile decoration in the buildings’ interiors and façades.

7bd0767f-b448-56ce-8a8e-6180b326ce87.name: "Alexander is Lowered into the Sea"
7bd0767f-b448-56ce-8a8e-6180b326ce87.alternate_name: Folio from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Amir Khusrau Dihlavi
7bd0767f-b448-56ce-8a8e-6180b326ce87.description: The Khamsa of the Indian poet Amir Khusrau includes a section on the philosopher-king Alexander the Great, who in Khusrau’s telling of his life led expeditions to China, Russia, and the Western Isles. In this copy of the Khamsa made for the Mughal emperor Akbar (r. 1556–1605), Alexander is shown being lowered into the sea in a glass diving bell. While underwater, he will receive a visit from an angel who foretells his death.
7bd0767f-b448-56ce-8a8e-6180b326ce87.obtention: Gift from Alexander Smith Cochran in 1913

7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.name: *Tabica* (small board).
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.description:
The splendid collar-beam framework of Teruel Cathedral, which has been erroneously described as a coffered ceiling, is one of the examples of Mudéjar carpentry most studied by art critics for several reasons, including its extraordinary iconographic and iconological complexity and its significance in the social context, and the interest generated by its style and dating, which has been helped by analysis of the wood. Among other items, the National Archaeological Museum holds two *tabicas* (small wooden boards) from the gables or planking, one of which shows a male figure and the other, the one examined here, a female figure.  
The woman is from the working class, a water bearer dressed in a long-sleeved, corded tunic or dress tied at the waist. The decorative horizontal lines give her a characteristic air. Her hair is short and her head appears to be uncovered, uncommon in figures on ceilings. She is carrying a two-handled jar. The flat colours are dominated by reds, whites and black outlines.  
It is possible to determine the *tabica*'s original position in the eighth section on the left, in the very place where a bomb fell during the war in 1936
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.short_description: This *tabica* (small wooden board) decorated the planks in the roof of Teruel Cathedral, showing the different classes of Mediaeval society. The figure is a water bearer dressed in contemporary costume: a long-sleeved dress tied around the waist.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.dimensions: Height 36 cm, width 23.8 cm, depth 1.7 cm.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.method_for_datation: From its style and from dendrochronological analysis of the wood.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.method_for_provenance: When giving this and three other pieces to the National Archaeological Museum, the donor, Pablo Gil y Gil, a professor at the University of Saragossa in 1869, reported that they came from the roof.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.provenance: Cathedral of Santa Maria de Mediavilla, Teruel, Spain.
7bf56987-b874-51e5-91e1-bf19f3afba07.obtention: The piece was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 19 August 1869.

7c3b1c92-51fd-5856-8367-ca91f32596a9.name: 'Mihr in a Bath House in Khwarazm'
7c3b1c92-51fd-5856-8367-ca91f32596a9.description:
Assar Tabrizi, who was active under the Jalayirid sultan Uways and died in c. AH 792 / AD 1390, was inspired by Nizami’s famous romances *Layla wa Majnun* and *Khusraw wa Shirin* when he wrote ‘Mihr and Mushtari.’ It tells the story of the love of Mihr, son of King Shapur, for Mushtari, the vizier’s son.  
  
In Persian mystical poetry, physical love is often a reflection of divine love, and the beauty of the beloved a reflection of God’s beauty. The beloved was just as often a man as a woman, and although love did not have to manifest itself physically, the sexual ambiguity of works like this was enough to awaken displeasure in more morally oriented circles.  
  
In contrast to the story of Khusraw and Shirin, who clearly have a sexual relationship, this does not seem to have been the case between Mihr and Mushtari. In any event, Mihr marries Nahid, the daughter of the Khwarazm shah.  
  
The bathing scene is unusual. The text explains that Mihr, the central seated figure, is having a knot in his long hair combed out
7c3b1c92-51fd-5856-8367-ca91f32596a9.bibliography:
Boghanim, H. and Carayon, A. (eds.), *Parfums d'Orient, Institut du monde arabe*, Paris: Beaux Arts, 2023: cat. 56, 115 and 215.  
  
Folsach, K. V. and Meyer, J., *The Human Figure in Islamic Art – Holy Men, Princes, and Commoners*, Copenhagen: The David Collection, 2017: cat.no. 66
keywords: Water; miniature; folio; Layla; Majnun; Khusraw; Shirin

7c5b0aa9-383a-5b52-bc5a-91c986d3c9eb.name: Toiletries
7c5b0aa9-383a-5b52-bc5a-91c986d3c9eb.short_description: In the 19th century the wealthy families of Tunis invented the notion of the knastrou l'aroussa (marriage basket) as a mark of their wealth. Made of engraved or watermarked silver, this basket would contain various toiletries for the bride: a perfume sprinkler (mrach), a khol phial with applicator for the eyes (mokhala), a round or rectangular-framed mirror with engraved floral motifs, and a knife and plate for henna. A pair of clogs (qobqabs) made of wood and covered in silver worn by the bride. As a traditional bath (hammam) was the bride's first event on her wedding day, all her toiletries were set out ready for her, with a series of tools for exfoliation, depilation, application of a clay face mask, and more.
7c5b0aa9-383a-5b52-bc5a-91c986d3c9eb.holder: Musée des Arts et Traditions Populaires

7c7c2cda-78e1-597a-b911-718576ff198a.name: *Hammam* (Arab Baths).
7c7c2cda-78e1-597a-b911-718576ff198a.description:
The *hammam* (Arab Baths) is a few kilometres outside Palermo in the municipality of Cefalà Diana. The building consists of an internal room measuring 11 m. by 7.5 m. covered by a slightly pointed barrel vault 7.5 m. high. The room is divided into two distinct areas separated by a partition with three pointed arches. The columns of the partition are a Corinthian variation with chalice-shaped terracotta capitals. The smaller room, next to the hot water spring, has one bath and the larger room has three, each lower than the last, ensuring a variety of water temperatures. The walls contained niches to store personal effects and the vault had vents to allow the stream to escape. The underground system of channels used to fill and empty the baths is still partially visible immediately around the baths.  
Outside, a *kufic* inscription, now very deteriorated, runs along the frieze on at least three of the four sides.
7c7c2cda-78e1-597a-b911-718576ff198a.short_description: The Arab Baths are found just a few kilometres from Palermo and are fed by naturally hot spring water. The building consists of an inner room measuring 11 m by 7.5 m divided into two distinct areas by a partition wall and housing a series of baths of different temperatures. On the outside of the building there is a much-deteriorated inscription in *kufic* characters. Recent research leads us to believe that the building dates back to Norman times.
7c7c2cda-78e1-597a-b911-718576ff198a.method_for_datation: Through architectural analysis of different parts of the building.

Bellafiore, G., *Architettura in Sicilia nell’età Islamica e Normanna (827–1190)*, Palermo, 1990.

7c7c2cda-78e1-597a-b911-718576ff198a.history: There is no definite data on the date of construction. It has been suggested that construction first started during the Hellenistic-Roman period (outer wall) and then continued during the period of Arab domination (the columns of the dividing partition) and the Norman period (stringcourse). It has also been suggested that it is an entirely Norman building on the basis of structural similarities with other buildings from the reign of Guglielmo (William) II.

7ca0b66c-4942-5ae1-ba7a-8fd1e3d1a12d.name: Water flask
7ca0b66c-4942-5ae1-ba7a-8fd1e3d1a12d.description:
The shape of this characteristic type of water flask is based on flasks made of leather without a base. The handle for filling water and spout for pouring it were made of wood or metal and attached to the leather with the aid of a collar.  
  
Although fairly few Indian bronze flasks of this type have been preserved, they are familiar features on Indian miniatures, where they appear from around AH 932 / AD 1525. Chinese porcelain flasks with this shape are slightly older, however, and it is probable that both Indian and Chinese flasks hark back to a leather prototype used by Central Asian nomad peoples. The engraved decoration that embellishes the flask is unusual.

7dbe5f26-102f-5a9b-a9c9-3dbff17febde.name: "The Clever Hare with the King of the Elephants at the Spring of the Moon"
7dbe5f26-102f-5a9b-a9c9-3dbff17febde.alternate_name: Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
7dbe5f26-102f-5a9b-a9c9-3dbff17febde.description: This manuscript contains seventy-eight paintings and many text folios telling the famous tales of the jackals Kalila and Dimna. Based on the book of ancient Indian animal fables, the Panchatantra written by Vidyapati (Bidpai), the stories spread all over the Middle East where they became wildly popular. This manuscript has a strong flavour of Mamluk Egypt in the figure styles and bold drawings, with hints of Ottoman tulips and Safavid turbans. However, the burnt orange palette and darkly-inked lines have led to an attribution to Sultanate Gujarat where it is suggested this manuscript was copied from an Egyptian original. Its life in India is also attested by a Devanagari inscription at the end, although the rest of the Arabic text is written in a strong, left-leaning naskh-like script.

7e932bea-47e5-5386-9498-0e48388f3e95.name: Fountain
7e932bea-47e5-5386-9498-0e48388f3e95.short_description: Water fountains such as these were common in Ottoman government buildings in Lebanon, and were turned on whenever there was a meeting to prevent outsiders overhearing or eavesdropping. This marble fountain is octagonal in shape and is decorated with embossed semi-cylinders on each side. The exterior of the structure is decorated with a mosaic of black, white, beige and brown marble organised in geometric designs. A second, circular level of the fountain rests on this first octagonal structure.

7edf0ccd-d66d-5870-9c4a-05240e9d59ce.name: The Aflāj of Al Ain — Ancestral Water Systems Sustaining Oasis Life
7edf0ccd-d66d-5870-9c4a-05240e9d59ce.description:
This photograph from Al Ain Oasis captures one of the traditional *Aflāj* channels — ingenious irrigation systems that have supported agriculture and human settlement in the region for over 3,000 years. The word *Aflāj* (singular: *Falaj*) comes from the Arabic root ف-ل-ج (F-L-J), meaning to divide, split, or distribute. This reflects the system’s core purpose: the controlled and equitable distribution of water among community members.  
  
The *Aflāj* carry groundwater from underground channels or wells through a network of open canals, delivering life-sustaining water to palm groves, fields, and communal gardens. Their design ensures continuous flow, fairness, and sustainability — principles that shaped the social and agricultural identity of oasis communities.  
  
Today, Al Ain Oasis is inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, while the *Aflāj* irrigation system is recognised as part of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Together they are evidence of the deep environmental knowledge, engineering skill, and cooperative traditions that enabled life to flourish in the desert landscape.
7edf0ccd-d66d-5870-9c4a-05240e9d59ce.author: Dina Turkieh

7ef4da57-b989-5c8a-b7bd-e74673870ad0.name: Aqueducts around Jericho No.7
7ef4da57-b989-5c8a-b7bd-e74673870ad0.description: An original plan from the survey of Western Palestine showing the aqueducts bringing water from the wadies Fara, Kelt and Nuwayimeh into the Jericho oasis. These aqueducts date from the Hellenistic era onwards, and were used and added to for centuries well into the Islamic era. Note in particular how they feed into the Umayyad period Khirbet al Mafjar, a huge agricultural estate and palace, and the Mamluk period sugar mill, Tawaheen es Sukkar.

7f95a1e1-30bf-5b30-abfb-8955cb750a4b.name: *Isbiya* or *Kaiya* barge (model)
7f95a1e1-30bf-5b30-abfb-8955cb750a4b.description:
The *isbiya* (also known locally as the *kaiya*) is a cargo barge traditionally built in the town of Hit on the Western bank of the River Euphrates in Anbar province. It is documented in archival photographs and texts from the AH 13th / AD 19th and AH 14th / AD 20th centuries, and is believed to have existed in a similar form for several millennia, although its organic construction left no known physical remains.  
  
It is built using a technique comparable to wattle-and-daub architecture, with no use of metal (tools or fixings) or planked wood. Like many traditional boats, the *isbiya* is a technology specific to its place of origin, made with locally sourced materials. It is a vertical-sided box, constructed using a framework of branches and sticks, including palm fronds (*isb*) from which it derives its name, mulberry wood and gharb wood. These are bound together with palm leaf cordage, and ringed with thick coils of halfa grass before being waterproofed with several layers of tar. The community are involved in a collective construction process known as *fezaa*.  
  
Archaeological evidence suggests that cargoes of stone, lime and bitumen used to build Ur (3800 – 500 BC) and other ancient cities in southern Mesopotamia were transported using *isbiyas* or similar boats. This trade continued into the AH 14th / AD 20th century to supply tar used to waterproof roofs, boats and as an adhesive. Each *isbiya* made a one-way journey, propelled by the river, and was broken up on arrival, with the materials sold mainly for use as fuel.  
  
Production of the *isbiya* ceased in the late 1950s, when its function was replaced by metal barges, then by road cargo transport. In 2019 a full-sized *isbiya* and its smaller guide-boat, the *delil*, were reconstructed in a workshop organised by Safina Projects with community members in Hit, including elder Haji Noaman, who had assisted in building the last *isbiya* as an apprentice in the late AH 1370s / AD 1950s. In 2024 a scale model *isbiya* was produced for the collection of the Open Museum for Water Culture (Basra).

800c391d-1714-509b-9718-f253f7cec93e.name: *Jendoul* (reconstruction from illustration by al-Wasiti from the Maqamat al-Hariri)
800c391d-1714-509b-9718-f253f7cec93e.description:
The Arabic term *jendoul* here refers to a boat class that exists across many cultures, the Venetian Gondola being the best-known example. Designed as passenger transport for canals, a *jendoul* features a seating area (usually cushioned and sometimes canopied or featuring a cabin) and is typically no longer than 11 metres in length, enabling it to manoeuvre around canal junctions (although similar craft for open waters may be larger). Whether rowing or poling, the boatman or crew usually stands at the back, overlooking the passenger area and steering the boat (sometimes with another crew member at the front).  
  
A *jendoul* typically includes ostentatious ornamentation, representing the status and affluence of its passengers. The materials used are of high quality, and an array of artisan crafts may be exhibited, such as decorative metalwork, wood carving, inlay, lacquerwork, textiles and upholstery, cordage, tassels, and glass lanterns.  
  
Examples of the *jendoul* boat class can be found in historical cultures including Ottoman Turkey, Fatimid Egypt, Kish, Phoenicia, and in South and South-East Asia. A Sumerian boat with the characteristics of a *jendoul* is depicted on a cylinder seal impression (4th millennium BC, Uruk 3 period) found in the wetlands of Uqair in Diyala, Iraq.  
  
A specific type of *jendoul* is depicted by Yahya al-Wasiti in one of his AH 7th / AD 13th century miniatures illustrating the “Maqamat” of al-Hariri: a richly ornamented boat, rowed by three men standing aft. Safina Projects’ work to reconstruct it from this single image was an unusual challenge. The study process included using artist’s impressions and technical drawings, scale modelling, and experimentation with rowing methods to understand how this *jendoul* worked and to calculate its proportions before the first full-sized prototype Abbasid *jendoul* reconstruction was built in AH 1446-7/ AD 2024-25.

8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.name: Bowl
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.short_description: Some *mina’i* ceramics enjoy a particularly close relationship to poetry. Many examples are inscribed with verses, and others are decorated with figures referring to well-known poetic themes and tales. Several of these colorful wares, including this bowl, appear to depict the act of poetic recitation itself: taking place at a *majlis* (an assembly of courtiers and literati for the purpose of poetic recital), it can be imagined that the performer here, seated at the left before a courtly audience, is delivering the verses inscribed along the exterior rim of the bowl, which begin: "If the beloved leaves me, what am I to do? If s/he does not see the wisdom of our union, what am I to do?"
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.method_for_datation: The bowl is dated Hegira Muharram 583 / AD March 1187. It is one of five *mina’i* bowls dated to the month of Muharram in its inscriptions. Among these, three have very similar scenes of a literary *majlis*. Two of them, the LACMA bowl and another in the British Museum (1945,1017.261) are dated Muharram 583, the third, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (64.178.1), dated 4th Muharram 582 / AD 27th March 1186, is signed by Abu Zayd. Both the Metropolitan Museum and LACMA bowls share the same curious figure at far left, a young man standing with his right leg bent and foot pointing downward; in the former, the figure is clearly holding his leg as though tired from standing. The LACMA bowl can be attributed to Abu Zayd, who not only created works in both *mina’i* and luster but was a talented poet. He is known to have included some of his own verses among the poetic inscriptions on his luxury ceramic wares.
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.method_for_provenance: The bowl is decorated in the *mina’i* technique. A modern designation from the Persian word for "enamel", *mina’i* is almost entirely restricted to Seljuq Iran. While *mina’i* wares once were variously attributed to several sites on the basis of archaeological finds, the evidence demonstrates at present that the central Iranian city of Kashan was the nucleus for the production of these objects as well as contemporary luster wares; in fact, both types of wares were made by some of the same potters, in the same workshops. The *mina’i* technique involves the application of as many as seven colors, resulting in a well-controlled, polychromatic decorative surface not possible in other contemporary pottery types. The method for producing the polychrome enamel pigments is described in a treatise on pottery making by Abu’l-Qasim of Kashan, completed in Hegira 700/1301 AD, by which time *mina’i* or haft rang (“seven colors”) wares, as they are known in the textual tradition, were no longer being produced.
8153536b-21de-5451-826b-5c0aed191888.obtention: Possibly acquired by Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch (1864-1943, and 1863-1943, respectively) from MacDermid Parish-Watson, New York (d. 1948). Collection of Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch, until 1945 (gifted to); LACMA, gift of Mr. and Mrs. Allan C. Balch.

8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.name: Aquamanile in the form of a ram.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.description:
This standing animal sculpture has lost its front paws, ears and horns. With its long neck and head too small for its body, it exudes a feeling of great strength. On its breast is a crescent which seems to have a medicinal significance. Around its neck it wears a collar, decorated with an incised saw-tooth pattern, from which the crescent hangs. The eyes are circles sculpted around globular protrusions for the iris. This aquamanile was probably a fountain-head embellishing one of the local palaces or large houses. The water ran up a tube from under the ram's belly and emerged from the open spout of its mouth.  
This example can be included within a whole series of animal-shaped aquamaniles discovered in various Muslim countries, especially Egypt and Spain. They were generally deer, dogs or birds.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.short_description: Aquamaniles were probably used as fountain heads to decorate palaces and grand residences. This example belongs to a series of aquamaniles in the shape of animals, usually stags, dogs or birds, found in some Muslim countries including Egypt and Spain.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.method_for_datation: This aquamanile has definite affinities to other pieces found at Madinat al-Zahra, dating from the mid-4th / 10th century, and in Egypt, dating from the 5th century (11th). From the Ifriqiyan historical context and the simple decoration the piece can be dated to somewhere between the 4th–early 5th / 10th–11th centuries.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.method_for_provenance: This piece was a fortuitous discovery made at Beni Khalad probably during the 1930s. In spite of its resemblance to the aquamaniles of al-Andalus, its Ifriqiyan origin appears beyond doubt.
8181fe27-473a-532e-986e-e0786c511a39.obtention: This piece was presented to the Museum by the Friends of the Bardo in May 1941, where it has been on display since.

820a47e5-8aaa-59ae-93fc-e4b386f5f8b4.description: It is made of terracotta. The rim protrudes very slightly. The body is encircled by five parallel chain-like incised lines. Between the two central lines are trapezoidal incisions arranged in a chain-like geometric pattern.

821515fd-cabe-5567-8bf4-25c6db38bf00.name: Three-handled jar
821515fd-cabe-5567-8bf4-25c6db38bf00.description:
Discovered in an unbuilt area adjacent to a complex of five houses, this three-handled transport jar was found during the 2007 excavation by the Qatari-French Mission. The unbuilt space between the houses served as an area with temporary installations, potentially functioning as open-air kitchens featuring fireplaces.  
  
Fashioned from red clay and enveloped in a cream slip, this jar exhibits a high neck atop a globular body. The body is adorned with horizontal and wavy incised lines, while three vertical leaf-like patterns are incised on the upper part, positioned between the handles. These leaf patterns feature short double lines incised within them. This jar would have been utilized for the storage, transportation, and serving of liquids.
821515fd-cabe-5567-8bf4-25c6db38bf00.dates: Hegira late 2nd to late 3rd century / AD late 8th to late 9th century

823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.name: Ewer and basin set.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.description:
A set comprising two pieces: a ewer and a basin that was used for ritual ablution. The basin is large with a flaring rim. The ewer has a pear-shaped body, a curved handle and a lid. The flaring rim of the basin and the body, lid and lower part of the spout of the ewer are decorated with lozenges formed by small grooves. Vertical and horizontal grooves in the lozenges also form square motifs. On top of the lid are a flower-bud and leaf in keeping with the fashion of the time.  
  
The set is decorated in a gilding technique known as *Tombak* and engraved. In Turkish metalwork gilding, especially of pure copper artefacts, appears in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. Technically, this method of gilding involves spreading an amalgam of powdered gold and mercury on the surface of the object, which is then fired in a kiln. The mercury evaporates during the firing, while the gold powder adheres to the surface. Sometimes gold leaf is placed on a mercury-coated metal surface, and when the mercury evaporates during firing, the gold leaf is fixed to the object.  
  
The inscriptions on the ewer and the basin inform us that the objects were dedicated to the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, and they give the date of AH 1286 (AD 1870). Pertevniyal was the second *iqbal* (lit. 'fortunate one') of Sultan Mahmud II (r. AH 1223–55 / AD 1808–39). When she gave birth to Abdülaziz, she ascended to the highest female rank at court and when Abdülaziz ascended the throne in AH 1278 / AD 1861 she became the Valide Sultan (Mother of the Sultan, i.e. the Queen Mother). She had a complex built in her own name in the Aksaray Quarter of Istanbul. It comprised a mosque, a *maktab* (school), a *sabil* and a public fountain, and a tomb which was built for her in the courtyard of the mosque and in which she was buried when she died in AH 1300 / AD 1883. The Museum owns several objects taken from this tomb, some of which are in this exhibition.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.short_description: Gold has been the expression of economic power in all periods of history. *Tombak* is a technique that gives the look of gold to items and is used to decorate this ewer and basin set used by Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, mother of Sultan Abdülaziz, during religious ceremonies.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.initial_owner: Possibly Pertevniyal Valide Sultan (d. 1300 / 1883; queen mother from 1277–92 / AD 1861–76).
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.dimensions: Basin: height 12 cm, diameter 60 cm; ewer: height 30.5 cm.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.method_for_datation: Both the ewer and basin bear an inscription stating that they were dedicated to the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan and giving the date of 1286 (1870).
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.method_for_provenance: Both the ewer and basin were dedicated to the tomb of Sultan Abdülaziz's mother, Pertevniyal Valide Sultan, in Istanbul and, due to the fact that the *tombak* technique was used especially in Istanbul, it is highly likely that this set was produced there.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.obtention: The ewer and basin were transferred to the museum in 1926 from the Tomb of Pertevniyal Valide Sultan in Istanbul, to which they were dedicated.
823fdade-8900-58b3-bcda-59a5e61574cf.bibliography: *Anadolu Medeniyetleri III, Selçuklu-Osmanlı (Anatolian Civilizations III, Seljuqs-Ottomans)*, Istanbul, 1983, p.305.

keywords: Tombak; ewer; basin; Pertevniyal Valide Sultan; Mahmud II; Abdülaziz.

825ea881-372b-5499-bcbe-096246ecd917.name: Import/export activities between Egypt and Venice in 1868 and the first six months of 1869
825ea881-372b-5499-bcbe-096246ecd917.short_description: The items imported from Egypt were cotton, natron (a hydrous native sodium carbonate, used in chemical industry; Egypt had a rich deposit of it in Wadi el-Natrun), coffee, hides, fruit, copper and tamarind roots. The items exported to Egypt included wood and pieces of furniture, fruits and vegetables, butter, bricks and tiles, glass beads, lime, wine, cloth, medicaments, books, and various other products.

8267bfa4-2166-51d7-8e12-263939dcfc97.name: Calligraphic Galleon
8267bfa4-2166-51d7-8e12-263939dcfc97.description: The hull of this sailing ship comprises the names of the Seven Sleepers and their dog. The tale of the Seven Sleepers, found in pre-Islamic Christian sources, concerns a group of men who sleep for centuries within a cave, protected by God from religious persecution. Both hadith (sayings of the Prophet), and tafsir (commentaries on the Qur'an) suggest that these verses from the Qur'an have protective qualities.

82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.name: *Habb* water cooler
82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.description:
The *habb* is a large ceramic water storage jar and filtration device, used in domestic and communal contexts throughout Iraq. It is known for being used in public spaces to provide water for travellers, an offering known as *ma’ al-sabil*, “the water of the way”.  
  
The ceramic structure is slightly porous, which has a cooling effect on the water inside due to evaporation from external surfaces. When it is placed on a metal or wooden support structure, Water drips slowly through the base and is collected in a container below, having been filtered by the clay. Placing charcoal inside the *habb* can also help to purify the water. Water ladles (traditionally made from basketry) and ceramic cups used with the *habb* are coated with pitch, which has antiseptic qualities.  
  
The form of the *habb* is evidenced since ancient times, for example in cylinder seal impressions; similar vessels were also used as fermentation vats for beer.  
  
The *habb* is still made in various parts of Iraq including Diwaniya, Najaf, Babylon and Baghdad, where traditional ceramic craft remains; the example in the collection of the Open Museum for Water Culture (Basra) was bought from a Basra street market but had been imported from nearby Iran.
82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.holder: Open Museum Initiative for Water Cultures
82e33e2c-cc80-5d60-961b-f1c561116311.author: Hannah Lewis, Rashad Salim

82e816ee-f687-53d4-8c4b-2f9b2c03144a.name: Electric Kettle
82e816ee-f687-53d4-8c4b-2f9b2c03144a.description:
Electric kettles, widely found in households across the Islamic world, reflect how contemporary societies are embracing modern technologies in everyday life. Once heated over open flames, water is now boiled instantly using electricity, an efficient technological advancement.  
  
In our globalised and consumer-oriented world, many of these kettles are imported from manufacturing hubs such as China, a result of economic interdependence and global trade networks. The kettle reflects how Islamic communities adapt to modern living while preserving their shared cultural traditions.
82e816ee-f687-53d4-8c4b-2f9b2c03144a.author: Dina Turkieh

840c6c73-9390-5b9c-ad84-481ed38f888d.name: Waterway in Nizwa, Oman
840c6c73-9390-5b9c-ad84-481ed38f888d.description: The *aflaj* (singular *falaj*) are one of the oldest irrigation systems still in use today. Its origins date back to 5,000 years ago, though the example here is from AD 500. Its channels convey water from underground sources, springs and stream flow to villages and towns all around Oman. This system is employed as a primary water source for agricultural and domestic purposes, accounting for more than 30% of water usage across Oman. Using gravity forces to maintain the flux of water and its distribution, it has emerged as a distinguished social, cultural and economic emblem of the Omani landscape. The responsibility for the maintenance of working falaj and the distribution of water to different settlements lies with these communities. Despite the existence of numerous wells that provide potable water, the presence of aflaj waterways is of pivotal significance to the agricultural prosperity of Oman. The Falaj Daris, seen here, are the largest of the aflaj in Oman, and played a big part in Nizwa’s former prosperity as the capital of Oman in the 6th and 7th centuries AD. In 2006, the Aflaj Irrigation System was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and consequently granted governmental protection.
840c6c73-9390-5b9c-ad84-481ed38f888d.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

8417a7db-dd62-56ca-887b-404da568f48b.name: "Design for the Water Clock of the Peacocks"
8417a7db-dd62-56ca-887b-404da568f48b.alternate_name: from the Kitab fi ma'rifat al-hiyal al-handasiyya (Book of the Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices) by Badi' al-Zaman b. al Razzaz al-Jazari
8417a7db-dd62-56ca-887b-404da568f48b.description: Al-Jazari, the author of this treatise on a variety of practical and fanciful mechanical devices, served at the Artuqid court in Diyar Bakr in the late eleventh to the early twelfth century. Some of the elements of the peacock clock, run by water, are shown in this illustration. In the completed device, the arch containing two peacocks would be surmounted by another containing a peahen that would turn from right to left in the course of a half hour, causing the peacocks to whistle.

84a2af32-23c5-5782-9961-db81e133a30a.name: "The Hare, the Lion, and the Well"
84a2af32-23c5-5782-9961-db81e133a30a.alternate_name: Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
84a2af32-23c5-5782-9961-db81e133a30a.description: This manuscript contains seventy-eight paintings and many text folios telling the famous tales of the jackals Kalila and Dimna. Based on the book of ancient Indian animal fables, the Panchatantra written by Vidyapati (Bidpai), the stories spread all over the Middle East where they became wildly popular. This manuscript has a strong flavour of Mamluk Egypt in the figure styles and bold drawings, with hints of Ottoman tulips and Safavid turbans. However, the burnt orange palette and darkly-inked lines have led to an attribution to Sultanate Gujarat where it is suggested this manuscript was copied from an Egyptian original. Its life in India is also attested by a Devanagari inscription at the end, although the rest of the Arabic text is written in a strong, left-leaning naskh-like script.

84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.name: Umayyad Mosque
84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.description:
The Umayyad Mosque was built on the site of the Roman Temple of Jupiter, converted into the Church of St John the Baptist in AD 379. After the Islamic conquest of Damascus, the holy site was shared between the Christians and the Muslims of the city. By the succession of the Umayyad Caliph al-Walid bin Abd al-Malik, the church was demolished and a vast congregational mosque constructed instead. The outer wall of the mosque is formed by the Roman *temenos*, an oblong enclosure with pilastered walls, measuring 158 m x 100 m. Of the mosque's three minarets, the one on the southeastern corner is known as the Jesus Minaret, and the one in the centre of the northern wall is known as Minaret of the Bride; both are dated to the early AH 5th / AD 11th century. The southwest minaret was rebuilt by Sultan Qaytbay after the fire of AH 884 / AD 1479.  
The 122.5 m-long and 50 m-wide rectangular courtyard of the mosque is surrounded by a colonnaded portico (*riwaq*) on three sides. Along the southern wall is a triple-aisled 136 m-long and 37 m-wide prayer hall, a layout reminiscent of Byzantine churches. It is divided by two rows of arcades supported by re-used antique columns with Corinthian capitals. A lavish domed transept cuts the arcades into two equal halves; its court façade distinguished by a monumental gabled entrance in the centre, again evoking Byzantine palaces. At one time glass and gold-leaf mosaics covered all the facades in the courtyard. Only the “Barada mosaic” is preserved, so named after the Barada River in Damascus, depicting a landscape with rivers, trees and architectural structures.  
The portico walls were covered with a 3.5 m-high, coloured marble decoration. Today only a few marble slabs in the corner of the southeastern portico are preserved. It was once topped by the *karma* frieze; a long, undulating vine stem of acanthus scrolls carrying grapes, echoing that of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem. The fine mosaic, stone carving and marble decorations are all antique elements, revealing continuity with Greco-Roman artistic traditions as well as Byzantine architectural features. These features were combined with an Islamic consciousness predicating the lack of human representation in religious spaces. Such 'conscious eclecticism' is the hallmark of the new Umayyad architectural language.  
The speed of construction of this monumental Umayyad Mosque, along with its brilliant decorations and its rich materials, stood as a challenge to the finest Christian churches and an awe-inspiring status-symbol for the Muslim believers. Like the Mosque at Córdoba, a similarly early masterpiece of sacral Muslim architecture, it became a prototype for the “hypostyle mosque” consisting of a simple, spacious courtyard (*sahn*) articulated by a colonnaded portico (*riwaq*) on three sides, and a covered area for praying (*haram*). The division into three aisles and the transept also became influential for mosque architecture throughout Syria, as well as Egypt, Tunisia and Spain.
84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.short_description: When the Caliph al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik decided to build the first monumental mosque in Islamic history he used the most lavish material at his disposal and set the standard for subsequent religious monuments. Situated on top of an ancient sanctuary in old Damascus, the mosque has a courtyard, 122.5 x 50 m, surrounded by a colonnaded portico and a domed transept along the southern wall reminiscent of Byzantine churches. It was completed in AH 96 / AD 714–15 and some of its original marble panels and magnificent mosaics in blue, green and gold still survive along the western portico of the courtyard, particularly the 'Barada Panel'.
84f6b107-47b2-5cd1-a520-3a4f89856221.method_for_datation: The foundation inscription no longer exists but the text was preserved by the medieval Arab historian, traveller and geophrapher Ali ibn al-Husayn al-Mas'udi in his *Muruj al-dhahab wa-macadin al-djawhar \[Meadows of Gold and Treasury of Jewels*\], written in 332–45 / 943–56.

85859ee1-f41f-5403-935b-5caa9c428488.name:
Young men carried off by a Simurgh  
Possibly from a dispersed *Khamseh* (quintet) of Amir Khusrow (d. 1325)
85859ee1-f41f-5403-935b-5caa9c428488.short_description: A young man grips the feet of an enormous technicolour simurgh flying above choppy waters filled with giant turtles, fish and a crocodile which looks like a makara, the mythical sea creature with magic powers. This painting may depict the story by Bahram Gur’s Indian princess wife in the *Haft Paykar* of the Persian poet, Nizami. King Bahram Gur had seven wives who told him tales from their separate, coloured pavilions each day of the week. In the Indian princess’s story, the hero is dramatically rescued by holding onto the feet of a simurgh who brings him to a paradise-like land. Anthony Welch notes that the two figures in the beak of the simurgh may be the artist’s personal addition to the story (Welch and Welch 1982, p. 170). In any case the theme fits the Indian interest in adventure-romances featuring heroes who travel through (or above) strange lands and seas, as in Akbar’s Hamzanama. The painting has been attributed to Basawan, Akbar’s outstanding painter known for his sensitive observations, lush landscapes and use of perspective (Welch and Welch 1982, p. 170). In about 1635 CE the painting was mounted onto an album page decorated with magnificent gold-outlined flower paintings by the anonymous ‘Master of the Borders’ and bound in an album for Shah Jahan, Akbar’s grandson. The reverse of this page contains an Arabic prayer with Qur'anic expressions in black *nasta‘liq* script signed by Muhammad Husayn (d. 1020 H/1611-12 CE), the master calligrapher who was honoured by Akbar (r. 1556-1605 CE) with the title, ‘Zarin Qalam’ (Golden Pen). There is a portrait of Muhammad Husayn as a teacher painted by Basawan’s son, the luminary Mughal painter Manohar. It must be one of Manohar’s earliest portraits since the artist included himself as a pupil in the composition and he looks to be no more than fifteen years old (Royal Asiatic Society; see Welch 1979, p. 179).

85c59150-e031-57be-b9c0-d8ea356538dc.name: *The Renaissance*
85c59150-e031-57be-b9c0-d8ea356538dc.description: This painting is inspired by the late Sultan Qaboos bin Said's effort to build a mosque in even the most remote villages in Oman as part of an architectural revitalisation program that sought to preserve old buildings while adding new civic structures. In this artwork, the mosque stands amid traditional architecture while the tree trunks and water symbolise the revival of a once-barren land.
85c59150-e031-57be-b9c0-d8ea356538dc.artist: Ahmad bin Said bin Khalifa al-Adwi

85f6d251-61ee-5b5c-8da6-7a5d3c60074f.name: Asian conical hat
85f6d251-61ee-5b5c-8da6-7a5d3c60074f.description: This hat, with its wide brim, is used by farmers to protect themselves against the rain or extreme heat, providing essential protection for farmers and labourers in the fields. It too is made from locally sourced materials such as palm leaves and bamboo.
85f6d251-61ee-5b5c-8da6-7a5d3c60074f.author: ActionAid Bangladesh

85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.name: Painting.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.description:
The painting shows a topographical view of Mecca with the Great Mosque in the centre surrounded by the houses of the city and the hills of the Meccan neighbourhood. In the middle of the large open court of the Mosque stands the nearly cubic, black veiled building of the Ka'ba, the holiest sanctuary of Islam. The simple structure of the Ka'ba has been little modified throughout the centuries although the building has been restored, in contrast to the Great Mosque which has been reconstructed several times. The painting depicts a view of it after the Ottoman rebuilding period of the AH 10th century / AD 16th century. Inspired by the imperial architecture of Istanbul, arcades with small domes arranged in a line surround the court on either side and the seven minarets were provided with two or three balconies. The painter has tried to show a town-planning measure of the Ottomans. The old Meccan districts were densely inhabited and the houses reached the exterior walls of the Great Mosque. It was decided to tear down houses that immediately bordered the walls in order to create a large area of open space before the Mosque and its façade, as was the rule within the mosque complexes in Istanbul, Bursa or Edirne.  
Representations of Mecca and the Ka'ba illustrate itineraries used by pilgrims for orientation during the *hajj* or appear on tiles and tile panels of the second half of the AH 11th / AD 17th century to the first half of the AH 12th / AD 18th century. They show detailed descriptions of the function of the different buildings. The dome in front of the Ka'ba on the left side of the *minbar* (pulpit), for example, covers the footprints of Abraham. The open building beside it houses the *Zamzam* well whose water the pilgrims drank and took home. The choice of the represented buildings, their arrangement and their execution resemble those of copperplate engravings in European descriptions of Mecca more than depictions of the same scene in contemporary prayer books or on the tiles mentioned above.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.short_description: Painting showing a topographical view of the city of Mecca with the Great Mosque in the centre surrounded by houses. In the middle of the large open courtyard is the black veiled building of the Ka’ba.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.dates: Hegira early 12th century / AD early 18th century.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.method_for_datation: The painting was acquired by the theologian and orientalist Michael Eneman (1676–1714), probably in Istanbul, where he was sent by the Swedish King Charles XII (1682–1718) as his envoy in 1709. After a journey through Syria, Palestine, Sinai, Egypt and Cyprus in 1711 and 1712 he came back once more to Istanbul before he returned to Sweden. It is assumed that the painting is a contemporary work because representations of Mecca and Medina were common at that time.
85fb094d-1ff0-508b-bb75-cfcae0c77625.method_for_provenance: The painting was purchased by the theologian and orientalist Michael Eneman during his stay in Turkey, probably in Istanbul, at the beginning of the 12th / 18th century. At that time, representations of Mecca and Medina were a common subject of Ottoman painting not only in oil but also on tiles or as illustrations of pilgrim and prayer books.

86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.name: Public drinking fountain.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.description:
This fountain was designed for the Mosque of Mustafa Lala Pasha. It resembles a bench and is made of fine marble decorated with calligraphic carving and geometric mosaics composed of coloured marble and mother-of-pearl. The upper section consists of a marble panel grandly engraved with two lines of Arabic inscriptions written in the busy and rhythmically over-lapping *diwani* script, a calligraphic type popular during the Ottoman era. A thin band of vegetal motifs divides the two lines of inscription. This central panel is flanked by a pair of curvilinear brackets that are also heavily ornamented with vegetal and calligraphic carvings.  
The inscription conveys that the fountain, referred to as a *rub*' (a unit of water measurement), was built and made available to the public in honour of Sultan Sulayman by the High Aristocrat Mustafa Pasha in AH 971 / AD 1564. The date seems to have been important as it is written numerically and alphabetically in three different locations within the inscription. This is the date upon which Mustafa Lala Pasha became the governor of Damascus and he would remain in this prominent position for the next five years. Of his *waqf* endowments to Damascus, he built a new mosque and a new *khan* with lavish water supplies. During the reign of Sultan Salim II (AH 973–81 / AD 1566–74) Mustafa Lala Pasha was assigned as the military commander to conquer Cyprus in AH 977 / AD 1570, one of the greatest victories of the Ottoman military.  
The inscription on this fountain translates as follows:  
“The one who built this public *rub'*, may God make it the most useful, during the era of the most God-fearing sultan, the Sultan Sulayman Khan son of the Sultan Salim Khan, may God the Most Exalted raise him to the throne of the sultanate, is the High Aristocrat Mustafa Pasha, may God include him in the intercession of his mediator, the heir of the Ottoman kingdoms of the Sultan Salim Khan, the most God-fearing, may God light up his realm with his brilliant light, the utterance of this text was dictated and inscribed in the year nine hundred and seventy-one, 971 \[1564\].”
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.short_description: An important marble fountain made in Damascus and dedicated to Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent by the powerful military aristocrat and governor of Damascus, Mustafa Lala Pasha.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.initial_owner: The ruler of Damascus Mustafa Lala Pasha (r. AH 971–6 / AD 1563–9) in honour of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent (r. AH 926–74 / AD 1520–66).
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.method_for_datation: The inscription on the object includes the date of its completion in 971 (1564).
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.method_for_provenance: The fountain is dated by the documentary records at the Museum.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.provenance: Mosque of Mustafa Lala Pasha, Damascus, Syria.
86141f73-f2d4-5de6-b66c-a5955dcb470a.obtention: The Mosque of Lala Mustafa Pasha in Damascus was demolished between 1928 and 1930 so that the Suq al-Hal could be built. However, this piece along with a number of other archaeologically valuable objects, were relocated to the Museum for preservation. This piece was registered at the Museum in 1931.

869b29bc-51fe-528b-b3a2-1d11954beeb5.name: The Jami‘ al-Mabadi’ wa’l-Ghayat of al-Marrakushi
869b29bc-51fe-528b-b3a2-1d11954beeb5.description:
Abu ‘Ali al-Hasan al-Marrakushi’s treatise, compiled c. 680 AH (AD 1281–2) in Cairo, is the most important written source for medieval Islamic astronomical instruments and includes discussions of sundials, armillary spheres, astrolabes and quadrants for determining time from solar altitude.  
  
It is copied in *naskh* script with 28 lines to the page.

86a596e6-b986-58ee-a208-14ec3fe50206.name: Footed bowl (*tazza*)
86a596e6-b986-58ee-a208-14ec3fe50206.description: Footed bowl. A thick-walled vessel with scalloped rim which flares out from a deep cavetto (curved profile) bowl on a large, flared, hollow-pedestal base. Overall white underglaze decorated with deep blue designs. On the rim, a rock-and-wave pattern; on the interior wall, a band of trefoil arcades with small trilobed "cloud" patterns above the space between each arcade. Above each "cloud" element and arcade is a vertical L-shaped spike which fills the space. The trefoil arcade register surrounds the central medallion filled by a freely-drawn  bouquet with an elaborate central lotus surrounded by eight symmetrically arranged, stylized blossoms and leaves. The bundled stems grow from a cloud-like horizontal ground line with tendrils filling the space below. All registers are separated by concentric blue lines. On the exterior, horizontal lines define the changes in profile between rim, bowl and base while a freely drawn line traces the undulating curvilinear edge just under the scalloped rim. The body of the bowl and the pedestal foot are decorated with small circular sprays of stylized flowers surrounded by leaves and buds or fruit. Just above the bottom of the foot is a thickened horizontal rib thrown in the profile; this is highlighted above with a wide blue band. The underside of the pedestal foot is glazed overall, the juncture of the foot and body highlighted with a blue line and the bottom edge of the foot is unglazed. Some chips in the rim and foot have been filled and inpainted, while there is some wear on the interior glaze.

86b8321d-1511-5aba-a8cf-ce33f27cf40c.name: "Khusrau Catches Sight of Shirin Bathing"
86b8321d-1511-5aba-a8cf-ce33f27cf40c.alternate_name: Folio 50 from a Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami of Ganja
86b8321d-1511-5aba-a8cf-ce33f27cf40c.description: One of the five stories related in Nizami's Khamsa (Five Tales) concerns the love affair between the Iranian king Khusrau and the Armenian princess Shirin. This beautifully-detailed painting captures the moment when Khusrau first catches sight of Shirin, bathing in a stream. While the pond has now tarnished to near black, it was originally painting in shining silver, complementing the golden sky above.
