8750b2ef-ed27-560f-a5b8-9740d8ab180c.name: 'A Palace Complex with Harem Gardens'
8750b2ef-ed27-560f-a5b8-9740d8ab180c.short_description:
The miniature, whose primary motif is a fantastic palace complex populated by a prince’s concubines along with their female servants and guards, in a way depicts the world as one great garden. In the distance we see the prince on the back of an elephant, and on the other side of the river all manner of activities are taking place that form a powerful contrast to the perhaps pleasant but enforced idleness of the women of the harem.  
  
The painting has been attributed to Faiz Allah, one of the many skilled artists who worked in the growing provincial courts at the time when the Mughals’ power was waning. He was familiar with the concept of European linear perspective, but he disregarded its laws, either deliberately or unintentionally.

8838f3d0-31b0-5466-9a13-570fd28e82f1.name: Jar fragments with incised décor
8838f3d0-31b0-5466-9a13-570fd28e82f1.description:
This fragment, a kitchen ceramic, was excavated in 2007 by the French-Qatari Mission in one of the houses in Murwab. The water jar features a globular body and a high, straight neck with an unpreserved rim. Crafted from creamy white clay with inclusions of sand and basalt, the porous nature of the material makes it well-suited for keeping water cool.  
A vertical decoration, created with a comb, adorns the entire upper part of the body up to the midpoint of the globular section. Additionally, a rounded handle was attached to the neck of the water jar.

893a0815-f9f4-52c7-8775-ffe7b752a7e5.description: The apricots are pressed using a press installed in the orchard or in the sheltered part of the facility. This press is equipped with two superimposed sieves, one with large holes to remove the stones and another with a much finer mesh to remove the fibres, leaving only the juice to pass through. The juice is collected in a large-capacity basin of more meticulous construction; the interior is tiled and surmounted by a fixed metal structure. The model of press dates from the 1970s. This operation takes place when the heat dies down at the end of the afternoon.

896034df-5b65-5b50-921e-f52b7e844979.name: Large Jar
896034df-5b65-5b50-921e-f52b7e844979.short_description: The origins of this object are from Southern Mesopotamia; it’s a complete pottery jar with rolled edges, a short-straight neck, and a globular body. This piece is considered rare, made from fine clay with opaque white glaze and copper, blue, and black manganese splashes on the sides. Archaeologists were able to find many different pottery pieces from different historical periods, and this piece dates back to the 9th century AD. A vessel like this is usually used as a goblet. Typically, it’s a multi-use jar which could have been used for storage and cooking or storing water to keep it cold or to drink from directly.

8a6532ff-cf2a-5f34-9f53-a4d9192c2490.name: A folio from the Maqamat al-Hariri representing a *Jendoul* (folio 61r)
8a6532ff-cf2a-5f34-9f53-a4d9192c2490.description:
The boat depicted by Yahya al-Wasiti in this AH 7th / AD 13th-century miniature, illustrating the "Maqamat" of al-Hariri, is a richly ornamented boat rowed by three men standing aft. The story it illustrates mentions that it was used on the river Euphrates. The fact that three oarsmen were needed suggests that it may have been rowed upstream, as well as carrying several passengers and perhaps cargo.  
  
In AH 1444 - 1445 / AD 2023-24, artist Rashad Salim and the Safina Projects team studied this image in detail in preparation to reconstruct the historic boat. This was an unusual challenge, as the image is not proportionate. The study process included creating artist’s impressions and technical drawings, scale modelling by three different modelmakers experienced in different kinds of boatbuilding, and experimentation with rowing methods to understand how this boat worked and to calculate its proportions before the first prototype Abbasid Jendoul reconstruction was built in AH 1444 - 1445 / 2024-25.
8a6532ff-cf2a-5f34-9f53-a4d9192c2490.initial_owner: The manuscript was probably produced for the Turkic emir shown in the left-hand frontispiece (folio 1v), a lieutenant of the Abbasid Caliph al-Mustansir (r. AH 623–639 / AD 1226–1242)
8a6532ff-cf2a-5f34-9f53-a4d9192c2490.method_for_datation: Colophon in the manuscript provides the name of the artist and date of completion.
8a6532ff-cf2a-5f34-9f53-a4d9192c2490.method_for_provenance: Similarity with other Baghdadi manuscripts, and the appearance of the name of the Abbasid Caliph al-Mustansir in one of the paintings (AH 8th / 15th maqama, fol. 164v).

8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.name: Cock
8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.description:
It was difficult to make and fire large ceramic figures like this one and the sphinx (Isl 56) with the technology of the day. They easily crackled or simply collapsed. The manganese, turquoise and blue glazes as well as the carved decoration are typical of laqabi ware, but while the glazes on a horizontal surface are kept in place by the carved decoration, this is not the case on an upright object like this one.  
  
Although both animals must be considered mythical creatures, the artist managed to depict the watchful and aggressive cock with all of this animal’s natural characteristics.
8b2820f2-b570-5834-a941-6d905377879a.dates: AH 2nd half of the 6th / AD 2nd half of 12th century

8b569dc5-e1b2-50a0-b4d0-c169fc260f13.name: Engraved rock
8b569dc5-e1b2-50a0-b4d0-c169fc260f13.description:
This engraved rock bears an inscription of a poem consisting of 12 verses composed by Khalfan bin Rashid. The prose documents the completion of a well in the Wilayat of al-Hamra for the Governor Saif bin Muhammad ibn Sayyar in AH 1177 / AD 1763, during the reign of Imam Ahmad bin Said al-Busaidi, the founder of the al-Busaid Household.  
  
The poem reads as follows:  
  
The Almighty granted the efforts with success  
The well has been built with mold and rocks.  
Its omens were like a magic,  
The area around seems heavenly, a garden full of trees bearing fruits.  
What a garden that burying sadness, with its flourishing beauty  
Blessed be its owner, the builder and those who dwelled in it.  
  
He , who had been freehanded to build the well, is Saif, son of Mohammad ibn Sayyar,  
And is the wise Wali of Oman, and the best leader.  
( )  
May the Almighty Allah protect him from the enviers, and those who are disloyal  
The best we conclude is by prayers upon the prophet Mohammad (Peace be Upon Him) as much of rainy clouds and more.  
In AH 20 Safar 1177, was written by (), Khalfan bin Rashid, ().

8bc18f76-661e-508b-92b4-e262c93b5aa3.name: Jar with turquoise-blue glaze
8bc18f76-661e-508b-92b4-e262c93b5aa3.description:
This small ceramic jar is decorated in a turquoise-blue glaze. As the glaze covers the outside as well as the inside, liquids such as water, vinegar, oil and so on could be transported and conserved in the vessel. The jar has a short neck with a wide flat rim, allowing for a lid or flexible cover of fabric or leather to be fastened to it. Two small handles, one of which has broken off, indicate the jar could have been carried or suspended.  
  
This type of turquoise-glazed pottery is very common on archaeological sites dating to the early Islamic period. These wares were produced in the workshops of Basra in southern Iraq and then exported all around the Abbasid Empire and beyond. Examples have been found around the Indian Ocean region, including East Africa, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.

8c713d6f-f859-5642-9f8e-6432126cff05.name: Tray
8c713d6f-f859-5642-9f8e-6432126cff05.short_description: This water-cooler tray stands on three legs and has circular recesses for holding cooling earthenware jugs. The inscriptions attest that the tray was made for the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun who was a lavish patron of the arts. The decoration is distinguished by its gold inlay and by the use of large lotus blossoms. This type of chinoiserie design was introduced from Mongol Iran to Mamluk Egypt in the early decades of the 14th century.

8d580ca5-2f15-5f82-9f15-cc5c1c0c7b42.name: 'The Dervish from Faryab Crosses the River on his Rug'
8d580ca5-2f15-5f82-9f15-cc5c1c0c7b42.description:
In his *Bustan* (The Flower Garden), Sadi described an amazing experience that he had on a ferry. While the author paid for his journey, an old dervish from the town of Faryab did not have the money and was left on the riverbank. As the boat made the crossing, Sadi heard laughter in its wake. It was the dervish, sailing over the river on his prayer rug.  
  
In this rendition, the ferry is shown as a western carrack, with Sadi dressed in a green caftan and standing in the bow. The page comes from a manuscript calligraphed by Mir Ali Haravi in Herat in AH 932 / AD 1526. At this point, the volume evidently had only a few illustrations, while others were added later in a style in keeping with the original ones.  
  
The richness of detail on this painting harks back in time, though the young man standing next to Sadi is wearing a turban typical of the Shah Abbas period (r. AH 995- 1039 / AD 1587-1629). This shah was responsible for the completion of the manuscript, and the stamp at the top shows that it was donated to the family sanctuary in Ardabil in 1608/1609.

8da71d19-da0a-5d1f-9e5b-ab417d6238f7.name: *Mudhif* meeting house
8da71d19-da0a-5d1f-9e5b-ab417d6238f7.description:
The *mudhif*, with its distinctive *kawser* (decorated face) and *shebbat* (arched columns) constructed of reed, is the traditional communal meeting and hosting space found throughout the Euphrates Delta and in the marshes of southern Iraq.  
  
The earliest Mesopotamian civilization, the Sumerian, arose in this region from the 6th millennium BCE. The archaeological remains of its city states are largely mud brickwork and ceramics, but imprints and remains of organic material such as reed mats are also found, as are textual references to the use of reeds in construction, and depictions of structures resembling today’s *mudhifs*. From this we may surmise a continuity of the architecture of the Marshes from antiquity to modern times, with the *mudhif* being the most iconic representation of this ancient vernacular tradition.  
  
When a new *mudhif* is built, the community gathers to help the master builder and his team. The main structural element is gathered reeds (*qasab*), stripped of leaves and tied together into a bundle column, the *shebba*. After being set in the ground at a 15-degree (outward) angle, each opposing pair are pulled together with ropes so that their tops meet, spliced and bound together to create the *mudhif's* arches. The number of *shebbat* column pairs is always odd: 5, 7, 9 etc, with the largest recorded *mudhif* at 25 *shebbat*.  
  
Long, thin bundles called *huttar* form beams laid across the *shebbat* to support woven *baria* roofing mats. All sides of the *mudhif* are finished with lattice panels that permit light and the circulation of air modulated by outer flaps. *Mudhifs* are oriented towards the prevailing wind, so fresh air enters through one entrance and exits from the other side, causing a natural cooling process.  
  
Reeds contain a high percentage of silica, making them waterproof and insect-repellent. An excellent heat and sound insulator, fast-growing, durable and flexible, they are used to build shelters, fences, mats, rafts, floating islands (*chibasha*) and other structures.

8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.name: Strainer.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.description:
The greyish earthenware fragment showing openwork at the centre was part of a jug with strainer. The slightly convex strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the vessel and was intended to protect the stored liquid from pollution and insects. Its design is inscribed in a circle and shows a quadruped passing to the left. The motif is set against a filigree background of rhombs. The major outlines of the animal, usually called a gazelle, are incised into the material. The remaining surface of the body is left plain. A striated zigzag line between two circles surrounds the quadruped.  
Decorated strainers are known from excavations of sites dated to the AH 2nd–9th / AD 8th–15th century. Strainers of the Fatimid period, which was the high point of their development, show not only the most varied patterns, but also the most elaborated compositions and the finest execution. As well as gazelle-like quadrupeds, other zoomorphic motifs such as elephants, lions, hares, birds or fish are depicted on the strainers.  
The strainers are only small fragments of vessels, but they call attention to themselves. One reason might be the unexpected combination of simple earthenware, mostly undecorated on the outside, with costly designs inside the neck of the jugs. Another might be that the potters created a highly aesthetic form for a simple utilitarian object. The complex patterns of the openwork carried out within small areas reveal the skills of the craftsmen.
8eee28ae-e98c-58dd-82dd-0212290a8232.short_description: Earthenware fragment which was integrated in a vessel as a strainer. The latticework displays a quadruped, possibly a gazelle, passing to the left. The strainer was placed at the juncture of neck and shoulder of the earthenware vessel to protect the stored liquid from insects and pollution.

8f0498f0-0ced-550b-8d87-d24b4ee4d5c9.name: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts Park
8f0498f0-0ced-550b-8d87-d24b4ee4d5c9.alternate_name: Previously known as the *Jabal al-Luweibdeh* Park
8f0498f0-0ced-550b-8d87-d24b4ee4d5c9.description:
The park covers an area of approximately 7500 square metres and provides a pleasant green space surrounded by residences in what was once one of Amman's most elegant neighbourhoods. Following the rehabilitation programme of the early 2000s, the park incorporates the domain of the Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts, presenting different areas of the garden that have been fully reinterpreted in terms of sustainability and contemporary landscape architecture.  
  
The new public installations include outdoor sculpture displays, children's play areas, a performance/exhibition space, a café/restaurant and model educational gardens demonstrating water-conservation landscape practices. It also includes a Japanese garden, elaborated in partnership with the Japanese Embassy in Amman, and an Andalusian fountain, also a fruit of the collaboration with the Spanish Embassy in Amman.  
  
The park also includes a 160 cubic metre reservoir that harvests rainwater for use in a drip irrigation system. All existing trees and mature ornamental plants were carefully preserved and incorporated into the new landscape design. To enhance the park’s vegetation, a diverse selection of drought-tolerant trees, ornamental species and ground covers were introduced to complement the original greenery. Additionally, a specialised variety of turf grass (Bermuda grass) has been introduced in select areas to further reduce water usage.  
  
Radiating from the platform, the pathways retrace the layout of the park’s original circulation routes. The irregular stone paving panels from the former design have been preserved to maintain a visual and tactile connection to the park’s historic character.
8f0498f0-0ced-550b-8d87-d24b4ee4d5c9.history: Originally known as *Jabal al-Luweibdeh* Park, the National Gallery of Fine Arts Park was established in AH 1371 / AD 1953 as one of the first public parks in Amman. Situated in one of the city’s oldest neighbourhoods, it became a cherished meeting place and an early example of civic planning in Jordan’s growing capital. However, over time, neglect and insufficient maintenance led to its deterioration. In AH 1423 / AD 2002, the Center for the Study of the Built Environment (CSBE) proposed comprehensive rehabilitation works. In collaboration with the Greater Amman Municipality, work began in the spring of AH 1424 / AD 2004 and was completed in AH Rabi 1426 / AD May 2005. The park was officially renamed to emphasise its integration with the Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts, linking the original gallery building and its new extension. The entire complex was inaugurated under the royal patronage of Their Majesties King Abdullah and Queen Rania, restoring the park as both a public amenity and a model of sustainable landscape design. In AH 1437 / AD 2016, the park won a Global Gold award by Green World Organisation in "Sustainability".

8fa09327-47d4-5dce-9649-b4f26818817e.name: Jar
8fa09327-47d4-5dce-9649-b4f26818817e.description: A hollow wooden jar with a rounded base and a large rhomboid-shaped body designed to store a greater quantity of water. It has a slightly protruding circular mouth, while on either side of the body are small recessed areas for fastening a rope to secure it to an animal. The jar is lightweight enough to be carried or transported over short distances. It was used for storing and transporting water in rural or Bedouin settings and was designed to facilitate drawing water from wells or troughs and preserving it for a period of time.

9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.name: Small bucket.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.description:
The small bucket is a metal container with a handle used for throwing water over hot marble paving to produce steam needed for the baths. The mouth is deformed, probably as a result of use. The decorative elements are contained within compass-drawn lines around the circumference. The engraving was done with two points, one sharp and the other blunter. The plant-arabesque decoration was added to fit the piece.  
The outer surface is totally covered with compartmentalised decoration, with ribbons that mark the boundaries between an inscribed strip in the upper part, a frieze of scrolls and palmettes, another strip (split into two circles and two poly-lobed medallions) and lastly another frieze of scrolls and palmettes in the lower part. In the upper strip, the inscription 'Continuous happiness' appears several times, while in the medallions 'Happiness, wealth, blessing and the fulfilment of desires' can be read. One of the medallions has a geometric pattern: two shapes spiralling away from one other that end in fanciful groups of stems and leaf buds make up the background of an inscription written in elegant cursive characters. The other, less dense, is made up of a group of scrolls finished with asymmetrical palmettes. The spandrels between the medallions develop the idea of the 'tree'. The structure relates to the Persian world, which from the AH 6th / AD 12th century revitalised the old Roman forms.  
This piece belongs to the type of domestic object used in refined environments and influenced by oriental trends, which had a great impact on al-Andalus.
9019f587-868b-5467-91b0-7b17a50a99bd.short_description: Fascinated by this magnificent gilded bronze bucket from the Alhambra, the powerful Cardinal Cisneros took it and added it to his private collection. Its exquisite and refined geometric, plant and epigraphic decoration show that it was a luxury piece for use only in a palace setting.

914eb4c5-9b5a-549c-b385-fee293bdb38a.name: Cogged well wheel (*al-manjūr*)
914eb4c5-9b5a-549c-b385-fee293bdb38a.description: The central hub of a cogged well wheel (*al-manjūr*) is made from a single cross-cut section of local hardwood such as the Christ's thorn jujube (Zisiphus spina-christi, locally known as *sidr*). To form the cogs, a double row of hand-shaped wedges, also of hardwood, are fitted into the hub individually. The wheel is then lashed together with shark skin or goat leather.

91c00825-34dc-5126-9e4f-7ae6ce0eed5a.name: The Bridge-Dam of al-Battan
91c00825-34dc-5126-9e4f-7ae6ce0eed5a.description: Throwing itself over across the Medjerda, 2 km downstream from Tbourba, this bridge-dam was built around AH 1101 / AD 1690 by the Bey Mohamed, son of Murad II. It is one of the most commendable works, pierced by 16 arches that stand raised up on an invert that serves as its foundation. Gates closed the arches and raised the water-level to set the press mills in action and to irrigate the river plains. The bey ordered for a summer house to be built next to this bridge.
91c00825-34dc-5126-9e4f-7ae6ce0eed5a.author: Ahmed Saadaoui

9245b827-e2b3-5d39-ad6f-d1f2358eaffb.name: Fatwa on water management
9245b827-e2b3-5d39-ad6f-d1f2358eaffb.alternate_name: Legal opinion on water rights; Islamic jurisprudence manuscript
9245b827-e2b3-5d39-ad6f-d1f2358eaffb.description: This manuscript presents a fatwa—an Islamic legal opinion—concerning the management and distribution of water in Moroccan society. Issued by a religious jurist (*faqih*) in Marrakech during the AH mid-14th / AD mid-20th century, it reflects the pivotal role of Islamic law (*fiqh*) in regulating access to water as both a natural resource and a sacred trust. The fatwa provides guidance on conflicts between water users, allocation of irrigation turns, and the religious duty of ensuring fairness and equity in distribution. Written in Arabic script in clear, formal calligraphy, the text embodies the enduring connection among law, faith, and environmental stewardship in Morocco. Such documents illustrate how water, a scarce and precious resource, was historically governed through ethical and religious frameworks, complementing customary practices and communal agreements. Today this manuscript serves as a testimony to the moral and spiritual dimensions of water management, highlighting how Islamic scholarship reinforced the idea of water as a collective right entrusted by God. The manuscript’s presence in the museum underscores the continuity of faith-based governance and its influence on Moroccan hydraulic traditions.

93e8ae64-547f-5c2e-a1a2-19aee2c4d694.name: *Birkat al-Hajj*
93e8ae64-547f-5c2e-a1a2-19aee2c4d694.description:
The *Birkat al-Hajj*, the "pilgrimage’s reservoir", marks the most south-easterly extension of the Muslim city. The open, trapezoid-shaped reservoir measures 155 m x 122 m, edged by massive 3.5 m-thick walls of roughly hewn basalt-stone blocks. Three metre-wide projections divide the inner walls. The reservoir itself is between 6 m and 12 m deep. Stairs at the north-western, south-western and southeastern corners provide access to the water. The Birkat al-Hajj and another, slightly smaller, reservoir to the east secured the water supply for the city, collecting rain and melted ice from the Jabal Hauran and the Wadi al-Zaidi to the west of the city.  
  
In his description of Syria, the historian Ibn Shaddad al-Halabi mentions that the Ayyubid ruler of Damascus, al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa (d. 624/1227), built a huge reservoir in the outskirts of Bosra, to serve as a drinking trough for the pilgrim’s caravan that passed on its annual journey to Mecca before entering the desert region. Describing his participation in the pilgrimage from Damascus in 726/1326, the traveller Ibn Battuta gives a vivid description of Bosra as pilgrim’s halt: “…we travelled on to the town of Bosra; it too is a small place. It is the usual practice of the caravan to stop there for four nights. The inhabitants of the Hauran flock to this town with their produce  
and the pilgrims supply themselves here with provisions for the journey.”  
  
The huge dimensions of the reservoir suggest that it must have provided water for a large city and not just for the  
pilgrims’ caravans that passed through twice a year. Therefore the initial structure may date to the Roman period (5th century AD) while the historically documented efforts of al-Mu‘azzam ‘Isa  
indicate a medieval renovation. This supposition matches very well with the extension of the citadel into a palatial residence for the lord of Bosra, the brother of al-Mu‘azzam, al-Salih Isma‘il,  
since the citadel with its newly constructed mosque and hammam required a sufficient and well-functioning water supply that the Birkat al-Hajj may well have provided.

95fa67f4-e90b-5049-aefb-6e44fd542a80.name: Small Metal Ewer
95fa67f4-e90b-5049-aefb-6e44fd542a80.description:
A small ewer with a spherical body and a tall cylindrical neck, featuring a slightly flared mouth opening. The handle is thin and curved, with breaks or corrosion at the top. The surface patina exhibits some green-blue oxidation characteristic of copper or bronze. The absence of decoration may indicate domestic or utilitarian use.  
  
In that period people referred to such a small vessel as *al-sāqī al-awwal* (the first server), as it was typically placed near a sleeping area. It was used by a traveller arriving late at night who would rise at dawn to wash his face with cool water in preparation for prayer.

9649e657-d081-5990-b3dd-ee2b6d2ee696.name: Washing Set (Pitcher and Wash Basin) with Chamber Pot
9649e657-d081-5990-b3dd-ee2b6d2ee696.description:
The 19th century witnessed major changes in the political, social, cultural, and economic spheres in Serbia. The uprisings against centuries-long Ottoman rule, in 1804 and 1815, led to the enactment of Sultan Mahmud II’s hatt-i sharif in 1830, the establishment of the autonomous Principality of Serbia, Serbia’s full independence, confirmed at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and the proclamation of the Kingdom of Serbia in 1882. The transition from a feudal to a capitalist society was accompanied by cultural pluralism, which implied the establishment of new cultural models with a local Ottoman-Balkan imprint, as well as the adoption of cultural models common in bourgeois Europe. In this context, the items imported from Central and Western Europe got a significant place in everyday life and the visual culture of Serbia. While European influences in Serbia signified a gradual breaking up with Ottoman traditions, at the same time, due to the extensive reforms that permeated all spheres of society, they also significantly shaped the visual culture of the Ottoman Empire.  
The washing set with a chamber pot originates from the renowned ceramics production centre of Stoke-on-Trent in Staffordshire, England. This area was home to a collective of workshops that produced majolica, stoneware, and porcelain. One of these manufacturers was S. Fielding & Co. Adapting to fashion trends and market demands, the company exported high-quality ceramic pieces worldwide from 1870 to 1982.  
The wash set preserved in the Museum of Applied Art, and created in the Historicist style, is characterized by its subtle decoration and the combination of a green pastel ground with floral motifs. A floral garland follows a restrained black line running along the central section of each vessel. The black band is edged with delicate touches of gilding. On the bottom of the pieces is the mark of the workshop: Crown Devon, Fieldings, Stoke-on-Trent, England, indicating that the set is part of the Crown Devon collection, which was produced from 1880, while from 1912 onward, the items were made in series.

964a5e5c-38f2-52e1-916c-5aa787fad913.name: "How a Braggart was Drowned in a Well"
964a5e5c-38f2-52e1-916c-5aa787fad913.alternate_name: Folio 33v from a Haft Paikar (Seven Portraits) of the Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami of Ganja
964a5e5c-38f2-52e1-916c-5aa787fad913.description: This miniature is an illustration of the most dramatic episode in the tale told by the Moorish princess in the Green Paviliion on Monday. While traversing the desert, Bashr, a good and pious man, and his bragging and evil-minded traveling companion come upon a jar filled with pure water sunk into the sand. After they have quenched their thirst, the selfish companion insists upon bathing in the water, in spite of Bashr's pleas against polluting it. The water turns out to be a deep well fed by a spring, and the heedless companion drowns. The tale ends happily for the deserving Bashr. The well is shown from two different perspectives to aid the viewer's comprehension of the scene.

97a74e08-c680-51a4-9ff3-a40be3a5d9ea.name: *The Source*
97a74e08-c680-51a4-9ff3-a40be3a5d9ea.description: Mona Saudi sculpts abstract forms imprinted by feelings. Her perfect mastery of gesture allows her to work with dexterity in all materials. Although she has a particular fondness for marble, she also works with granite, pink Jordanian stone, and bronze. Two versions of *The Source* were realised: the first in bronze (AH 1405 / AD 1984), shown here, and the second in pink Jordanian stone in a larger format (AH 1407 / AD 1986). Circles emanating from the central eye, which symbolises the water source, bring movement to the work. The terms "eye" and "source" are the same word in Arabic.

9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.name: *Egyptian village scene*
9844c72d-8d2f-50e5-8d5b-86ef15a82164.short_description: Egyptian men and women are seen here in a town or village on the Nile. In the shade of an overhanging tree a market stall displays its wares, including paper lanterns and bread. At the stall behind, sugar cane is for sale. In the background is a mosque with a white minaret, though not distinctive enough to establish the scene's locality. Pilleau had visited Egypt in the winter of 1842-43 with Lieutenant Colonel George Everest (after whom Mount Everest was named) and two other companions, on their way home from India. On his return to England he published a set of twelve coloured lithographs, Sketches in Egypt (1845), which, like the better-known publications of Wilkie, Roberts and Owen Jones in the same decade, fuelled popular interest in Egypt and the Holy Land.

keywords: Economy; Market; sugar cane; Egypt; local product; rural life; eating; paintings

99eb7578-9253-520d-8e15-f2005c79e229.name: Table jar with blue glaze
99eb7578-9253-520d-8e15-f2005c79e229.description: This table jar, unearthed in 1981 during the French mission at the Murwab site in one of the houses with a plaster floor, exhibits a well-recognized design inspired by early Islamic metal needles. Featuring a notably tall (10cm) and wide (11cm rim diameter) straight neck with a slightly projecting rim, the jar boasts a mildly globular body that accommodates two handles on its upper portion. The straight handles suspend from the upper part of the neck. Although the blue glaze is considerably damaged, it reveals a very fine cream paste akin to eggshell. This artefact likely originated from the workshops of Basra.

9ac8d0d2-823f-5dcf-8834-a73fe5588a48.name: Merida Citadel.
9ac8d0d2-823f-5dcf-8834-a73fe5588a48.description:
The city of Merida, founded by Augustus in AD 25, was one of the main urban centres of Roman Hispania and it was the second most important metropolis in the Visigothic period, after Toledo. The city went on to be the most important city in Gharb al-Andalus (western al-Andalus) after the Muslim conquest. However, continuous rebellions against the centralist Umayyad power sent Merida into obvious decline. In AH 220 / AD 835, following a succession of rebellions and sieges, ‘Abd al-Rahman II ordered the construction of a fortress where troops loyal to Córdoba could shelter in order to secure the city and guarantee the submission of an area so prone to uprisings.  
The citadel sits on the bank of the Guadiana River next to the bridge and its wall is built on a Roman containment-dyke. It is a square enclosure of some 130 m2 with a perimeter of 550 m. The walls, 2.70 m thick and 10 m tall, are built of granite ashlars taken from existing Roman and Visigothic buildings. The wall is strengthened by a series of large quadrangular towers that act as buttresses. The main entrance to the enclosure is a horseshoe arch situated on the north side and flanked by two towers. This entrance was protected by a rectangular courtyard with another two gateways (one to the bridge and one to the city) that acted as a barbican or initial defensive area.  
Inside the enclosure in the western section there has survived a rectangular reservoir, also constructed of granite ashlars, that dates to the same period. The building providing access to the water store is decorated with salvaged Visigothic pillars and has two flights of stairs that go down to the pool. The reservoir was continuously filled with river water filtering through the ground and would provide water to the people in the citadel in times of siege.  
After the *Reconquista* the fortress was given to the Order of St. James, which added towers and other medieval structures in order to convert it into a convent and a residence, which explains why the building is also known as the 'Merida Convent'.
9ac8d0d2-823f-5dcf-8834-a73fe5588a48.short_description: This is the oldest surviving Muslim fortification on the peninsula. Having put down the continuous revolts against Merida, the Amir of Córdoba ‘Abd al-Rahman II ordered the city walls to be dismantled and a new fortress to be built from the salvaged ashlars using a header/stretcher bond in accordance with existing Roman and Byzantine military tradition. The new fort was located next to the Roman bridge over the Guadiana River in order to defend it. It was also used as the governor’s residence and as refuge for servants loyal to the amir in the event of a revolt.
9ac8d0d2-823f-5dcf-8834-a73fe5588a48.method_for_datation: A surviving inscription tells us the exact date when the citadel was constructed. It was commissioned by the Amir ‘Abd al-Rahman II in 220 / 835.

9b465241-9dbe-5697-82cb-f32fd4f23628.name: Magical Bowl
9b465241-9dbe-5697-82cb-f32fd4f23628.description:
The small, apodal cup has curved walls. The interior is entirely engraved with magical, astrological, and Kabbalistic symbols: two numerical squares, five-pointed stars, and zoomorphic representations, including the zodiac sign of Aries in the center, Scorpio below, and the double-headed knot of the Dragon of Eclipses. The engraved inscriptions contain invocations and Qur'anic quotations, as well as instructions for using the cup, referring to its restorative properties.  
  
Inscription on the outer edge: Work of the destitute Muhammad b. Yanus, may God have mercy on him

9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.name: Fountain basin.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.description: Oblong basin in grey marble. A sculpted decorative element consisting of two poly-lobed arches that end in serpentine motifs can be found at both ends of the cavity. The four cornerstones of the basin's edge are adorned with four full medallions. The cavity of this fountain consists of a hollow with a bordering edge. One of the two sides features an orifice that was once connected to piping. The basin's exterior form becomes narrower towards its base.
9b8ab3ff-1008-5ce8-b032-994aad3a8bf4.short_description: This rectangular basin is decorated with sculptures consisting of two poly-lobed arches finished with snake motifs. There are four full medallions in the four spandrels around the basin. This basin was probably used to provide water to the Palace of the Sea (Dar al-Bahr).

9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.name: Basin
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.description:
This basin was discovered in pieces at the end of the 19th century in the centre of Seville. Restoration work has reconstructed the bands of inscriptions, as well as the decoration on three of its sides.  
The front is decorated with three tri-lobed arches, framed by alfiz (frame) panels supported on columns. Each arch contains a plant sprouting leaves, palmettes, pinecones and intertwining stems. The space between the arch and the alfiz panel shows the same type of decoration, and the whole thing is framed by an inscribed strip.  
The right-hand side shows a space divided vertically into three parts. The central area is undecorated, probably to allow space for the water to come out, and the other two sides show similar scenes: eagles, seizing deer with their talons, bear two lions face to face on their outspread wings, while beneath them two griffins facing each other complete the scene. This iconography, of Sassanid origin, refers to power, abundance and eternity.  
Only the inscribed band is preserved from the third side, a strip with ducks and fishes, and, underneath it, the remains of a lion attacking a deer.  
We know from the inscription that this basin was commissioned for the royal palace of al-Zahira on the orders of al-Mansur, prime minister and favourite of Hisham II, who was still a child when he became Caliph in AH 366 / AD 976, following the death of his father al-Hakam II. The unstoppable rise to power of al-Mansur started shortly after the accession of Hisham II. With the intention of establishing a parallel dynasty to the legal Umayyad one, al-Mansur built a palatine city called Madinat al-Zahira. This new city, rival to Madinat al-Zahra, was in the eastern part of Córdoba, but limited material remains have survived to the present day. The city was burnt to the ground in AH 399 / AD 1009.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.short_description: Emulating the Umayyad caliphs who built Madinat al-Zahra, the hajib of Córdoba al-Mansur built the palatine city of Madinat al-Zahira, and he commissioned this ablutions basin for it, as stated on the inscription. Animal-shaped spouts would have emerged from the attached side pillars, of which only traces have survived.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.dimensions: Height 68 cm, width 150 cm, depth 77 cm.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_datation: The inscription in *kufic* lettering says: '…Almanzor Abi Amir Muhammad ben Abi Amir and glory to God. \[This was\] ordered to be made for the royal palace of al-Zahira and was finished with the help and assistance of God under the direction of the great Amiri Fata in the year seven seventy and three hundred'. Consequently, the basin has been dated to 377 / 988.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.method_for_provenance: There are two other basins attributable to the same period and place, one of which can be found in the Alhambra Museum, Grenada, and the other in Marrakesh (Morocco). This latter was made for ‘Abd al-Malik, son of Al-Mansur. The three pieces have similar decorations of eastern origin on one of their sides.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.provenance: The missing royal palace of Madinat al-Zahira (Córdoba), Spain.
9b938f78-dd1b-5b00-a709-62c11978cdc8.obtention: The basin arrived at the National Archaeological Museum in stages. The two most important parts, the front and part of one of the sides, were bought on 22 November 1882. Another fragment arrived in 1923. Finally, on 30 July 1930, the last piece arrived from the Provincial Archaeological Museum of Seville.

9bc77e5d-4437-5fe8-99a0-82dd01f0d23c.name: He who Gives the Drink
9bc77e5d-4437-5fe8-99a0-82dd01f0d23c.description:
The artistic work entitled *He Who Gives the Drink* (1979) by the artist Mohanna Durra, which is currently on display at the Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts, is a prime example of Durra's unique combination of social realism and expressive modernism. The image portrays an elderly man attired in traditional Jordanian clothing, meticulously pouring a beverage (potentially water or tea) into a bowl. This unassuming, quotidian act evolves into a poignant meditation on human generosity, humility, and resilience. Durra's adept handling of light and shadow accentuates the man's weathered face and hands, lending spiritual gravity to an intimate, commonplace gesture.  
The warm colour scheme, characterised by ochres and browns, interspersed with soft blues, serves to evoke the arid yet luminous atmosphere of Jordan's landscape. The architectural background, which is not rendered with great precision, situates the figure within a traditional urban setting, reminiscent of the old quarters of Amman. The subdued brushstrokes and tonal gradations capture both the material texture of the scene and the emotional depth of the subject, characteristics that are indicative of Durra's mature style.  
This painting is indicative of the artist's sustained interest in the dignity of labour and the moral strength of ordinary people. Durra's depiction of such figures positions him within a broader movement in Middle Eastern modern art that seeks to honour local identity through everyday realism. His work *He Who Gives the Drink* engages in a profound visual dialogue on charity, endurance and the cultural ethos of giving that defines Jordanian and Arab life.
9bc77e5d-4437-5fe8-99a0-82dd01f0d23c.holder: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts

9c040e27-f568-54de-b5a4-cbbcdf66d29c.name: Gourd Growing
9c040e27-f568-54de-b5a4-cbbcdf66d29c.description:
This type of gourd, grown in Hit, Anbar Governorate, Iraq, is among a number of varieties of calabash or "bottle gourd" of different shapes and sizes that were historically used as multipurpose vessels, including water bottles and containers for agricultural produce including beer and wine, milk and other dairy products, honey or grains. Cut segments of these gourds could also be used to make kitchen utensils such as ladles and bowls. They have been cultivated in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas for thousands of years for similar purposes.  
  
While the same gourds can be harvested young for consumption as a vegetable, if grown as containers or utensils they are left to grow for longer and harvested when mature. After harvesting, they are dried for several months until the outer shell becomes hard. The dried gourds are usually cut at the top to make an opening through which the seeds are removed and contents added for storage.
9c040e27-f568-54de-b5a4-cbbcdf66d29c.holder: Open Museum Initiative for Water Culture
9c040e27-f568-54de-b5a4-cbbcdf66d29c.author: Hannah Lewis

9c17568a-e2ca-5524-b5ae-c2d13aa4c2ac.name: The Beirut water factory
9c17568a-e2ca-5524-b5ae-c2d13aa4c2ac.short_description: Located in the suburb of Dbayeh, this factory provided the daily water supply for all of Beirut. The company was founded in 1873 and the factory was first opened in 1896. The water was taken from the Nahr al-Kalb river and distributed across a large water network.

9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.name: Irrigation bucket
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.description:
The cylindrical object features a straight mouth and pointed base, with retaining recesses located at the start of the mouth and base. The surface shows traces of hand modelling, leaving indentations on the body in the form of perimeter circumferences and on the base in parallel lines following the conical shape.  
  
Made of whitish porous, unglazed clay, it retains traces of *almagra* (reddish pigment) drips on both the exterior and interior. Functionally, such objects can be understood within the context of irrigation and hydraulic systems in al-Andalus. Their development enabled the introduction of new plant species, the expansion of arable land, and the diversification of the diet. These innovations changed working methods, the agricultural cycle, and the landscape.  
  
Waterwheels spread throughout the Iberian Peninsula. The waterwheel buckets, which were secured with ropes at the top and halfway down their cylindrical body, underwent technical improvements. These elements reflect a series of small but significant technical advances. The earliest ones, with an annular or pointed bottom, gradually were replaced by others with a perforated bottom that prevented their tilting and breakage in addition to the backward movement of the wheel.
9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.method_for_datation: Comparative study of typologies; references provided by previous owner.

9fe1e828-67e2-5249-a654-e86e4a5b6c0c.obtention: The bucket was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 1 January 1987.

a07c1b97-5ce9-5d4e-a870-1d3149e2561d.name: Badi Palace.
a07c1b97-5ce9-5d4e-a870-1d3149e2561d.description:
On 3 Sha'ban 986 / 4 October 1578, Ahmad al-Mansur achieved a resounding victory against the Portuguese at the Battle of Wadi al-Makhazin (also known as the Battle of Alcazarquivir / al-Qasr al-Kabir or the Three Kings), after which he was proclaimed sultan and received the title of 'Mansur' (the Victorious). Having achieved international renown, he decided to build a luxurious reception palace in the *kasbah* of Marrakesh.  
The work lasted 16 years and the palace was named 'Badi' (the Incomparable), one of the 99 names of Allah (moreover, *ksar l-bdi* in Moroccan Arabic means 'the porcelain palace', which could refer to the rich ceramic panels that profusely decorated the building). Montaigne, in his *Voyage en Italie*, reported that Italian craftsmen near Pisa were cutting, 'for the King of Fez in Barbary', 50 very tall marble columns which were paid for in sugar, weight for weight. And al-Ifrani reported that workmen from different countries, including in Europe, were recruited to execute the work.  
For three-quarters of a century, the Badi was the venue for all of the great ceremonies and parties given by the Sa'did sovereigns, and ended up with a reputation, more or less deserved, for excess and debauchery. This was the main reason why the 'Alawid king Mulay Isma'il (AH 1083–1140 / AD 1672–1727) ordered the complete destruction of the building and consequently all that remains today is a section of the 2 metre-thick outer wall, the esplanade, with remains of its pools and orchards, one of the pavilions with its columns and some decorative elements (stucco, marble, *zellij* – small tiles).  
However, excavations carried out in the 20th century, the discovery of two drawings of the palace (one Portuguese and one English) and the reports of contemporary chroniclers and foreign visitors give us a reasonably precise idea of how the Badi would have been in its heyday.  
The palace was constructed around an enormous rectangular courtyard measuring 135 m by 110 m, including a long central pool measuring 90 m by 20 m that contained a monumental fountain and had hollows on either side planted with trees and flowers and four small rectangular basins at the ends whose ceramic mosaic paving is still visible. The east side of the palace looked out over a large garden known as 'the crystal garden'.  
Two pavilions measuring 15 m by 16 m were built half way along the shorter sides of the courtyard and two more measuring 23 m by 15 m in the middle of the longer sides. Truncated-pyramid towers stood in the corners of the courtyard.  
The pavilions were crowned with domes whose ceilings were encrusted with gold and precious *muqarnas* (honeycomb work) supported by marble columns with capitals covered with golden leaves. The floors and walls were covered with faience mosaics, the doors were made of sculpted wood and, throughout, the fountains gushed water from the mouths of lions, leopards and pythons sculpted in solid silver.
a07c1b97-5ce9-5d4e-a870-1d3149e2561d.short_description:
For 75 years the Badi, destroyed under the 'Alawids, hosted all of the celebrations held by Sa'did sovereigns.  
The palace was built around an enormous courtyard endowed with five ceramic-tile pools and leading to large garden. Central pavilions flanked by two towers were built at the centre of each of the sides. Its decoration was extremely sumptuous, with gold-encrusted *muqarnas* (honeycomb work), Italian marble, mosaics and solid-silver fountain heads. Part of the outer wall, the esplanade with remains of the pools, one of the pavilions with its columns, and some decorative elements have survived.
a07c1b97-5ce9-5d4e-a870-1d3149e2561d.method_for_datation: According to al-Ifrani, based on the poetic inscriptions that decorated the palace (now lost), work started in the month of Shawwal 986 (December 1578) and was completed in 1002 / 1594.

a082fcd1-6ab8-5065-913f-e8b18e48249c.name: Acte habous
a082fcd1-6ab8-5065-913f-e8b18e48249c.description:
This historical and religious document, dated 1952, records the donation of a tour d’eau (water turn) as a waqf—an Islamic charitable endowment. Issued in Marrakech, it reflects a long-standing tradition in Islamic societies where essential resources like land, property, or water rights are donated for the benefit of the community or religious institutions.In this case, the water right was endowed to ensure ongoing access to irrigation or domestic water use, often for a mosque, madrasa, or a public fountain (*sabil*).  
  
Such donations were considered acts of piety and social responsibility, intended to bring spiritual merit to the donor while serving the collective good. The document is not only a legal record but also a cultural artefact that illustrates how water was governed as both a sacred trust and a communal asset in Moroccan society.It highlights the intricate connection between Islamic law, environmental ethics, and local governance, where water—an essential and scarce resource—was managed through deeply rooted moral and religious frameworks. This *waqf stands as a testament to how water endowments helped structure equitable access, social cohesion, and religious devotion in everyday life.*

a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.name: Alhambra vase.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.description:
This piece is one of the so-called 'Alhambra vases'. Formally, all of these are similar: a large egg-shaped body and a narrow, unglazed base from which two large, flat handles emerge, and an octagonal neck reinforced with vertical mouldings.  
The decoration of pale gold on a white base is arranged horizontally in broad bands of different widths that are separated from one another by other smooth, narrower bands. The central, and widest, band contains vegetal motifs and an inscription in *kufic* characters in white on a golden background, in which the word 'forgiveness' is repeated several times. Both above and below the central band there are other similar bands decorated with plant arabesques and gold circles, all joined by a thread. The decoration of the main body is completed by another two bands, one on the lower part with small arches and another nearer the neck with a *kufic* inscription, now almost completely disappeared.  
The neck, which has eight sides separated by mouldings, is decorated with stylised vegetal motifs. The handles, attached close to the body, are decorated with the hand of Fatima (*hamsa*) on each side.  
The Alhambra vases constitute the most important examples of Nasrid ceramic production. These pieces became extremely well known for their delicate decoration and large size, and were exported to other places. The best-preserved examples are to be found in Palermo (Regional Museum of Sicily), St Petersburg (Hermitage), Stockholm (National Museum of Fine Arts) and Madrid (Institute of Valencia de D. Juan and the National Archaeological Museum). Some are decorated exclusively in gold and others in gold and cobalt-blue, always on a tin-glaze background.  
Although its form derives from large storage vessels, its cumbersome size and the absence of any strengthening elements in the handles suggest a purely ornamental function.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.short_description: The so-called ‘Alhambra vases’ were luxury items because of the technical complexity of their manufacture and the beauty of their decoration and lustrework. The intended use is not known, but their renown led them to be exported to Sicily and Mamluk Egypt.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_datation: It is difficult to determine the date of manufacture of these vases. Nonetheless, all writers agree that, on the basis of the inscription, the oldest examples are those decorated solely with gold on white, which were produced from the last third of the 7th / 13th century and, in particular, during the 8th / 14th century.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.method_for_provenance: Although all of these pieces are known generically as the Alhambra vases, they were produced in Malaga and exported. From the 7th / 13th century, Arab writers begin to mention Malaga as a large centre for the production and export of ceramics with gold or metallic highlights.
a0a31a62-7361-5268-8ad7-1a7b0126f09d.obtention: The piece was found by chance at the beginning of the 20th century during work to shore up vaults in the monastery of Santa María de la Defensión in Jerez de la Frontera (Cadiz). It was donated to the National Archaeological Museum on 29 July 1930.

a2abf9d6-891e-59a0-9c6b-0f36d803394d.name: Beaded Water Glass
a2abf9d6-891e-59a0-9c6b-0f36d803394d.description: A massive glass made of transparent, grey-toned glass with bubbles, cylindrical shape, set on a low, round pedestal base, from Avram Petronijević's Manufacture. The walls of the glass are wrapped with a bead embroidery with floral motifs. The central decoration is a wreath pattern, displaying the Cyrillic initials "M.C.", with the year 1855 shown on the opposite side of the glass. The initials are those of the embroiderer, Marija Stojković (Cyrillic: Марија Стојковић) from Belgrade, with the year reflective of the time of the ornamentation. The appearance of glassware items decorated with beads was very popular in the bourgeois houses of the 19th century where women's hand-made works were highly appreciated. Several similar items with beads originating from Belgrade families, including this beaded water glass, have been preserved in the collection of the Museum of Applied Arts.
a2abf9d6-891e-59a0-9c6b-0f36d803394d.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.

a2b8f43a-d5fd-57c1-a88e-b1fc3a6097b2.name: *Laylā visits Majnūn in the Wilderness*
a2b8f43a-d5fd-57c1-a88e-b1fc3a6097b2.description: Majnūn, emaciated and clad only in loincloth, is seated in the wilderness under a large tree. Reclining about him are wild beasts and waterfowl along the stream. On the further bank facing Majnūn sits Laylā, four maids standing behind her. The nearer one salutes Majnūn, her hand raised to her forehead, the second carries a large peacock plume, and the third holds a scarf in her hands, while the fourth (dark-skinned), whose head only is seen, stands behind the other two. Laylā is wearing a *coli* (tight fitting bodice) and a figured skirt. On her head is a large conical-shaped *mukuta* (crown) with *sarpes* (plume). She also wears a *keyura* (armlet), and a *mala* (necklace). In the foreground, where Majnūn sits, recline a gazelle, a tiger and a lion; on the other side of the stream recline an antelope and its mate. Along the bank are herons, cranes and ducks. In the background are high rocky hills and a large river seen to the right with a heavily forested bank. Cranes fly across the sky and songbirds can be seen in the tree above Majnūn. The sky is dark.

a2bff875-de56-5054-ba77-30b1b3d100cd.name: *Au bord du Nil* (On the Banks of the Nile)
a2bff875-de56-5054-ba77-30b1b3d100cd.description:
Often called the father of modern Egyptian sculpture, Mahmoud Mokhtar united the art of his country's pharaonic past with the 20th century to convey the spirit of a newly independent Egypt. The artist aspired to create an artistic language that would reconcile contemporary Egyptian society with its cultural and historical identity.  
Throughout his career, Mokhtar drew inspiration from scenes of everyday life in Egypt's countryside and he frequently depicted the fallaha (peasant woman). Au Bord du Nil is a life-size statue that shows a fallaha wearing a tarha (traditional Egyptian veil) and holding a balas (jug used to transport water) on her head. The fallaha was a leitmotif in the artist's output, representing Egypt and the Nile Delta as an intrinsic part of the nation. The sculpture exemplifies Mokhtar's clean, bold and angular lines, evoking the ancient priestesses who walked the Nile's banks.  
  
*Au Bord du Nil* sends a clear, powerful message in response to the turbulent political climate of the 1930s (AH 1348), when Egypt was under British military administration. At the time, the Egyptian people's desire to reclaim national sovereignty had grown, prompting Mokhtar to transform the fallaha into a nationalist emblem.
a2bff875-de56-5054-ba77-30b1b3d100cd.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art

a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.name: "Amr has the Infidels Thrown into the Sea"
a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.alternate_name: Folio from a Khavarannama (The Book of the East) of ibn Husam al-Din
a507b49f-de2b-5383-b587-8eef58a18a27.description: This painting, with its vibrant color palette and lively action, is taken from a manuscript of the Khavarannama (Book of the East), a gathering of tales relating the adventures of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad. These mostly imaginary accounts of the exploits of 'Ali and his companions against demons, dragons, and kings were composed in emulation of the great Persian poet Firdausi’s Shahnama, but have the important religious figure of 'Ali as their main protagonist.

a51d8bae-57d0-5565-9480-72d8b94775ba.name: 'The Paths of Paradise'
a51d8bae-57d0-5565-9480-72d8b94775ba.description:
The miniature, which like 13/2012 and 14/2012 comes from a manuscript describing Muhammad’s mystical ascension to heaven (*miraj*), shows the Prophet and the Archangel Gabriel (*Jibril*) at the pond of al-Kawthar before one of Paradise’s richly ornamented gates. Both the ribbed domes and tiled walls are covered with rich vegetal ornamentation of various types, in keeping with contemporary architecture from Central Asia. Beside the pond are countless vessels of gold and jade and celadon-glazed ceramics from which the believer can quench his thirst after the tribulations of the Day of Judgment.  
  
The Garden of Paradise itself, with its many spiritual and sensual delights, is not depicted in this beautiful painting, and no artist would probably have been able to describe it to the believer as intensely as accounts in the Koran and later writings.  
  
Of the museum’s seven paintings from this manuscript, the refined ‘Gates of Paradise’ is the one that most clearly points toward the artistic zenith of Timurid painting at the end of the AH 9th / AD 15th century.

a56a9bf0-2b17-5702-8aa1-d72790e9ec02.name: Tumbler
a56a9bf0-2b17-5702-8aa1-d72790e9ec02.description:
The glass is bell-shaped and rests on a wider, cylindrical base. It is embossed with engraved motifs. The front displays the initials "A.K." encircled by a garland. The opposite side and rim display a floral motif. An 1844 Austrian coin was placed inside the glass' stand.  
It was determined by comparison and stylistic analysis that the glass was most likely created in the first glass manufactory of the Principality of Serbia, which was owned by Avram Petronijević, the then Minister of Foreign Affairs and the envoy at the Sublime Porte. At the invitation of Avram Petronijević, glassmakers came from Bohemian and Bavarian glasshouses. Considering that the manufactory operated during a very short period, from 1846 to 1852, only a small number of items can be reliably linked to its production and few have been preserved. Most items were caste or mould blown. They are distinguished by their common characteristics: a greyish tone of glass that testifies to the presence of lead, the presence of bubbles in the glass mass, and the thick walls of the object. They were heavy, but harmonious shapes, such as this very rare example that was most likely made for a particular person.
a56a9bf0-2b17-5702-8aa1-d72790e9ec02.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.

a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.name: Two Chinese blue-and-white porcelain sealed ‘Zamzam’ water bottles
a5f7ac5a-c7e3-5149-8a1c-17cd76006305.short_description:
Prophet was known to drink from the well and use the water for significant purposes. The most famous *hadith* (Prophetic saying) regarding Zamzam states that the water is good for whatever purpose it is intended. Thus, over time, the water has been used for many purposes: in graves, to prevent harm, to cure and in ceremonies to obtain blessings.  
Similar examples to these bottles are in the Topkapi Palace in Istanbul and were used during ceremonies involving the mantle of the Prophet. During these ceremonies the mantle was dipped in Zamzam water and what dripped from the cloth was then collected in bottles similar to these. Other comparable types were simply sent from Mecca to Istanbul containing Zamzam water and closed with leather, string and sealed with wax.  
The well is believed to have been discovered by Hagar and Ismael, after being abandoned by Abraham in Mecca. It was later rediscovered by ‘Abd al-Muttalib, Prophet Muhammad’s grandfather, who is credited with having dug several wells, most importantly that of Zamzam. From then on the responsibility of giving water to pilgrims was to remain in the lineage of one of his sons.  
Water from the well of Zamzam was previously collected in buckets by a rope pulley mechanism and then transferred to earthenware vessels. Now the well is entirely managed subterraneously by electric pumps and the King Abdullah Zamzam Water Factory produces approximately 200,000 bottles of water a day.

a672ca3f-2b88-56b6-9ef8-4b188d9eb591.name: Jug
a672ca3f-2b88-56b6-9ef8-4b188d9eb591.short_description: This jug, with its rounded body, cylindrical neck with cover and dragon-shaped handle, is one of the few surviving examples of sixteenth-century Ottoman silver. Several similar objects are currently preserved in museums and collections outside Turkey. The jug is reminiscent of the metal or jade Timurid vessels inspired by the art of the Mongol period. The differences concern not so much the shape as the various decoration techniques: whereas the Timurid metal vessels are inlaid with silver, the Ottoman wares feature hammered, engraved, and chiselled motifs. The raised decoration on the body, neck and cover is characteristic of the first half of the sixteenth century: the composition combines *rumi* (half-palmettes) arabesques and motifs of Chinese origin. This decorative repertoire, still closely linked to Timurid traditions, but likewise indebted to Balkan silver, was also typical for the Ottoman ceramics of the time. The jug was probably donated to the Monastery of Bistriţa (Vâlcea County) by a boyar or a voivode. Its exquisite workmanship testifies to the opulence and refinement of the Romanian princely courts, extensively documented, but illustrated only by a few extant objects.

a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.name: Süleymaniye waterway map.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.description:
The Süleymaniye waterway map is handmade on unfinished paper. The waterway was designed to supply water to the entire complex of the mosque, including its *imaret* (soup-kitchen), *maristan* (hospital), *maktab* (school) and public fountains. Fed by the Aypah (Kirazlı) and çınar springs, the highest-capacity branches of the Halkalı water supply system, this waterway supplied the Süleymaniye Complex as well as 80 other points in Istanbul. The map shows the waterway in detail from its source all the way to its end, including the places where it is joined by other waterways, the points where it enters the city through the walls, and especially the water-distribution centres and aqueducts.  
  
The map was prepared without a scale and has a schematic style. Therefore, many structures and neighbourhoods cannot be precisely placed. At the far end of the map there is the drawing of the Süleymaniye Complex.  
  
Such waterway maps tell the story of water from springs being conveyed via pipes, crossing valleys in aqueducts, its pressure adjusted at certain points, being sent off in various directions at distribution centres and reaching public fountains. These maps also provide information about the urban structure; how people lived, and the infrastructure and buildings in a given quarter. For example, the Roman Aqueduct of Valens (AD 375), known as Bozdoğan Aqueduct in Turkish is introduced as 'the big aqueduct in the Horse Market'. The names of the people and the structures receiving water from this aqueduct are also given. The water of the Halkalı network could be distributed to private estates only on the written permission of the sultan. For instance, we find the house of Süleyman the Magnificent's dentist, Moshe Hamon, (AH 899–962 / AD 1490–1554) listed as 'House of Hamudoğlu'.  
  
From the Süleymaniye Complex waterway map, we learn not only how the water was brought to the city but also about the quarters where the courtiers and dignitaries resided. Therefore, the waterway maps are important for describing the social topography of the city.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.short_description: Istanbul has always suffered from water shortage due to a lack of sufficient springs nearby and its demand was met by conveying water via aqueducts from afar. Waterway maps provide information about the routes from the springs to the city, monuments on the way and the social structure of the city.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.dates: Hegira second half of the 12th century / AD 18th century.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.method_for_datation: Although the map does not have a date it is clear from the names of people and structures therein that this is an 18th-century document. For example, it is known that water was supplied to Taygun Palace in 1161 / 1748, a building shown on this map; therefore, this map must have been prepared after 1161 / 1748.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.method_for_provenance: The map does not bear any date. However, that our copy is an 18th copy is clear from the names of people and structures given therein. For example, it is known that water was supplied to Taygun Palace in 1161 / 1748, a building shown on our map; therefore, this map must have been prepared after 1161 / 1748. Public services such as the water supply were under the supervision of the state and due to this fact the waterway would have been designed and constructed by the official architects of the Topkapı Palace.
a7ce0231-54e8-5757-928a-48c3c0b66585.obtention: The map was transferred to the museum in 1923 from the Directorate of Supplies for Pious Foundations.

a842940f-0cc2-5088-a04d-869d51b9464b.name: Pitcher, with one handle
a842940f-0cc2-5088-a04d-869d51b9464b.description:
Uncovered in an unbuilt area adjacent to a cluster of five houses, this pitcher was discovered during the 2007 excavation by the Qatari-French Mission. The unconstructed space between the houses featured temporary installations, potentially serving as open-air kitchens, marked by ash and fireplaces.  
This jar features a single handle, a flared globular body, and a small flat base. Its body is adorned with a horizontal incised line as a decorative element. Crafted from red clay and adorned with a cream slip, the entire lower section of the body retains traces of red pigment. This kitchen vessel likely served the purpose of storing and transporting liquids.

a8c174f0-6099-5aad-945f-087eadc119af.name: Zawiya al-Ahmadiyya
a8c174f0-6099-5aad-945f-087eadc119af.description:
The zawiya is attributed to the shaykh Ahmad Ibn Ibrahim Ibn Muhammad Ibn Bakr, known as al-Badawi (d. AH 675 / AD 1276). He was a famous sufi who lived in Tanta, Egypt, with many followers both inside and outside the area. The foundation inscription above the entrance portal reveals that the Amir Tarantay al-Yukandar the wali of Gaza, constructed the zawiya in AH 731/ AD 1330–1331, during the reign of the Amir Tankiz al-Nasiri.  
  
The zawiya consists of two main sections: the prayer hall and the lodging wing. The square-plan prayer hall lies in the southern part of the building, and its side is 8.5 m. long. A stone dome that stands on a polygonal drum, pierced by many windows for ventilation, covers the prayer hall. The mihrab is in the Mamluk style. The lodging wing consists of a large, square interior courtyard, covered with a cross vault. In the centre is an octagonal fountain, used for ablutions. The water for the fountain was supplied from the neighbouring rivulet, which also supplied water for the air-cooling system. The hall overlooks the front courtyard from the west through two pointed arches. Three rectangular vaulted iwans surround it and each overlooks the external courtyard through a doublevaulted window.

a96d02ab-fea4-5e29-9dc5-16c7773c9331.name: Ewer for Zamzam water
a96d02ab-fea4-5e29-9dc5-16c7773c9331.short_description: The ewer is unsual in that the cover for the mouth and the stopper for the spout are both screw-threaded, which allows them to be securely sealed in place. This implies that their purpose was more than keeping insects and the like away form the contents; rather, they were meant to minimize evaporation, a factor which has lead to the designation of such vessels as containers for Zamzam water. The somewhat flattened sides also allowed the ewer to be carried suspended from a saddle during the journey back from hajj. An almost identical ewer in the Louvre, Paris, which was on display at the Louvre Abu Dhabi in March 2018, still retains the chain which allowed the ewer to be suspended from the two loops on its sides, and which is now missing from the Khalili ewer.

a9aec9e3-3257-571d-870d-3f39027411af.name: Basin
a9aec9e3-3257-571d-870d-3f39027411af.description:
Carved from a single piece of marble, the basin is rectangular in shape and shallow. One of its short sides has a semicircular recess, while its interior has a drain hole with a cover. The rim of the basin is wide and decorated with a flat frieze. The interior of the piece features bas-relief decoration. This consists of wading birds flanking intertwined fish on the long sides; on the short sides, there is a bird devouring a fish. On the outside, in addition to a perimeter moulding, there is an unfinished relief of a dromedary.  
  
In this regard, the basin is part of the wider water architecture of al-Andalus. After a period of ruralisation, urban life was revived there and the ancient water supply systems were renovated and expanded. Basins, decorative fountains and irrigation channels were essential components of Andalusian spaces where gardens and architecture coexisted to create cool and relaxing atmospheres enriched by the sounds and scents of water. Within this context, the supply and display of water symbolised wealth, power, and well-being, reflecting the image of paradise.  
  
From a technical view, this basin could be a reused Visigoth cymatium, hollowed out and engraved in relief. The decoration is concentrated on the interior walls, where wading birds and fish seem to dive and jump with the flow of water and the incidence of light.
a9aec9e3-3257-571d-870d-3f39027411af.place_of_production: Unknown, probably province of Córdoba, Spain

aa5417bd-aa61-5f36-9773-6c9fbf9885ab.name: Customised Toyota Truck
aa5417bd-aa61-5f36-9773-6c9fbf9885ab.description:
Almost unrecognisable, this Toyota Land Cruiser, once produced in Japan, is transformed into a decorated Pakistani truck. Fitted with a barrel, it was used for the transportation and distribution of water. The truck exhibits a large tank with a painted mural: decorative vegetal motifs of branches, leaves, and trees, along with lobed arches, ornamental oval medallions, intersecting geometric designs, architectural depictions and bird motifs such as the peacock.  
  
Mughal traditions of embellishing carts and carriages survived as an expression of art, national identity and personal taste. Motifs, such as the peacock, religious sites like the Kaaba, and flowers and vegetation narrate the storied heritage of Pakistani truck art and their owners.

ac1f2fa2-5a55-53f8-9fa5-bd7d22b5f627.name: *al-Qanatir*
ac1f2fa2-5a55-53f8-9fa5-bd7d22b5f627.description: *al-Qanatir* refers to two massive stone dams located south of al-Qastal and the town of Zizya. The word *al-qanatir* is derived from the Arabic word qanat, referring to water systems in the form of chains of wells or dams that were used to irrigate agricultural estates. These dams were used to collect and store rain water for the dry summer months. Even though the exact date of these two dams cannot be ascertained, it is more or less certain that they date back to the Umayyad period.
ac1f2fa2-5a55-53f8-9fa5-bd7d22b5f627.author: Lara Tohme

acc57934-ae32-5e43-8f31-305447337577.name: Water pumping equipment in Kağıthane, Istanbul
acc57934-ae32-5e43-8f31-305447337577.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902 at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique monument to the history of the architecture industry in the Ottoman Empire. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – in the direction of Tophane, moving water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane using steam pump machines.

keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; History of Water in Ottoman Empire; Water Pump Station

ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.name: Blossoming almond trees.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.description:
One of Portugal's most well-known legends tells of how it was that almond trees came to be part of the landscape of the southern region of the country. An Arab prince, married to a Christian from the north, noticed that his wife lived in a permanent state of melancholy, and so one day he asked her for the reason for this enduring mood. She told him that she missed the snow, frequent in the north of the Peninsula, but which rarely fell in the more southerly regions. The prince then ordered the planting of almond trees, whose blossoming at the end of the winter would create the illusion of fields covered with snow.  
This romantic and highly lyrical legend does nevertheless contain some basis of truth and demonstrates deep links with the Portuguese land.  
Al-Mu'tamid, a poet and lord of the Abbadid dynasty (AH 461–84 / AD 1069–91), one day set a challenge to Ibn Amar, as they were travelling along the Guadalquivir: 'The breeze turns the river / into a coat of mail'. The response came from Itimad, a slave woman of Romaik: 'A better coat of mail cannot be found / since the river freezes it'. Impressed by the slave's beauty and by her poetic inspiration, al-Mu'tamid took her as his wife and made her queen. The family and geographical origins of Itimad were confined to helping construct the legend. Although the story told relates to the region of Seville, al-Mu'tamid was born in Beja and was a lord of Silves, having later governed a large part of the south of the Iberian Peninsula.  
Deposed from power, al-Mu'tamid ended up living in exile in Morocco, where he died on 30 Dhu'l-Hijja 487 / 10 January 1095. Itimad lies at his side in a mausoleum in Agmat.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.short_description: Towards the end of the winter, the landscape of the Algarve is marked by blossoming almond trees. Legend has it that they were planted by an Arab prince in homage to his beloved, who came from the north, in order to create the illusion of snow, which is rare in the south. The legend is based on the romance between the Abbadid prince Al-Mu‘tamid and the slave girl Itimad. Impressed by her beauty and poetic inspiration, Al-Mu‘tamid married her and made her queen. Itimad’s geographical and family background helped to create the legend.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.dates: From the earliest Muslim presence in the region.
ada30dbf-d7f6-59db-9686-df60e9f94fc9.author: Isabel Cristina Ferreira Fernandes
keywords: almond trees; Southern Portugal; landscape; legend; traditions; al-Mu'tamid

ada80603-3bb0-5613-bff0-989bc6936a22.name: Calligraphy
ada80603-3bb0-5613-bff0-989bc6936a22.description:
This composition features the Qur’anic declaration:  
Arabic: وَجَعَلْنَا مِنَ الْمَاءِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَيٍّ  
Transliteration: *Ve cealnâ mine’l-mâ’i kulle şey’in hayy*  
English: “And We created every living thing from water.”  
Renowned calligrapher Hasan Çelebi presents the verse with his characteristic mastery of classical Ottoman *sülüs* and *nesih* forms. The sweeping curves and disciplined strokes create a rhythmic visual structure that mirrors the verse’s theme: the emergence and vitality of life through water.  
The work’s balanced layout and refined linework reflect the artist’s dedication to traditional aesthetics, while the verse’s universal message invites viewers to contemplate the sacred origins of life and the sustaining role of water in the natural world.
ada80603-3bb0-5613-bff0-989bc6936a22.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
ada80603-3bb0-5613-bff0-989bc6936a22.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece.
ada80603-3bb0-5613-bff0-989bc6936a22.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

ae5a92a8-98ae-588a-a771-9a2c3a38eb09.name: *Al Rahaa* (Millstone)
ae5a92a8-98ae-588a-a771-9a2c3a38eb09.description: *Al Rahaa* (millstone) is used to grind grains, such as wheat and barley to make flour. Grain is fed between the two stones through the central hole. The top stone is turned using the handle and this action crushes the grain.

afa75823-03d1-5b8b-9466-52bd507fdea6.name: *al-azīzi falaj* log
afa75823-03d1-5b8b-9466-52bd507fdea6.description:
This manuscript, completed in February 1891 CE by the skilled Omani scribe Rabiʿah bin Majid bin Suleiman al-Kindi, offers a vivid glimpse into the life and rhythms of Seiq Town, in the Jabal Bani Riyam range of al-Jabal al-Akhdar (ad-Dakhiliyah Governorate). Written in a clear and confident hand, it records the intricate water-sharing system of the ʿFalaj al-ʿAzīzī, a vital lifeline for the community.  
  
Unlike most *falaj* logs in Oman, this copy replaces common distribution units with the ṭāsah, a pierced copper vessel whose draining time measured each turn of irrigation. Within its pages are the names of landowners, gardens, mosques, and endowments, each evoking the people and places that shaped this mountain community. Sixty-two irrigation cycles, alternating between day and night, are marked with care, the beginnings signalled by graceful elongated letters.  
  
Its final section sets out the rules for calculating the *falaj*’s rotation, preserving the knowledge and order on which the community’s survival depended, a timeless record of both master engineering skills and human cooperation.
afa75823-03d1-5b8b-9466-52bd507fdea6.provenance: Moved from Ministry of Heritage and Culture, Oman (now Ministry of Heritage and Tourism)
