aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.name: *Hajj Day*
aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.description:
Abdulhalim Radwi often evoked his hometown of Mecca, emphasising the importance of the Ka’ba as a source of universal energy and a religious symbol.  
In Hajj Day, the Ka’ba is surrounded by a central circle around which various elements of the composition revolve. The artist manipulates perspective so that near and far elements converge and intersect around the Ka’ba. Facial features are absent, and the artist has stripped the city of Mecca of all detail except for the main elements - the Ka’ba, the overlapping mountains and the pilgrims coming for the Hajj.  
  
In contrast to his colourful scenes, Radwi removes the vibrant colours in this work, opting for a monochrome palette to emphasise the unity of the elements under this universal energy. In his series depicting Mecca, the artist emphasises the importance of Mecca as a place of peace, where there is no difference between people, who are all there for the same reason regardless of their cultures or social status.  
  
Radwi often uses Arabic words and letterforms in his artwork, including religious expressions such as Allah; *bismillah*, or 'in the name of God'; *and la illah ila Allah*, or 'there is no god but God'), as well as other Arabic expressions. This demonstrates Radwi's commitment to incorporating an Arab and Muslim identity into his work. In addition, his continued use of visual symbols such as crescents and other motifs underlines the importance of these symbols as signs of cultural heritage.
aff8cde7-1f94-523b-b92a-5dd0a0feaca4.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art
keywords: Hajj; day; Mecca; Zam Zam; Zamzam

b00aafcf-8e21-51f7-9183-e6c70742dd92.name: Glass bottle
b00aafcf-8e21-51f7-9183-e6c70742dd92.description:
This small green blown-glass bottle was discovered during the 2003 excavation of the city of al Zubarah. It dates from the AH 12th–13th century / AD 18th to 19th centuries.  
  
Due to its small size, this container was used to store perfume or precious oils and was probably manufactured in the Levant
b00aafcf-8e21-51f7-9183-e6c70742dd92.author: Alexandrine Guerin, Tania Abdulmonem Al Majid

b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.name: *Haal* (Cardamom)
b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.description:
*Haal* (Cardamom) used to flavour the coffee.  
Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving dallah referred to as a mezallah, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the mezallah with their left hand and distribute the fanayeel (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.*
b01b60d5-e457-5cea-b280-e145d44183d1.dates: Hegira mid 14th century / AD mid 20th century

b0b32448-07f0-5aaa-8b81-cade08d4c6f4.name: Fountain and *sabil* of Ahmed III.
b0b32448-07f0-5aaa-8b81-cade08d4c6f4.description:
The Fountain of Ahmed III is located between the Bab-ı Hümayun (the Imperial Gate of Topkapı Palace) and Ayasofya Museum. It is a square structure with a *sabil* in each corner. In the centre is an octagonal water tank encircled by a corridor.  
In the centre of each façade there is a fountain crowned with a pointed arch and flanked with a niche crowned with *muqarnas* on both sides. On the rear side, the niches are replaced with two doorways providing access to the *sabils.*  
Each of the semi-circular corner *sabil*s has a low wall-surround of about one meter; the walls support four columns connected to each other with multifoil arches. The arches in between the columns are closed off by metal latticework. The walls that continue above the latticework are also semi-circular.  
The entire structure has a timber roof protruding in wide eaves. Plated with lead, the roof is crowned with five domes, a large one in the centre and four smaller ones above the *sabil*s. These timber domes rise on octagonal drums. The domes are also plated with lead and crowned with gilded bronze standards. The decorative schema is evidently based on *horror vacui*. The marble facades are entirely decorated with various motifs from both Turkish and European art.  
On the façades, the horizontal bands of *muqarnas*,arabesquesand palmettes as well as the foliate compositions around the fountains are noteworthy. Flowers in a vase executed in low-relief are found on both the façades and the lower walls of the *sabil*s. The use of decorative tiles and calligraphic script, together with the tulip motifs on the latticework, are also exceptional. The wide, timber eaves have decorative woodwork. The upper sections of the façades are decorated with compositions of coffers, while above the corner *sabil*s are various floral and fruit compositions.  
Many fountains and *sabil*s were built in the so-called 'Tulip Era' (AH 1130–42 / AD 1718–30), when the Westernisation period of Ottoman art began. Fountains, which up until this period had been placed on walls or in courtyards, now started to be built as independent structures. As new elements in the city's silhouette, such fountains and *sabil*s are seen as the first structures to reveal the foreign influence on Ottoman architecture. The most monumental of the square fountains, the Fountain and *Sabil* of Ahmed III with its design and decorative programme is an important structure revealing the transition from the Classical Ottoman period to that of Westernisation period.
b0b32448-07f0-5aaa-8b81-cade08d4c6f4.short_description: Ottoman fountains built in public squares, of which the Fountain of Ahmed is an important example, assumed a monumental character in the AH 12th / AD 18th century. On each of the four corners is a *sabil* (water-dispensary kiosk) and in the centre of each of the four sides is a fountain. Located in front of the Imperial Gate of Topkapı Palace, it is an important example of the so-called Tulip Era with its wide eaves and rich decoration.
b0b32448-07f0-5aaa-8b81-cade08d4c6f4.method_for_datation: The inscription on the fountain itself and on the *sabil*s is a *qasidah* by Seyyid Vehbi. It is inferred from this inscription that the structure was built on the suggestion of Damat Ibrahim Pasha of Nevşehir, the grand *vizier*, in AH 1141/ AD 1729. The couplet giving the date was composed by Sultan Ahmed III himself. A document dated to Ramadan 1141 (April 1729) provides evidence that there was a demand for local pure white, veinless marble from Marmara Island, indicating that the structure had not yet been completed by this date.

b0b32448-07f0-5aaa-8b81-cade08d4c6f4.architects: The name of the architect is unknown, but it is inferred that the structure was built during the time when the head-architect at the Topkapı Palace was Mehmed Agha of Kayseri, who also gilded the alems (standards) and latticework of this Fountain.

b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.name: Hornos vase
b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.description: Pear-shaped vase with a narrow base decorated with six rings. It has a tall, faceted, flared neck, a wide, protruding rim, and wing handles. The decoration combines gold and cobalt on a cream ground, forming segments of blue listels on the main body which are filled with vegetal compositions based on palms, palmettes, and pines. This vertical partition is repeated on the neck where, over two friezes framed in blue and decorated in reserve over a gold ground, salient edges are added. The first of the friezes features a cursive calligraphic inscription; the second, interlaces. The wing handles also feature small-scale vegetal decoration, overlaid with palmette scrolls. Reflecting the splendour of the Nasrid courts, the so-called Alhambra vases were considered luxury items. They were frequently mentioned as gifts and praised in the chronicles of Medieval travellers. These vases were manufactured in specialised workshops using complex lusterware techniques in gold and cobalt blue; they often included short poems of the fajr genre, or boastful style, reflecting on the object's beauty, contents, and use. Specifically, as translated by Eduardo Saavedra in 1875, the inscription around the neck of the Vase of Hornos praises the value of water: "Every fountain springs forth, resembling the most perfect stream, and increases abundant kindness and excellent joys. And it affirms the memory of happiness and poverty that faded away morning and evening with the fortune of time."
b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.provenance: Church of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, Hornos (province of Jaén, Spain)
b2223947-ef0b-51d1-93ae-384d3496e7ab.obtention: Unearthed during plowing, the vase was moved to the Church of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción, where it served as holy water stoup. First acquired by V. Juan y Amat, then deposited at the Valencia Institute of Don Juan. Later purchased by the Spanish State for the National Archaeological Museum.

b2e397c6-490b-55a7-9d8c-c7b2478e307e.name: Metal ewer with decorated handle
b2e397c6-490b-55a7-9d8c-c7b2478e307e.description:
A metal ewer with a swollen, rounded body and a short conical neck. The handle is decoratively shaped and more elaborate than earlier forms. The surface shows corrosion with traces of patina.  
This ewer was known as *Rafīq al-Jumʿah* (The Friday Companion), as it was used specifically on Friday mornings. The men of the household would gather around it to perform ablution one after another, and the sound of water striking the metal would rise like a purifying melody, restoring clarity to the soul before they engaged with the world. These ewers were always placed in elevated spots, as people believed that vessels used for ablution were not merely tools, but honoured hosts for water that would touch the body before reaching the heart.

b338f0aa-7763-5cb1-95e1-558ff691b64d.name: Bowl
b338f0aa-7763-5cb1-95e1-558ff691b64d.short_description: This round-bottomed brass bowl with bulging sides was raised from a single sheet of brass and was finished by turning and polishing. Its engraved designs have been thickly inlaid with silver. Used for washing, it would have been proffered at arms’ length by a servant while another servant poured scented water from a similarly decorated jug or ewer over the hands of the bowl’s owner or guest. From that distance, the detail of the decoration as well as the Arabic inscription running around the exterior of the bowl could be appreciated. The fish within the bowl would have appeared to wriggle and swim as the water splashed over them.
b338f0aa-7763-5cb1-95e1-558ff691b64d.author: Alessandra Cirelli
keywords: Brass; bowl; inscription; roundel; silver; engraved
materials: Brass; engraved and inlaid with silver

b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.name: *Sabil* of Sultan Qaytbay.
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.description:
The *sabil*, which is approximately 13 m high, consists of three sections. The first section is the square base, the walls of which open up to high windows in three directions, and a door that leads inside the *sabil* and opens out on to the fourth, east-facing direction. In each corner of the structure there is a pillar that is supported by the base and ends with a *muqarnas* capital with hewn-out decoration. The second section of the *sabil* edifice is the middle section comprising the drum of the dome, and the zone of transition between the base and the dome. At the corners of the drum, small piers are erected which are pyramidal in shape and facilitate the transition from the high square of the base to an octagonal, and then into a 12-sided polygon. The third section of the building is the high stone dome which is decorated with distinctive arabesque ornamentation. This dome is considered to be a unique example of Egyptian Mamluk architecture outside Cairo. The courses of the *sabil* were built of alternating red and yellow stone, known as *ablaq*. At the top of the building there is a carved inscription band that includes verses from the Qur'an and which holds a foundation inscription written in prominent Mamluk *naskhi* script.  
The architectural and decorative elements of this *sabil* were inspired principally by Egyptian building traditions which predominated during the Mamluk period. The Sabil of Qaytbay is considered to be one of the most famous and grandiose *sabil*s built in Jerusalem, and is also seen as one of the most exquisite small-domed buildings in the region of the Haram al-Sharif. The edifice is a good example of late Mamluk architecture in general, and of the architectural style that dominated in Cairo in particular. The *sabil*, which is still replenished, continues to provide visitors to the Haram al-Sharif with fresh water.
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.short_description: The decorative and architectural elements of this *sabil* (public fountain) was inspired principally by Egyptian building traditions. The building has a square ground plan (4.80 m x 4.60 m) and it towers about 13 m from the ground. It is surmounted by a very high stone dome which is decorated in the arabesque style. Each of its facades contains a large window. Scattered throughout the building are inscriptions, which are primarily Qur’anic verses in addition to the foundation inscription. This *sabil* is considered to be one of the most famous and beautiful of the many *sabil*s in Jerusalem.
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.dates: Built in AH 887 / AD 1482, then renovated in AH 1300 / AD 1882–3.
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.method_for_datation: The building is dated by an inscription band which goes around the top of the all four sides of the facade. The date is further verified by the writing of the historian, Mujir al-Din al-Hanbali (d. 928 / 1521) who describes the works of Sultan Qaytbay in Jerusalem.

Burgoyne. M., *Mamluk Jerusalem: An Architectural Study*, London, 1987.  
Al-Hanbali, Mujir al-Din, (d. 927 / 1520), *Al-Uns al-Jalil fi Tarikh al-Quds wa al-Khalil \[The Significant Ambiance in the History of Jerusalem and Hebron\]*, Amman, 1973.  
Kessler, C., and Burgoyne, M., “The Fountain of Sultan Qaytbay in the Sacred Precinct of Jerusalem”, in R. Moorey and P. Parr (eds), *Archaeology in the Levant: Essays for Kathleen Kenyon,* Warminster, 1978, pp.250–69.  
Walls, A., “Ottoman Restorations to the Sabils and the Madrasa of Qaytbay in Jerusalem”, *Muqarnas*, No. 10, 1993, pp.85–97.  
  
*Pilgrimage, Sciences and Sufism: Islamic Art in the West Bank and Gaza*, pp.83–6.
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.patrons: Sultan Sayf al-Din Inal (r. AH 857–65 / AD 1453–61) founded the *sabil* where the Sabil of Qaytbay is located today; nothing remains of this original Sabil of Inal. Then Sultan al-Ashraf Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96) completely renovated the structure and made it an extension to his neighbouring Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya. The Sabil of Qaytbay was renovated by the Ottoman Sultan ‘Abd al-Hamid II (Adülhamid II, r. AH 1293–1327 / AD 1876–1909).
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.architects: It is probable that the same team of engineers, architects and builders constructed both the Madrasa al-Ashrafiyya and the Sabil of Qaytbay, and that they were sent by Sultan Qaytbay from Egypt to Jerusalem to execute the work.
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.dynasty: The building dates to the Mamluk period and was renovated in the Ottoman period.
b35cbc07-d87d-5f89-b803-e7930fc1b57b.author: Yusuf al-Natsheh
keywords: Naskhi script; Mamluk naskhi script; sabil; water fountain

b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.name: Public fountains.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.description:
Al-Djazaïr and its *fahs* (rural surroundings) possessed a large number of fountains. Their number, for the walled town, varied from seven according to Haëdo in the AH 10th / AD 16th century, to 125 according to the knight of Arvieux in 1674–5, and to 'seventy-three as recorded in 1840' (S. Missoum, *Alger à l'époque ottomane* – see Bibliography). A large number of these fountains were built during the AH 12th / AD 18th century by *deys*.  
Benefactors were responsible for the creation of these fountains. Attached to each one, on a plaque of marble or shale, in Arabic or Ottoman Turkish, is an inscription extolling the merits of the benefactor. Under the auspices of a *khudjat al-'uyun* – a sort of 'fountains secretary' – an administrative body was responsible for managing the *habus* (estate donations) that were collected on behalf of these fountains.  
One of these fountains, known as the fountain 'de la Calle aux Vins', has ended up on an exterior wall of the present National Museum of Antiquities and Islamic Art. Built by the *dey* Husayn in AH 1235 / AD 1820 outside Bab al-Djazira (Gate of the Island', also referred to as Gate of the Holy War) and below the battery of al-Andalus, it was moved for the first time in 1867 to 'underneath the stairway of the present bastion of the Gate of France' (undated report on the proposition of making an endowment to the state; but the agreement on the endowment is dated 13 May 1905). Then it was moved a second time to the Park of Liberty (formerly Gallant Park), to be placed against the wall of the Department of Antiquities, where, in correspondence dated 27 May 1968, it is the subject of an account of the maintenance work carried out by the chief architect of historic monuments.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.short_description: The town of Al-Djazaïr had a number of public fountains, most of which were built during the AH 12th / AD 18th century by the Ottoman *deys*. These fountains bore, on a marble or slate plaque, the names of the benefactors who commissioned them and were managed by an body under the aegis of the 'fountains secretary'. In AH 1235 / AD 1820, *dey* Husayn had a fountain built outside Bab al-Djazira, the gateway that bears an inscription in his honour.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.method_for_datation: Through an inscription in Arabic and Osmanli: 'Everything lives through water. The governor of Algiers along with his sultan, who is Husayn Pasha, incessantly strives, with virtuous intentions, to accomplish good deeds. His bounty attempts above all to bring running water in sufficient quantities to all places. It is he who commissioned the building of this fountain. He gives life to him that is thirsty and deprived, in this place that lacks water. Drink fresh water thanks to the generosity of Husayn and his love. Year 1235 [1820].'
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.bibliography:
Belhamissi M., *Alger par les eaux XVIe–XIXe*, Algiers, 2004.  
Missoum, S., *Alger à l'époque ottomane*, Aix-en-Provence; Algiers, 2003.  
National Archaeological and Historic Monuments Agency, Archives, notably the report on endowments to the state, undated.
b381524f-09dd-5a75-8920-d87af44e1cd5.author: Ali Lafer

b3b30c50-746b-58e7-9d2b-8bf0e782271e.name: Tiraz Textile
b3b30c50-746b-58e7-9d2b-8bf0e782271e.short_description: This linen textile with its regal purple inscription naming the Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir has lost much of it original length due to its use as a burial shroud. However, it preserves almost its full width, spanned by the decorative inscription band. Known as a “*tiraz*” textile, it is unusually wide and was perhaps a shawl. The term “*tiraz*” actually means “embroidery,” but came to denote an inscription band as one sees on these textiles and on anything else, including architecture. Most of the medieval textiles discovered in excavations in Egypt had been used as burial shrouds and have suffered similar deterioration. Only those that found their way into European church treasuries are well preserved and give us an idea of how the full garment appeared. *Tiraz* textiles, despite their Arabic inscriptions, were highly valued in Europe as relics of the Holy Land and appear as the costumes of Christ and the Virgin in Italian Renaissance paintings.
b3b30c50-746b-58e7-9d2b-8bf0e782271e.author: Alessandra Cirelli
keywords: Textile; tiraz; tiraz-textile; linen; tabby; tapestry; woven; inscription; linen-textile
materials: Linen tabby; with purple, yellow, and blue silk, and undyed linen tapestry-woven inscription

b5c0e36b-46e4-5ee6-b561-8e69e064e0cc.name: Fountain
b5c0e36b-46e4-5ee6-b561-8e69e064e0cc.description:
Most Islamic gardens – including those in India – are very formal, with geometrically organised beds, paths, and irrigation channels. Fountains might stand in strategic places. The fountains that have been preserved are often made of marble, but there must have been many made of bronze, like this one, that were melted down later for other purposes.  
  
The fountain’s elegant form, which looks mostly like a stylised, open lotus with everted, pointed petals, is found in various forms in architecture and decorative art from the Deccan. The demon-like head that spewed water into the fountain is of Hindu origin, like many other creatures found in Indo-Islamic art.
b5c0e36b-46e4-5ee6-b561-8e69e064e0cc.dates: AH 1st half of 11 / AD 1st half of 17th century

b64a1bbb-e3ff-5209-9c78-7304ea9b3d7d.name: Water Well
b64a1bbb-e3ff-5209-9c78-7304ea9b3d7d.description:
This powerful and emotional drawing reflects everyday life, community and endurance. The artist uses a limited colour palette of dark, soft tones to create a haunting atmosphere. At the centre, a group of women stand close together around a dark well, while a solitary figure stands apart, carrying heavy containers. The scene is both quiet and heavy, conveying the physical and emotional weight of their daily labour.  
The well itself becomes more than just a source of water; it also symbolises life, connection and memory. The women's bent figures and joined forms suggest unity and cooperation, as if they rely on one another for strength and survival. Their faces are not clearly visible, giving the image a universal quality and turning the women into symbols of resilience and shared struggle rather than individuals.  
The artist’s use of shading and blurred lines gives the drawing a dreamlike and timeless quality, as if the moment exists in both the past and the present. The open space and faint background add to the sense of isolation and endurance in a harsh environment.  
Overall, *Water Well* powerfully and poetically captures the intersection of women’s labour, community and survival. The simple composition and muted tones draw attention to the emotional depth of the scene, reflecting not only daily life in rural Jordan, but also providing a broader commentary on strength and perseverance.
b64a1bbb-e3ff-5209-9c78-7304ea9b3d7d.holder: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts

b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.name: Zamzam Water Bottle
b705e8a3-17fc-5217-8640-d86017b77c66.short_description: This simple, circular Zamzam bottle has been constructed from copper-alloy sheet and decorated with hammered and incised decoration. A very narrow cylindrical neck gives access to the body of the vessel, and a chain secured to its shoulder allows it to be carried. Every pilgrim to the Holy City of Makkah will make a point of drinking and collecting water from the sacred well of Zamzam, located near the Ka’bah within the precinct of the Holy Mosque at Makkah al Mukarramah. Its never ceasing flow is considered a miracle, and its properties are believed to aid good health and wellbeing. To this day, pilgrims to Makkah make a point of taking as much Zamzam water as they can back with them, not least to distribute it to loved ones and treasured friends in order to allow them to partake in the water's beneficial properties.

b8b74d6c-8bd5-5f15-9490-e1dfa1ca07b9.alternate_name: Folio 18v from the Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Shah Tahmasp
b8b74d6c-8bd5-5f15-9490-e1dfa1ca07b9.description: In the introduction to the Shahnama, God launched seventy ships, bearing adherents to the religions of mankind, into a stormy sea. Clearly depicted on the central ship are the Prophet and his son‑in‑law and successor 'Ali sitting beneath the red canopy, while 'Ali’s sons, Hasan and Husain, stand nearby. Details such as the inlaid stars and figures with very small elliptical pupils are characteristic of works attributed to Mirza 'Ali, the son of the master painter Sultan Muhammad.

b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.name: Cistern.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.description:
A water tank or cistern, circular in cross-section, almost 20 m deep (the depth reached with cleaning and excavation, but thought to be much greater) and 3 m in diameter at the mouth. As 2 to 3 metres of water can always be seen it is possible that the construction is linked to phreatic (underground) waters.  
It is a very rare work of hydraulics, built of local stone – Silves red sandstone – giving it a high quality of construction. Architecturally it is a fine example of technical craftsmanship and functionality: a vaulted spiral staircase descends alongside it for 16 metres in a gallery to the lower level.  
The entire staircase, consisting of four flights, is roofed by a magnificent segmented tunnel vault. Three windows, with semi-circular-shaped vaults, form the link between the gallery of the staircase and the well, allowing access to the water at the different levels of filling, and also provide the gallery with ventilation and natural light.  
This monument was built at the end of the AH 6th / AD 12th century or the beginning of the AH 7th / AD 13th century, close to the inner surface of the wall which runs around the *medina* (town) and which was rebuilt at the same time. In this area the wall is wider and has a watchtower built against the outside.  
Undoubtedly these three structures (wall, watchtower and cistern), built at the same time, functioned as a defensive, structural and architectural whole.  
The function of this monumental cistern was probably to supply water to most of the lower part of the town, namely the *hammam* (public baths) which was very close, some 100 m away.  
The cistern was filled in with earth and rubbish and its function abandoned with the arrival of the Christians at the end of the AH 7th / AD 13th century. It was only rediscovered in 1979, when reconstruction and repaving work was begun in that area. The archaeological excavations which followed brought to light not only the magnificent structure itself but also an extraordinary haul of ceramics, with pieces dating from the AH 3rd–4th / AD 9th–10th centuries to the AH 11th / AD 17th century, now on display in the Silves Municipal Archaeology Museum.  
The cistern is today part of the Silves Municipal Archaeology Museum, where it plays a central role, with the whole permanent exhibition arranged around it.  
This unique example of a cistern linked to phreatic waters has been classified as a National Monument since 1990.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.short_description: This Almohad water tank or cistern was fed from the Silves water table. A vaulted spiral staircase descends into a gallery to a depth of 16 metres. The entire four-flight staircase is covered by a segmented barrel vault. Three windows with semi-circular vaults link the stairwell to the well, giving access to the water as well as naturally lighting and ventilating the gallery. The cistern is now the centrepiece of the Municipal Museum of Archaeology around which the other exhibits are arranged.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.dates: Hegira second half of 6th–first half of 7th century / AD second half of 12th–first half of 13th century.
b8c3263e-bcad-57f1-85f6-7e684aea8d52.method_for_datation: From the style, construction and architecture of the structure. There are documentary records of the existence of a cistern close to the *hammam*.

bab7404e-f6da-51e5-bfe3-7f236f4ef2b2.name: *Wadi el-Tuffah*
bab7404e-f6da-51e5-bfe3-7f236f4ef2b2.short_description: In this image, a Palestinian lady uses a traditional spinning wheel for cotton. 19th-century Palestine became an increasingly viable, agricultural producer of cotton, whose importance on the world market was steadily increasing. Mainly supplying European countries  Palestine's cotton became a key commodity. 6% of its cultivated land was given up for its production. Throughout the 1860s, concerted efforts were made to meet the ever growing demand, but as early as the 1870s, the industry, which was merely based on expanded cultivation rather than industrialisation, declined again.This print originally appeared on page 192 in Charles William Wilson's  'Pituresque Palestine, Sinai and Egypt, published between 1881 and 1884. The caption reads: ''Wady et Tuffah, commonly called the vale of Eshcol. The peasants grouped in the foreground are under the southern branches of Abraham's oak. In the distance the minaret of the great mosque of Sheikh Ali Bakka, Hebron, may be distinguished'.

bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.name: Painted wall-hanging: The Day of Judgement (*Ruz-e mahshar*)
bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.short_description: A painted wall-hanging depicts the *Day of Judgement* from a Shi'ite perspective in Isfahan. The main theme is the reward given in paradise to the martyrs who fell at Kerbala on 10 October 680, corresponding to the Islamic date 10 Muharram 61, and the agonies of their enemies on Judgement Day. Elements of Christian iconography are present. There is the trumpeting angel who blows into the bugle at the Last Judgement; the receiving of the arisen into heaven; the two angels who attend to the weighing scale of the souls; the chosen ones who await their entry into paradise; the blood witnesses who in advance enjoy the delights of paradise; and finally those of different faiths and traitors, who, already condemned, stand before the infernal ground. There are also new elements: the prophet of Islam is now an established, important figure, and Christ, the judge of the world, assumes the part of a precursor-prophet.
bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.method_for_datation: Entry in the general inventory and archival documents.
bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.method_for_provenance: Entry in the general inventory book.
bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.obtention: Catalog entry: "Purchased from Saeed Motamed, Frankfurt am Main, 1958."

bb8218af-c329-56aa-9fd9-9570b638e2b2.name: Sickle (*mikhlab*)
bb8218af-c329-56aa-9fd9-9570b638e2b2.description: The sickle is a tool that has been employed worldwide for its utility: it is a manual agricultural tool that consists of a curved blade that is usually used for harvesting grain crops or cutting weeds used to feed livestock.

bc1be694-23e7-57dc-8d0e-5dd013cff796.name: Bath scraper or pumice stone
bc1be694-23e7-57dc-8d0e-5dd013cff796.description:
This object has been associated with a series of bath scrapers and pumice stones attributed to AH 5th-6th / 11th-12th century Middle East. They are characterised by an animal shape or motif made from a coarse material.  
  
This model represents a rodent or a hedgehog recognisable by its long ears and the spines on its back. The bottom of the piece is incised with a grid that would have accentuated its abrasive quality. Deliberately left unglazed and unrefined, such scrapers were used during hamam rituals to exfoliate and purify the skin.  
  
This bath scraper could be considered an early version of the traditional exfoliating washcloth (ar. *kessa* , tr. *kese*), an emblematic item from the hamam. It is also plausible that they coexisted, given that the *kessa* was made from natural perishable material that would have disappeared in places where ceramic has survived.

bca1f6e5-4534-5831-b044-f283753ceae7.name: Calligraphy
bca1f6e5-4534-5831-b044-f283753ceae7.description: This verse, from Surah Al-Insān (76:21), describes a symbolic moment of divine generosity in Islamic tradition. The phrase, ‘"And their Lord will give them a pure drink (*wa saqāhum rabbuhum sharāban ṭahūrā*)" evokes spiritual purification and ultimate reward. In Islamic theology, this "pure drink" is often interpreted as a metaphor for inner peace, moral elevation, and closeness to the divine granted to the righteous in the hereafter.

bcc67bdc-c7be-5340-9052-eebc133a1ba7.name: Prayer Book
bcc67bdc-c7be-5340-9052-eebc133a1ba7.description: This small prayer book, or du'anama, belongs to a corpus of illustrated devotional texts produced in the Ottoman Empire in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Unlike most prayer books created at the time, this one contains twenty-nine drawings of traditional Islamic themes and subjects, which are outlined in gold and filled with prayers in ghubar naskh, an especially fine or "dust-like" variety of the naskh script. These include representations of the Ka'ba, the footprints (kadem) of the Prophet Muhammad, the Seal of Solomon, the bifurcated sword of 'Ali (zu'l fiqar), Noah's Ark, the lamp of the Prophet, the trumpet of the Archangel Israfil, and the cave from the story of the Seven Sleepers in the Qur'an, among others. The manuscript is signed and dated by the calligrapher, a prominent mid-eighteenth-century master known for his calligrams and pictorial calligraphic compositions, such as the galleon with inscriptions referring to the story of the Seven Sleepers also in the Metropolitan's collection (2003.241). It also contains collectors' stamps dating to the first half of the nineteenth century. The leather binding is decorated with stamped and gilded medallions within a simple border. Prayer manuals enjoyed wide popularity in the Ottoman Empire in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, a time of political reform and religious revivalism. Used for individual prayer, they also served as mediational devices to protect, comfort, and heal their owners.

be67f016-2a91-567e-bfb3-ab20f22a18de.name: Noria at the Mohammed VI Museum for the Civilisation of Water in Morocco
be67f016-2a91-567e-bfb3-ab20f22a18de.dates: This reconstructed noria is displayed in the museum to highlight traditional urban water engineering. As a functional exhibit, it demonstrates historical methods of lifting and distributing water and engages visitors directly. In doing so, it illustrates how water infrastructure has shaped urban life while connecting engineering, public education and cultural heritage in a modern museum context.

bf3bbec5-16fa-5c53-92d5-f939cdb22f28.name: Water-Scoop
bf3bbec5-16fa-5c53-92d5-f939cdb22f28.description:
This is the only precisely dated Ottoman silver object of the AH 10th / AD 16th century. The exterior of the bowl bears an inscription in a rounded script with careful pointing, engraved and inlaid with a black composition. The inscription begins with the *basmalah* followed by a quote from the surah *al-Anbiya’* (XXI), verse 30, ‘and \[we made\] from water every living thing’, and the date, AH 985, in figures.  
  
The tubular handle, with a band of semi-precious stones set in collar-mounts, is constructed in sections and terminates in a knob with a ring set in a polyhedron.

bfe37257-aff0-5289-b8c5-59ecbe78ace2.name: Yıldız Palace Greenhouse Kiosk
bfe37257-aff0-5289-b8c5-59ecbe78ace2.short_description:
The palace has an inner garden which is called “Hasbahce” with a pool inside resembling a natural creek. In different points of this garden there are small independent resort kiosks.  
In the Palace garden winter gardens and greenhouses were constructed for growing plants appropriate for the natural topography. Some greenhouses had unique designs where then-fashionable iron and glass elements were expertly used and it is known some of them had been heated. Especially the Limonluk Köşkü, designed by Raimondo D’Aronco and found just behing the Harem Gate is one of the most distinguished structures in the Palace.
bfe37257-aff0-5289-b8c5-59ecbe78ace2.history:
Yildiz Palace, which is the last architectural example of Turkish Ottoman palace, is located on the Yildiz hill in the district of Beşiktaş. Sultan Ahmed I was the first to build a pavilion, over this land registered at the time to the Private treasury of the Ottoman Sultan as a hunting place sultans beginning during the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-1566).  
The main construction in the palace started in the period of Sultan Abdulhamid II (1876-1909) and it was called Saray-i Humayun (Central palace). During this period the palace comprised of buildings for private use of the sultan as well as buildings, allocated for the officials, repair shops and carpentry like repairing shop, carpenter’s shop and the buildings of culture and art such as theatre, museum and library. The Palace begun to serve as a museum under the name of "Directorate of the Museum of Yildiz Palace" since 1993.

bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.name: Ewer and Basin Set
bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.description:
This set is comprised of three elements: an ewer, a basin, and a lid strainer. They are made of cast brass, and the surface is coated with nickel, thereby creating a gold and silver appearance.  
The ewer has a pear-shaped body, a slender neck with ring moulding, a curved spout and a handle, and is topped with a domed lid bearing a tall finial. All surfaces of the ewer are decorated with ornamental bands, engraved with leaves and stylised floral motifs.  
The circular basin is deep, with a flaring rim and a perforated decorative edge. It is ornamented in the same manner as the ewer. The lid is perforated and features a raised circular central section, which serves as a stand for the ewer.  
These types of sets were very popular and widely used for ritual ablutions, as well as for washing hands between meals. Some examples were distinguished by the refinement of their decoration or the preciousness of the material, and thus served not only a practical but also a decorative function in everyday life.
bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.dates: AH early 14th century / AD early 20th century
bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.

bff32db0-47a0-5fc9-88e2-12d073ff5354.author: Mila Gajić

bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.name: *Works for the opening of the Corinth Canal*
bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.short_description:
The Corinth Canal under constuction, circa 1885. Photographer unknown.  
The Corinth Canal separates the Peloponnesian peninsula from the Greek. The idea of the canal was revived after Greece gained independence but soon abandoned due to economical reasons. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 gave an new impetus and the following year, the Zaimis government passed a law authorising the construction of the canal, which was formally inaugurated on 23 April 1882. Zaimis assigned the project to the Hungarian István Türr who set up the Société Internationale du Canal Maritime de Corinthe but the company failed and the project was finished by the company of Andeas Syngros. The canal was designed by the Hungarian engineer Béla Gerster with the assistance of the French Vincent Dauzants, a chief engineer of the Suez canal.
bff5b327-dd8c-55ac-a7f0-49d5bbc62548.author: Maria Dimitriadou

c030f281-39a4-5826-98d8-b68d6a9cb3a7.name: Basin of al-Malik an Nāsir
c030f281-39a4-5826-98d8-b68d6a9cb3a7.description:
The large basin is circular in section and rests on a flat base. The walls taper towards the flared rim with projecting lips. The interior and exterior surfaces are entirely incised and feature thuluth inscriptions on a background decorated with vegetal and floral elements, including peonia, leaves, and birds in flight. Three large polylobed medallions decorated with peonies and rosettes interrupt the thuluth inscription.  
The basin, along with other Islamic objects, entered museum collections thanks to King Ferdinand I of Bourbon's purchase in 1817 of the eighteenth-century collection of Cardinal Stefano Borgia (1731-1804).  
Thanks to his position as secretary of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith, Cardinal Borgia collected a diverse array of artistic material through Catholic missions around the world, evidence of distant and exotic cultures, which reflects his erudite and encyclopaedic interest in the history of civilizations, of which this collection of Islamic objects is a part.  
  
Inscriptions in thuluth:  
Outer wall: Glory to our lord Sultan al-Malik/al-Nasir, helper of the world and religion, Muhammad ibn/al-Malik al-Mansur ibn \[sic\] Qalawun al-Salihi  
  
Inner border: Glory to our lord Sultan al-Malik al-Na-/sir, helper of the world and religion, slayer of unbelievers and poly/theists, Muhammad ibn Qalwun al-Salihi, may his victories be glorious

c0d80368-9101-5330-9c94-206d3ccd6cb3.name: Umm al-Walid.
c0d80368-9101-5330-9c94-206d3ccd6cb3.description:
The site of Umm al-Walid, situated 14 km southeast of Madaba, consists of an agglomeration of buildings which include both large and small structures, a late Roman temple, mausoleum, cisterns and barrages. In the Umayyad period, during the first half of the AH 2nd / AD 8th century, a large settlement sprang up on an area extending 400 m north to south, and 300 m, east to west. On the eastern periphery a *qasr* (palace) and a small mosque were built.  
The *qasr* is a square enclosure, measuring 70 m on each side. It has round buttresses at each of its corners and three-half round ones on the sides between them, except on the east side, which has only two. The walls are carefully built of local limestone and also include some embossed blocks apparently taken from earlier buildings. The entrance, set in between two quarter-round towers in the middle of the eastern side, opens onto a passageway which has stone benches, with armrests, along its sides. The entrance passageway leads into a paved courtyard measuring 33 m sq. Excavations have revealed that a portico ran all around this courtyard, and behind it ran low walls that separated the apartments from the central courtyard.  
The low walls enclose five narrow rectangular courts, and behind them are five self-contained residential units (*bayt*s). At the corners of the portico are narrow rooms each provided with a latrine. In addition to the pottery and steatite vessels, two incense burners with spherical covers, jugs and bowls, all in bronze, were recovered from the southeastern room. Also notable is a monolithic lintel decorated in plaster relief depicting a panther chasing a gazelle that was found in the northwestern room.  
Some 60 m to the east of the *qasr* is a small mosque measuring 14 m x 10.30 m; it has two doors, one in the northern and one in the eastern side, the latter leading to a walled enclosure with stone benches along its western side.  
The interior of the mosque, which shows two phases of construction, is divided into three aisles by two arcades of three arches, each running parallel to the south (*qibla*) wall. In the middle of the *qibla* wall is a projecting concave niche (*mihrab*), which indicates the direction of prayer. It should be noted that the Umayyad settlement at Umm al-Walid was implanted in the middle of a predominantly Christian area, and without peaceful coexistence and close cooperation with neighbouring Christian communities in Madaba, Nitl and Umm al-Rasas, the Umayyad settlement could not have existed; it was in need of local markets to supply the sustenance required for the community. In other words, Umm al-Walid tells a story of integration rather than an attempt on the part of the Umayyads to live separately from the rest of the community.
c0d80368-9101-5330-9c94-206d3ccd6cb3.short_description: Umm al-Walid lies 14 km southeast of Madaba. It includes a late Roman temple, a mausoleum, cisterns and barrages. During the first half of the AH 2nd / AD 8th century, a large settlement was built with a small mosque and a qasr (palace), where a substantial collection of pottery, steatite and bronze vessels was found. The Umayyad settlement at Umm al-Walid was implanted in the middle of a Christian area, and had close co-operation with neighbouring Christian communities. It tells a story of integration rather than an attempt by the Umayyads to live separately from the rest of the community.
c0d80368-9101-5330-9c94-206d3ccd6cb3.dates: Hegira, first half of the 2nd century / AD third quarter of the 8th century.

c13e07a9-25e9-500c-a2eb-4f7568251a1e.name: Qajar Carpet -Hunting Scene
c13e07a9-25e9-500c-a2eb-4f7568251a1e.short_description: The pictorial carpets of Qajar Iran illustrate royals and famous people in various scenarios. This Persian Kashan wool rug displays a hunting scene with a portrait of a king or a nobleman sitting on a chair embellished with crowns, drinking and holding a copper ewer in his other hand, and a wide variety of animals and plants. The phoenix above the nobleman, a popular creature in Persian mythology, represents immortality. Hunting dogs symbolize honour and glory, while the gazelle symbolizes innocence. The imagery of water is significant, denoting purity and the source of life, and in which the fish embody undying love. The cypress tree signifies Persian perseverance and pride.

c2d89824-82fc-5b0b-b842-57fa1d2f9bf8.name: Ceramic boat model
c2d89824-82fc-5b0b-b842-57fa1d2f9bf8.description: This is one of many clay models of flat-bottomed boats with vertical sides found at Ur, of varying shapes and sizes. It is among several examples that bear a resemblance to the *isbiya* barge (see item 2024.8.2 in the collection of the Open Museum Initiative for Water Culture), particularly in the lip protruding from the bottom edge of the boat. This feature is called *leffa* in Hit, where *isbiyas* were traditionally made, and is unique to the *isbiya*.

c30fb9aa-8248-5b4a-84f5-a4be2f553315.name: Oasis of Madkhal Meski
c30fb9aa-8248-5b4a-84f5-a4be2f553315.description: The subject of this image is 'The Blue Source' in the oasis of (Madkhal) Meski, near Er-Rachidia, in Morocco, distinguished by its expansive body of water encompassed by palm trees. This oasis is a paradigm of the urban landscape in desert regions, where water functions as a nexus for communities and urban life. It is enveloped by residential dwellings and commercial establishments.

c37ffe04-f331-50a3-8853-714465f7a769.name: The *tali'* (water system) of Damascus.
c37ffe04-f331-50a3-8853-714465f7a769.description:
The water-distribution system in Syria is important for the region's success as a centre of civilisation. The availability of running water nourishing both private houses and public buildings is tribute to the ancient Damascene heritage of irrigation and underwater canals that survives to this day. One of Damascus's most famous neighbourhoods is known as 'Hayy al-Qanawat' after the Roman water canals that supplied it, and which were well maintained under Islamic rule.  
During the period of prolific construction begun by Nur al-Din Mahmud bin al-Zangi (d. AH 569 / AD 1174) Damascus was renowned for its luxurious bathhouses (*hammams*), its public drinking fountains(*sabils*), andthe accessibility of running water within its mosques, *madrasas* and hospitals (*bimaristans)*.The water fountain and running stream attached to the courtyard basin at the Madrasa Nuriyya, built in AH 563 / AD 1167–8, is an example of the Nuri creativity in water provision, for this visible abundance of water was a mark of good governance.  
The Barada River is the main water source, springing from the Anti-Lebanon Mountains near the Zabadani district at an altitude of 1100 m. Water reaches Damascus via six main channels, although the total tributaries are around 40. The underwater canals of Syria have been ingeniously used throughout history to transform a dry and desert-like region into a green one.  
There is a system of water distribution in the city called a *tali'*, which distributres a share of water to each neighbourhood based on a unit known as a *qirat*. The *qirat* is a unit of measurement equalling 1 out of 24. The total water supply in a *tali'*' is therefore 24 qirats and, as stated in the lease of any given property, each building has the right to a ratio of this water allocated by the *tali* system and measured as a number of *qirats*. This system of water distribution withan an urban setting was the hallmark of Atabeg and Ayyubid Damascus. Hammam Nur al-Din, for example, was constructed adjacent to its *tali'* and the Madrasa Adiliyya is located near Hayy al-Sabi' Tawali', a neighbourhood named after the seven *tali*'s supplying it.  
The official controller who oversees the distribution process is known as *al-faradi*, an aqua-specific counterpart to the *muhtasib* who ensures that water distribution is fair and legal. As a result of this *tali*' system, water from the Barada River reaches every home; the Demascene home, unlike any other, is known to this day for its central courtyard basin and sprinkling fountain, the sight and sound of water always symbolic of good living.  
Similarly, in Aleppo, there is an important system of channelled water distribution known as *al-qastal*. The Madrasa al-Shu'aybiyya, built by Nur al-Din in AH 545 / AD 1150 was erected next to the Qastal al-Shuaybiyy which still carries his inscription and marks the extent of his work in water distribution. Also, the city of Hama is famous for its waterwheels or *noria*s, a number of which were built during Nur al-Din's reign.
c37ffe04-f331-50a3-8853-714465f7a769.short_description: The supply of water for the city of Damascus relies on the River Barada, which springs from the Anti-Lebanon mountain range and reaches Damascus via six main channels and numerous minor ones. The expert manipulation of these precious waters to ensure water supply for every public institution and private house of the city was the hallmark of the rule of Nur al-Din Mahmud bin Zangi (d. AH 569 / AD 1174). Each neigbourhood was equipped with a *tali'* through which water was measured and distributed to the surrounding properties.
c37ffe04-f331-50a3-8853-714465f7a769.dates: Hegira mid-6th century / AD mid-12th century.
c37ffe04-f331-50a3-8853-714465f7a769.method_for_datation: The historian Ibn 'Asakir (d. 571 / 1176) describes a significant number of *hammams*, *qanats* (water channels) and *sabils* in Damascus during the mid-6th / 12th century.

c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.name: Water-basin.
c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.description: A brass water-basin originally inlayed with silver and divided into six sections with the aid of six roundels. Decorated with a band of bold calligraphic inscription, the text reads: 'This is one of the things made for his highness, the lordly, the kingly, the learned, the treasure house of excellence, the just, the conqueror, the warrior, the defender, the protector of frontiers, the fortified by God, the victorious, the planner, the well-ordered, the masterful, the complete, supporter of the khan, the Seal Bearer, the king the Nassiri.' The inscription indicates an official of high rank in charge of the Sultan Al-Malik Al-Nasir's correspondence and other administrative responsibilities. Al-Malik Al-Nasir (who ruled during three phases between AH 692 and 740 / AD 1293 and 1340) commissioned the basin. Three of the roundels enclose the design of a blazon. The other three roundels have a symmetrical composition of six birds: two facing each other, two looking away from each other; and two moving away from each other but looking back at each other. The compositions of these roundels with their birds or waterfowl are a distinctive feature of Egyptian Mamluk metalwork, distinguishing it from contemporary Syrian, Iraqi and Iranian work.
c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.short_description: Vessels like this one were quite expensive. The script round the basin is in the *thuluth* style, and describes the titles of the high-ranking Mamluk official who owned it. The blazon incised in the roundels that divide the text indicates that the owner was in charge of the sultan’s correspondence.
c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.holder: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum, Glasgow Museums
c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.owner: on temporary display at Glasgow Central Mosque.

c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.method_for_provenance: Identification of the 8th- / 14th-century Mamluk blazon and titles.

c3846b74-8446-5391-a0bc-02dca834176f.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: Water; Ruling classes; patronage; calligraphy; coat of arms
materials: Brass; beaten and inlayed with silver.

c42ca69a-f7fd-5764-8954-9f2bbd201575.name: Ewer (*Aftaba*)
c42ca69a-f7fd-5764-8954-9f2bbd201575.description: A ewer, adorned with vegetal motifs and geometric designs, composed of a base, body, neck, mouth, lid, handle and spout. The base is circular, with a lobed contour and ornamented with arrowheads using the chasing technique. The body is spherical and lobed. Each lobe is ornamented with a meandering vegetal branch, while the field is adorned with rosettes of four petals in varying sizes. The neck is short, circular and lobed, beginning with a plain metallic band, followed by a frieze of arrowheads. The circular mouth is covered with a hemispherical helmet-shaped lid, topped by a small spherical knob entirely undecorated. The spout is cylindrical, beveled, and tapering towards the tip, narrowing upwards, with a central protrusion. It is adorned with longitudinal framed motifs of arrowheads, beginning with a row of broken arches. The handle is curved, extending from the middle of the body and ending in a lotus flower, attached to the lid by hinges fixed with circular pins.
c42ca69a-f7fd-5764-8954-9f2bbd201575.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
materials: Metal, hammering, mold casting, engraving, and incising

c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.name: Minbar of Burhan al-Din.
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.description:
The *minbar* occupies an elevated position in Islamic Art. The *minbar* is an essential piece of furniture within the mosque for it is where the preacher stands to deliver his *khutba* specifically on religious occasions; for the Friday *khutba* it is not permissible to conduct prayers without the *minbar*. Thus the *minbar* is an important object linked closely with prayer one of the five pillars of Islam, and one of the most important Islamic rites after the *Shahada.* The *minbar* is found predominantly in congregational mosques, although it is found in some *madrasa*s as in, for example, the Mamluk *madrasa*s in Cairo, the *madrasa*s in Jerusalem, do not have *minbar*s.  
The Minbar of Burhan al-Din is a rarity for it is a purpose-built construction made specifically for open-air use and constructed out of stone and marble and not from wood as is more commonly seen. It seems that this *minbar* replaced the need fora wooden one, which normally would be towed on wheels as necessary.  
The present *minbar* contains a number of sections, the most prominent of which is the front panel, for this is the principle façade. The front of the *minbar* is composed of a rectangular opening flanked between two marble columns. Each column has a cylindrical base and a capital. Both columns bear stone lintels directly above them, where there is a stone panel that ends in the form of an arch. The panel has a carved inscription in *naskhi* script which dates the restoration of the *minbar* to the Ottoman period in AH 1259 / AD 1843. A series of stone steps at the front of the *minbar* lead to the *jawsaq* where the orator stands. The *jawsaq* consists of a small square platform covered by a segmented dome (known as the *Qubbat al-Maizan*), which is erected on top of a hexagonal drum. The drum is supported by six small tri-lobed arches, held up by marble pillars. The architectural elements of the *minbar* were not made specifically for it but were taken from sites and buildings dating to the Crusader period.  
The *minbar* has two sides designated the *risha* of the *minbar*. Both sides are triangular with corners that are characterised by marble side-panels. In the east corner of the *minbar,* on the supporting arches of the dome, a surface-*mihrab* has been erected which terminates in a tapered arch consisting of seven voussoirs. The *mihrab* is decorated with simple geometric forms on the upper and lower sections, and with natural vegetal forms in the central section.  
This *minbar* was used to preach to the masses in al-Aqsa Mosque on occasions which necessitated guidance, the strengthening of resolution and the calling for patience, especially in the execution of prayers for rain. The *minbar* was used particularly in the summer months to present religious lessons.
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.short_description: This *minbar* (pulpit) is built from marble and stone and is located in the open plaza of the Dome of the Rock. It is the only *minbar* in Jerusalem which is located in an open area and was most probably used to deliver the *khutba* (Friday sermon) and lessons on summer days and on important occasions. It is therefore also known as the ‘summer *minbar*’. The *minbar* is an artistic piece characterised by vegetal and geometric decoration, columns and capitals and inscription panels. All of this has been implemented in the Mamluk style.
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.dates: It is not known when the minbar was constructed but it was restored in the AH mid-8th / AD 14th century, and again in AH 1259 / AD 1843.
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.method_for_datation: The *minbar* was dated by historical information from several sources; for example in the work of the historian Mujir al Din Hanbali (d. 928 / 1521) and in the writing of Ibn Fadl Allah al-'Umari (d. 749 / 1348), which dates to around 745 / 1345.
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.bibliography:
Berchem, M. van, *Matériaux pour un Corpus Inscriptionum Arabicarum*, Vol. II, Cairo, 1922.  
Burgoyne, M., *Mamluk Jerusalem: An Architectural Study,* London, 1987.  
Al-Hanbali, Mujir al-Din, *Al-Uns al-Jalil bi Tarikh al-Quds wa al-Khalil \[The Magnificent Ambiance in the History of Jerusalem and Hebron*\], Amman, 1973.
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.patrons: It is not known who sponsored the *minbar* but Qadi Burhan al-Din Ibn Jama’a (AH 725–90 / AD 1325–88) supervised the initial restoration.
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.dynasty: Restored in the Mamluk period and again in the Ottoman period during the rule of Sultan ‘Abd al-Majid (Abdülmecid, r. 1255–77 / AD 1839–61).
c4f03920-d58d-553e-895b-4f8dadfb02e3.author: Yusuf al-Natsheh
keywords: Jawsaq; khutba; preacher; minbar; marble; summer minbar

c58426af-004d-5e5c-b305-8352f7786889.name: Water elevation towers of Tameslouht
c58426af-004d-5e5c-b305-8352f7786889.description:
Water elevation towers relied on siphoning and pressurisation, allowing water to overcome elevation differences between the source in the village and the higher agricultural lands, specifically the Agdal, a vast olive grove. Each tower consisted of two adjacent cylinders: a main one, about 60cm in diameter, to hold water, and a smaller one, about 15cm wide, to regulate pressure. Built with local materials like brick, stone, and terracotta, the towers operated by creating progressive hydraulic pressure. Water, captured in the village or from lower springs, was directed into the first cylinder. The pressure difference then pushed it to the next tower, overcoming obstacles. Repeated successively, this process carried water to the heights where the olive groves were located.  
  
This mechanism, based on an inverted siphon, saved manual or animal labour, which was once required for pumping and transporting water. Thanks to this innovation, Tameslouht’s inhabitants irrigated dozens of hectares, strengthening economic stability and food self-sufficiency. A territory marked by harsh climatic constraints was transformed into a productive agricultural area where olive cultivation flourished, sustaining the community and producing a valuable export.  
  
Beyond their technical role, the towers fostered community cooperation in water management, with clear rules governing distribution and maintenance, thus reinforcing social cohesion. With the advent of modern irrigation technologies in the AH 14th century / AD 20th century, the use of elevation towers gradually declined. However, in some remote rural areas, the Tameslouht elevation towers still function today, either for local use or within heritage valorisation projects.  
  
Today, these structures symbolise sustainable water management and the resilience of Moroccan rural societies, offering valuable lessons for contemporary environmental challenges.
c58426af-004d-5e5c-b305-8352f7786889.bibliography: Aïssaoui, H., 'Hydraulique traditionnelle et systèmes d'irrigation dans la vallée de l'Ourika : étude des tours élévatrices de Tameslouht', *Revue Marocaine d’Hydrologie*, 12(2; 2013), 115-130.
c58426af-004d-5e5c-b305-8352f7786889.history:
Built at the end of the AH 13th / AD 19th century and located in the Tameslouht region, about twenty kilometres southeast of Marrakech, the water elevation towers played a crucial role in local agricultural development, particularly for irrigating the vast olive groves of this semi-arid region.  
  
Tameslouht is marked by a semi-arid Mediterranean climate with irregular rainfall and rugged terrain. These conditions required water management to be both tactful and strategic to ensure crops and secure livelihoods. Historically, olive oil production was a major economic activity in the region, demanding an efficient irrigation system where water was precious and limited.
c58426af-004d-5e5c-b305-8352f7786889.author: MUSEUM Staff, Layan Shahin
keywords: Water elevation tower, Tameslouht, Marrakech, traditional irrigation, water management

c59e402b-a53f-58e3-8f66-a2b8da7df255.name: Leather container
c59e402b-a53f-58e3-8f66-a2b8da7df255.description: Used for watering camels and animals in the desert and steppe, this container was filled with water after being drawn from the well. Made of leather, it is lightweight and easy to carry. Its primary function was to facilitate the drinking of camels and animals during desert journeys or while grazing. The vessel is deep in form, widening at the top to allow the animal’s head to drink without spilling the water. It is supported by branches arranged as intersecting semicircular arches, fastened with ropes. It was also placed beside wells and filled with water for livestock to drink. In some regions, it is known as a *Shann*
c59e402b-a53f-58e3-8f66-a2b8da7df255.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum

c689fa52-52dc-59c4-be4e-613916e848a5.name: Water Museum
c689fa52-52dc-59c4-be4e-613916e848a5.description: This is the first water museum of South Asia. The Water Museum was created to spread information and raise awareness among communities, stakeholders, and policymakers about the importance of safeguarding rivers. It serves as a strong foundation for the policy advocacy of the "Water Commons" campaign by ActionAid Bangladesh and a call to action to save rivers in South Asia.
c689fa52-52dc-59c4-be4e-613916e848a5.author: ActionAid Bangladesh

c7284cbb-74d2-54e9-8467-e6e99021b1f4.name: Small hoe (format 2)
c7284cbb-74d2-54e9-8467-e6e99021b1f4.description: This wider hoe was designed for maintaining irrigation plot boundaries and managing shallow water channels. It reflects adaptive agricultural practices developed to ensure efficient water use in oasis environments.
c7284cbb-74d2-54e9-8467-e6e99021b1f4.holder: Mohammed VI Museum for the Civilisation of Water in Morocco

c7b92ca6-0fb1-5ef1-be15-6d03a8406b7f.name: Small hoe (format 1)
c7b92ca6-0fb1-5ef1-be15-6d03a8406b7f.description: This small hoe was widely used in oasis agriculture for light soil work, including weeding and the creation of shallow irrigation channels. Its modest size allowed farmers to manage water distribution with precision, reflecting an agricultural system closely adapted to limited water resources.
c7b92ca6-0fb1-5ef1-be15-6d03a8406b7f.holder: Mohammed VI Museum for the Civilisation of Water in Morocco

c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.name: Photograph pitched wooden boats by the River Euphrates in Hit, Iraq
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.description:
This photograph, taken by explorer, archaeologist, writer, and colonial diplomat Gertrude Bell during her AH 1327 / AD 1909 travels in Mesopotamia, depicts traditional boats at shore beside the River Euphrates in Hit. The boats, which have been made using woven reeds, wood and bitumen, are one of many examples of traditional trade and craft captured within the Gertrude Bell Archive. The image was featured in Bell's AH 1329 / AD 1911 publication 'Amurath to Amurath', alongside many others taken during this trip.  
  
The photograph has been digitised using the original negative, which is held along with the original print in Bell's photograph album ('Album K'), within the Gertrude Bell Archive at Newcastle University Special Collections. It is contextualised by original diary entries and letters, also held within the Archive.
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.method_for_datation: Date and origin documented by Gertrude Bell, and confirmed by contextual material in Gertrude Bell Archive.
c7e1ed38-295a-5272-b536-f559755ccd2b.provenance: Photograph taken by Gertrude Bell in Hit, Iraq, during her AH 1327 / AD 1909 trip there, included in Photograph Album K, part of the Gertrude Bell Archive.

c7ea01bb-8303-57dd-b186-861681adf109.name: Hot and Cold Water Dispenser
c7ea01bb-8303-57dd-b186-861681adf109.description:
This object has become a familiar fixture in kitchens, office pantries, and public spaces across the Islamic world. Designed to provide instant access to hot and cold water, it reflects how convenience and functionality shape modern domestic and professional environments.  
  
Most dispensers are imported from industrial centres such as China. In Islamic communities global technologies are integrated into local habits, as water remains a basic necessity and shared social element.
c7ea01bb-8303-57dd-b186-861681adf109.author: Dina Turkieh

She holds a water jug, which presumably she has just filled. Behind her a man descends into the tunnel to access the spring.

ca166fd8-40d8-5568-b817-4999a1ea04de.name: "The Eavesdropper"
ca166fd8-40d8-5568-b817-4999a1ea04de.alternate_name: Folio 47r from a Haft Paikar (Seven Portraits) of the Khamsa (Quintet) of Nizami of Ganja
ca166fd8-40d8-5568-b817-4999a1ea04de.description: This folio once illustrated a magnificent manuscript of Nizami’s Haft Paikar (Seven Portraits). The story of the Seven Portraits comprises a series of moralizing tales as told to the Persian hero Bahram Gur by seven princesses. This lively and lyrical scene illustrates a story in which a youth spies upon maidens swimming in a garden pool by moonlight. The voyeur is barely visible here, peering out of the shuttered window, unbeknownst to the playful bathers below.

ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.name: *Women grinding corn in Sinai*
ca84a358-0e08-5345-bc08-43570cf84e04.short_description: Many of the most popular subjects of stereographs were of topographical views or of scenes unfamiliar to the western audience for whom they were generally produced. This group of Islamic women from Egypt's Sinai Peninsula is shown grinding corn. Their faces are hidden by veils. The veil turns away the gaze while at the same time attracting it. The secrecy of the veil prompted fascination for what was often seen as the mysterious and exotic world of the East or the 'Orient' to 19th-century western viewers. In contrast, the men in the background confront the camera.

cb8f8517-5780-5bcc-bee9-849860cd610e.name: *Sabil* Birkat al-Sultan.
cb8f8517-5780-5bcc-bee9-849860cd610e.description:
The Sabil Birkat al-Sultan is one of the six *sabil*s that were erected in Jerusalem by order of Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent. The *sabil* is built with cut white stone in a multiplicity of sizes, which form a rectangle 3.70 m long and 1.5 m wide. In front of the *sabil* block there is a recess 71 cm deep and 1.9 m long. Above the recess is a pointed arch composed of stone voussoirs decorated with saw-like ornamentation, in a style known as a Persian arch. The voussoirs are surrounded by moulded decoration. On each of the two sides of the arch there is a projecting circular stone medallion devoid of decorative elements. Around the bulk of the *sabil,* on both sides and above it, there is a frame of moulded decoration that terminates with more embellishment where the base of the *sabil* starts to form.  
The recess of the *sabil* is composed of three decorative architectural units. In the lower part of the recess there is a rectangular marble plaque which has an opening in the middle to allow water to flow from the *sabil* reservoir (located at the back) to the basin. At the top of the recess there are three tiers of *muqarnas* crowned by a small ribbed shell. In the middle of the niche, below the *muqarnas* tiers, there is an inscription panel. The panel is composed of three lines carved in Ottoman *naskhi* script which allude to the command to construct the *sabil*, the titles of the builder and the date of its construction. The inscription reads:  
“The construction of this blessed *sabil* was ordered by our lord the Sultan, the Great Ruler, The Sovereign, The Noble, the Lord of Nations, the Sultan of Rome \[Byzantium\], the Arabs and the 'Ajam \[Persians\], Sultan Sulayman, son of Sultan Selim Khan. May God grant him a long reign and sovereignty on the date of the 10th of Muharram in the year AH 943 \[29th June 1536\].”
cb8f8517-5780-5bcc-bee9-849860cd610e.short_description: This was the only *sabil* (public fountain) of the six commissioned by Ottoman Sultan Sulayman the Magnificent to be built outside the walls around Jerusalem. It is located on the road that connects Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Hebron. The *sabil* is provided with water from a canal linked to Solomon’s Pools. Inside a recessed niche, open at the front, in the middle of a rectangular plaque an opening allows water to pour into a wide basin. Above the basin is a large foundation inscription. The *sabil* is constructed of cut stone in different sizes with rich decorative motifs. Behind the building is a reservoir which collects the water.

cdef497c-1efa-5c25-b7ef-048f71a83d64.name: Blue glazed jar
cdef497c-1efa-5c25-b7ef-048f71a83d64.description:
This jar, with two small handles, a narrow neck and a globular body is covered externally with a turquoise-blue glaze, while the interior is covered with a white glaze. The lip of the neck is protruding, which may have allowed for the placement of a small ceramic or wooden lid held by a textile.  
  
This functional object used for the storage and transportation of liquids, such as oil, water, wine or syrup. t was discovered at the Murwab archaeological site in northwest Qatar. The production of this type of jar appears to have ceased in the middle of the 9th century, according to the stratified archaeological findings of Susa (Iran), Samarra and Basra (Iraq). The most important workshop for this production was the centre of Basra.

ce0fc758-0578-5c82-a0bf-76b98283bf9c.name: "The Concourse of the Birds"
ce0fc758-0578-5c82-a0bf-76b98283bf9c.alternate_name: Folio 11r from a Mantiq al-Tayr (Language of the Birds)
ce0fc758-0578-5c82-a0bf-76b98283bf9c.description: The illustration on this folio depicts a scene from a mystical poem, Mantiq al-tair (Language of the Birds), written by a twelfth-century Iranian, Farid al-Din 'Attar. The birds, which symbolize individual souls in search of the simurgh (a mystical bird representing ultimate spiritual unity), are assembled in an idyllic landscape to begin their pilgrimage under the leadership of a hoopoe (perched on a rock at center right). The careful, harmonious composition is consistent with that of the late fifteenth-century Timurid miniatures also in the manuscript, but three factors indicate that this image is later: the presence of the hunter, who has no place in the narrative; his firearm, a weapon that gained currency in Iran after the mid-sixteenth century; and the signature of the late sixteenth- to early seventeenth-century artist Habiballah.

ce13dcdd-26d4-51f9-be00-2236cb4965f4.name: Ewer and basin
ce13dcdd-26d4-51f9-be00-2236cb4965f4.description: The basin is made of brass, with a wide, shallow rim and a concave body with a flat base. The bowl-shaped opening supports a soap holder, which sits as a plate and, after a slight neck, has straight sides folded upwards. The soap holder features a star at its centre and curved, three-pointed openwork perforations on the edges and underside. The rim of the basin is inscribed in Arabic with the words: “Mahmud Paşa’da Duyun-i Umumiye Caddesi'nde Osmanlı İmalathanesi,” which translates as “Ottoman Factory on Duyun-i Umumiye Street in Mahmud Pasha.”

ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.name: Cup
ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.description: This copper cup is of a characteristic bell-shaped form, with a rounded base. Owing to its shape, it fits comfortably in the hand. The surface is entirely decorated with leaf motifs, arranged either as vine tendrils or within petal-shaped medallions. Vessels of this type were used for drinking water or wine, and parallels can be found in the AH 13th / AD 19th century metalwork collection of the National Museum in Niš, Serbia.
ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.
ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.obtention: The item is a part of the collection of Serbian painter and engraver Ljuba Ivanović (1882–1945). The collection was purchased by the Museum of Applied Art in Belgrade in 1951 and comprises 3,116 items, bearing witness to the early modern and modern visual culture of the Balkans: urban and folk dress,  jewelry, metalwork, casting molds and tools, items carved in wood, horn, and mother-of-pearl, wood-carved and painted icons, etc. The items were collected in the field, mostly during the interwar period.
ceddedce-74b1-58a0-9e37-95a0cdedcef0.author: Mila Gajić

cf314a7e-b71e-5876-a94f-3e498400a91f.short_description: This elaborate flask dates from the late 16th century. Its wooden body is covered with a linen and chalk ground that was gilded and painted where we see lovers and musicians in a garden filled with flowers.

d04d6038-8121-55a2-8b2e-c0971ba15d5d.description: This bronze pump was made by a Greek artisan in Trabzon. The mouth section of the pump is designed in the form of a stylised dragon head, while the body features floral motifs and bears the inscription "[M.] 1810."

d0f77700-ba50-5c79-bdd6-b7a71456cf55.name: Banknote
d0f77700-ba50-5c79-bdd6-b7a71456cf55.description: The Syrian banknote depicting the Norias of Hama presents one of the country’s most iconic water monuments. The great wooden water wheels, rising above the Orontes River, symbolise traditional hydraulic ingenuity and the centrality of water in Syrian urban life. Rendered with fine engraved detail, the image links national identity to heritage, memory, and the enduring relationship between society and river landscapes.
d0f77700-ba50-5c79-bdd6-b7a71456cf55.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

d1df60cc-7f00-5222-836d-c786e82473ca.name: Water jug filter
d1df60cc-7f00-5222-836d-c786e82473ca.description: The decorative openings on the necks of this type of water jugs (fired clay vessels that cool their contents through a process of gradual evaporation) are evidence of the inventiveness of Cairo potters. They would trace the design onto wet clay with a sharpened reed similar to a calligraphy pen, in a technique similar to *al fresco* painting.
d1df60cc-7f00-5222-836d-c786e82473ca.obtention: Formerly in the collection of Mr. and Mrs. Jean-François Bouvier.
