materials: Unglazed ceramic clay, incised and perforated

d2293b15-b277-5cf9-b55b-a5c86bba494e.name: Waterway in Nizwa, Oman
d2293b15-b277-5cf9-b55b-a5c86bba494e.description: The *aflaj* (singular *falaj*) are one of the oldest irrigation systems still in use today. Its origins date back to 5,000 years ago, though the example here is from AD 500. Its channels convey water from underground sources, springs and stream flow to villages and towns all around Oman. This system is employed as a primary water source for agricultural and domestic purposes, accounting for more than 30% of water usage across Oman. Using gravity forces to maintain the flux of water and its distribution, it has emerged as a distinguished social, cultural and economic emblem of the Omani landscape. The responsibility for the maintenance of working falaj and the distribution of water to different settlements lies with these communities. Despite the existence of numerous wells that provide potable water, the presence of aflaj waterways is of pivotal significance to the agricultural prosperity of Oman. The Falaj Daris, seen here, are the largest of the aflaj in Oman, and played a big part in Nizwa’s former prosperity as the capital of Oman in the 6th and 7th centuries AD. In 2006, the Aflaj Irrigation System was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and consequently granted governmental protection.
d2293b15-b277-5cf9-b55b-a5c86bba494e.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

d2881aa5-0ddf-52cc-b17f-a2d9d686b2fe.name: Calligraphy
d2881aa5-0ddf-52cc-b17f-a2d9d686b2fe.description:
This artwork centers on the Qur’anic phrase rendered in the form of a water droplet:  
Arabic: وَجَعَلْنَا مِنَ الْمَاءِ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ حَيٍّ  
Transliteration: *Ve cealnâ mine’l-mâ’i kulle şey’in hayy*  
English: “And We made from water every living thing.”  
  
The piece merges modern calligraphic expression with classical Islamic aesthetics. The water-droplet form highlights the verse’s central theme: the origin of life through water, a motif deeply rooted in Islamic cosmology. The fluid lines, layered strokes and turquoise tones evoke movement, purity and renewal. On the right, the intricate calligraphic motif adds a devotional dimension, inviting contemplation on divine creation and the sustaining nature of water.  
  
Through its interplay of text, form and symbolism, the artwork invites viewers to reflect on life’s elemental foundations and the spiritual significance of water in Islamic thought.
d2881aa5-0ddf-52cc-b17f-a2d9d686b2fe.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
d2881aa5-0ddf-52cc-b17f-a2d9d686b2fe.method_for_datation: Date and origin are written on the piece
d2881aa5-0ddf-52cc-b17f-a2d9d686b2fe.author: Ercan Topçu, Barış Topçu

d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.name: Konch
d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.description:
The Konch is a fishing device made from bamboo and iron spikes, and is specifically designed to catch larger fish. It is similar to the Juti, but employs at least 10 pieces of bamboo splits, which are firmly fixed in a bunch. In order to increase its effectiveness, the tips of the bamboo are topped with sharp and pointed iron caps. To use it, fishermen must wait with great patience until they find a fish, often spending hours on a boat or at the water's edge. Once they eventually find one, they hurl the implement with great force, pinning the fish down and striking it. The species of fish caught with this device include Rui (Labeo rohita), Catla (Catla catla), Shoal (Channa striatus), and Gozar (Channa marulius), amongst others.  
Traditional fishing gear consists of a long bamboo handle (2-4m) with a 60-65cm iron rode at the base, and is fitted with multiple iron hooks at the apex. The iron rode is securely attached to the bamboo handle using coconut thread or iron wire.
d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.bibliography: Siddiq, M., *et al.*, “Fishing Gears of the Meghna River Estuary of Chandpur Region, Bangladesh”, in *Trends in Fisheries Research, 2(1; 2018): https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325120382\_FISHING\_GEARS\_OF\_THE\_MEGHNA\_RIVER\_ESTUARY\_OF\_CHANDPUR\_REGION\_BANGLADESH \[last accessed: 04/10/25\]*
d330f255-e6aa-5ada-a3e4-633faa06f950.author: ActionAid Bangladesh

d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.name: Font.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.description: Font with eight lobes. The inside is hollowed out, with the rim moulded on the top and on the outside. It has a hole at the bottom. The base is truncated, with a base or foot missing. The exterior moulding has a decoration of small engraved geometric patterns (lozenges, squares and circles). The upper rim has an Arabic inscription in *kufic* script running all the way round, in which it is possible to read the expression ‘al-Mulk’, repeated in a chain.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.short_description: The evidence for the prolonged presence of a Muslim community in Lisbon is supported by this octagonal ablutions font sculpted from local *pedra lioz* (lias) limestone. It was found during restoration work in Lisbon’s Moorish quarter, to whose mosque it belonged.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.method_for_datation: External, historical dating. The mosque in the Moorish quarter, to which it is supposed to have belonged, was dismantled in the early 16th century, in the reign of Dom Manuel I of Portugal.
d39f33c7-ab99-570d-9745-2ca9481fd5e0.method_for_provenance: Found during urban regeneration work, re-used in the masonry of one the walls of the building on no. 67 Rua João do Outeiro (Moorish quarter, Lisbon). The building probably dated originally from the 16th century.

keywords: font; lias stone; Kufic script; al-mulk

d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.name: Pearl Diver’s Finger Protectors
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.short_description: These finger guards are known as khabt (pl. khabta). They were an essential part of a pearl-diver's equipment, as they protected his finger tips from the sharp oyster shells and other unexpected dangerous objects the pearl-diver might brush his fingers against while searching the murky seabed. Much of his work had to rely on touch, as visibility was minimal and few dangers could be anticipated by sight alone. When not used, the finger guards were kept in a container filled with water to keep them supple.
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.type: 15 leather finger protectors with cotton bag
d3ddaba2-605a-593a-84dc-d55cd6a60174.holder: Sharjah Maritime Museum / Sharjah Museums Department

d3e76481-492c-566e-9282-18576527dae4.name: Farmer with Dried Gourd
d3e76481-492c-566e-9282-18576527dae4.description:
This type of gourd, grown in Hit, Anbar Governorate, Iraq, is among a number of varieties of calabash or "bottle gourd" of different shapes and sizes that were historically used as multipurpose vessels, including water bottles and containers for agricultural produce including beer and wine, milk and other dairy products, honey or grains. Cut segments of these gourds could also be used to make kitchen utensils such as ladles and bowls. They have been cultivated in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas for thousands of years for similar purposes.  
  
While the same gourds can be harvested young for consumption as a vegetable, if grown as containers or utensils they are left to grow for longer and harvested when mature. After harvesting, they are dried for several months until the outer shell becomes hard. The dried gourds are usually cut at the top to make an opening through which the seeds are removed and contents added for storage.

keywords: Water, gourd, calabash, container, vessel, utensil.

d4e323fc-c4f2-52d4-94cb-5c4f2e01828f.name: Map of the Üsküdar Waterways
d4e323fc-c4f2-52d4-94cb-5c4f2e01828f.description: A scroll-shaped map of the waterways of Üsküdar, backed with cloth and painted in watercolours. This image shows a section of the map, which measures 17.86m in total.

d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.name: Basin.
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.description:
A spectacular piece of Mamluk metalwork in the form of a large basin with a flared rim, covered inside and out with silver and gold inlay decoration. A striking *thuluth* inscription surrounds the central panel of the bowl giving the name and titles of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun, who ruled between AH 692 and 743 / AD 1293 and 1341. This basin is one of a number of metalwork vessels from this period featuring bold inscriptions as the main decorative element. The principal inscription is set against arabesques whose tendrils transform into ducks or birds. Dividing the inscription are three medallions filled with lotus flowers, and a small epigraphic blazon in the centre that reads: ‘Glory to our master, the sultan’. Above and below this central panel are two friezes of floral scrolls alternating with six roundels containing further inscriptions.  
The presence of lotus blossoms and peonies derives from chinoiserie designs, imported by the Mongols in Iran; these floral designs are also found in Iranian art at this time. The inscription around the rim of the interior reads: ‘Glory to our master, the Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir the wise, the efficient, the warrior, the champion of the faith, the defender Nasir al-Dunya wa’l-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun, may his victory be glorious’. Large basins such as this one were used for a number of ceremonial functions. However, the circling fish in the base suggest that this basin was used as an ablution vessel.
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.short_description: A large brass basin covered in silver and gold inlay, probably used as a vessel for ritual ablutions. A bold inscription band around the body of the basin is the main decorative feature, and displays the name and titles of the Mamluk Sultan al-Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qalawun (AH 692–743 / AD 1293–1341).
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.method_for_datation: The object is inscribed with the name Sultan Nasir al-Din Muhammad (r. 692–743 / 1293–1341). He was a great patron of the arts, commissioning many buildings as well as numerous fine objects; this object was made during his reign.
d5f6e50a-98c0-5ed7-8aca-8f6313966465.method_for_provenance: The basin would have been made in Egypt or Syria as both countries were under the rule of the patron, Sultan Nasir al-Din Muhammad.

d637d366-909f-55c1-86c7-bd60b9d571e9.name: Water flask
d637d366-909f-55c1-86c7-bd60b9d571e9.description: A wooden oval flask with metal edges decorated with zigzag (sawtooth) and wavy branch motifs. The body is ornamented with domed studs and rosettes of multi-petaled flowers with zigzag borders and simple cross-hatched lozenges. Metal fittings include rings for suspension. It features two cylindrical necks (one small, one large, pierced), with covers. One attached by a chain, the other missing.

d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.name: Basin.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.description:
This piece, a deep copper basin inlaid with silver, is decorated with an epigraphic band written in *thuluth* script whose text reads: 'Made for the honourable Excellency, the sublime master, the learned, the just, the warrior (of the frontiers), the defender (of the faith), the masterful, al-Sayfi Tabtaq al-Maliki al-Ashrafi.' The name carried by this vessel is linked to Amir Tabtaq, one of the officers under al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, who ruled from AH 689–93 / AD 1290–4. Tabtaq was the governor of Qus a city in Upper Egypt, during the third reign of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun (AH 709–41 / AD 1309–40). A number of blazons depicting a goblet, a symbol for the position of cupbearer, intermingle with the inscriptions. The inside centre base of the basin holds a design composed of six fishes arranged in a spiral format.  
The basin was used for hand-washing and at times for washing clothes. During the Mamluk period, the wardrobe or storeroom for clothing was known as '*tast khana*' meaning the 'abode of the basin' and all that was allotted to the sultans by way of basins, apparel, jewellery, swords, chairs and carpets was stored there. There were various types of basin and a variety of decorative styles, including gold and silver inlay, especially during the Mamluk period.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.short_description: A basin would form a pair with a ewer as an indispensable item in hand-washing and cleanliness in general. This basin, inlaid with silver, bears the blazon of its owner, the cupbearer Amir Tabtaq.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.dimensions: Height 17 cm, diameter (of the opening) 44 cm.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.method_for_datation: The basin was dated based on studies of the inscriptions which bear the name of Amir Tabtaq, one of the officers of al-Malik al-Ashraf Khalil, and a governor of the City of Qus during the reign of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.method_for_provenance: This piece was produced in Egypt, for in addition to having been discovered in the Egyptian City of Qus, it was commissioned specifically for Amir Tabtaq. Furthermore, the inlay technique used on this basin is in the mode that flourished in Egypt during the Mamluk period. There are a number of pieces, acquired by museums, that have been made in an identical manner to this piece, and whose provenance has been attributed to Egypt.
d6880977-13ca-5aa6-b786-648161801155.obtention: The basin was uncovered during the course of archaeological excavations in 1966 at Qus.

d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.name: Women by the Well
d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.description:
This painting elegantly encapsulates a quotidian moment imbued with the rural essence of Jordanian tradition. The scene under consideration depicts a group of figures, predominantly female, congregated around a stone well situated beneath a clear blue sky, with lush greenery and palm trees serving as a backdrop. The utilisation of vibrant hues and meticulous attention to detail serves to elicit a sense of concord between humans, architecture and nature.  
The composition is centred on the well structure, which is composed of warm, sandy stones and framed by an arched entrance that serves as both a practical and symbolic focal point. This concept encompasses not only the physical source of water but also serves as a nexus for community and social interaction. The women's actions, drawing, carrying and pouring water reflect cooperation and rhythm in everyday life, while their vibrant clothing, rich in blues, reds and greens, highlights cultural identity and regional craftsmanship.  
The artist's employment of colour and light engenders an atmosphere that is serene and almost celebratory. The distinct contours and vivid colour scheme bear resemblance to folk painting and naïve art, placing emphasis on storytelling and collective memory as opposed to strict realism. This approach encourages viewers to recognise the aesthetic value of simplicity and to acknowledge the dignity of routine activities.
d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.holder: Jordan National Gallery of Fine Arts
d69ce4c6-4db6-5eba-bc2f-4c16c9bf8894.author: Dina Turkieh

d6d69c7b-e931-5628-b682-41484e297c16.name: *Woman with a Branch of Dates*
d6d69c7b-e931-5628-b682-41484e297c16.description:
Faiq Hassan was among the pioneering artists in Iraq who obtained formal art education and was awarded a government scholarship to pursue studies in Paris. In AH 1356 / AD 1938, he assumed the directorship of the recently established *Ma’had al-Funun al-Jamila fi Baghdad* (Institute of Fine Arts in Baghdad), a role he held until AH 1382 / AD 1962.  
Hassan belonged to the cohort of *'al-Ruwwad'* (the Pioneers), a group of painters that integrated elements of everyday Iraqi life into their artwork and defied conventional studio methods. He followed the artistic principle of istilham al-turath, which focused on taking inspiration from heritage. This principle was developed by *Jama'at Baghdad lil-Fann al-Hadith* (Baghdad Group for Modern Art), which was founded in AH 1370 / AD 1951.  
  
'A Woman with a Branch of Dates' shows an Iraqi woman wearing a black traditional garment and holding a basket of dates , before an abstract, flattened village background. Hassan preferred to depict everyday life in rural areas. He merged the artistic traditions of ancient Mesopotamia with modernism to cultivate an awareness of Iraqi national identity.
d6d69c7b-e931-5628-b682-41484e297c16.holder: MATHAF, Arab Museum of Modern Art

d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.name: Water pumping equipment in Kağıthane, Istanbul
d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.short_description: During the 19th century, new technologies radically transformed both travel and communications. Cendere Hamidian Water Pump Station was built by Abdülhamid II in 1902 at an altitude of 34 metres above sea level. With its function, architectural design and mechanical equipment, the station is a unique monument to the history of the architecture industry in the Ottoman Empire. It pumped to Balmumcu and Beşiktaş – in the direction of Tophane, moving water coming from 20 different pipes in Kağıthane using steam pump machines.
d86bffa6-0320-50d5-b0a4-c47134d7d642.holder: Istanbul University, Nadir Eserler Kütüphanesi (Rare Books Library)
keywords: Yıldız Album; II. Abdulhamid Han; Photograph; History of Water in Ottoman Empire; Water Pump Station

d88746c7-cbe9-5e02-9b69-27f81f2ed7e5.name: Nilometer
d88746c7-cbe9-5e02-9b69-27f81f2ed7e5.description:
The Nilometer is the oldest extant Islamic structure in Egypt, built on the Nile island of al-Rauda in Cairo in AH 247 / AD 861. It consists of a shaft that is connected with the Nile through three channels. In the middle of the shaft stands a column, and its markings from the bottom up make it possible to measure the water level, providing information that is of fundamental importance for people and crops in the Nile river valley.  
  
The Nilometer’s interior is decorated with inscriptions that primarily consist of passages from the Koran. Similar friezes, since demolished, once embellished the entrance, from which this inscription frieze probably came.  
  
It was purchased in Cairo in AH 1240 / AD 1824 by F. C. Münter, Bishop of Zealand, Denmark.
d88746c7-cbe9-5e02-9b69-27f81f2ed7e5.bibliography: Meyer, J., *et al.*, *Beyond words: calligraphy from the World of Islam*, Copenhagen: Strandberg Publishing, 2024: fig. 12, 22 and 25.

"*Eba Eyyûb el-Ensârî aleyhir-raḥmeti’l-bârî’de Kur’an ve Mevlid-i Şerif için, Şevketli, Kerametli, Mehabetli Sultan Mahmud Han-ı Gazi Hazretlerinin Vakf-ı Hümâyun-ı Mülûkânesindendir. Sene 1161.*"

d8e1d81f-2112-5652-987b-f417b3f15ad1.name: Scalloped ewer
d8e1d81f-2112-5652-987b-f417b3f15ad1.description:
This pitcher with gadrooned (scalloped) body is used to rinse the hands and face of a guest who has arrived at a host’s residence. The shape of the object is well known in Türkiye and India; it was also reproduced in ceramics.  
The mark of the owner is visible in two places: under the spout, in an almond cartouche, and again in a hexagon whose sides are extended by a three-lobed floret.

The lower part of the body is decorated with a row of rounded reliefs. The lid has a rounded handle that expands slightly outward. A small brass spout is fitted to the lower part of the body.

da60db2e-b27e-5914-9284-ae2e7d5378d4.name: Astrolabe-quadrant
da60db2e-b27e-5914-9284-ae2e7d5378d4.description: One side of the instrument carries a Prophatius astrolabe-quadrant for latitude 41°, with an unequal hour diagram (horary quadrant) above. The other side is a sine-cosine quadrant with arcs of sine and versed sine. There are brief instructions in Turkish and Arabic on the sides and edges. The maker’s name and the date appear on each side, with slight variations in some details of the signature. The *nisbah* of the maker, al-Uﬁ, indicates that he was from Of, a small town on the Black Sea.

daf0a019-2f3a-548e-8b57-dc323f10cd15.name: Cisterns of Sidi Bou Othmane
daf0a019-2f3a-548e-8b57-dc323f10cd15.description:
The cisterns of Sidi Bou Othmane, in the Haouz region near Marrakech, are an outstanding example of medieval Moroccan hydraulic engineering. Built in the AH 6th / AD 12th century under the Almohad dynasty, they show how crucial water management was in a semi-arid environment. Designed to collect, store, and distribute water, they supplied local populations, commercial caravans, and military garrisons in a water-scarce region. The complex comprises several basins and tanks linked by a system based on the impluvium principle, where channels run off into settling basins for filtration before reaching the main cisterns. At its core are nine large cisterns, each about 4 metres wide, 5 metres high, and 25 metres long, holding over 3,250 cubic metres of water. Thick walls of roughly 1.5 metres provided stability, and roof openings allowed ventilation and maintenance. Water flowed through a network of canals, with a nearby dam regulating the supply.  
  
Built from local stone and mortar, the cisterns were waterproofed with fine finishes. Fragments of decorated ceramics, now preserved at El Badi Palace, reflect the attention paid to durability and aesthetics.  
  
These cisterns had multiple roles: they irrigated surrounding lands, supporting cereals, fruits, and other crops. Strategically, they supplied garrisons and caravans moving between Marrakech, southern Morocco, and Saharan trade routes. Socially, many cisterns were managed through *waqf* endowments, a type of Islamic charitable donation where property or income is dedicated to public or religious use, funding mosques, madrasas, and aid for the poor. Though their use declined with modernisation, they remain a vital heritage site showcasing historical water management and human adaptation to environmental challenges in Morocco.
daf0a019-2f3a-548e-8b57-dc323f10cd15.bibliography: Allain, C., ‘Les citernes et les margelles de Sidi Bou Othman’, *Hespéris*, vol. 38 (3–4), 1951 : 423–434.
daf0a019-2f3a-548e-8b57-dc323f10cd15.history: During the Almohad period (c. AH 524–667 / AD 1121–1269), Marrakech, then the empire’s capital, saw major developments in urban planning, agriculture, and water infrastructure. The dynasty inherited knowledge from the Almoravids and introduced new structures adapted to the local climate and terrain. In Haouz, capturing rain and floodwaters was essential. The Sidi Bou Othmane cisterns collected runoff from the surrounding mountains, ensuring a year-round supply.
daf0a019-2f3a-548e-8b57-dc323f10cd15.author: MUSEUM Staff, Layan Shahin
keywords: Almohad, cistern, water storage, irrigation, Haouz, hydraulic system, waqf

dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.name: Vat
dc123c01-a94a-53ca-b79e-5fb7aeb83571.description:
Globular vat with a conical base, a flaring neck, a flanged rim and winged handles. The paste is whitish and unglazed. Its decoration consists of a stamped, alternating series of lozenges and eulogetic epigraphy arranged in perimeter friezes.  
  
A common feature of Andalusian homes, these large earthenware vats were strategically placed in the courtyards or in interior rooms to preserve goods such as oil, cereals, or water, as well as to store domestic objects. In this case, the porous nature of the unglazed clay suggests that this example functioned specifically as a water vat, as it would have filtered and cooled the water, keeping it clean and fresh.  
  
Beyond their practical function, some vats had also an aesthetic value, as can be seen in the stamped decoration or glazing. Decorations included epigraphic motifs invoked to protect the vats' contents. The production and use of these vats continued after the Castilian conquest.

The globular body and stamped decoration are particularly present in the Almohad world, evolving towards more stylised forms, with more pronounced winged handles.

dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.name: Ablution jug.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.description:
A cylindrical jug of leaded bronze without a handle and with a tall neck divided into two unequal parts by a decorative 'rope' band. The cylindrical body is plain, although the shoulder is divided into narrow bands that are filled with short vertical strokes.  
  
This vessel may once have been used as an ablution jug for ritual washing before prayer; many other such metal and ceramic jugs have been found associated with this ritual. This particular jug was found during archaeological excavations in the hammam that was part of the qasr (palace) at Umm al-Walid.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.short_description: A jug of leaded bronze, without a handle and made from four parts welded together. Found during excavations at the baths of the Umayyad qasr at Umm al-Walid, it may have been used as an ablution jug for ritual washing before prayer.
dc345fef-438d-5088-994a-47a78663e585.owner: Now on display at Jordan Museum

dc5b965f-e339-5f91-bede-06c101b7ce46.name: Water mills
dc5b965f-e339-5f91-bede-06c101b7ce46.description:
Water mills, locally known as *maṭḥana*, date back to the AH 5th-16th / AD 11th–12th centuries during the Almoravid and Almohad dynasties. They played a vital role in Morocco’s rural and agricultural history, supporting traditional economies where farming was the main livelihood. These dynasties promoted the development of hydraulic infrastructure and the rational use of water in both cities and countryside.  
The concept of the water mill was not new, but it was refined in Morocco through the blending of Berber, Andalusian, and Eastern influences, enriching local know-how in construction, hydraulics, and community organisation.  
Built in rural regions near rivers and irrigation canals, these mills harnessed the power of flowing water to grind cereals such as wheat, barley, and corn: staples of Moroccan agriculture. Water was diverted through a small canal or pipe to a horizontal wheel, typically wooden or metal, which rotated and turned the upper stone. This efficient system turned grains into flour—an important step in preparing bread, the cornerstone of the Moroccan diet.  
In Morocco’s semi-arid climate, water management was always crucial to the survival of communities. Water mills were often integrated into larger hydraulic systems, linked to khettaras (traditional underground canals), norias (water wheels), dams, and retention basins. Beyond their agricultural function, water mills had a social and religious dimension. They might be incorporated into waqfs or habous (religious endowments), whose revenues were used to fund mosques, Quranic schools (madrasas), or hostels for travellers. The miller, often a respected figure in the village, played the role of mediator and overseer in ensuring fair access to milling services. More than functional structures, these mills served as social hubs and symbols of cooperation, sustainability, and spiritual value.  
With the advent of modern industry and the introduction of electric mills in the AH 16th / AD 20th century, the use of traditional water mills gradually declined. Some survive in mountainous areas, such as the Middle Atlas, or in remote regions of the Rif and Souss, preserved as part of Morocco’s cultural heritage. These mills stand as evidence of Moroccan hydraulic genius, of the ability of rural societies to adapt to their environment, and of the harmonious integration of nature, technology, and spirituality.

dc96172a-d522-545b-a1c3-052bebfe5e6c.name: "Device for Raising Water" from al-Jazari's "Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices"
dc96172a-d522-545b-a1c3-052bebfe5e6c.description: In the AH 7th / AD 13th-century, a scholar and engineer named Isma‘il Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari wrote a famous treatise called *Kitab fi ma‛rifat al-hiyal al-handasiyya*, or The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices. The text offered detailed descriptions of a series of elaborate machines designed to delight and impress the elites at the court where he served, in eastern Anatolia. Al-Jazari’s text and its illustrations belong to a long tradition of studies about these kinds of devices, including Greek compendia on mechanics and mathematics. This page belongs to a copy of the text that was produced in Mamluk Egypt in AH 755 / AD 1354, and was copied by Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Izmiri for a Mamluk ruler.
dc96172a-d522-545b-a1c3-052bebfe5e6c.obtention: By 1912, Victor Goloubew (b. 1879 - d. 1945), Paris; 1914, sold by Goloubew through M. Meyer-Riefstahl to the MFA.

dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.name: Safi ibn Vali’s Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’)
dd7c1d21-573b-5dd3-8f6f-94141d1320e3.short_description:
Written during the year-long pilgrimage undertaken by the author, Safi ibn Vali, in 1676–77, the Anis al-Hujjaj (‘Pilgrims’ Companion’) gives advice to prospective pilgrims on every aspect of the journey: which ships to choose, how to stay healthy, the places to visit, the rituals to be observed and the people one is likely to encounter. Safi ibn Vali’s own pilgrimage (he commenced his journey on 12 Rajab 1087/ 20 September 1676) was made possible through the financial help of Zib al-Nisa, a daughter of the Mughal emperor Awrangzeb, for whom he had written a commentary on the Qur’an.  
  
This manuscript belongs to a long-established tradition of guides to the Holy Places (see MSS 1038), although the illustrations here differ in that they combine the diagrammatic views normally found in such guides with vivid and colourful scenes of the pilgrims and their caravans. The illustrations are simple in their conception yet their attention to detail is acute. They provide a cogent picture of camp life of pilgrims in the late 17th century.  
  
The illustrations:  
  
View of the port of Surat and the ships carrying pilgrims (folio 2b). Surat, on the Western coast of India, north of Bombay, was one of the main points of departure to Arabia. The view is oriented to the south.  
The pilgrims’ ships crossing the Sea of Oman (folio 3b). The two larger ships carry pilgrims; one, on the right, appears to be casting (or raising) anchor. The smaller vessels may be fishing boats.  
The mish‘ar al-haram and the ritual of collecting pebbles (folio 10a). The painting shows the pilgrims in the region of Muzdalifa, in a state of ihram (ritual purity), collecting pebbles.  
The pilgrims in the town of Mina, being shaved, making sacrifices and casting pebbles at the Devil (folio 10b). This day corresponds to ‘Id al-Adha on 10 dhu’l-Hijjah, the feast commemorating the Sacrifice of Abraham. By this stage, the pilgrims, who are in a full state of ihram indicated by their white garments, have already completed their initial circumambulation of the Ka‘bah (the welcome tawaf); the ritual of running between the hills of Safa and Marwa (sa‘iyy) recalling Hagar’s desperate search for water for her son Isma‘il; the day of prayer at ‘Arafat – a most holy time when every pilgrim stands alone with God; and the gathering of pebbles at Muzdalifa in preparation for the stoning of the Devil at Mina. This recalls yet another chapter in the Abrahamic narrative in which Isma‘il stones the Devil seven times (the ritual is illustrated in the upper right-hand corner of the painting). After this a sacrifice is made. The pilgrims are released from most of the restrictions imposed by the state of ihram; men shave their heads and beards; women have their hair clipped. Pilgrims can now wear their normal clothes and leave for Mecca, where they perform another essential rite, a further circumambulation of the Ka‘bah known as the tawaf al-ifadah, which takes place on the same day.  
The birthplaces of the Prophet Muhammad; Fatimah; Abu Bak al-Siddiq; as well as the Madrasah of Sultan Sulayman, and a Bektashi lodge (folio 11b). These are shrines to visit in the vicinity of Mecca, which are not part of the hajj rituals.  
Plan of the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca with the Ka‘bah (folio 12a).  
The camp of North African caravan of pilgrims (folio 15a).  
The camp of Egyptian caravan of pilgrims (folio 15b).  
The camp of the Syrian caravan of pilgrims (folio 16a). Unlike the pilgrims from North Africa and Egypt, the Syrian pilgrims are richly dressed and carry swords and gold daggers. Ahmad Pasha, the Syrian Amir al-Hajj, is identified by a caption (top left).  
The camp of the desert Arabs and the people of Najd (folio 16b).  
The camp of the caravans of the Indian (top) and Iranian pilgrims (folio 17a).  
Officials, scribes and secretaries (folio 17b). This is a small illustration, which is not captioned.  
Sharif Barakat, hakim haramayn sharifayn (‘Governor of the two Holy Sanctuaries’), riding to meet the envoy of Sultan Mehmed \[IV\], the Emperor of Rum (folio 18a).  
‘Abdi Pasha, the Amir al-Hajj of the Egyptian caravan, on his way from Mecca to Medina (folio 18b).  
The port of Mucha, in the Yemen (folio 21a). The illustration shows the pilgrims’ ships departing from the port as well as Sayyid Husayn, the Governor of Mucha, riding his horse (bottom right).  
The port of Jeddah (folio 22b). This view is very similar to that of Mucha (folio 21a) in that it combines views of the city and the pilgrims’ ships with one of the Governor of the city, Sunjuq.  
Man attacked by a lion (folio 21b); Man saved from the jaws of a lion (folio 23a); A feast (folio 23b). The three small-scale paintings are illustrations to a parable about a very poor woman taking pity on some beggars passing by and feeding them; her act of generosity was rewarded when a stranger saved her son from being eaten by a lion. The feast is probably in celebration of the son’s safe return to his mother.  
Script:  
  
Persian text copied in nasta‘liq; with 23 lines to the page.

dddd9f2e-9bbf-52e9-b0c9-6daa195c732b.description: A view of Jebel Kuruntul from the Jericho plain with the remains of Mamluk sugar mills and aqueducts in the middle distance. Charles Warren describes the scene in his book *Underground Jerusalem*, AH 1293 / AD 1876: p 167, and pp 185–189. This picture was taken from Warren's campsite. “Our way lay over some low swelling hills, on which the ruins of the sugar mills remain, and the aqueduct which brought water to work them from ‘Ain ed Duk. These mills appear to have been put up after the Moslem conquest, when the plain of Jericho was in a high state of cultivation; even as late as the 12th century it was accounted the garden of Palestine”: 186.

de4d9eaf-e78d-5c74-9efd-dd68d0c7fae9.name: Entrance of the Hammam of the Mouassine Mosque (Marrakech)
de4d9eaf-e78d-5c74-9efd-dd68d0c7fae9.description: The entrance to the *hammam* of the Mouassine Mosque in Marrakech is situated within an area of the city that dates back to antiquity. This area demonstrates the interconnection between water, buildings and the quality of life of the inhabitants of the medina. The Mouassine complex was constructed during the Saadian period in the 16th century. The architectural design of the building was conceived with the intention of creating a multifunctional civic foundation, thereby ensuring its versatility in terms of utilisation. The complex included a mosque, fountain, hammam, madrasa and public amenities. The entrance to the hammam is modest and integrated into the urban fabric, reflecting the traditional Moroccan approach to architecture where public buildings are an integral part of the city.
de4d9eaf-e78d-5c74-9efd-dd68d0c7fae9.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

df3db103-55c2-57af-a18e-f9b924273ff5.name: Soap box
df3db103-55c2-57af-a18e-f9b924273ff5.description:
Soap boxes such as this example were part of the AH 13th / AD 19th century Turkish dowry tradition. Known as *sabunluk*, *kildence* or *kildan*, they were offered to the bride as part of grooming trousseau which would include a personal toiletry set and refined objects that she would bring with her to the hamam.  
  
This box is made of tinned copper. The sides are decorated with repoussé semi-circles running along the edges and encircling a row of diamond-shaped motifs finely engraved with a lotus-like pattern. Similar delicate vegetal engraving adorns the upper level which is indented on the top, most probably to leave a comfortable resting space for the knuckles during transportation. The rectangular handle is supported by two slightly leaning hinges. Two further hinges house a bird-shaped lock to safely protect the contents of the box.  
  
It currently holds a silver pumice case and its bottom is pierced allowing it to serve as a sieve so that any residual moisture could drain off. The *kildence* could vary in size and contain a variety of other items such as *kese* (exfoliating washcloth), combs, mirrors, makeup, perfumes, etc.  
  
A treasured family item, the quality of the *kildence* matched the refinement of the set it was part of and would act, like every object in the dowry trousseau, as a statement on the social status of its holder.  
  
As the traditions fade away and the utilitarian objects of the hamam turn into plastic, this carefully crafted item is a testimony to the refinement of the often overlooked material culture of the hamam tradition in Türkiye.

dfc454bd-a4c8-5e09-bb84-93b4d6b1629f.name: Basin
dfc454bd-a4c8-5e09-bb84-93b4d6b1629f.short_description: A brass basin with splayed rim; raised, chased, and inlaid with silver and niello. The main decorative element on the exterior is a large band of flowing *Thuluth* (elaborate Arabic script) inscription against a floral background, broken by three circular medallions. Each medallion has an inner circle of *Nashki* (more standard Arabic script) bordered by a floral band. The large register is bordered top and bottom by narrow registers decorated with pinwheels and diamonds filled with a fleur-de-lis pattern. The top register has crowning element of upward pointing leaves. The exterior *Thuluth* inscription reads, "The seat of power, the lord, the princely / the great, the conqueror, the defender of the faith, the frontier warrior / the protector of frontiers, the rendered victorious by God the \[mamluk\] of al-Malik al-Nasir." The *Nashki* inscription reads, "The seat of power, the lord, the learned, the diligent, the defender of the faith, \[mamluk of al-Malik\] al-Nasir." The underside of the lip has a roughly engraved inscription. The edge of the rim is decorated with a running vine scroll. A wide register of script is on the interior of the lip broken by six medallions, each with a pinwheel surrounded by a floral border. The Arabic inscription on the interior of the lip reads, "The seat of power / the lord, the / princely, the great, the lear / ned, the diligent the / conqueror, the defender of the faith / the master, \[mamluk of al-Malik\] al-Nasir." Below the remaining decorative register is an elaborate floral band with leaves pointing downward. On the interior floor is a large engraved circular medallion of fish with the same border of flowers and outward pointing petals.

dfc454bd-a4c8-5e09-bb84-93b4d6b1629f.method_for_datation: The stately Arabic inscriptions encircling the exterior of the basin and its interior rim indicate it was created for a high-ranking officer of the Mamluk ruler al-Malik al-Nasir (ruled 1293–1341).

dfeaa653-0f75-546d-8c39-7cac8ec05374.name: Planispheric Astrolabe
dfeaa653-0f75-546d-8c39-7cac8ec05374.description: Astrolabes of this size were not precise enough for astronomical observations, but served well for telling time, and astrologers could use them to determine the position of a planet relative to the different astrological houses. The intricate calligraphic faceplate of this example is typical of Safavid‑period astrolabes; it reads: "In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate" (bismallah al‑Rahman al‑Rahim).

e0cacb7c-8356-5070-a4ca-e40684822c68.name: Solomon’s Pools
e0cacb7c-8356-5070-a4ca-e40684822c68.description: The so-called Solomon's Pools at Artas near Bethlehem. These pools date from the Roman period and have a complex history of use, disuse and reuse lasting into the Mandate period. They were significantly refurbished in the Mamluk and early Ottoman periods. They were built to bring water into Jerusalem through a series of pipes and aqueducts, a process facilitated by the slightly higher ground at Artas relative to Jerusalem, and also for use in Artas and Bethlehem. They are fed by four nearby springs.

e0f43983-a8c9-5141-b857-a481b15f6d1d.name: *Ashari Balam*
e0f43983-a8c9-5141-b857-a481b15f6d1d.description:
The *ashari Balam* is the iconic boat of Basra, with a graceful shape and distinctive scroll-shaped stem head, pictured on many postcards and photographs of the British Mandate era (AH 1339-1351 / AD 1920-1932) that celebrated Basra’s reputation as “the Venice of the East”. The *ashari* may be either punted (propelled by pole), rowed, or sailed. It is not coated with tar, but caulked.  
  
There are three main boat types known as “*ashari*” (named after the al-Ashar area of Basra): the open water *ashari*, often under sail, a working boat that carried cargo; the marsh *ashari*, which is wider and used for net fishing and cargo; and the canal *ashari*, mainly used for passenger transportation and leisure trips, comparable in its function to the Gondola of Venice. Some of the latter type were fitted with canopies or shaded booths.  
  
Production continued into at least the AH 1400s / AD 1980s with a design that had changed little since the Ottoman era. The canal *ashari* can be considered as the last of the “gondolas” of Iraq, a category of boats that may have existed continuously since (at least) the early Islamic period: the historian al-Shabushti (AH 4th / AD 10th century) described how the people of Baghdad travelled in pleasure boats where they enjoyed playing music and games, eating and drinking. Even as far back as the 4th millennium BC (Uruk 3 period), a Sumerian boat with the characteristics of a gondola – a small but luxurious passenger craft – was depicted a cylinder seal impression found in the wetlands of Uqair in Diyala.  
  
Safina Projects has made extensive studies of these boat types, including models of several variants and full-sized reconstructions of the canal *ashari* and the open water *ashari*, which have been returned to use on Basra’s waterfront. The latter (pictured here) was built in AH 1444-43 / AD 2022-23 by Basra maritime historian Asaad Dawood in consultation with an experienced local boatbuilder, drawing on Rashad Salim’s research into archival imagery of the *ashari* and oral history interviews with former boatbuilders.

e1235680-19c3-5988-a988-34caaf7813e1.name: Rosewater bottle
e1235680-19c3-5988-a988-34caaf7813e1.description:
This bottle, used for storing rosewater or perfumes, is decorated with floral motifs, geometric patterns, and pictorial scenes. Structurally, it consists of a base, a body and a mouth.  
  
The base is slightly elevated and round in shape, decorated with twisted floral branches made of half palm fronds.  
  
The body is spherical, slightly tapered upwards, and is divided into three round bands, the middle one being the largest. These bands are framed with decorative borders composed of twisted floral branches and segments of palm fronds. The middle band features intersecting circular shapes, adorned with pictorial scenes set against a background of plant decorations made of multi-petaled rosettes and bird illustrations. The surfaces of the shapes are decorated with images of women wearing various types of hats and Iranian garments. Some are shown standing in tilted positions as if dancing, others are sitting, and some appear in whimsical or clownish poses. The upper band is adorned with touching circular shapes featuring seated women, some with sorrowful expressions and others in dancing postures. The lower band also contains touching circular shapes, depicting people wearing various hats and a mix of Iranian and fantastical clothing.  
  
The neck, shaped like a swan’s neck, begins and ends with a raised part decorated with zigzag patterns. The neck is decorated with oval shapes showing figures wearing various hats and Iranian garments – some standing, some sitting and some as mythical beings.  
The mouth, shaped like a teardrop, is adorned with the same pictorial scenes as those on the body and neck.  
  
Some Persian legends mention this vessel, known as “Ashkdan” or “Eshqdan” (meaning Vessel of Tears), suggesting that such bottles were used to collect women's tears during the long absence of their husbands. Upon their return, the amount of tears would be measured as an expression of love. In Shia mourning rituals, it is believed that tears are kept to commemorate martyrs, and these tears are thought to possess healing powers. However, the more accurate historical use of such bottles among the Persians was for applying perfume or rosewater to the hands and clothing.

e1eb944d-493e-5695-ab8f-d78784aef708.name: "Elias and Khizr at the Fountain of Life"
e1eb944d-493e-5695-ab8f-d78784aef708.alternate_name: Folio from a Shahnama (Book of Kings) of Firdausi
e1eb944d-493e-5695-ab8f-d78784aef708.description: Alexander the Great figures prominently in Persian literature and histories, including in both the Shahnama and the Khamsa of Nizami. This scene, which occurs in both texts, depicts Alexander and the Prophet Khizr’s search for the Fountain of Life. Although they begin the journey together, they are separated and only Khizr is successful. Here, he appears with the Prophet Elias at the Fountain, while Alexander continues his search in the background.

e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.name: Large dish with poly-lobed decoration.
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.description:
This dish is elegantly decorated with a large polylobed motif painted in black beneath a turquoise glaze.  
The side of the dish does not have the usual inscription of good omens, but a verse from the *Divan*of the Persian poet Hafez, which tells of the lament of an unhappy lover: "I have washed \[with tears\] the courtyard of the home of my eyes, but why / since this house is not \[even\] worthy of imagining your form?". The date is written at the end of the inscription: "finished in the year 873" (AD 1468).
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.short_description: This dish belongs to a group of ceramics known as *kubachi* after the village in the Caucasus where they were found. They would have been hung on the walls of homes as decoration.
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.holder: Museum of Civilisations | Museum of Oriental Art “Giuseppe Tucci”
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.owner: Istituto Italiano per l’Africa e l’Oriente (Is.IAO).
e44f9b93-0fc9-58a0-8f0b-14d05df5157e.method_for_provenance: This piece belongs to a specific group of ceramics known as *kubachi* from the name of the village in Daghestan in the Caucasus where they were found hung on walls for decoration. Ceramics of this type are of exceptional interest as they bear witness to the intense commercial exchanges between Persia and Kubachi, a place known for its production of steel weapons that were particularly sought after by the Iranian market and exchanged for a large quantity of Persian ceramics of unknown origin.

e4921c14-8d40-54c3-8c3f-a824cbf0cac3.name: Diwan Muhibbi
e4921c14-8d40-54c3-8c3f-a824cbf0cac3.short_description:
This precious and richly decorated divan is a manuscript by the poet and Sultan, Süleyman I, whose pen name, Muhibbi, literally translates to “lover" or God lover." The divan contains 213 folios with 614 poems written in *ta’liq* script. Each poem is framed by naturalistic, gilded floral illuminations. The leather binding is also decorated with gilded floral ornaments and bears the following inscription: “This is the Third Diwan from the speech of the sultan of sultans of the rime, from Ghazi Sultan Suleyman Khan may his rule last until Judgement Day”. Other known divans by Süleyman are held at the Süleymaniye Library in Istanbul (Inv. No. T 3873) and in the University of Istanbul.  
The calligrapher and illuminator can also be identified through a colophon which reads: “Haci Mehmmed has finished this whilst praying wholeheartedly for lasting conquests and victories at the last ten days of the month Rabi as-sani in the year 961 (March 25-April 4, 1154).” The illuminator, Kara Memi, worked in the court of Süleyman and is well-known for his innovative floral ornaments which replaced the Safavid tradition of book illumination. A unique example of Ottoman book decoration, each of Memi's folios has an individual, unrepeated design. Each realistically-depicted plant can be individually identified through their precise botanical rendering, giving the illuminations a nearly encyclopaedical character.  
In 1886, the divan was purchased from the art dealer Franz Bock by the founder and initial director of the Museum of Arts and Crafts in Hamburg, Justus Brinckmann.
e4921c14-8d40-54c3-8c3f-a824cbf0cac3.method_for_provenance: Purchased by Franz Bock (1823-1899), clergyman and art historian. He traveled to Syria and Egypt and owned a large textile collection which he started to sell in 1850 to major museums in Europe (Paris, Berlin and the South Kensinton Museum (now V&A, London).

e498d8ba-123c-5475-862a-85cede317ae0.name: Marble water jar
e498d8ba-123c-5475-862a-85cede317ae0.description:
This jar bears inscriptions in Greek, Armenian, and Ottoman Turkish reading:  
"A’ la Kayışdağı Suyu, \[M.\] 1868" ("Kayışdağı Water, \[M.\] 1868").  
  
The spout is attached to the jar's body. On the left side of the lower base, when viewed from the side where the spout is mounted, a piece of the marble base is broken off. The marble of the lower base has areas darkened with black patina, and surface erosion is visible.  
  
On the outer surface of the jar’s body, there are traces of paint, as well as scratches and erosion on the marble surface. At the mouth of the jar, on the side where the spout is fixed, there are linear cracks, with the crack line visible on both the inner and outer surfaces.

e500a55c-8788-5600-85fa-bfffc127c785.name: Two-man plow (*qiraz*)
e500a55c-8788-5600-85fa-bfffc127c785.description: The *qiraz* is used to divide fields into manageable, level plots and to create water channels and basins in freshly ploughed soil. The channels are connected to the local *falaj* system, after which seeds are sown and irrigation can commence. The shovel-like blade is moved back and forth by two men working together in a steady rhythm.

e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.name: Ewer.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.description: A ewer with missing foot and spout, inlaid with silver and copper. The delicate inlay decoration covering the body and neck is exceptionally fine. A remarkable range of figurative scenes of contemporary court life is depicted in a series of medallions. The medallions are surrounded by a geometric pattern alternating with bands of inscriptions and figures. Men have covered heads and wear tunics with straight sleeves. Their costumes reflect the Turkish origin of the Zangid dynasty. The princes have ornamental tiraz bands around the sleeves of their robes. Soldiers have swords with straight blades and round buckles. Two noble women are depicted: one is shown looking in a mirror accompanied by an attendant; another is riding on a camel in a camel litter with a servant. A lute-player has the bottom of her face veiled. Other medallions depict a hunting scene with a man shooting an arrow at his prey; another hunter with a cheetah on the back of his horse; musicians, dancers and drinking revellers. There is even a scene from the Persian epic poem the Shahnama representing Bahram Gur shooting an arrow while Azadeh plays the harp on the back of his horse. Given the outstanding quality of the decoration and the scenes of courtly life the ewer was probably intended for use at court. The patron may have been Badr al-Din Lu'lu', who ruled Mosul (AH 629–59 / AD 1232–59), or a member of his court. A number of objects inscribed with his name reveal that he commissioned a number of metalwork objects. Although the technique of inlaid metalwork originated in Iran, new shapes were introduced in Mosul often inspired by Byzantine forms. Ibn Said, a Spanish Muslim, travelled all over Syria, Mesopotamia and Iraq in AH 648 / AD 1250. In his book, Geography, he mentions inlaid brass vessels made in Mosul that were exported and presented to various rulers. Therefore, Mosul metalwork with its glittering inlay had clearly gained sufficient status to compete with gold and silver.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.short_description: The craftsman of this exceptional ewer has signed his work stating he is from Mosul. Made from brass inlaid with silver, it is covered with figures performing many different activities that include playing music, drinking and hunting.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.dimensions: Height 30.4 cm, width 22 cm, depth 21.5 cm.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.method_for_datation: The ewer is inscribed with the date 629 (1232).
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.method_for_provenance: An inscription describes the craftsman as 'Shuja ibn Mana al-Mawsili' (Shuja, son of Mana of Mosul). Therefore he was from Mosul where there was an active metalwork industry in the early 7th century / 13th century.
e5089d3e-3231-5064-9958-45c0890fde1c.obtention: The ewer is named after the Duc de Blacas whose collection was acquired by the British Museum in 1866.

e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.name: Water seller's jar
e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.short_description: The egg-shaped jar has a narrow neck the top of which is covered by a dome-shaped lid. There is a curved handle on each side of the neck base and a long, straight spout. The lower part of the jar is made of unglazed and undecorated earthenware, a common material for water vessels that enables water evaporation thus keeping the water inside cool. The upper part is made of copper alloy, engraved with decorative bands of intertwined floral motifs; knot work patterns; stylised four-legged animals amongst a vegetal design; and two calligraphic bands. The jar sits in a knotted rope net with handle for carriage on the water seller’s back.
e58c69db-bd74-5185-a678-96228b8d0ba3.author: Hazelle Page
keywords: Water jar; Water seller; Everyday life; Egypt

e644ef1f-80d7-52bf-aa24-7ee45fbf092e.name: Ewer
e644ef1f-80d7-52bf-aa24-7ee45fbf092e.description: The handle is ornamented, while the body is flattened on the sides and decorated with engravings. The lateral surfaces feature geometric motifs within a border, while animal depictions are present in the center. The object stands on a base.

e68c9926-6b22-5aab-b71e-e3faba6e95e4.name: Halabja, Iraq
e68c9926-6b22-5aab-b71e-e3faba6e95e4.description: As demonstrated in this image, the city landscape of Halabja, in Iraq, features Kurdish individuals attired in traditional attire, namely knickers and turbans, traversing the city's souk. In the immediate foreground of the scene is depicted a pitcher of water, offered for the passers-by's use. On March 16, 1988, Halabja was the victim of a large-scale chemical attack by Saddam Hussein's army, which killed thousands and injured many more. The attacks destroyed the city, and parts of the city remained contaminated by the toxic gases for decades to come. Little remains of the city life seen in the image.
e68c9926-6b22-5aab-b71e-e3faba6e95e4.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

e6c5512c-0d14-5feb-be93-2db1988939f5.name: *Bir Barruta*
e6c5512c-0d14-5feb-be93-2db1988939f5.description:
Sources attribute the digging of Bir Barruta to the Governor Harthama Ibn A‘yan, in AH 180 / AD 796. However it seems that the Bey Mohamed, son of Murad, carried out a renovation of the whole construction in 1101/1690, to which he added a marble fountain. Although it is not amongst the first wells to be dug out at the centre of the town, it is an object of special veneration for part of the population.  
  
According to legend, the wells are linked to those of Zemzem in Mecca. Another legend states that whoever drinks water from Barruta is sure to return to Kairouan. The room that houses the wells, reached via a staircase, is covered by a dome on squinches based on the Kairouanese dome type. It stands out for its profound bareness, and rests on four arches that lean against the walls. It is doubtless a contemporary of the dome covering the dome room in the Mausoleum of Abu Zama‘a al-Balaui, built at the time of Mohamed Bey. Both are the works of the master mason Mohamed al-Zakraui whose name features on a panel of fretted stucco. The room is occupied by a noria that is worked by a camel. This system of drawing water, which dates back to the Middle Ages, exists here as one of the last that work at the centre of Tunisian city life. Outside the building, standing up against the north wall, there is a fountain with a drinking trough and marble taps.
e6c5512c-0d14-5feb-be93-2db1988939f5.author: Mourad Rammah

e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.name: Sphinx
e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.description:
This sphinx was found in Rafiqa, Raqqa’s twin city, in AH 1343 / AD 1924 together with the cock (Isl 57) and the figure of a horseman in Syria’s National Museum. As ceramic sculptures, they are unique not only in Syria, but also in the rest of the Islamic world.  
  
They are fountain figures, and all have pipes to carry water up to the figures’ heads. The North African historian al-Maqqari wrote that the Iberian Umayyad caliph Abd al-Rahman III had a fountain made with 12 figures: a lion with a gazelle, a crocodile, a serpent, an eagle, an elephant, a dove, a falcon, a peacock, a hen, a cock, a hawk and a vulture.
e705767c-f39f-5e1f-b8fc-8f075dc24a4f.dates: AH 2nd half of the 6th / AD 2nd half of 12th century

e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.name: Midhat al-Sultan (ablutions room).
e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.description:
The right–hand door of the building leads into a narrow hallway. On the right is a large archway opening onto the ablutions room. On the left, opposite the archway, the hallway wall is lined with arch-stones forming blind arcades. In the recess of each arcade is a square rosette of braided strap-work in black marble on a white background.  
The ablutions room consists of a courtyard surrounded by four single-arched galleries. One of these is the archway giving access to the courtyard from the hallway. Under the three remaining galleries narrow basins and benches have been provided for the faithful to perform their ablutions. The arches of layered black and white marble rest on columns with winding scroll capitals of the Hispano-Maghrebin type. The walls and spandrels of the arches have been ingeniously inlaid with decorative slabs of black on white marble.  
In the middle of the courtyard stands an octagonal marble dado. Each of its faces has an arch, either multifoil or recticurvilinear. In the centre remain the nozzles of the fountain which poured water into individual basins facing small stone benches.
e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.short_description: This Hafsid monument is one of the few surviving parts of a hot-water conveyance system, now lost. Although the National Institute of Art and Archaeology restored it in the 1960s, the building is not functional today. The ablutions room consists of a courtyard surrounded by four single-arched galleries. The arches are made of black and white marble voussoirs and spring from columns with Hispano-Maghrebin meanders and capitals.
e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.dates: Begun in hegira 852 / AD 1448, finished in 854 / 1450.
e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.method_for_datation: The poet al-Damamini evokes the beauty of Midhat al-Sultan in a famous poem. The historian Zarkachi comments on this poem in his book on Ibn Achamma edited by Mustapha Kaak.
e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.bibliography:
Daoulatli, A., *Tunis sous les Hafsides, Tunis, 1976, pp.213–21.*  
Marcais, G., *L'architecture musulmane d'Occident*, Paris, 1952, pp.22–4.  
“Notes sur les coupoles de la Grande Zitouna de Tunis”, *Revue de l'Occident musulman et de la Mediterranee*, 1966, pp.95–105.
e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.history: Historical sources describe the inauguration of the building by the Sultan himself and explain the hot-water system, now defunct. According to an inscription, the wooden ceilings were restored in the 12th / 18th century. In 1380 / 1960 the National Institute of Archeology and Art began restoring the building, but it is not yet functional.
e82e7a90-67b5-5656-a132-7a7975bceb31.author: Jamila Binous

e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.name: Nilometer.
e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.description:
The Nilometer (Kiosk of the Nile; known in Arabic as *al-Miqyas*) is considered among the enduring architectural foundations tied to the Egyptian culture and way of life. It is in fact unique in the Islamic world. Its importance goes back to a time when measuring the rise of the waters of the Nile was closely related to the levying of taxes on agricultural lands. Taxes were levied only when the waters of the Nile had risen to a certain designated level, which would irrigate the land during flood season.  
The Nilometer itself is the equivalent of a well whose walls are built from skilfully hewn stone blocks. The thickness of the walls increases the greater the depth. The well consists of three levels: the lowest level is a circular base, while the middle level is a square whose sides measure more than the diameter of the level below. The highest level is also square in shape, and bigger than the middle level. It is due to this design that the walls can bear the horizontal pressure of the earth that increases the greater the depth.  
The waters of the Nile would flow into the well by means of three tunnels, which discharged their waters into the well by means of three 'mouths' on the eastern side that are in the form of subterranean entrances in the wall. These openings are oriented towards pointed arches supported by compact decorated columns with globular bases. These arches are considered to be not only the oldest known examples in Islamic Egypt, but precede the European Gothic type by three centuries. We may also view similar examples on the arches of the Ibn Tulun Mosque in Cairo (AH 265 / AD 879).  
A staircase curves around the inside walls of the well and extends all the way to the bottom. Adorning the upper reaches of the well on two sides, the northern and the eastern internal walls, are inscriptions in *kufic* script, which represent the oldest (dated) Arabic inscription in Egypt ever recorded. In the centre of the well stands the principal component of the monument, an octagonal marble pillar whose length extends to 16 cubits (10.50 m). It is engraved with measurements in cubits *(kirat*) and inches *(zira')*, which demarcate the water inundation levels.  
Ahmad ibn Tulun (r. AH 254–70 / AD 868–84) carried out restoration of al-Miqyas in AH 259 / AD 873 and replaced the two bands of ancient inscriptions with more contemporary ones on the south and west sides. He placed his name within the new inscription, but kept the original date of construction untouched. Throughout the ages the building has been subject to many restorations and renovations (Fatimid, Mamluk and Ottoman). It was renovated in the modern age in 1925 when the Mamluk dome crowning the outside of the building was replaced by a conical-shaped roof covered by lead panels.
e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.short_description: Set on Roda island in the Nile, the Nilometer is a unique structure in Islamic architecture. It gained its importance from being the means for calculating tax levies on agricultural lands according to the size of the Nile flood every year. Its design and the building materials used in its construction helped it to resist corrosion by water for over one thousand years.
e9446de8-0118-5c68-aa90-cc7965c9040a.method_for_datation: Historians concur that al-Miqyas was built in the year 247 / 861 by order of the Abbassid Caliph al-Mutawakkil, although some scholars trace its foundation back to the Caliph al–Ma'mun (r. 169–217 / 786–833). However, the historian Ibn Khalkan (d. 681 / 1282) mentions that the name of the al-Mutawakkil and the year the Nilometer was constructed (247 / 861) was engraved within an inscription on the walls of the well, and that this inscription dated to the foundation of the monument. This inscription has now been lost and may have been removed when Ibn Tulun carried out his restoration of the building in the year 259 / 873.

e967434e-06ff-5cc3-88d8-9786fd216273.name: Spout
e967434e-06ff-5cc3-88d8-9786fd216273.description:
This bronze spout, dated to the AH 13th / AD 19th century Ottoman period, features a stylized lion’s head and was used as a fountain nozzle in the water pools of Alevi–Bektaşi lodges in Anatolia.  
  
In Alevi–Bektaşi symbolism, the lion represents Ali, embodying courage, spiritual authority and protection. Such zoomorphic forms were integrated into ritual architecture to express sacred meaning while enhancing the aesthetic and symbolic character of lodge water features. The object’s date and typology were identified by experts from the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.

e99f19c5-2155-5385-857a-049be3d918d9.name: "Man's Fate or the Man Taking Refuge in a Well Inhabited by a Dragon"
e99f19c5-2155-5385-857a-049be3d918d9.alternate_name: Folio from a Kalila wa Dimna
e99f19c5-2155-5385-857a-049be3d918d9.description: This manuscript contains seventy-eight paintings and many text folios telling the famous tales of the jackals Kalila and Dimna. Based on the book of ancient Indian animal fables, the Panchatantra written by Vidyapati (Bidpai), the stories spread all over the Middle East where they became wildly popular. This manuscript has a strong flavour of Mamluk Egypt in the figure styles and bold drawings, with hints of Ottoman tulips and Safavid turbans. However, the burnt orange palette and darkly-inked lines have led to an attribution to Sultanate Gujarat where it is suggested this manuscript was copied from an Egyptian original. Its life in India is also attested by a Devanagari inscription at the end, although the rest of the Arabic text is written in a strong, left-leaning naskh-like script.

ea99bbf2-1d63-5510-96b0-82bb57bbc44b.name: Traditional clepsydra
ea99bbf2-1d63-5510-96b0-82bb57bbc44b.description:
Locally known as *tanast*, *tassa* or *tighira*, the traditional clepsydra is a water clock used in the oases of southeastern Morocco, particularly in Tafilalet, to measure irrigation turns. Farmers rely on it to know exactly how long they can access water from canals, springs, or reservoirs to water their fields. It consists of a small perforated copper bowl that floats inside a larger bucket of water. As water slowly seeps into the bowl, it becomes heavier until it sinks, and the moment it sinks marks one fixed unit of irrigation time. By repeating this cycle communities could divide water fairly among rights-holders, according to customary law.  
The device embodies the principle of hydraulic justice—time, rather than volume, becomes the standard, allowing a constant and transparent distribution even when flow varies. Its durable copper construction, portability, and ease of calibration made it ideal for communal use beside canals and reservoirs.  
Beyond its utilitarian value, the clepsydra reflects deep cultural meanings: the sanctity of water, the moral duty to share, and the sophisticated know-how of rural artisans who crafted reliable instruments without modern technology.  
  
Though many oases now use pumps and clocks, the Tanast remains a powerful symbol of Morocco’s living hydraulic heritage and community self-governance.

eae5c274-7b09-5dc1-a70e-37e8ae1488d8.name: Vase neck
eae5c274-7b09-5dc1-a70e-37e8ae1488d8.description:
Neck belonging to a vase of the type known as ‘Alhambra’. It has the typical flared shape of the necks of these vases, with a polygonal structure that opens upwards. The lip is thick and ends in a series of outward scrolls. The body is divided into alternating vertical bands of blue and light cream, the latter being approximately twice as thick, which have probably lost their original golden sheen. The lower part has two horizontal grooves that run around the entire perimeter of the piece. There is loss of enamel across the entire surface.  
  
Representative of Nasrid luxury, these vases are a very specific type of container, of which few examples remain. They are notable not only for their rich and luxurious decoration, but also for their monumental size, measuring around 130 cm in height and 60–70 cm in diameter. Given these characteristics, it is difficult to imagine that their function was primarily practical, despite the fact that some of these vases feature epigraphic decorations referring to water, as in the case of the Jarrón de Hornos, also in the National Archaeological Museum (Spain). One possibility that has been suggested is that they contained perfumed water or water to be distributed at certain ceremonies.

ecbfd555-c941-5154-8936-9832dbbd13cf.name: Bowl
ecbfd555-c941-5154-8936-9832dbbd13cf.description:
The brass apodal bowl features an exterior decoration with a dense vegetal weave and large inscriptions in thuluth on a foliate background, interrupted by circular medallions with peonies.  
The inner base of the cup is decorated with a school of engraved fish following a circular pattern and a potentiated cross, the latter likely added when the object arrived in Europe.  
The inscription reads: "The high, lordly, sovereign, wise, active, just, ordering, zealous, Treasure, Help, Support, Assisted, \[official\] of Al-Malik an Nasir, may his victory be glorious."  
The epigraph follows the typical formula of Mamluk protocol for high-ranking figures. Although neither his name nor his specific function are indicated, the inscription suggests that the owner was an official of Sultan al-Malik al-Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn Qulawun. This is the sultan who owned the large Borgia Collection Basin, also in the museum's collections. From this, it can be deduced that the bowl was made by 1341, that is, during the sultan's lifetime, according to the customary formula used in the inscription, which ends with the phrase "may his victory be glorious."  
The bowl, as also underscored by the decorative motif of engraved fish within, was used to hold drinking water or for ritual purposes.  
The bowl entered the museum collections thanks to Mario De Ciccio's donation to the Italian state in 1958, consisting of 1,300 pieces. These primarily consist of applied art objects from various periods and typologies, collected by the collector over a period of over 50 years, first in Palermo, his hometown, then in Naples, his adopted home since 1906, and also on the most highly regarded international art markets.

ecc253f4-eace-5315-af2c-f64f071f89e0.name: Flask
ecc253f4-eace-5315-af2c-f64f071f89e0.description:
Reddish clay vessel, flattened spherical in shape. It has two ribbon handles that extend from the middle of the vessel to its upper part. The two flattened sides are asymmetrical, one inverted truncated cone-shaped and the other convex with an incised decoration of several small concentric circles inserted in turn within a larger circle. The neck is not too high, cylindrical and slightly flared. The entire body is decorated with a schematic red design consisting of thick parallel brushstrokes in groups of three. The entire piece is fractured.  
  
Historically, this type of container was very common not only during the medieval Islamic period, but also in different eras and cultures, even today. Its function, carrying small amounts of water for consumption, is essential for everyday work in rural areas. In addition, the use of unglazed pottery allows the flask to breathe, keeping the water cool. Even today, cork stoppers and ropes tied to the handles are generally used for transport.

edd94d46-2a69-592f-80d7-0c535b109eff.name: Coffee
edd94d46-2a69-592f-80d7-0c535b109eff.description: Coffee is always served at the beginning of a visit and is repeatedly offered until guests politely signal that they have had enough by rocking their cup from side to side. In order to keep coffee hot and fresh for unexpected guests it goes through many stages. After roasting and grinding the coffee beans the grains are added to boiling water inside a large *dallah* (coffee pot) called a *khamra*. Next, the liquid is poured into a medium-sized coffee pot called a *taljeemah*. At this stage cardamom seeds, saffron and rose water may be added for flavour. From this jug, the coffee is poured into a serving *dallah* referred to as a *mezallah*, where the coffee is refined and filtered. The server must hold the *mezallah* with their left hand and distribute the *fanayeel* (coffee cups) using the right hand. The coffee should fill less than half of the cup.
edd94d46-2a69-592f-80d7-0c535b109eff.dimensions: Varies and depends on the coffee bean. Length: 10mm, width: 7mm

efef0d6f-3f4f-5566-89c1-caa1ae554c20.name: Spout (*Horhor lüle*)
efef0d6f-3f4f-5566-89c1-caa1ae554c20.description:
This bronze spout, known as a '*horhor lüle*' in traditional water terminology, dates to the AH 6th-7th / AD 12th–13th century Seljuq period and was used in street fountains where water flowed continuously without a stop mechanism. Its form features a stylised dragon figure, a powerful animal motif widely employed in Roman and Seljuq art as a symbol of strength, protection and divine force.  
  
In belief systems of the era, objects decorated with such motifs were thought to transfer this protective power to their users and surroundings. As Islamic artistic conventions evolved, especially in the Ottoman period, figurative animal motifs were gradually replaced with vegetal and geometric designs due to religious preferences. This spout exemplifies both the aesthetic language and symbolic worldview of its time, embodying the transition from mythic animal imagery to the more abstract ornamentation of later periods.
efef0d6f-3f4f-5566-89c1-caa1ae554c20.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
