f0e5d0e1-0d9f-5dac-9166-a688b53727f8.name: Zaghwan aqueduct
f0e5d0e1-0d9f-5dac-9166-a688b53727f8.short_description: The hydraulic works are described in the general administration's 1883–1889 Public Works report as follows: "89 km of brick canal between Zaghwan and Goulette were refurbished, 41 km of metal piping has replaced the huge aqueducts at Djouggar, Oued Miliane, Djedeida and the Aryanah plains". Water supplies for Tunis and the beylical residences were thus assured. The piping was put into operation for the first time on 19 May 1862. You can still see the impressive row of columns and arches today.
f0e5d0e1-0d9f-5dac-9166-a688b53727f8.history: Water problems were one of the Tunisian governments' constant preoccupations. It was the custom for wealthy people to build public fountains called *sabils*. Rulers, however, were preoccupied with the organisation of large scale water conveyance. In 1859, just before the establishment of the French protectorate and on the advice of the French consul Léon Roches, Mohamed Bey tasked the engineer Pierre Colin with the restoration of the old Roman aqueduct running from Zaghwan to Carthage, and its Hafsid era diversion towards Tunis, which had been out of use and abandoned for a long time. The works were completed in 1862, during Mohamed Sadok Bey's reign.
f0e5d0e1-0d9f-5dac-9166-a688b53727f8.author: Saloua Khadhar Zangar

f290264c-83b5-5e47-b429-b0232354c1d8.name: Water sharing of Figuig
f290264c-83b5-5e47-b429-b0232354c1d8.description:
In Figuig, water is not shared by volume, but by time. Locals use a unit called a *nouba*, meaning a turn to use water, and a smaller unit called a *kharrouba*, which lasts 45 minutes. Each family or village owns specific turns, overseen by guardians known as *amnay*, who are responsible for enforcing the schedule, ensuring the fair distribution of water, and resolving conflicts.  
  
Figuig is made up of seven fortified villages, located on two types of land: the plateau, called the *jorf*, and the plain. Each village has its own water sources, canals, reservoirs, and irrigation systems, but they all follow the same general rules and customs.  
  
Water comes from springs and underground foggaras, flowing by gravity through canals (séguia) and reservoirs. It is then divided using devices like valves and small distribution boxes, allowing people to direct the water based on their needs. Figuig has around 200 storage basins and over 110km of canals, all managed by families and villages. Each branch of the network has modular valves that can open or close certain channels, or combine or split water flows. This flexibility allows the system to constantly adapt to weather conditions and the changing needs of users, which helps keep peace and balance in the community. While each group controls its own water, they all follow shared rules.  
  
Unlike many oases, Figuig still relies on its traditional, electricity-free methods — balancing private rights, community cooperation, and environmental sustainability. The water is free and shared according to a community calendar, which helps prevent overuse and maintains strong social bonds. In this way, Figuig preserves not only its water but also the social and cultural fabric that has sustained its community for centuries.
f290264c-83b5-5e47-b429-b0232354c1d8.bibliography: Madani, T., ‘Le partage de l’eau dans l’oasis de Figuig (Maroc oriental)’, in *Le partage de l’eau* , vol. 36(2 ; 2006) : 61–81.
f290264c-83b5-5e47-b429-b0232354c1d8.history: Figuig, an oasis town in southeastern Morocco, has a very old and unique system of managing water, passed down through generations. This system began in pre-Islamic times and became more organised during early Muslim dynasties. It was based on fairness and community sharing — very important principles in a dry area.
f290264c-83b5-5e47-b429-b0232354c1d8.author: MUSEUM Staff, Layan Shahin
keywords: Water sharing, Figuig, ancestral system, community management, traditional irrigation, Morocco

f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.name: Saint Christophorus with the Infant Jesus
f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.short_description:
According to Emperor Jahangir's (r. 1014-1037 / AD 1605-1627) inscription, the image of St. Christopher carrying the infant Jesus and accompanied by a dog was painted by the court painter Miskin (a pen name meaning "the humble one"). Miskin contributed to the codification of the Mughal style and played an increasingly important role in the illustration of the chronicles of the Mughal emperors. He is known for his keen observation of humans and animals. For this work, he probably drew inspiration from European engravings with Christian themes, which were brought to India by Jesuits at the end of the 16th century.  
  
The border with the prominent hazelnut branch was originally part of a larger album project completed under the Persian artist Muhammad Baqir (active Hegira late 1160s-1204 / AD late 1750s-1790) between Hegira 1178 / AD 1765 and Hegira 1183 / AD 1770. Parts of the album with Mughal and Safavid miniatures and calligraphies were rebound for the Qajar ruler Fath ʿAli Shah (r. Hegira 1211-1250 / AD 1797-1834) in the Hegira year 1237 (AD 1822). The individual leaves of this album were sold at auction by Drouot in Paris on 23 June 1982. Other leaves that originally belonged to this convolute known as the Drouot or Baqir album are currently scattered. The leaf seen here has another miniature pasted on the reverse.
f2ab9cfb-bbce-54c1-b8c6-caafd9c9b90a.initial_owner: Shahram Pahlavi; 2002-2013: Mehdi Metghalchi, London; 2013-2014: Catharina Dohrn, Münsingen

f31eb58f-b7d0-56f8-b129-225b701d5561.name: Ewer
f31eb58f-b7d0-56f8-b129-225b701d5561.description: The wide base is decorated and fluted. A doughnut-shaped body rises from the base, with eight outward-pointing projections along its upper edge. The body narrows towards the top. The handle is attached to the body and the mouth with double rivets; a clasp at the very top of the handle secures the lid. The handle tapers towards the mouth with a serrated edge. The lid, shaped like a small minaret, incorporates a spout that extends from the body to its top; it is inclined outward, with its surface decorated with a diamond motif. Both the lid and neck are further adorned with fluted decoration.
f31eb58f-b7d0-56f8-b129-225b701d5561.dimensions: Base diameter: 12.5cm, height: 50cm, body width: 24cm, lid height: 12cm

f4487135-c3dd-52d4-aace-e368bdb407e4.name: Aqueduct.
f4487135-c3dd-52d4-aace-e368bdb407e4.description:
The idea of building an aqueduct to carry water to the Citadel of Salah al-Din, known also as Citadel of the Mountain (*Qala'a al-Jabal),* goes back to the period of Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi (r. AH 564–89 / AD 1169–93) who erected Cairo's city wall, the beginning of which was close to Fustat. A canal to convey water was constructed on top of the wall; the water being carried up to it by means of a series of waterwheels from one of the wells. The water flowed through the canal to the citadel where it was used for drinking and irrigation of the surrounding fields.  
During the Mamluk period the population of the citadel expanded, with many Mamluk citizens residing there and, as their numbers grew, so Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun was forced to consider another plan to increase water flow from the River Nile to the citadel.  
In AH 712 / AD 1312, al-Nasir Muhammad put into practice his plan and ordered the construction of a great tower to contain four waterwheels in the region of *Fum al-Khalij* (which is today known as Qasr al-Ayni Street), on the banks of the River Nile. These waterwheels were designed to raise water up to a canal system (an aqueduct) located on top of a series of raised arches that were supported by large stone piers. The structure was designed to form a slope in order that it connected with the aqueduct, which Salah al-Din al-Ayyubi had earlier masterminded. Al-Nasir Muhammad's aim was to provide the citadel with enough water to satisfy the thirst of residents, soldiers and beasts of burden; to irrigate the surrounding fields and to expand his planned construction works within the citadel, which included the Qasr al-Ablaq and the Mosque of al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun.  
Sultan Qaytbay (r. AH 872–901 / AD 1468–96) undertook major renovation works to the aqueduct in AH 885 / AD 1480. In AH 912 / AD 1506, Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri further restored some parts of the aqueduct, as well as renovating the waterwheel tower, at which time he placed his emblem on the tower. Al-Ghuri brought the water system up to date; the water now pooled in the square at the foot of the citadel, before being raised by waterwheels to water cisterns inside. The aqueduct was functional until the Ottoman period (AH 13th / AD 19th century). It fell into disuse during the French expedition against Egypt under the leadership of Napoleon Bonaparte (AH 1213–16 / AD 1798–1801), when French soldiers transformed some parts of the aqueduct into a fort by blocking up some of the arches and turning them into fortifications.  
The length of the remaining section of the aqueduct is about 3 km. It is considered to be one of the most beautiful examples of aqueduct architecture not only in Egypt but also in the entire Islamic world. In 2005 the High Council of Antiquities undertook the implementation of a plan to restore the waterwheel tower and the aqueduct walls.
f4487135-c3dd-52d4-aace-e368bdb407e4.short_description: The greatest project designed to provide the Cairo Citadel with drinking water, the huge stone aqueduct extends about 3 km from the banks of the Nile towards the Citadel. Water was hauled up by four great waterwheels and poured into sedimentation cisterns. The cisterns were then opened so that the water flowed in a canal on the top of the aqueduct to the Citadel.
f4487135-c3dd-52d4-aace-e368bdb407e4.method_for_datation: Dating of the aqueduct is supported by allusions made to its construction by al-Maqrizi in his book (see below), where he suggests that the aqueduct was built in 712 / 1312 during the reign of Sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun. Furthermore, there is a blazon on top of the waterwheel-tower that is specific to Sultan Qansuh al-Ghuri, which may well indicate that he undertook restoration work on the aqueduct during his reign.

f4aca485-b1db-583e-b83d-c9c533f030c1.description:
Discovered in a house during the 1959 excavations in Murwab, northwest Qatar, this partially reconstructed jug must have had a striking and shiny appearance.  
  
It originally had three rounded handles on the shoulder, two of which are preserved, and is entirely covered with a monochrome yellow glaze. The small size of this jug and its decoration make it a delicate piece of tableware. It could have been a 'table vinegar jar' used to hold sweet and sour sauces that were very popular in the 9th century, as shown in ancient

f4d003ac-43de-5b52-ab57-a2e3b9bf6a98.name: *Khettaras*
f4d003ac-43de-5b52-ab57-a2e3b9bf6a98.description:
*Khettaras* are an old and clever way of bringing underground water to the surface without using machines or electricity. Found mostly in dry or semi-dry areas, they manage water sustainably. They work using gravity, so no energy is needed, making them perfect for desert regions. A *khettara* has a wellhead at the highest point, a gently sloping underground tunnel, and vertical shafts every 10 to 30 metres for ventilation and maintenance. Water flows naturally to the surface, entering irrigation canals, séguias, pools, or fountains, and is shared by communities according to traditional rules. Some *khettaras* are 10–15 kilometres long, showing the skill of their builders.  
Beyond their design, *khettaras* shaped life in Morocco’s deserts. They allowed oases to grow, influenced farming, settlement, and local governance. Control over them was linked to political power. Over centuries, these systems helped shape not just the land but the way of life in Morocco’s driest regions.

f4d003ac-43de-5b52-ab57-a2e3b9bf6a98.history:
*Khettaras* began in ancient Persia (modern-day Iran) as *qanats*, an underground tunnel system that taps into groundwater from an aquifer and carries it across long distances to the surface. As Muslim empires expanded, this technique spread to North Africa, especially Morocco, during the Islamic conquests. They became more common in the 11th century under the Almoravid dynasty. The first *khettaras* in Morocco were built in the central Haouz region near Marrakech, a politically and economically important area that needed water for farming and its residents.  
Khettaras brought water from underground aquifers to the fields without pumps. By 1987, over 650 existed in this region. Later, during the Saadian and Alaouite dynasties, *khettaras* spread further south, to oasis regions like Errachidia, Figuig, Tinghir, and Skoura, where they supported farming and palm trees.

f5030f3c-8af5-552d-8913-157bc3d6732c.name: Marina Square, Reem Island
f5030f3c-8af5-552d-8913-157bc3d6732c.description: This image of Marina Square on Reem Island (Abu Dhabi) reflects the transformation of modern Arab cities, where architecture and urban planning increasingly embrace blue spaces: areas designed around proximity to water. Alongside residential towers, these coastal developments integrate museums, cultural centres, promenades, and commercial hubs, merging urban living with leisure and cultural life. In many contemporary Arab cities, waterfront development symbolises progress, prosperity, and global connectivity, echoing the historic relationship between water and civilisation in the region. Just as ancient settlements flourished near rivers and coasts, today’s skylines continue to grow along the shores, redefining how water shapes identity, lifestyles, and the rhythms of urban experience.

f50d39b2-f8db-5777-9fdd-bfe1a5755107.name: Sickle (*mijaz*)
f50d39b2-f8db-5777-9fdd-bfe1a5755107.description: The sickle is a tool that has been employed worldwide for its utility: it is a manual agricultural tool that consists of a curved blade that is usually used for harvesting grain crops or cutting weeds used to feed livestock.

f5e1356e-4954-59b0-9bd4-b25d1b12ff38.name: Banknote
f5e1356e-4954-59b0-9bd4-b25d1b12ff38.description: The Iraqi banknote depicting Dukan Dam presents a visual articulation of state-led modernisation and hydraulic sovereignty. Constructed on the Great Zab River in the mid-twentieth century, the dam represents the strategic harnessing of water for irrigation, flood control, and hydroelectric power. Its inclusion in national currency frames large-scale water infrastructure as a symbol of economic progress, territorial integration, and technological advancement within modern Iraq.
f5e1356e-4954-59b0-9bd4-b25d1b12ff38.author: Yelyzaveta Basysta

f5efa1b5-e76e-5603-80c4-2602ee925386.name: Bag for hauling water with draft animals (*ad-dalū*)
f5efa1b5-e76e-5603-80c4-2602ee925386.description: This huge leather bag (*ad-dalū*) is designed for lifting water by means of draft animals. An angled pathway allows the animals to walk uphill while lowering the bag into a well or reservoir, and downhill when pulling against the weight of the water-filled bag. A single *dalū* has a capacity of 10 to 40 litres.

f60e24ce-c1de-5b4b-9219-cfb0c187f885.name: Qanat (inside the Psychiatric Hospital).
f60e24ce-c1de-5b4b-9219-cfb0c187f885.description:
*Qanats* are underground drainage channels that collect aquifer water and bear it from considerable depths to within a few metres of ground level. The *qanats* discovered in Palermo are of the Arab-Persian type, but differ from their Eastern counterparts in that they are not fed by a real well, but by a transversal drainage gallery located upstream.  
This network of underground channels, which extends over tens of kilometres, ensured a continuous and spontaneous supply of water from the underground aquifer to the surface, making it possible to construct fishponds, fountains and public baths and to water the lush gardens described in medieval sources.
f60e24ce-c1de-5b4b-9219-cfb0c187f885.short_description: In the ground beneath Palermo there is a network of drainage channels that carry aquifer water from significant depths up to ground level. These complex Arabo-Persian-inspired hydraulic engineering works are known as the *qanat*, and they guaranteed the continuous and spontaneous flow of water from underground aquifers to the surface.
f60e24ce-c1de-5b4b-9219-cfb0c187f885.method_for_datation: The discovery of ceramic fragments from the 12th and 13th centuries in two *qanats* in the central area of the Piana dei Colli (Castelforte and Scalea I) confirm their existence in Sicily from that time at least.

f85a3c6e-5d92-5e2a-9503-9f763a9619cb.name: A set of two reverse-glass paintings
f85a3c6e-5d92-5e2a-9503-9f763a9619cb.short_description:
The technique of reverse-glass, or *églomisé*, painting became popular in Iran in the early 19th century, possibly as a result of imports from Europe. In this technique, the paint is applied behind the glass in reverse order, with the highlights and details applied before the background colours. The technique had also been practised in China since the 18th century.  
Both the prince and the courtesan are depicted in bejewelled Qajar costume against European-inspired landscapes which are typical of Qajar paintings of the period. The paintings are not signed but have been compared to paintings by Mirza Baba, who may have been responsible for a cycle of reverse-glass paintings in the Marble Throne Hall of the Gulistan Palace in Tehran.  
The carved and richly painted frames, with their bird-and-dragon openwork scroll borders, are contemporary.

f8d95dbb-56af-5611-a814-9a73ceff888e.name: "The Beaker Water Clock" from al-Jazari's "Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices"
f8d95dbb-56af-5611-a814-9a73ceff888e.description: In the early thirteenth century, a scholar and engineer named Isma‘il Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari wrote a famous treatise called Kitab fi ma‛rifat al-hiyal al-handasiyya, or The Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices. The text offered detailed descriptions of a series of elaborate machines designed to delight and impress the elites at the court where he served, in eastern Anatolia. Al-Jazari’s text and its illustrations belong to a long tradition of studies about these kinds of devices, including Greek compendia on mechanics and mathematics. This page belongs to a copy of the text that was produced in Mamluk Egypt in AH 755 / AD 1354, and was copied by Muhammad ibn Ahmad al-Izmiri for a Mamluk ruler.
f8d95dbb-56af-5611-a814-9a73ceff888e.obtention:

1914, sold by Goloubew through M. Meyer-Riefstahl to the MFA.

f8f46999-1429-5208-8d79-17b9a2715883.name: Vessel with tap
f8f46999-1429-5208-8d79-17b9a2715883.description: Made of copper using the forging technique, the vessel has a narrow, rounded mouth, a cylindrical, flattened shoulder, a wide belly, and a flat base. A copper pipe is fitted to the edge of the base. A single-spouted tap made of brass is soldered to the end of this pipe. The vessel consists of three sections, and the forging marks on the surface are distinct. Both interior and exterior are tin-plated, but have darkened over time due to oxidation. The lid is missing, and the rim shows nicks and cracks.

f99b0b36-e5fc-56c8-9a6f-400862cc44ab.name: Glazed bowl with cobalt-blue decoration
f99b0b36-e5fc-56c8-9a6f-400862cc44ab.description:
This large, straight-sided bowl has a continuous loop-and-circle design painted in cobalt blue on a white or cream opaque glaze. The shape and colour of the bowl are highly typical of early Abbasid decorated glazed wares and were originally inspired by AH 2nd-3d / AD 7th–8th-century Chinese ceramics.  
  
Muslim, Christian and Jewish merchants from the Gulf region, Iraq and Iran had trading posts in southern China and imported various products, including ceramics. These imported ceramics reached the great port of Basra (Iraq) by the middle of the 8th century. Famous potters' workshops in Susa (Iran) or Samarra (Iraq) produced their own designs for this type of ware. Their products were distributed throughout the Middle East and the Gulf, including Qatar.

fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.name: Spa Glass
fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.description:
The 'Collection of Ceramics, Glass and Porcelain' at the Museum of Applied Arts houses a large number of spa glasses from Central Europe. Initially, water at spa resorts was drawn using vessels made of natural materials, but with the development of industry in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, glass cups began to be produced. Glass was considered a very suitable material, as it preserved the qualitative properties of mineral water. Patients would wait in line, and following doctors' recommendations, pour precisely the prescribed number of millilitres of healing water into their cup.  
  
This spa glass, from the Collection, features a depiction of the Church of St. George in Oplenac and represents a type of souvenir glass. It has a flat shape, made of moulded glass, with a hand-painted application and enamel detailing. It is dated to the 1930s, during the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, and was most likely produced by the Serbian Glass Factory in Paraćin. This is supported by stylistic features, as well as evidence from numerous factory catalogues of the period, in which spa glasses with painted motifs were part of the product range.  
The Cyrillic inscription on the application also points to a local and national identity, while the motif of Oplenac is associated with the Karađorđević dynasty, making this spa glass a piece of promotional memorabilia as well.
fa5c1124-b044-520c-9b3b-fc5775babc56.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analysis with related material.

fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.name: Lion from a fountain.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.description:
A sculpture such as this hollow lion – standing erect with its uplifted tasselled tail in the shape of a handle – is testament to the variety of Fatimid art. The open jaw of the lion once held a water pipe. The lion’s shape is based on a composition of very abstract forms. Thus its paws are flat, its ribs drawn out linearly, and the lines to describe both the extension of its ears and its bulging eyebrows are simple. The surface of its body along its back, chest and upper legs, is decorated with a spiral pattern that reinforces the sculpture’s stylised form. The engraved inscription found on both sides of the neck can be seen clearly and may date from the AH 7th / AD 13th century. It refers to bi-rasem al-amir Shams al-Din wali Misr, who was probably the governor of ‘Misr’ (Lower Egypt and Cairo).  
A fully modelled sculpture of a living creature is of interest, as it does not conform to the specifications of Islamic dogma. However, such sculptures emerged from the Egyptian Court because, within its circles, the prohibition of the representation of living forms was not always enforced or adhered to, and also because the Fatimid Shi’ites adopted a liberal view. The Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo holds a sitting lion figure. The Berlin lion could have formed part of a sculptured fountain that featured a variety of figures. Thus, it would correspond to the lions of the well-known, bigger lion fountains of the Alhambra in Granada, Spain. Given its small size, the lion could have been part of a larger construction featuring a number of sculptures such as those represented in Iraqi manuscripts from the AH 7th / AD 13th century onwards. Bronze figures like this lion were widespread across the Mediterranean, and especially across Spain. One of these Spanish lions can be seen in the Louvre Museum in Paris. One can assume that most of these bronze lions did not survive the test of time and were melted down.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.short_description: This lively little lion with an open mouth and upturned tail was used as a fountain spigot during the Fatimid period in Egypt. It is made of cast bronze that has been decorated with scrolls on the back and the legs. Fountains with animal decoration were widespread in Mediterranean countries.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.method_for_datation: Similar figures, cast in bronze, were made especially in Fatimid Egypt. Both the design and the decoration of the lion fountain demonstrate parallels to similar pieces that were created during the Fatimid period. Additionally, it features an inscription that names an apparent governor of Egypt.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.method_for_provenance: The inscription appears to name a governor of Egypt. Furthermore the stylistic markings testify to having originated from the Egyptian Fatimid period.
fa6093d9-67a1-536f-b0bb-38a5d07cb915.obtention: From a private art gallery in 1911.

fb4ff4be-b094-5d1b-b95d-4c9739ad33d1.name: Oil Lamp
fb4ff4be-b094-5d1b-b95d-4c9739ad33d1.description:
This bronze oil lamp, dated to the AH 7th-8th / AD 13th–14th century and attributed to the Great Seljuq cultural sphere in Persia, represents a refined example of medieval metalwork used for domestic illumination.  
  
Shaped in the form of a small ewer, the lamp reflects the Seljuq aesthetic preference for elegant, functional household objects crafted with durable materials. Oil lamps of this type provided steady light in homes, workshops and religious settings, playing a central role in daily life before the widespread adoption of glass lamps and later mechanical lighting technologies. The dating and typological assessment of the piece were carried out by experts from the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.

fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.name: Watermelon-shaped bottle
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.short_description:
Glass vessels in the shape of fruits were made in Syria-Mesopotamia and Egypt as early as the mid 2nd millennium BC. With the introduction of glass-blowing in the Roman period, they became much cheaper and, by the 2nd century AD, flasks and jars in the form of bunches of grapes or dates were popular all over the empire, persisting into the 6th and 7th centuries.  
The deliberately matt surface of this bottle gives an added dimension of naturalism. There are, however, no known parallels for its shape and size.
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.type: Blown, tooled, wheel cut and polished glass
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.holder: Khalili Family Trust – Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.method_for_datation: There are no known parallels, but according to S. Goldstein, the thick walls and rim are reminiscent of Sasanian and early Islamic flasks, including some found at Jerash and Shiraz. The treatment of the surface and the cutting also suggest a late Sasanian date.
fbb1ba22-98ad-5080-bfbe-53a4a9d43d9f.bibliography:
Goldstein, S.M., *et al.*, *Glass. From Sasanian Antecedents to European Imitations*, London: The Nasser D Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, volume 15, 2005: cat.42, pp.54–5.

keywords: glass; wheel-cut; blown glass; Iran; Iraq; Sasanian art; glass-blowing
materials: Dark emerald-green glass, blown, tooled, wheel cut and polished

fbcae9a7-567e-5281-9355-f85aa3d91744.name: Ewer
fbcae9a7-567e-5281-9355-f85aa3d91744.short_description:
According to an inscription found on a large number of ewers of this type, this group can be assigned to a craftsman called Ahmad or a related workshop.  
Characteristic for this group of cast bronze ewers are the distinctive pear-shaped body on a splayed foot, a tall faceted neck, a spherical upper part with hinges for fastening the lid and a large beak-shaped spout. The composite shape results from a blending of forms originating in functionally different objects: oil lamps attached to a bulbous vase. Both parts are connected by a strongly curved handle of angular cross-section surmounted by a diamond-shaped thumb rest and leaf-shaped projection on the lower part.  
In total, 30 ewers of this type are known so far. Twelve of them bear an inscription “‘amal Ahmad” (the work of Ahmad), eponymous for this group. The ewer at hand belongs to the group with a band of two rows of cavities around the widest part of the body. Additionally, three triangle-shaped medallions with a tripartite vegetal ornamentation are engraved above the double row of cavities.  
The find context of the 15 pieces found in archaeological excavations point to a production in or near the Ferghana Valley. A hoard of bronzes found at Budrac – medieval Saghaniyan – in Southeastern Uzbekistan contained ewers of this type and a mortar signed by Ahmad. This was possibly the production site from which the ‘Ahmad ewers’ were distributed.
fbcae9a7-567e-5281-9355-f85aa3d91744.holder: University Museum of Islamic Art | The Bumiller Collection
fbcae9a7-567e-5281-9355-f85aa3d91744.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and comparison with material found in excavations

fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.name: Fountain spout
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.description:
Small gilded bronze sculpture in the form of a hind. The figure is fragile and disproportionate. Almost all of the surface is covered with delicate oriental plant decoration (lotus flowers inscribed in circles) which make it look as if it is swathed in a rich fabric. Judging from the remains left in the grooves of the engraving and various parts of the body, the piece would have been completely gilded.  
The simple forms of the body, its facial characteristics and its legs, which end with discs and are extremely short in relation to its body, are reminiscent of representations of animals that appear in Fatimid ceramics.  
This sculpture undoubtedly served as a fountain spout because, apart from the legs, its body is hollow and there is a hole in its belly to allow water to pass through and cascade out of its mouth.  
The presence of water in Umayyad gardens was a sign of wealth, luxury and well-being. Fountains were an important aesthetic element in Islamic palaces in the West and in al-Andalus in particular. This hind would probably have been accompanied by other bronze animals.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.short_description: Its cloven hoofs, the base of its horns and its short pointed tail suggest that this animal is a fawn. It would undoubtedly have been used as a spout in a basin or fountain in a Córdoban palace, with the water entering through a duct beneath the belly and coming out through the mouth.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis. Although the Madrid hind is smaller and less stylised, it is clearly similar to other pieces found in the 10th / 16th century among the ruins of the Madinat al-Zahra palace, one of which can be found in the Archaeological Museum of Córdoba. The second disappeared at the start of the 19th centuryfrom the Monastery of Guadalupe, where it was being stored, but has recently been recovered and has been in the Qatar National Museum since 1997.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.method_for_provenance: Some researchers believe that this piece could have been imported from Fatimid Egypt. However, its discovery in the province of Córdoba and the similarities to the deer of Córdoba and Qatar suggest that the three sculptures were produced, if not in the same workshop, at least in the same geographical area of al-Andalus, where metalwork workshops developed.
fc0f934c-a60f-5984-b826-24611c304045.obtention: The hind was bought by the National Archaeological Museum on 3 February 1940.

fcd8d02e-bbbb-5ff5-aa2f-64ac381a7cbf.name: Rope
fcd8d02e-bbbb-5ff5-aa2f-64ac381a7cbf.description: A thick braided rope made of animal hide, tied at one end to a bucket with a strong knot and extended into the well to draw water. The rope must be durable enough to bear the weight of the filled bucket. It is plaited using several leather strips, a technique that provides strength and sustainability. The rope passes through a wooden or stone pulley to protect it from friction against the edge of the well and to facilitate pulling the bucket. This type of leather rope embodies an aspect of traditional life in desert environments, where leather was a primary material due to the scarcity of alternatives. It also reflects the craftsmanship involved in utilising available natural resources.
fcd8d02e-bbbb-5ff5-aa2f-64ac381a7cbf.holder: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani Museum FBQ Museum
keywords: Rope; water; wells; leather; arabian peninsula

fd4b59a9-ae59-534d-a8b4-6d56ba4420f8.name: Sa'di, Abu 'Abd-Allah Musharrif ad-Din b. Muslih (ad-Din), *Bustan* (Fruit Garden)
fd4b59a9-ae59-534d-a8b4-6d56ba4420f8.short_description: Sa'di, Abu 'Abd-Allah Musharrif ad-Din b. Muslih (ad-Din) (died 691 AH/ 1292 AD), wrote the *Bustan* (‘Fruit Garden’), which was his first published work. It contains ethical anecdotes incorporating the accounts of the author’s travels and his manifold experiences, and would later become one of his major works. This copy was written in *nasta’liq* script in Tabriz around 937-47 AH / c. 1530-40 AD. The manuscript contains five nearly full-page paintings. The paintings are reminiscent of the style of the Timurid school of Herat. In 1677, it was acquired in Constantinople for 36 gold ducats.
fd4b59a9-ae59-534d-a8b4-6d56ba4420f8.method_for_provenance: On fol. 1a, inscription by Peter Lambeck: *Bostan, seu Hortus Scheichi Saadi, celebris Poetae ac doctoris Persici. Liber moralis. 36 auriis*.
fd4b59a9-ae59-534d-a8b4-6d56ba4420f8.obtention: Acquired for the Austrian National Library for 36 gold ducats in 1677 in Constantinople by Peter Lambeck.
fd4b59a9-ae59-534d-a8b4-6d56ba4420f8.bibliography: Duda, Dorothea, *Islamische Handschriften I. Persische Handschriften, Die illuminierten Handschriften und Inkunabeln der Österreichischen Nationalbibliothek*, vol. 4, Vienna: Verlag der Österreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1983: 37-40.
fd4b59a9-ae59-534d-a8b4-6d56ba4420f8.binding_desc:
The luxuriously painted lacquer binding has a leather spine and leather edges. On the front cover, a group of people are depicted within a lush garden of flowering shrubs spread across the black background. A prince is sitting behind a spread-out red cloth with plates of food and a jug in the centre. He is holding a golden wine bowl while a kneeling courtier on the left serves a plate of pomegranates. In a semicircle around and above them, various figures sit or stand with drinking vessels or pomegranates in their hands. Below them, on the right, is a (poorly conserved) seated group; on the left are three musicians with a tambourine, a flute, and a lute. All figures wear the Safavid staff turban and a long two-piece robe covered with gold patterns in bright saffron, orange, and red colour as well as in dark green and blue.  
On the back cover, a courtly hunting scene is depicted within dense foliage and clouds at the top, including archers on horseback chasing lions, panthers, gazelles, and hares, as well as one falconer at the top right. It is a dynamic composition with five riders approaching from different sides, the movement of the horses and gestures of the figures are animated and varied. Fine mother-of-pearl dust is mixed into the colours that comprise the clouds, stones, and rocks. Related lacquer bindings can be found in the British Library (Or. 1374) and in the British Museum (no. 1948 12-11027-8).
fd4b59a9-ae59-534d-a8b4-6d56ba4420f8.author: Theresa Zischkin
materials: Ink, opaque watercolour and gold on paper. Calligraphic *nasta'liq* script of 16 lines.

fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.name: Basin
fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.description:
Ablution basin of Süleymaniye Workmanship.  
Inscribed in Ottoman Turkish with the text:  
  
"Sâhibi İmam-ı Evvel Hazret-i Şehriyârî Hâfız Ahmed Kâmilî Efendi, H. 1226."  
  
"Belonging to His Eminence Hâfız Ahmed Kâmilî Efendi, the İmam-ı Evvel Hazret-i Şehriyârî \[Chief Imam to the Sultan\], Year \[Hijri\] 1226."  
  
The phrase "İmam-ı Evvel Hazret-i Şehriyârî" signifies the Chief Imam of the Sultan.  
  
Hâfız Ahmed Kâmilî Efendi served as the Chief Imam to Sultan Mahmud II.
fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.holder: İstanbul Su Müzesi / Istanbul Water Museum
fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.method_for_datation: Determined by the experts of the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
fd6a5a94-fc7a-51b0-bb4a-c9c81f9f84c3.method_for_provenance: It was determined by the experts of the Istanbul Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.

These marks and craftsmanship identify pieces as “Süleymaniye work.”"

fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.name: Tumbler
fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.description:
Cylindrical, red tumbler whose walls on the outside are covered with red translucent paint. The painted decoration consists of the yellow coat of arms of the Principality of Serbia with crossed green oak branches. The opposite side of the tumbler displays a painted cornucopia, covered with a wide ribbon and a Cyrillic inscription, Споменъ (Memento).  
During the 19th century, along with the establishment of its state, Serbia sought to align with developed countries through modernization. One important component of this process was industrial production, and amidst challenges posed by the trade lobby and competing imports from Austro-Hungary one of the first steps made included establishment of the Glass Manufacture of Avram Petronijević. The owner himself had a flair for creating new processes and was very persistent, obtaining the exclusive right of production from the state, along with some benefits, including the ability to use raw materials from the environment where the factory was built and a twelve year tax exemption. The Manufacture did not operate for very long (1846-1852), but its work represented a significant shift, marking the beginning of Serbian industrialization. The largest number of the items preserved from this Manufacture originate from the period around 1850, consisting largely of glasses of simple shape and massive look, decorated with the heraldic motifs of the Principality of Serbia, including this tumbler from the Museum of Applied Arts collection. Whether painted with red or yellow translucent colours, they bear the image of the state coat of arms as decoration and a heraldic inscription in Cyrillic.
fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material and technique, and comparative method using other objects made in the same period in the same place.
fe669a8f-cbb8-5366-9aa0-68b03247a027.method_for_provenance: By stylistic analysis and historical documentation
